docs.title: Page Template
docs.text: This page defines the structure every other page in this docs site follows. It isn't linked from anywhere except the site's own "Meta" nav section — copy its shape when adding a new page, don't link to it from content pages.

docs.title: Why a single template
docs.text: Before this docs site existed, project documentation was scattered across README.md (grown well past what a landing page should hold), scattered code comments, and one-off files like CONTRIBUTING.md and .github/BRANCH_PROTECTION.md, each with its own structure and level of detail. A single template keeps every page predictable to both read and write: anyone opening a new page already knows where the summary is, where the real content starts, and where to look for related reading.

docs.title: The structure
docs.text:
Every page in docs/ (except this one and index.md, which is deliberately a landing page) follows this shape:

# Page Title

*One-sentence summary of what this page covers and who it's for, in italics, directly under the title.*

## Overview

A short paragraph (2-4 sentences) of context: what this page covers and why
it matters, before diving into specifics.

## <First real section>

Content. Use H2 (`##`) for top-level sections within the page, H3 (`###`)
for subsections. Prefer tables for reference material (flags, fields,
defaults); prefer prose for anything that needs to explain *why*, not just
*what*.

## See also

- [Related Page](relative-link.md) — one line on why it's relevant.

docs.title: Conventions within that structure
docs.text:
• The italic summary line is mandatory and must fit on one line. It's what a reader scanning the nav decides "is this the page I want" from — if it needs two sentences, the page is probably trying to cover too much and should split.
  • "Overview" is always the first H2. Even a page that's mostly a reference table (like Configuration Reference) gets 2-4 sentences of "what this is and when you'd look at it" before the table starts.
  • Code blocks are fenced with a language tag (```bash, ```go, ```yaml, ```json) so syntax highlighting and the copy button both work.
  • Internal links are relative ([Detection Algorithm](detection-algorithm.md)), not absolute GitHub URLs — they need to work both on the rendered site and when reading the raw Markdown in the repo.
  • "See also" is optional but encouraged, and only lists pages, not external references — external links belong inline, in context, next to the claim they support.
  • Reference tables document defaults, not just types. A flag/field table always has a "Default" column, even when the default is "(required)" or empty string — an absent default is itself information.

docs.title: Alerting
docs.text: How a detected regression gets reported, and to what.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
When the Correlation Engine detects a regression, internal/alerting.WebhookNotifier POSTs it to a webhook endpoint. What that payload actually looks like is decided by a Formatter — this project ships four:

Format Destination Notes slack (default) Slack (or Slack-compatible, e.g. Mattermost) incoming webhook This project's original, and still default, format. teams Microsoft Teams Incoming Webhook connector Classic MessageCard payload — the same shape Teams' own webhook connector documents today. pagerduty PagerDuty Events API v2 Opens (or updates, on a repeat notification for the same regression) an incident; always posts to PagerDuty's fixed Events API endpoint, authenticated by a routing key rather than a per-integration URL. custom Anything A Go text/template you supply renders the body — see Custom format.

Every format reports the same underlying fields (deploy event, query ID/text, latency before/after, change factor, confidence, change point, and — when --capture-plans/spec.capturePlans is enabled — the plan-diff summary), just laid out however each destination expects.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
CLI (cmd/operator, or the unified pg-regression-radar operator subcommand):

pg-regression-radar operator \
  --dsn "$DSN" \
  --alert-format teams \
  --alert-url "https://example.webhook.office.com/webhookb2/..." \
  ...
Flag Default Description --alert-format slack slack, teams, pagerduty, or custom --alert-url `` Webhook URL for slack/teams/custom; ignored for pagerduty. Falls back to --slack-url when unset --alerting-allowed-destinations `` Optional strict allowlist: comma-separated exact hostnames, IPs, or CIDRs. When set, the alert destination must match one of them --alerting-destination-policy permissive Destination strategy: permissive (default), allowlist, or relay-only --alerting-destination-policy-relay-url `` Fixed relay endpoint required when --alerting-destination-policy=relay-only --pagerduty-routing-key `` Required when --alert-format=pagerduty --alert-template `` Go text/template source, inline; required (or use --alert-template-file) when --alert-format=custom --alert-template-file `` Path to a template file — alternative to --alert-template

--dry-run validates the alerting configuration (unknown format, missing routing key, unparseable template) before touching Postgres, so a typo'd --alert-format fails immediately instead of on the first detected regression.

cmd/manager accepts --alerting-allowed-destinations, --alerting-destination-policy, and --alerting-destination-policy-relay-url and applies them cluster-wide to every reconciled PostgresWatch.

CRD (PostgresWatch.spec.alerting, cmd/manager):

apiVersion: radar.pgregressionradar.io/v1alpha1
kind: PostgresWatch
metadata:
  name: prod-db
spec:
  clusterName: prod
  dsnSecretRef: {name: prod-db-dsn, key: dsn}
  alerting:
    format: pagerduty
    pagerDutyRoutingKey: R0UTE1NG-KEY
Field Default Description format "" (→ slack) slack, teams, pagerduty, or custom url "" Webhook URL for slack/teams/custom; ignored for pagerduty pagerDutyRoutingKey "" Required when format is pagerduty customTemplate "" Required when format is custom — inline, since a CR spec has no local filesystem to reference

spec.alerting supersedes spec.slackWebhookUrl entirely when set — there is no field-by-field merge between the two. Leave alerting unset to keep using slackWebhookUrl (or no alerting at all, if that's empty too) exactly as before this field existed.

Helm chart: the alerting.* values (format, url, allowedDestinations, destinationPolicy, destinationPolicyRelayUrl, pagerDutyRoutingKey, customTemplate, alongside the pre-existing slackWebhookUrl) feed both mode: operator (as CLI flags) and mode: manager (as manager flags plus spec.alerting on the default PostgresWatch) — see Installation.

docs.title: Destination validation (SSRF hardening)
docs.text:
--alert-url/spec.alerting.url (and the deprecated --slack-url/spec.slackWebhookUrl) are free-text: whoever can pass the flag or edit the PostgresWatch controls where every detected regression's payload gets sent. Since that payload can include query text and, with --capture-plans/spec.capturePlans on, plan-diff content, an unvalidated destination is both a spoofing/notification-injection risk and a potential exfiltration/SSRF path. BuildNotifier (the one place both the CLI and the manager controller construct a notifier from that configuration) rejects a configured URL outright, before ever making a request, when it:

  • uses a scheme other than http/https (rules out file://, ftp://, gopher://, and similar);
  • is a literal loopback or link-local address — this covers 127.0.0.1/::1 and, notably, 169.254.169.254, the cloud instance-metadata address shared by AWS, GCP, Azure, DigitalOcean, and Alibaba, which can hand back the node's own cloud credentials to whatever reaches it; or
  • targets a well-known cloud metadata hostname (metadata.google.internal, etc.).

Separately, WebhookNotifier never follows HTTP redirects — a 3xx response from the configured endpoint is treated as a delivery failure rather than a hop to a second, unvalidated destination, closing the usual way around an up-front check like the one above.

This check is intentionally narrow, not a complete SSRF defence: it validates the URL's literal host, not whatever address it eventually resolves to (so it doesn't defend against DNS rebinding), it still permits plain http:// destinations, and it does not block ordinary private (RFC1918) addresses, since a self-hosted, in-cluster webhook receiver — an internal Alertmanager, a homegrown relay — legitimately lives at exactly one of those addresses, and blocking them by default would break that deployment shape rather than an attack.

For clusters where untrusted users can create or edit PostgresWatch objects, treat the built-in validation as a best-effort mitigation for obvious targets, not an authoritative SSRF control. Use one or more of:

  • --alerting-allowed-destinations on operator or manager to enforce a strict, opt-in allowlist of approved hostnames/IPs/CIDRs;
  • a NetworkPolicy that only allows egress to your approved alert receivers; and/or
  • an admission policy (AdmissionWebhook, Kyverno, Gatekeeper, etc.) that rejects unapproved spec.alerting.url / spec.slackWebhookUrl values before they ever reach the controller.

The allowlist is evaluated in addition to the static blocklist above — it narrows what is accepted, but it does not make hostname-based destinations immune to DNS TOCTOU/rebinding on its own.

pagerduty is exempt from all of the above: its destination is always PagerDuty's own fixed Events API endpoint, never the configured URL.

docs.title: Custom format
docs.text:
--alert-format=custom / spec.alerting.format: custom renders the notification body from a Go text/template you supply, for any destination that isn't Slack/Teams/PagerDuty-shaped — a generic HTTP endpoint, an internal on-call tool, an n8n/Zapier relay, or anything else with its own expected JSON (or non-JSON) body.

The template is executed against these fields:

Field Type Example .ClusterName string prod-east .DeployEventID string deploy-abc123 .QueryID int64 987654321 .QueryText string SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = $1 .ConfidenceScore float64 0.97 .ConfidencePercent string (pre-formatted) 97% .PValue float64 0.03 (0 when the significance test did not run) .PValueText string (pre-formatted) 0.03 (empty when the test did not run) .MeanLatencyBeforeMs string (pre-formatted) 12.50 .MeanLatencyAfterMs string (pre-formatted) 84.20 .LatencyChangeFactor string (pre-formatted) 6.74x .ChangePointRFC3339 string 2026-08-12T10:00:00Z .ExternalCauseSuspected bool false .PlanDiffSummary string ` (empty unless--capture-plans/spec.capturePlans` is on)

ConfidenceScore is 1 - PValue, a significance score and not a probability; see Detection Algorithm. The Slack, Teams and PagerDuty layouts show it as 97% (1 − p) next to the p-value.

The pre-formatted fields (ConfidencePercent, MeanLatencyBeforeMs, etc.) match exactly what the built-in Slack/Teams/PagerDuty formatters render, so a template author gets the same numbers without reimplementing that formatting.

Example — a minimal generic JSON body:

{
  "cluster": "{{.ClusterName}}",
  "query_id": {{.QueryID}},
  "confidence": "{{.ConfidencePercent}}",
  "summary": "query {{.QueryID}} latency changed {{.LatencyChangeFactor}} on {{.ClusterName}}"
}

The rendered body is sent with Content-Type: application/json by default; a non-JSON template (plain text, form-encoded, etc.) can pass a different content type — the CRD/CLI surface doesn't expose this today (it defaults to application/json), since every destination worth templating for accepts JSON.

A broken template (bad text/template syntax) is rejected at construction time — --dry-run, or the first reconcile of a PostgresWatch with a bad customTemplate — rather than only failing the first time a regression is actually detected.

docs.title: Destination policies
docs.text:
By default any webhook URL that passes the static SSRF blocklist (no loopback, no link-local, no cloud-metadata hostnames) is accepted. Two additional, opt-in policies let operators lock down where alerts can be sent — useful in shared or multi-tenant clusters.

flowchart TB
  U["Alert destination URL"]:::radar
  B["Passes the SSRF blocklist?<br/>no loopback, link-local or metadata"]:::gate
  P["destinationPolicy"]:::gate
  AL["Host in the<br/>allowed destinations?"]:::gate
  REL["Send to the relay URL<br/>(spec.alerting.url ignored)"]:::out
  SEND["Send to the configured URL"]:::out
  NO["Rejected: the watch<br/>fails to reconcile"]:::gate
  U --> B
  B -->|"no"| NO
  B -->|"yes"| P
  P -->|"permissive"| SEND
  P -->|"allowlist"| AL
  P -->|"relay-only"| REL
  AL -->|"yes"| SEND
  AL -->|"no"| NO

What each policy decides before an alert is sent.

docs.title: permissive (default)
docs.text:
The URL configured in spec.alerting.url (or via --alert-url / --slack-url in the standalone operator) must only clear the built-in SSRF blocklist. No other restriction applies. This is the default and is fully backward-compatible.

# No explicit destinationPolicy — permissive is implied.
spec:
  alerting:
    format: slack
    url: https://hooks.slack.com/services/T000/B000/XXX

docs.title: allowlist
docs.text:
The webhook URL's host must also appear in the manager-level --alerting-allowed-destinations list (comma-separated hostnames, IPs, or CIDRs). Reconciliation of a PostgresWatch whose URL's host is not in the list fails immediately with a clear error message.

Use this when only a pre-approved set of alert receivers should be reachable from any watch in the cluster.

Manager flag:

--alerting-destination-policy=allowlist
--alerting-allowed-destinations=hooks.slack.com,alertmanager.monitoring.svc.cluster.local

Or per-watch, when running the standalone operator:

--alerting-destination-policy=allowlist
--alerting-allowed-destinations=hooks.slack.com
--alert-url=https://hooks.slack.com/services/T000/B000/XXX

CRD — the destinationPolicy field is honoured when no manager-level policy is configured:

spec:
  alerting:
    format: slack
    url: https://hooks.slack.com/services/T000/B000/XXX
    destinationPolicy: allowlist

docs.title: relay-only
docs.text:
The CRD-level URL (spec.alerting.url) is ignored entirely. All alerts from every watch are forwarded to a single, centrally configured relay endpoint supplied via --alerting-destination-policy-relay-url. Reconciliation fails if that flag is empty.

Use this when you want a single egress point that individual watch owners cannot override.

Manager flags:

--alerting-destination-policy=relay-only
--alerting-destination-policy-relay-url=https://relay.example.com/webhook

Startup validation ensures the relay URL is set before the manager starts.

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text: The JSON shape of the two types that cross a process boundary: DeployEvent and PerformanceRegression.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: These are the two types every webhook source normalises into and every alert is built from. Both are plain Go DTOs in pkg/apis/v1alpha1 — see Architecture Overview's note on the difference between these and the real Kubernetes CRDs in api/v1alpha1.

docs.title: DeployEvent
docs.text:
{
  "id": "argocd-my-app-1234567890",
  "source": "prod-argocd",
  "app": "my-app",
  "cluster": "prod-cluster",
  "namespace": "production",
  "revision": "abc123def456",
  "imageTag": "my-app:v42",
  "timestamp": "2026-08-11T12:00:00Z"
}

Produced by the Ingester from any of the four webhook sources — see Deploy Sources & Webhooks for how each source populates cluster.

docs.title: PerformanceRegression
docs.text:
{
  "name": "argocd-my-app-1234567890-q8675309",
  "namespace": "production",
  "deployEventId": "argocd-my-app-1234567890",
  "queryId": 8675309,
  "queryText": "SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = $1",
  "status": "Detected",
  "confidenceScore": 0.98,
  "pValue": 0.02,
  "meanLatencyBefore": 4.2,
  "meanLatencyAfter": 13.7,
  "latencyChangeFactor": 3.26,
  "externalCauseSuspected": false,
  "planDiffSummary": "root node changed from Index Scan to Seq Scan",
  "createdAt": "2026-08-11T12:35:00Z"
}

Produced by the Correlation Engine for every query analysed against a DeployEvent — see Detection Algorithm for what status, pValue, confidenceScore, and the latency fields mean. confidenceScore is 1 - pValue, a significance score and not a probability, and pValue is omitted when the significance test did not run, and how Detected is decided. status is one of Detected, NoRegression, or InsufficientData. planDiffSummary is only populated when plan-diff correlation is enabled (--capture-plans / spec.capturePlans) — see Detection Algorithm: Plan-diff correlation.

docs.title: Dashboard API
docs.text:
internal/dashboardapi serves a read-only HTTP API for the observability dashboard. It is enabled with --dashboard-addr on cmd/operator and cmd/manager (see Configuration Reference) and is a pure read layer: every field returned already exists on the PerformanceRegression/PostgresWatch CRDs (api/v1alpha1) or in internal/storage/internal/collector/internal/ingester, with no new computed metrics. Fields the current detection pipeline does not compute — t-statistic, Cohen's d, confidence intervals, e-divisive permutation counts, cache-hit ratio, rows-examined, lock-wait time, p95/p99 latency — are not part of this API.

Each route returns 501 Not Implemented if the process serving it wasn't wired with the dependency that route needs. /api/v1/regressions and /api/v1/watches list Kubernetes objects and need a client.Client — only cmd/manager has one, so they always 501 on cmd/operator. /api/v1/deploys and /api/v1/queries need query-sample/deploy-event history, which only cmd/operator builds (via its Collector/deploy-event Store, or the postgres state backend when --state-backend=postgres) — they always 501 on cmd/manager.

Every route responds with permissive CORS headers (Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *, GET and OPTIONS only), so a browser-based dashboard served from a different origin can call this API directly without a proxy. This is safe precisely because the API is read-only and never combines the open origin with credentialed/cookie-based access.

queryId is a JSON string, not a number, on every route below (/api/v1/regressions, /api/v1/queries, and /api/v1/queries/{queryId}/samples) — pg_stat_statements queryids are arbitrary int64 values that routinely exceed JavaScript's Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (2^53-1), so a bare JSON number would get silently rounded by JSON.parse in any JS consumer. Treat it as an opaque string identifier: pass it back verbatim (e.g. into /api/v1/queries/{queryId}/samples), never parse it into a number.

docs.title: GET /api/v1/regressions?namespace=&status=
docs.text:
Lists PerformanceRegression objects (api/v1alpha1/performanceregression_types.go) via a client.Client, optionally filtered by namespace and status (Detected, NoRegression, InsufficientData). Each item:

{
  "name": "argocd-my-app-1234567890-q8675309",
  "namespace": "production",
  "clusterName": "prod-cluster",
  "queryId": "8675309",
  "queryText": "SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = $1",
  "deployEventId": "argocd-my-app-1234567890",
  "status": "Detected",
  "triggerType": "deploy",
  "confidenceScore": "0.98",
  "pValue": "0.02",
  "meanLatencyBeforeMs": "4.2",
  "meanLatencyAfterMs": "13.7",
  "latencyChangeFactor": "3.26",
  "externalCauseSuspected": false,
  "planDiffSummary": "root node changed from Index Scan to Seq Scan",
  "autoAbortTriggered": false,
  "detectedAt": "2026-08-11T12:35:00Z"
}

deployEventId is omitted for a periodic-triggered regression (no deploy involved); when present, cross-reference it against GET /api/v1/deploys (below) to show the real deploy that triggered the regression — app, image tag, revision, timestamp.

docs.title: GET /api/v1/deploys?since=RFC3339&until=RFC3339
docs.text: Returns DeployEvent (above), unmodified. Backed by storage.EventStore.EventsInRange when --state-backend=postgres, or otherwise directly by the operator's own in-process deploy-event history (internal/ingester.Store) — either way this works with cmd/operator's default configuration, not only when postgres persistence is opted into. Defaults to the last 7 days when since/until are omitted.

docs.title: GET /api/v1/queries?windowMinutes=60
docs.text:
Returns, per tracked queryId, an aggregate over samples recorded in the last windowMinutes (default 60). Backed by storage.SampleStore when --state-backend=postgres, or otherwise directly by the operator's own in-process query-sample history (internal/collector.Collector) — either way this works with cmd/operator's default configuration:

{
  "queryId": "8675309",
  "queryText": "SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = $1",
  "calls": 4213,
  "meanExecMs": 4.2,
  "sampleCount": 12
}

calls and meanExecMs mirror exactly what regression_radar.query_samples stores (calls, mean_exec_time_ms); there is no p95/p99 or cache-hit-ratio field, since that data isn't collected today.

docs.title: GET /api/v1/queries/{queryId}/samples?since=RFC3339&until=RFC3339
docs.text:
Returns the raw, per-scrape samples for one queryId in [since, until] — unlike /api/v1/queries above, which collapses a whole window into one aggregate, this is one entry per pg_stat_statements scrape, meant for plotting an actual time series (e.g. the real before/after curve around a specific regression's detectedAt) rather than a single before/after number. Defaults to the last 60 minutes when since/until are omitted, same as /api/v1/queries. Backed by the same SampleReader as /api/v1/queries, so it 501s under the same conditions.

[
  { "recordedAt": "2026-08-11T12:30:00Z", "calls": 4201, "meanExecMs": 4.1 },
  { "recordedAt": "2026-08-11T12:35:00Z", "calls": 4213, "meanExecMs": 13.7 }
]

docs.title: GET /api/v1/watches
docs.text: Lists PostgresWatch objects (api/v1alpha1/postgreswatch_types.go) as-is, with no transformation.

docs.title: Attribution API
docs.text: The attribution engine serves two read-only endpoints on their own listener, off by default: start the manager with --attribution-verdict-addr=:8082 (only the leader serves it) and expose that port with a Service. They are not part of the Dashboard API and do not share its port.

docs.title: GET /api/v1/attribution/verdict?namespace=&app=&revision=
docs.text:
The engine's verdict on the latest deploy of app in namespace (or of revision), shaped for an Argo Rollouts AnalysisTemplate web provider that reads $.verdict.

Field Meaning verdict pass, inconclusive (pause) or fail (abort). Anything undecidable, and every shadow-mode answer, is pass known true when the deploy is known to the engine; false (with pass) for an unknown one pending true while the deploy has not been evaluated yet; the verdict is pass until it has deployId, evaluatedAt The deploy the answer is about and when it was last evaluated enforced true when the watch is in enforce mode and the decision acts wouldBe What the verdict would be in enforce mode action, grade The engine's action (none, alert, hold, rollback) and evidence grade (A to D) impact Supported lower bound of the added database time, as a fraction attribution Probability that this deploy, not a concurrent one, is the cause reasons Why, including what caps the evidence at grade C when it does

docs.title: GET /api/v1/attribution/actions?namespace=&app=
docs.text: The action ledger, newest first: every pause or abort the manager made or skipped, with at, deployId, namespace, app, action (pause or abort), result (done, failed, skipped, recovered, persisted), reason (the stable reason code the log line for the same event carries, such as Acted or ActuationPaused) and detail. It also reports breakerOpen. The ledger keeps the last 200 entries and is lost on restart. See Letting the manager act.

docs.text:

  • Deploy Sources & Webhooks — how DeployEvent is produced from each source type.

docs.title: API Versioning & Compatibility Policy
docs.text: What v1alpha1 means in practice, what guarantees (and non-guarantees) come with it, and how the project plans to graduate CRDs to stable versions.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Every CRD shipped by pg-regression-radar today — PostgresWatch, DeploySource, and PerformanceRegression — is at version v1alpha1. This page explains what that version label commits to, what it explicitly does not commit to, and what a user who stores or depends on the schema of these resources should expect across releases.

docs.title: What v1alpha1 means
docs.text:
v1alpha1 follows the Kubernetes API stability convention documented in Kubernetes API versioning:

  • May change in incompatible ways in any release, including minor and patch releases. Fields can be renamed, removed, have their type changed, or have new required fields added without a deprecation window.
  • No guarantee that stored objects can be read after an upgrade. If a field is removed or renamed and you have live resources that use it, you will need to re-create or migrate those resources manually.
  • Recommended only for short-lived experimentation and development clusters, not for production workloads where schema stability is a hard requirement.

This is intentional and not a quality judgment — the CRD surface is still being shaped by real-world feedback, and v1alpha1 preserves the freedom to make the right design choice without a migration burden.

docs.title: What is (and is not) guaranteed today
docs.text: Guarantee Status Kubernetes API server accepts the CRDs ✓ guaranteed spec fields documented in Configuration Reference exist and behave as documented ✓ guaranteed within a release Fields and their types are stable across minor or patch releases ✗ not guaranteed at v1alpha1 Stored resources survive an in-place upgrade without manual action ✗ not guaranteed at v1alpha1 A conversion webhook exists to migrate old stored versions ✗ not implemented at v1alpha1 Schema changes are announced in release notes ✓ best-effort — breaking changes will be called out in the release note; check before upgrading

docs.title: Practical guidance for users
docs.text:
If you are experimenting or running in a non-production cluster: use the CRDs as-is. Check the release notes before upgrading; any field-level breaking change will be explicitly noted there.

If you need stability today: pin your Helm install to a specific chart version (helm install ... --version <chart-version>) and do not upgrade without reading the release notes for every version in between. Because there is no conversion webhook yet, upgrading may require deleting and re-creating PostgresWatch and DeploySource resources.

If you are writing automation or tooling against the CRD schema (e.g. a Crossplane composition, a GitOps repo, or a controller of your own): treat the schema as volatile. Subscribe to releases on GitHub to be notified when schema changes land.

docs.title: Planned graduation path
docs.text:
The project intends to graduate the CRDs through the standard Kubernetes API maturity ladder:

  1. v1alpha1 (current): schema is being shaped. Breaking changes permitted without deprecation period.
  2. v1beta1 (target: a future minor release): schema is considered mostly stable. Breaking changes require a deprecation notice in at least one minor release and a migration note in the release. A conversion webhook will be introduced to support stored-version migration.
  3. v1 (target: a future major release): schema is stable. No breaking changes without a full deprecation cycle (minimum two minor releases). Stored objects from any prior v1 sub-version are guaranteed to be readable after upgrade.

There is no firm timeline or committed version number for v1beta1 or v1. Graduation will follow demonstrated stability of the schema in real-world use, not a fixed calendar. Updates to the graduation timeline will be tracked in Roadmap.

docs.title: How breaking changes are communicated
docs.text:
Before v1beta1, any field-level breaking change in a v1alpha1 CRD will be:

  1. Called out explicitly in the GitHub release notes under a "⚠ Breaking changes" heading.
  2. Accompanied by a migration note describing what resources need to be updated (delete-and-recreate, field rename, etc.).
  3. Reflected in an updated Configuration Reference in the same release.

After v1beta1, the project additionally commits to a deprecation annotation (deprecated: true in the field's OpenAPI description) for at least one minor release before removal.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Configuration Reference — current PostgresWatch spec fields and their defaults.
  • Roadmap — what's shipped and what's still open.
  • Installation — pinning a specific Helm chart version.

docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text: How the four core packages fit together, the two ways to run them, and the repo layout.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: pg-regression-radar is built from four engine packages (internal/collector, internal/ingester, internal/correlation, internal/alerting) that never change depending on how the process is run. What changes is the entrypoint that wires them up: a single CLI-flag-configured binary, or a Kubernetes-CRD-driven controller. This page covers both, plus where everything lives in the repository.

docs.title: The four engine packages
docs.text:
1. Collector (internal/collector) — scrapes pg_stat_statements on an interval and keeps a bounded in-memory time series per queryid, with Prometheus metrics exposed. See Collector Internals for retention, queryid rotation, and version-detection details.
  2. Deploy Event Ingester (internal/ingester) — receives webhooks from ArgoCD, Argo Rollouts, and Flux and stores normalised DeployEvent records. See Deploy Sources & Webhooks.
  3. Correlation Engine (internal/correlation) — for every deploy event, extracts the pre/post latency windows and runs E-divisive change-point detection followed by Welch's t-test. See Detection Algorithm.
  4. Alerting (internal/alerting) — fires a Slack-compatible webhook with the query text, latency before/after, change factor, and confidence score.

An optional fifth package, Attribution (internal/attribution), judges each tracked deploy against a counterfactual control and records the action it would take. It reads the same collector samples, never writes to the cluster (in enforce mode it serves a verdict that Argo Rollouts or Flagger acts on), and is off unless a PostgresWatch sets spec.attribution.enabled. See Attribution engine.

docs.title: Two ways to run pg-regression-radar
docs.text:
Both entrypoints wire up the same engine packages in two different ways:

cmd/operator (standalone) cmd/manager (CRD-driven) Configuration CLI flags PostgresWatch / DeploySource Kubernetes CRs Postgres clusters watched exactly one any number, added/removed at runtime Kubernetes API access needed none yes (CRDs + a Secret read) High availability run 1 replica run N replicas with leader election; only the leader works, a standby takes over automatically on failure Regression history Slack/webhook alert only Slack/webhook alert and a PerformanceRegression CR (kubectl get performanceregressions -A) Recommended for quick trials, single-cluster setups, environments without CRD install rights production

Both binaries are built from this one module and neither modifies the other's code path — cmd/manager's reconcilers (internal/controller/postgreswatch_controller.go, internal/controller/deploysource_controller.go) call the exact same collector.New / correlation.New / alerting.NewWebhookNotifier constructors cmd/operator/main.go calls directly, just with one instance per PostgresWatch CR instead of one instance total, orchestrated by controller-runtime instead of main().

Note

pkg/apis/v1alpha1 holds plain Go DTO structs used internally between packages — they are not Kubernetes objects. The real CRDs (metav1.TypeMeta/ObjectMeta, runtime.Object, OpenAPI schemas) live in api/v1alpha1 and are only used by cmd/manager and internal/controller. This split lets the detection engine stay Kubernetes-agnostic while still getting a first-class CRD experience.

docs.title: When to use which
docs.text:
• Use cmd/operator if you have one Postgres cluster, don't need HA, and would rather not grant the process any Kubernetes RBAC at all — it never talks to the Kubernetes API.
  • Use cmd/manager (the Helm chart's mode: manager) if you want to watch multiple Postgres clusters from one deployment, want kubectl get postgreswatch,deploysource,performanceregression visibility, or need HA (multiple replicas with automatic failover via a coordination.k8s.io Lease).

docs.title: Multi-cluster: two independent axes
docs.text:
"Multiple Postgres clusters" and "Postgres clusters living in a different Kubernetes cluster than the manager" are two separate capabilities, easy to conflate:

  • Many PostgresWatch CRs, one Kubernetes cluster. cmd/manager has always supported this: internal/controller/registry.go's Registry tracks one independent Collector/Engine/Notifier/ingester.Store per reconciled PostgresWatch, however many DSNs (reachable over the network from wherever the manager pods run) that adds up to.
  • A PostgresWatch's DSN Secret living in a different Kubernetes cluster. This is what spec.remoteClusterRef (preferred, registry-backed) and the deprecated spec.remoteClusterSecretRef add: a hub-spoke model, matching the pattern Cluster API / Argo CD / Open Cluster Management use, where a kubeconfig Secret in the manager's own (hub) cluster lets PostgresWatchReconciler build a client.Client for a remote ("spoke") cluster and read that cluster's CloudNativePG-generated DSN Secret through it, instead of requiring an operator to manually copy the Secret into the hub. The same kubeconfig can also back spec.cnpgClusterRef, a remote CloudNativePG Cluster health check performed before the watch starts, and a separate PostgresRadarClusterReconciler proactively re-probes every registered cluster's kubeconfig on an interval, independent of whether any PostgresWatch currently uses it. See Multi-Cluster (Fleet) Mode for the full model, the RBAC split between "read a Secret in the hub" and "whatever the kubeconfig itself is allowed to do in the spoke," and the permanent operational considerations that remain (kubeconfig rotation still requires an external rotator, and cross-cluster Postgres data-plane reachability is always the operator's own responsibility).

DeploySource/the webhook Ingester need neither of the above: a DeploySource's whole job is registering an HTTP route that a remote system (ArgoCD, Argo Rollouts, Flux, or a custom CI job) pushes a webhook to — the connection is always initiated by the remote side, never by the manager reaching out, so there is nothing for a Kubernetes client (local or remote) to do here regardless of which cluster the deploy tooling runs in. See Deploy Sources & Webhooks.

docs.title: Attribution engine
docs.text: Decide whether a deploy caused a latency change by asking what would have happened without it, and act on how strong that evidence is.

docs.title: Why it exists
docs.text:
A latency change after a deploy is not proof the deploy caused it. A query's queryid changes when its text changes, the planner changes plans when statistics refresh, a cache runs cold after a restart, load moves, another deploy lands. Handling each of these with its own rule does not scale. The engine replaces the rules with one question: what would these queries have done without this deploy, and how sure are we that they did something else?

The engine judges every tracked deploy and, by default, only records the action it would take (shadow mode). In enforce mode it serves a verdict that your rollout controller acts on; the manager itself never writes to a Rollout. Turn it on per watch:

apiVersion: radar.pgregressionradar.io/v1alpha1
kind: PostgresWatch
spec:
  attribution:
    enabled: true
    mode: shadow   # or "enforce"

Decisions appear in the manager log (attribution (shadow): decision, not executed, attribution (enforce): verdict served… when a decision is enforced, or attribution (enforce): decision below the acting threshold… for an alert or nothing in enforce mode) and in the metric pg_regression_radar_attribution_shadow_decisions_total{action,grade}. It requires the watch to scrape its own collector (not a Prometheus sample source).

flowchart TB
  A["Tracked deploy<br/>(evaluated at +30, +35, +40 min)"]:::radar
  B["Identify each query by the<br/>fingerprint of its text"]:::radar
  C["Build the counterfactual:<br/>A canary arm, B synthetic control, C own history"]:::radar
  D["Step test per query, then<br/>e-BH across queries"]:::radar
  G["Guards: persistence, table-level cap,<br/>overlapping deploys, global shift"]:::gate
  P["Policy by evidence grade"]:::gate
  R["A: roll back"]:::out
  H["B: hold promotion"]:::out
  L["C: alert only"]:::out
  N["D or immaterial: none"]:::gate
  A --> B --> C --> D --> G --> P
  P -->|"A"| R
  P -->|"B"| H
  P -->|"C"| L
  P -->|"D"| N

docs.title: Acting on a verdict
docs.text:
By default the manager does not patch Rollouts. It serves a read-only verdict and the progressive-delivery controller acts on it, which is how Argo Rollouts and Flagger are designed to take an outside signal (to have the manager act itself, see Letting the manager act): Argo's analysis passes, fails (aborting the rollout) or is inconclusive (pausing it at its current step), and a Flagger webhook that does not return 2xx halts promotion. On this path the manager needs no new RBAC.

Start the manager with --attribution-verdict-addr=:8082 (off by default; only the leader serves it) and expose that port with a Service. The endpoint is GET /api/v1/attribution/verdict?namespace=<ns>&app=<name>[&revision=<rev>]:

{"verdict":"inconclusive","enforced":true,"wouldBe":"inconclusive","action":"hold","grade":"B","impact":0.12,"attribution":1,"reasons":["grade B evidence supports 12.0% added database time"]}
verdict Meaning Argo Rollouts effect pass Nothing to act on, no evaluation yet, unknown deploy, shadow mode, or an alert-only grade Rollout continues inconclusive Grade B evidence of a material regression, confirmed twice Rollout pauses at its step fail Grade A evidence (a concurrent control arm), confirmed twice Rollout aborts

Anything that cannot be decided is pass: the engine never blocks a release for lack of data. In shadow mode verdict is always pass, and wouldBe shows what enforce mode would have said.

An Argo Rollouts analysis that uses it:

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AnalysisTemplate
metadata:
  name: pgrr-attribution
spec:
  args: [{name: namespace}, {name: app}]
  metrics:
    - name: attribution
      interval: 5m
      successCondition: result == 'pass'
      failureCondition: result == 'fail'   # neither condition met = inconclusive = pause
      provider:
        web:
          url: "http://pg-regression-radar.<manager-namespace>.svc:8082/api/v1/attribution/verdict?namespace={{args.namespace}}&app={{args.app}}"
          jsonPath: "{$.verdict}"

Timing matters. On simulated workloads the engine cannot convict before about 15 minutes after a deploy, because its persistence check needs a late window (transients, such as a cold cache, must have decayed). A canary that is fully promoted in five minutes is out of reach: give the Rollout a pause step of at least 20 minutes, or the verdict arrives after the release is done and can only alert. Compare Flagger, whose rollback time is the analysis interval times its failure threshold, and the Google and Waze advice to run a canary long enough for a meaningful number of data points.

The ladder is the one Google and Waze describe for a new canary analysis: begin with a non-blocking stage, then a manual judgement, and automate only once the analysis has proved reliable. Run shadow mode, compare wouldBe with what happened, then set mode: enforce. With enforce, the first action you will see is a pause, which one click resumes; an abort needs grade A.

A copy-and-adapt walk-through is in Example: pausing a bad rollout, and Enforce mode explains why a deploy might only alert.

docs.title: Letting the manager act
docs.text:
The verdict endpoint needs a rollout controller that asks. When you want the radar to act on its own, with no AnalysisTemplate in between, turn on actuation:

spec:
  attribution:
    enabled: true
    mode: enforce
    actuate:
      enabled: true
      namespaces: [shop, payments]   # optional; empty means any

It follows the same ladder as the verdict, and only for a deploy that a DeploySource of type argo-rollouts reported:

Engine action What the manager does Same as hold (grade B, confirmed twice, material) sets spec.paused: true on the Rollout kubectl argo rollouts pause rollback (grade A, confirmed twice) sets status.abort: true on the Rollout kubectl argo rollouts abort anything else nothing

It never resumes, rolls back to a revision, scales, or deletes: a pause or an abort stops a bad rollout where it is, and a person decides what comes next. Each action is taken at most once per deploy, a pause can escalate to an abort if later evidence is stronger, and a failed call is retried at the next evaluation. Every attempt is counted in pg_regression_radar_attribution_actions_total{action,result} (result is done, failed or skipped) and logged with the grade, the impact and the reasons.

Every attempt is also written to an in-memory ledger, served newest first at GET /api/v1/attribution/actions (same port as the verdict endpoint; filter with ?namespace= and ?app=): the time, the deploy, pause or abort, the result, and the reason code of the log line for the same event (see Reason codes). It also reports breakerOpen. The ledger keeps the last 200 entries and is lost on a restart; the metrics and the logs are the durable record.

{"breakerOpen":false,"actions":[
 {"at":"2026-11-24T14:41:00Z","deployId":"d1","namespace":"shop","app":"checkout","action":"abort","result":"recovered","detail":"regression no longer supported after the action"},
 {"at":"2026-11-24T14:26:00Z","deployId":"d1","namespace":"shop","app":"checkout","action":"abort","result":"done","detail":"grade A evidence supports 12.0% added database time"}]}

Checking that it helped. Fifteen minutes after an abort the engine reads the deploy again. It leaves out what the deploy did until the abort (and three minutes more for the canary's pods to drain) and reads what came after, so a canary that ran slow before it was stopped does not count against the abort; a canary that is still serving does. If the regression is gone the result is recovered. If it is still supported at grade B or better, the abort did not help (the deploy was not the cause, or the abort did not take) and the result is persisted. When there is too little data after the abort to judge by, no check is made and nothing counts. Each persisted counts as a failure for the policy; after two in a row (BreakerLimit) the circuit breaker opens and the engine only alerts, until you close it with kubectl annotate postgreswatch <name> pg-regression-radar.io/reset-breaker="$(date +%s)" --overwrite (a change of the annotation's value; a value already on the object when the manager started is ignored) or the manager restarts. pg_regression_radar_attribution_breaker_open is 1 while it is open, and pg_regression_radar_attribution_verifications_total{result} counts the checks. A pause is not checked: a held canary keeps serving traffic, so its regression persists by design.

The Actuating condition of the PostgresWatch says whether the manager may act right now, and if not, which of the cases below applies: the breaker is open, the watch is in shadow mode, actuate is not enabled, there is no Rollout RBAC, or the kill switch is set. Enforce mode walks through each.

Four rules keep it safe to turn on:

  • Enforce mode only. In shadow mode nothing is written; the log says what would have been done.
  • One detector acts. While actuate is on, the older spec.autoAbort trigger is ignored for that watch, so one regression is never acted on twice by two detectors that disagree. The engine's guards (material impact, two consecutive confirmations, attribution of at least 0.8, a cooldown) apply to every action.
  • You can bound it and stop it. actuate.namespaces limits it to Rollouts in the listed namespaces (empty means any); a deploy elsewhere is still judged and logged, and the ledger records it as skipped. To stop all pausing and aborting at once, with no restart and no spec change, annotate the watch: kubectl annotate postgreswatch <name> pg-regression-radar.io/actuation-paused=true (remove the annotation to resume). If the watch cannot be read at that moment, the manager assumes it is paused.
  • It needs the Rollout RBAC. Set manager.autoAbort.rbacEnabled: true in the Helm chart (it grants patch on rollouts and rollouts/status). Without it, or without mode: enforce, actuate is ignored and the log says why.

Through the collector alone the best evidence is grade B, because pg_stat_statements carries no label saying which release served a call, so the manager pauses and a person aborts; an abort needs grade A evidence, which attribution.arms provides. The timing note applies here too: the engine cannot convict before about 15 minutes, so the Rollout needs a pause step of at least 20 minutes for the action to land in time.

docs.title: Telling a canary from the stable pods (grade A)
docs.text:
pg_stat_statements mixes every client together, so through the collector alone the best evidence is grade B and the strongest action is a pause. To abort, the engine needs to see the canary and the stable pods at the same time. It gets that from the Postgres log, which records for each statement the application_name of the session that ran it. Nothing is installed on the server: it takes core settings, and no extension.

spec:
  attribution:
    enabled: true
    mode: enforce
    actuate: {enabled: true}
    arms:
      enabled: true
      podLogs:                       # Postgres in the cluster (CloudNativePG, a StatefulSet)
        namespace: db
        selector: cnpg.io/cluster=pg
      # file: /var/log/postgresql/postgresql.json   # or a log file the manager can open

What you set up:

  1. The server. compute_query_id = on, log_destination = 'jsonlog' (PostgreSQL 15 or newer), log_min_duration_sample = 0, log_min_duration_statement = -1 (or leave a slow-query log on: the engine weights for it), and a small log_statement_sample_rate, for example 0.05. The manager reads these settings itself every five minutes and logs exactly which one is wrong. The log is not used until they pass. A rate above 0.25 only draws a warning, because it costs the database and the log pipeline.
  2. The application. Every pod must report an application_name that begins with the pod's name (<rollout>-<pod-template-hash>-<suffix>), which is the hostname. With an Argo Rollouts workload, set PGAPPNAME from the pod's own name:
env:
- name: PGAPPNAME
  valueFrom: {fieldRef: {fieldPath: metadata.name}}

The manager reads the Rollout's status.stableRS and status.currentPodHash, so the pods of the new version are the treatment and the pods of the old version the control. A pod that does not follow the naming is simply not counted; if none do, the engine behaves as it does without arms. 3. The manager. podLogs needs manager.arms.rbacEnabled: true in the chart (get and list on pods, get on pods/log). file needs nothing. Reading Rollouts needs manager.autoAbort.rbacEnabled, as for actuate.

How the evidence is built:

  • The manager keeps, per application_name and query_id, the number of sampled executions and their mean duration in each scrape interval. It joins a log line to a collected query by query_id. It never keeps the statement text or the bind parameters, which can hold personal data, and a line longer than 1 MiB is skipped.
  • Each sampled execution is weighted by the inverse of its chance of being logged, so the mean stays unbiased when slow statements are always logged (a slow-query log) and fast ones only sampled. The weight of a mean is the number of samples behind it, not the number of calls they stand for.
  • Before the deploy there is no canary, so the old version's pods are split in two alternating halves and one half stands in for the canary. The ratio of treatment to control is therefore flat by construction before the deploy; after it, the canary pods are the treatment and the old pods the control. A step in that ratio at the deploy time, which also passes the engine's placebo tests at fake deploy times, is grade A.
  • When the log is not flowing (no line for five minutes), its settings fail, the Rollout is already promoted (stable and current hash are equal), or the Rollout cannot be read, the evaluation falls back to what pg_stat_statements supports.

Two things decide how much a canary check can see: the traffic the canary receives and the sample rate. The number that matters is the sampled executions per minute the canary produces for a query: with only a handful, the engine cannot tell a regression from noise and says nothing, which is safe but silent. The Prometheus metrics pg_regression_radar_attribution_arms_usable, ..._arms_records_total and ..._arms_dropped_total say whether the log is usable and flowing.

docs.title: What a real test showed
docs.text:
The arm reader was run twice against seven PostgreSQL 16 servers (four stable pods and one canary pod per server, a real Kubernetes API server with the Argo Rollouts CRD, the manager in enforce mode with actuate, a canary at about 15% of the traffic, evaluations from 10 minutes after the deploy). The canary regression was a query that runs without its index in the canary only.

Case Round 1 Round 2 Canary regression, every statement logged (about 26 sampled executions a minute for the query) grade A at +15 min grade A at +15 min, abort at +20 min Canary regression, sample rate 0.2 (about 5 a minute) grade A at +15 min grade A at +15 min, abort at +20 min Canary regression, sample rate 0.05 (about 1 a minute) grade A at +15 min missed: stayed at grade C, alert only Canary identical to stable (A/A) no action no action A/A while a shared load shock hit both arms no action no action One stable pod degraded, canary healthy no action no action application_name not following the pod name alert only (grade C) alert only (grade C)

Read it for what it is: two rounds of seven scenarios, one workload, a 2-core machine. It shows that the mechanism works end to end and that no control case acted; it is not a rate. The one miss is the expected limit: at about one sampled execution a minute the canary leaves too little to tell a regression from noise, so choose a sample rate that gives the canary at least a handful of sampled executions a minute for the queries you care about (rate x canary traffic x the query's share). Round 1 also paused instead of aborting because the test had registered no earlier deploy, and the engine never aborts a first deploy. In round 2 the verification 15 minutes after each abort recorded persisted (the regression was still there), because nothing in the test acts on an abort: no rollout controller scales the canary down. The engine kept judging the deploy a rollback but did not patch the Rollout a second time, and the persisted check counts toward the circuit breaker, as designed.

docs.title: Reverting a convicted deploy
docs.text:
Pausing a rollout only helps while it is running. For a release that is already promoted, the durable fix is a revert in git: with Argo CD's automated sync on, Argo CD cannot roll the application back ("Rollback cannot be performed against an application with automated sync enabled"), and anything changed directly in the cluster is undone by the next sync. So in enforce mode the radar can open a draft pull request that reverts the change, and leave the decision to a person.

spec:
  attribution:
    enabled: true
    mode: enforce
    revert:
      enabled: true
      repository: my-org/my-deploy-repo
      tokenSecretRef: {name: github-token, key: token}
      maxPerDay: 3
      includeQueryText: false

It acts when the policy holds at hold or above (grade B or better, confirmed twice, material, attributed to this deploy). It then:

  1. Takes the deploy's revision, which must be a full 40-character commit SHA. An Argo CD source reports one; an Argo Rollouts source reports a pod hash and a tag is not a commit, so those are refused, not guessed at.
  2. Checks that no pull request for this deploy exists yet (a marker line pgrr-revert-id: <deploy id> is searched for, so a restart or a leader change does not open a second one).
  3. Finds the pull request whose merge commit is that SHA, merged into the default branch. A direct push, or a commit that is not the merge commit of a pull request, is refused.
  4. Asks GitHub to create the revert (the GraphQL revertPullRequest mutation, which "creates a pull request that reverts the changes from a merged pull request"), as a draft, with a body that gives the grade, the lower-bound added database time, the attribution, the most affected queries, and what to check before merging: database migrations, other changes in the same commit, and a warning if the radar has not seen an earlier deploy of the app.

What keeps this safe:

  • It never merges. The pull request is always a draft and a person reviews it. That is the one safeguard that does not depend on the statistics being right.
  • Once per deploy, and at most maxPerDay (default 3) per watch, so a bad day cannot bury a repository.
  • Query text is off by default. The body shows fingerprints and ratios. Turn on includeQueryText only if the repository is private, since a query's text names tables and columns. Everything written into the body is stripped of markdown, mentions and issue references.
  • The token comes from a Secret that carries the same consent label as every other Secret a PostgresWatch references (pg-regression-radar.io/allow-postgreswatch-access=true). It is read for each use and not kept, it is only sent to the configured API host, which must be https, and a redirect is never followed with it attached. Use a fine-grained token limited to that one repository. The documentation I read does not state which permissions revertPullRequest needs; start with Pull requests and Contents, both read and write, and check that against your GitHub.
  • In shadow mode nothing is called. The log says which pull request would have been opened.

Metric: pg_regression_radar_attribution_revert_proposals_total{result} with opened, already-proposed, skipped and failed.

Limits: a failed attempt is retried at the next evaluation, and the search that finds an earlier pull request lags by a short while after one is opened, so a restart within that window can, rarely, open a second draft. A revert does not undo a database migration that shipped with the change.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Identity. A query is identified by the fingerprint of its normalised text, never by queryid. A rewritten query is a new unit with no history, so it is never judged against a baseline.

  2. Counterfactual. For each query the engine builds the series it would have had without the deploy, from the best control available, and measures the difference after the deploy.

    Grade Control Needs A The same query on the arm the deploy did not reach (canary vs stable), with parallel pre-deploy trends Samples labelled by arm B A synthetic control from queries the deploy did not touch, validated by in-time placebos At least 5 untouched queries with history C The query's own history Nothing; cannot separate the deploy from anything else D Nothing Not enough data; never blocks

    A control query must have data for at least half of the pre-deploy window (45 of the 90 minutes), so after a manager restart the evidence stays at grade C, an alert, until about 45 minutes of history have been collected. Hold and pause are not available before then.

  3. Inference. A local-level state-space model with the step estimated inside the Kalman filter, ridge-regressed on the control series. Evidence is an e-process against "no regression beyond the margin" (default 20%), so it is valid at any stopping time, and the false-discovery rate across queries is controlled with e-BH, valid under arbitrary dependence.

  4. Guards. A persistence test (the shift must still be there after the grace period, so warm-ups do not count), a table-level cap (a shift concentrated on one table that the deploy did not declare is capped at grade C), attribution among overlapping deploys, and a global-shift flag. The global-shift flag only counts untouched units that moved the same way as the unit under test: a slow query that throttles a closed-loop workload makes the other queries faster, and that is not a cause shared with the regression.

    When the evidence stops at grade C, the decision says why (evidence is capped at grade C by: global-shift (3), few-donors (1)), in the log and in the verdict's reasons. 5. Policy. The action depends on the strongest grade whose supported lower-bound impact reaches the materiality threshold (5% of database time):

    Evidence Action A Roll back B Hold promotion C Alert D or immaterial None

    Rollback and hold need two consecutive agreeing evaluations, attribution of at least 0.8, a reversible deploy with a rollback target (a first deploy is held, not rolled back), a cooldown between actions, and a closed circuit breaker. Two actions that did not help open the breaker and the policy only alerts.

docs.title: What the test suite shows
docs.text:
Simulated workloads (120 queries, 90 minutes before and 30 after, with load shocks, statistics refreshes, cold caches, rewrites and concurrent deploys), 20 to 60 runs per scenario:

  • No change: at most the nominal share of runs flag anything, and none at grade A or B.
  • Load shock, statistics refresh, cold cache, rewritten queries, concurrent deploy, below-margin change: no conviction at grade A or B.
  • Real regression with a canary arm: about 98% of the affected database time found, no false positives.
  • Real regression with synthetic control only: about 94% of the affected database time found, no false positives.
  • A first deploy is InsufficientData; the policy never blocks on it.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• pg_stat_statements cannot split canary and stable. Grade A needs arm-labelled data, which attribution.arms reads from the Postgres log; without it the best grade is B.
  • A shift shared by every query, with no control arm, is capped at grade C: the engine cannot tell a slower deploy from slower hardware.
  • A real regression concentrated on one table, when the deploy does not declare that table, is capped at grade C.
  • Table extraction from query text is lexical. A mistake makes queries look related, never invents evidence.
  • A pause or abort only helps while the Rollout is still in progress. After a full promotion the verdict can only inform an alert; reverting a promoted release belongs to your GitOps flow.
  • Without attribution.arms the samples from pg_stat_statements carry no arm label, so the best grade is B and the strongest verdict is inconclusive (a pause). A fail needs the arms.
  • attribution.arms assumes the pod name is the application_name, a Postgres 15 or newer JSON log, and a canary that receives enough traffic to leave samples; it was tested against PostgreSQL 16 logs read from a file, and the CloudNativePG log wrapper is unwrapped as documented but has not been run against a live CloudNativePG cluster.
  • The revert proposal needs the deploy's revision to be a git commit SHA: Argo CD sources qualify, Argo Rollouts sources (a pod hash) do not.
  • The circuit breaker is fed only by the check after an abort. A pause cannot be checked (a held canary keeps serving traffic, so its regression persists by design) and a revert pull request is not checked yet, so neither can open it.

docs.title: Auto-Abort (Argo Rollouts)
docs.text: Closing the loop between detecting a regression and doing something about it — safely, and only when asked.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
By default, this project only ever alerts: the Correlation Engine detects a regression, internal/alerting sends it to Slack, and a PerformanceRegression CR records it. A human still has to read the alert and decide whether to abort the deploy.

PostgresWatch.spec.autoAbort optionally closes that loop for one specific, well-understood case: a canary rollout managed by Argo Rollouts. When a regression tied to an Argo Rollouts deploy clears a confidence bar you configure, this manager aborts the canary itself — the same effect kubectl argo rollouts abort has — instead of waiting for someone to see the alert.

This is opt-in at every level, on purpose:

  • Disabled by default. spec.autoAbort is nil unless you set it.
  • Per-PostgresWatch. Enabling it for one watched Postgres cluster doesn't affect any other.
  • Scoped to Argo Rollouts only. A regression whose deploy event came from an argocd, flux, generic, or kubernetes DeploySource is never auto-aborted, regardless of spec.autoAbort.enabled or confidence — none of those has an equivalent "abort mid-rollout" primitive to call, and ArgoCD's/Flux's own notion of "rollback" (re-syncing to a previous Git revision) is a materially bigger, more destructive action than pausing a canary, so it's deliberately out of scope here.
  • Gated behind its own RBAC. See RBAC below — a cluster that never sets spec.autoAbort.enabled doesn't need to grant this manager any access to Argo Rollouts at all.
  • A higher confidence bar than ordinary alerting. See Confidence threshold.
flowchart LR
  D["Regression detected"]:::radar
  A["Alert and<br/>PerformanceRegression"]:::out
  G1["spec.autoAbort.enabled?"]:::gate
  G2["Deploy event came from<br/>Argo Rollouts?"]:::gate
  G3["Confidence at or above<br/>the threshold?"]:::gate
  ABORT["Abort the canary<br/>patch rollouts/status"]:::k8s
  ALONE["Alert only"]:::gate
  D --> A
  D --> G1
  G1 -->|"yes"| G2
  G1 -->|"no"| ALONE
  G2 -->|"yes"| G3
  G2 -->|"no"| ALONE
  G3 -->|"yes"| ABORT
  G3 -->|"no"| ALONE

The alert is always sent. Aborting needs three conditions on top, and the manager also needs the optional Argo Rollouts RBAC.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
apiVersion: radar.pgregressionradar.io/v1alpha1
kind: PostgresWatch
metadata:
  name: prod-db
spec:
  clusterName: prod
  dsnSecretRef: {name: prod-db-dsn, key: dsn}
  autoAbort:
    enabled: true
    confidenceThreshold: "0.99"   # optional; this is the default
Field Default Description enabled false Turns on automatic abortion for this watch. confidenceThreshold "0.99" Minimum confidenceScore (1 - pValue, so "0.99" means pValue <= 0.01) required before aborting, on top of already having cleared pValueThreshold to be reported as Detected at all.

docs.title: Confidence threshold
docs.text: A regression is already reported as Detected once its p-value clears spec.pValueThreshold (default 0.05, i.e. confidenceScore ≥ 0.95; a significance score, not a probability that the regression is real — see what the confidence score means). autoAbort.confidenceThreshold defaults higher, at 0.99, deliberately: alerting a human on a 0.95-confidence signal costs nothing but their attention, but automatically aborting a production canary on the same signal is a more consequential action, and false positives are more expensive to get wrong in that direction. Set confidenceThreshold explicitly if your workload's noise profile calls for something other than the default — it must be a value the Welch's t-test p-value can plausibly clear; see Detection Algorithm for how confidence is computed.

docs.title: What actually gets changed
docs.text:
ArgoRolloutsAborter (internal/actuation) does exactly one thing: a merge patch setting status.abort: true on the Rollout object named after the deploy event's app, in the deploy event's namespace — the same field kubectl argo rollouts abort sets, which causes Argo Rollouts' own controller to stop the canary in place. It does not:

  • Delete, scale, or otherwise mutate anything else about the Rollout.
  • Roll back to a previous revision (that's kubectl argo rollouts undo, a separate, bigger decision left to whoever operates the Rollout).
  • Touch any other Kubernetes object.

The outcome is recorded on the PerformanceRegression's status — autoAbortTriggered (an attempt was made) and, if it failed, autoAbortError — so kubectl get performanceregressions and the Slack alert both show what happened, not just that a regression was detected.

docs.title: RBAC
docs.text:
Auto-abort needs the manager's ServiceAccount to reach Rollout objects, which is not part of this project's default RBAC (see Configuration Reference). Via the Helm chart, set:

manager:
  autoAbort:
    rbacEnabled: true

which grants exactly:

- apiGroups: ["argoproj.io"]
  resources: ["rollouts", "rollouts/status"]
  verbs: ["get", "patch"]

Leave this false (the default) on any cluster that doesn't use Argo Rollouts, or where no PostgresWatch sets spec.autoAbort.enabled — there's no reason to grant it otherwise. Outside Helm (e.g. config/rbac/role.yaml for a kustomize-based install), the equivalent rule is already present unconditionally; remove it if you don't need it.

If cmd/manager can't build a Kubernetes dynamic client at startup for any reason, it logs the failure and continues with auto-abort unavailable — every PostgresWatch.spec.autoAbort.enabled is treated as false regardless of what the CR says, and everything else (detection, alerting, the webhook/native-watch ingestion paths) is unaffected.

docs.title: Where this is heading
docs.text:
The attribution engine can now drive the same pause and abort itself: with spec.attribution.actuate.enabled, the engine decides and this page's p-value trigger stands down for that watch (see Letting the manager act). Pausing patches the Rollout's spec, so it needs patch on rollouts as well as on rollouts/status, which the RBAC above already grants.

Auto-abort acts on a confidence score from the detector, which says a query changed near the deploy, not that the deploy caused it. The attribution engine is the groundwork for acting on stronger evidence: it grades each finding by how good its control is and only calls for a rollback at grade A (a concurrent control arm). It does not change what auto-abort does: in enforce mode it serves a verdict that an Argo Rollouts analysis acts on, pausing at grade B and aborting at grade A, and the manager itself writes nothing to the Rollout.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Attribution engine — the evidence grades a future rollback decision would be keyed on.
  • Deploy Sources & Webhooks — the sourceType: argo-rollouts DeploySource that must be feeding the target PostgresWatch for auto-abort to ever have anything to act on.
  • Detection Algorithm — how confidenceScore/pValueThreshold are computed.
  • Configuration Reference — the full PostgresWatch spec field table.

docs.title: Backporting
docs.text: How a merged fix gets applied to older, still-maintained tool versions — the backport <branch> label, release-X.Y maintenance branches, and what happens when a cherry-pick conflicts.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Backporting is how a fix that lands on main also reaches a tool version that's already shipped and still supported — the maintainer decides which versions a merged pull request should affect, by applying one backport release-X.Y label per affected line. Everything from there — cherry-picking the change, opening a pull request per target branch, and recovering when a cherry-pick doesn't apply cleanly — is automated by korthout/backport-action (.github/workflows/backport.yml), not hand-rolled scripting. This page covers the full lifecycle: how a release-X.Y branch comes to exist, the label convention, what a conflict looks like and how to resolve it, and how a maintenance branch cuts its own patch releases afterwards.

docs.title: How to backport a merged pull request
docs.text:
Apply a backport release-X.Y label to the pull request — before or after it merges. One label per tool version line the fix should also reach, e.g. both backport release-1.5 and backport release-1.6 to backport to two supported lines from the same PR. Once the PR is merged, backport.yml takes over automatically:

  1. It confirms every backport <branch> label actually names an existing release-X.Y maintenance branch — a typo, or a label naming a line that's never had a branch created, fails loudly with a comment on the original PR rather than silently doing nothing or cherry-picking to the wrong place.
  2. For each valid target, it cherry-picks the pull request's squash-merge commit (see CONTRIBUTING.md: Squash merge only — there's always exactly one commit to pick) onto a new branch off release-X.Y, using -x so the resulting commit records which original commit it came from.
  3. It opens a pull request per target branch, titled [Backport release-X.Y] <original title>, labeled backport, with the original author added as an assignee.
  4. It comments back on the original pull request with the result.

Only a maintainer applies these labels — a contributor can request a backport in the PR description, but deciding which shipped versions are affected (and therefore need the fix) is a judgment call, not something to automate from the PR's own content.

docs.title: Maintenance branches: release-X.Y
docs.text:
A release-X.Y branch (e.g. release-1.6) is the only valid backport target, and is the branch that line's own patch releases (v1.6.1, v1.6.2, ...) get cut from afterwards — main keeps moving forward (v1.7.0, v2.0.0, ...) and never looks at that branch again.

These branches aren't created or maintained by hand. .github/workflows/release-branches.yml watches the exact same push: tags: v* event release.yml does (see below for why that doesn't put release.yml itself at any risk) and, whenever the pushed tag is the first release of a minor/major line (patch 0, e.g. v1.6.0, not v1.6.1), it:

  • creates release-X.Y pointed at that tag's commit, if it doesn't already exist, and
  • creates the matching backport release-X.Y label, if it doesn't already exist.

A patch tag (v1.6.1) does nothing here — its release-1.6 branch is assumed to already exist from when v1.6.0 shipped. A pre-release tag (v2.0.0-rc1, same convention docs.yml uses to decide what becomes the latest docs alias) never gets a maintenance branch either — only a real vX.Y.0 does.

In practice, this means every minor/major line this project has ever shipped becomes backport-eligible automatically the moment it ships, with zero manual setup — the label simply doesn't exist yet for a line nobody has asked to maintain further, and starts existing the instant someone does.

docs.title: Resolving a backport conflict
docs.text:
Not every cherry-pick applies cleanly — a maintenance branch can diverge from main in ways that create a real textual conflict. backport.yml sets experimental.conflict_resolution: draft_commit_conflicts (rather than the action's default, which is just to fail), so a conflict never dead-ends as a failed Actions run with nothing to act on:

  1. The action commits the conflict as-is (conflict markers included) and opens a draft pull request against the target release-X.Y branch.
  2. It comments on the original pull request with a link to that draft and instructions to continue.
  3. To resolve it:
git fetch origin <the backport branch the action pushed>
git checkout <that branch>
# resolve the conflict markers in the affected file(s)
git add <resolved files>
git commit  # no --amend - the conflicted commit stays as the audit trail of what was attempted
git push
  1. Once the branch builds and passes CI (see CI on backport pull requests below), mark the draft ready for review and merge it like any other pull request.

Auto-merge is never enabled on a draft created this way (GitHub doesn't allow auto-merge on drafts), so a conflicting backport always gets a human's eyes before it merges, by construction. Once the draft (or any backport PR) is merged or closed, branch-cleanup.yml deletes its branch automatically — see CI/CD: branch-cleanup.yml.

docs.title: Cutting a patch release from a maintenance branch
docs.text:
Once one or more backport pull requests merge into release-X.Y, that branch accumulates pending changelog.d/ fragments exactly like main does — each backported commit carries its original fragment file along with it (the cherry-pick reapplies that file's addition, unchanged). release-prep.yml now also runs on release-X.Y branches (not just main), and opens a ci: prepare release vX.Y.(Z+1) pull request the same way it does for main, with one important difference: the next version it computes is relative to that branch's own tag history (git describe, not a repo-wide "highest tag" search), so release-1.6 always proposes v1.6.(Z+1) regardless of how far main has moved on. It also refuses to compute a version at all if that branch's name and its own latest reachable tag ever disagree (e.g. release-1.6 whose history doesn't actually contain a v1.6.x tag) — a configuration problem on a maintenance branch should fail loudly, not quietly produce a wrong version.

From there, releasing a patch version works exactly like releasing from main: review and merge the release-prep PR, then

git checkout release-1.6
git pull
git tag v1.6.1
git push origin v1.6.1

docs.title: The release job is unaffected
docs.text: Pushing v1.6.1 from release-1.6 triggers release.yml exactly the same way pushing v1.7.0 from main does — release.yml's trigger (push: tags: v*) and every one of its jobs (images, manifests, helm-chart, release-notes) already only cares about the pushed tag and the commit it points at, never which branch it was pushed from. Nothing in this feature touches release.yml's own file or job graph at all: release-branches.yml and the release-prep.yml/ci.yml/go-quality.yml/pr-title.yml changes described on this page are each independent workflow files or additive trigger scopes, with no needs:/shared-job relationship to release.yml. See CI/CD for the full breakdown of what that workflow does.

docs.title: CI on backport pull requests
docs.text:
A backport pull request goes through the same quality bar as any other, with two deliberate exceptions:

Check Runs on backport PRs? Why ci.yml (build/test/integration), go-quality.yml (lint/fmt/vuln) Yes A cherry-pick that applies cleanly textually can still fail to build or pass tests against a branch that has otherwise diverged — these need to gate a merge into release-X.Y exactly as they would into main. pr-title.yml (Conventional Commits title) No The backport PR's title is machine-generated ([Backport release-X.Y] <original title>), which isn't itself a Conventional Commits type — and the original title already passed this check once, on main, before it was ever eligible to be backported. changelog-fragment-check.yml (news fragment required) No The fragment was already validated on the original PR and travels with the cherry-picked commit unchanged — requiring a second one here would be redundant, and would break on the same title-prefix mismatch as pr-title.yml. dco.yml (sign-off) No (scoped to main only, unchanged) The original commit was already signed off; this workflow's scope wasn't widened for backporting.

If resolving a conflict substantially changes the fix for that specific version (not just a mechanical conflict-marker resolution), nothing stops a reviewer from manually adding or adjusting a changelog.d/ fragment on the backport PR — it just isn't enforced by CI the way it is on main, since that's a judgment call about how different the backported fix really is.

docs.title: Safety and governance notes
docs.text:
A few things were deliberately built in rather than left to convention:

  • One source of truth for targets. backport.yml's validate-targets job is the only place target branches are computed from labels — it disables the backport-action's own independent label_pattern matching (label_pattern: "") and passes its already-validated list via target_branches instead, so there's no second mechanism that could ever disagree with the first.
  • Existence is checked, not assumed. A backport <branch> label that doesn't resolve to a real branch fails the run with a comment explaining exactly which label is wrong, instead of the backport-action failing deeper into its own run with a less actionable git-level error.
  • Maintenance branches only ever bump their own patch version. release-prep.yml's version-bump logic takes a different path on a release-X.Y ref than on main: it always increments the patch number there, even if a stray *.feat.md fragment somehow ended up on that branch, because a maintenance line's entire purpose is patch releases.
  • Concurrency is scoped correctly in both new workflows. backport.yml groups by the originating PR number (so re-triggers for the same PR queue instead of racing); release-prep.yml now groups by github.ref_name (so a release-1.6 prep PR and a main prep PR never share — or silently clobber — the same branch/PR).
  • Disposable branches never linger, and long-lived ones are never touched by the same mechanism. branch-cleanup.yml deletes every PR's head branch on close (merged or not) — including the per-target branches backport.yml creates and release-prep.yml's reused release-prep-<ref> branch — but is hard-coded to never delete main or any release-X.Y branch, even in the (unusual) case one of those is ever a PR's head rather than its usual role as a base.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• CI/CD — every workflow referenced on this page, including backport.yml and release-branches.yml's own entries.
  • Branch Protection — whether release-X.Y branches should carry the same required checks as main.
  • Contributing Guide — the contributor-facing summary of this page.

docs.title: Branch Protection
docs.text: The GitHub repository setting (not a file in this repo) that decides whether the CI checks in CI/CD actually block anything.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Nothing in this repository can enforce this — it's a GitHub setting only a repo admin can change — which is exactly why it's easy to add a CI check and forget that it isn't actually required anywhere. Without a ruleset or branch protection rule requiring each check by name, every check in CI/CD (build/test, real-Postgres integration, real-envtest, golangci-lint, gofmt, PR title, DCO) is purely informational: it can fail and a merge can still happen anyway.

GitHub's admin bypass permission is a separate setting from whether a check is required — an admin can have bypass and the checks can still be wired up as required, so they run and show pass/fail on every push and PR. The two aren't in tension; this page only covers the required-checks side.

docs.title: Where to configure it
docs.text:
GitHub has two mechanisms; use whichever this repo already has active. A push rejected (or, for an admin with bypass, accepted with a Bypassed rule violations for refs/heads/main message) mentioning "rule violations" specifically means a ruleset is active, not classic branch protection:

  • Rulesets (current): Settings → Rules → Rulesets → edit (or create) the ruleset targeting main.
  • Classic branch protection: Settings → Branches → Branch protection rules → edit (or add) a rule for main.

docs.title: Required status checks to add
docs.text:
These are the exact check names as they appear in the Checks tab (each is a job's name: field in the corresponding workflow file — see that file if a name ever needs to be cross-checked after an edit):
