Check name Workflow Runs on Build & Test .github/workflows/ci.yml push + PR to main Integration tests (real PostgreSQL): postgres:16 .github/workflows/ci.yml push + PR to main Integration tests (real PostgreSQL): postgres:17 .github/workflows/ci.yml push + PR to main Integration tests (real PostgreSQL): postgres:18 .github/workflows/ci.yml push + PR to main Controller tests (real kube-apiserver) .github/workflows/ci.yml push + PR to main golangci-lint .github/workflows/go-quality.yml push + PR to main gofmt .github/workflows/go-quality.yml push + PR to main Enforce Conventional Commits title .github/workflows/pr-title.yml PR to main Check sign-off (DCO) .github/workflows/dco.yml PR to main

Integration tests (real PostgreSQL) is now a postgres-version: [16, 17, 18] matrix (see Support Matrix), so it shows up as three separate checks above instead of one — require all three, not just one, or a regression against 17/18 only could still merge.

Integration tests (EDB Postgres): EDB Postgres Advanced Server (EPAS) / ... Extended Server (PGE) (also in ci.yml) are deliberately not in this list: that job is entirely skipped unless the EDB_SUBSCRIPTION_TOKEN repository secret is configured (see Support Matrix) and runs with continue-on-error: true even when it does run, so making it a required check would either block every fork PR (secret never present there) or silently pass on real failures — neither is what "required" should mean.

Manual E2E (real container) (e2e-manual.yml) is deliberately not in this list — it's workflow_dispatch-only, so it never runs against a PR and can't be a required check.

docs.title: Extending protection to release-X.Y branches
docs.text: Every release-X.Y maintenance branch (created automatically by release-branches.yml — see Backporting) is a real target branch for backport pull requests, so the same Build & Test / integration / golangci-lint / gofmt checks above apply there too, via ci.yml/go-quality.yml's release-* branch filter (see CI/CD). Whichever mechanism this repo uses (ruleset or classic branch protection), target it at release-* as a second rule/pattern alongside main's, requiring the same five rows from the table above — Enforce Conventional Commits title and Check sign-off (DCO) are the two exceptions, since those two checks are deliberately not extended to backport PRs (see Backporting: CI on backport pull requests for why) and so cannot be required there without blocking every backport PR from ever becoming mergeable.

docs.title: Other settings worth enabling alongside the checks
docs.text:
• Require a pull request before merging — confirm it's on and scoped to main.
  • Require branches to be up to date before merging — otherwise a status check can pass against a stale base and still land a broken merge.
  • Keep bypass scoped to repo admins only (not "everyone", not a public team) — bypass shouldn't be wider than "people who genuinely need to override CI".
  • Do not allow force pushes / Do not allow deletions — protects the commit history CI has already validated.
  • Require approvals — GitHub doesn't count a self-review as an approval, so this only makes sense once there's more than one maintainer or regular external contributors; turn it on (1 approval) at that point, per CONTRIBUTING.md's squash-merge policy.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• CI/CD — every check referenced in the table above.
  • Backporting — how release-X.Y branches come to exist and why two checks are deliberately excluded from them.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
All notable changes to this project are documented in this file. The format loosely follows Keep a Changelog; the category names are this project's own (matching the type/scope table in CONTRIBUTING.md) rather than Keep a Changelog's stricter Added/Changed/Fixed vocabulary, since a flat categorization loses the thematic grouping that makes these notes readable.

How this file is maintained: every PR that ships a user-facing feat, fix, or perf change adds its own newsfragment under changelog.d/ (format documented in CONTRIBUTING.md, enforced by .github/workflows/changelog-fragment-check.yml). Before cutting a release tag, the maintainer runs towncrier build --version vX.Y.Z --yes, which compiles every fragment currently in changelog.d/ into a new dated section here and deletes the consumed fragments — .github/workflows/release.yml's release-notes job then extracts that section verbatim as the GitHub Release body. See towncrier.toml for the category configuration.

Scope note on v1.0.0-rc1 below: that section was a one-time historical backfill — generated with git-cliff from git log v0.1.0..main (47 commits) and hand-reorganized into the thematic sections below — covering everything that shipped before the newsfragment process above existed. Since it predates any real changelog.d/ fragments, it was hand-labeled with this release's version rather than produced by towncrier build (there was nothing for that command to consume yet). git-cliff and cliff.toml are retired and not part of the ongoing process; every future entry in this file comes from changelog.d/ fragments via towncrier build as described above.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text:
• Fixed deploys being accepted and then never judged after the PostgresWatch they feed was edited: a DeploySource route now finds the watch's current event store on every request, and answers 503 with Retry-After while the watch is not running, so senders retry instead of losing the event. (#262)
  • The dashboard no longer leaves cells of its sheet open: a column that ends above its neighbour now gets its edges drawn like any panel, the Case board fills its left column with the activity feed, and a panel that scrolls inside its cell fades out at the edge where more content continues instead of cutting a row in half. (#264)
  • The check the engine makes 15 minutes after an abort now reads only what came after the abort, not the whole deploy window. Before, the slow stretch the canary ran before it was stopped still counted, so a correct abort was recorded as persisted and two of them opened the circuit breaker, leaving the engine alerting only until the manager restarted. (#265)

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Added attribution.mode and a read-only verdict endpoint (--attribution-verdict-addr) that an Argo Rollouts analysis can poll: inconclusive pauses a rollout on grade B evidence and fail aborts it on grade A, with shadow remaining the default. (#247.attribution-verdict)
  • Added an opt-in counterfactual attribution engine that judges each tracked deploy against a control built from queries the deploy did not touch, and records the action it would take (alert, hold or roll back) in shadow mode without executing it. (#246)
  • Added attribution.revert: in enforce mode the radar can open a draft pull request that reverts the commit behind a convicted deploy, once per deploy and never merged, with the evidence and a pre-merge checklist in its body. (#248)
  • The attribution engine can now act on its own decisions: with attribution.actuate enabled in enforce mode, the manager pauses the Argo Rollouts rollout of a held deploy and aborts the rollout of a rolled-back one, instead of waiting for a rollout controller to ask for a verdict. (#253)
  • The attribution engine now records every pause and abort it makes in an action ledger at /api/v1/attribution/actions, checks 15 minutes after an abort whether the regression went away and feeds that to its circuit breaker, and lets you bound actuation with actuate.namespaces or stop it at once with the pg-regression-radar.io/actuation-paused annotation. (#254)
  • The attribution engine can now tell a canary from the stable pods by reading the Postgres JSON log (attribution.arms, with the log settings checked and the comparison weighted for sampling), so it can reach grade A and abort a bad canary; it needs no extension on the server. (#259)
  • Added pg-regression-radar dashboard, a local web page, read-only toward the cluster, that shows what the radar saw, decided and did. It has editable boards, a per-panel view with settings and a filter query, and keeps your edits between runs in its own data directory. (#260)

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text:
• Queries executed by multiple roles or databases now keep independent counters before their intervals are combined. Partial row changes no longer create misleading latency samples, and saved intervals retain their reset and validity state after a restart. (#241)
  • The attribution engine no longer treats other queries moving the opposite way as a shared cause, so a regression that makes the rest of the workload faster (a slow query throttling it) can reach grade B and be paused instead of staying at an alert. (#256)
  • The attribution engine now says what holds its evidence at grade C (for example global-shift or few-donors) in the decision's reasons, the log line for an enforce-mode decision that is not acting is no longer labelled shadow, and a pause or abort that was skipped or failed no longer waits out the 10-minute cooldown before the next attempt. (#257)

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Added OpenTelemetry as a pluggable analysis input: OTLP/HTTP trace spans can now be turned into deploy events with the new otlp source type, every detected regression can be exported as an OTLP log record, and the Prometheus sample source gained bearer-token auth, failure metrics and a validated worked Collector pipeline. (#182)
  • Separated the two data floors that --min-executions used to blur: the new --min-samples (default 10) counts latency observations per window, while --min-executions now counts real executions (default 100, was 10 samples), so rarely-called queries report InsufficientData until enough calls back the verdict. (#210)
  • Detected regressions now expose the raw Welch's t-test pValue in the PerformanceRegression status (and a P-Value kubectl column), the dashboard API, alerts and OTLP export; confidenceScore stays as 1 - pValue and is documented as a significance score, not the probability that the regression is real. (#211)
  • Added a browser playground to the docs that runs the real detection engine, compiled to WebAssembly, against a real PostgreSQL with pg_stat_statements (PGlite): pick a scenario or write your own schema, workload and deploy, and see which queries are flagged, with no Postgres or Kubernetes to install. (#212)
  • Added opt-in false-discovery-rate control across queries (--multiple-testing=bh|by) and an autocorrelation adjustment for Welch's t-test (--adjust-autocorrelation), as operator flags and PostgresWatch fields, so a pass over hundreds of noisy queries reports fewer chance detections; both are off by default and change nothing until enabled. (#219)
  • Added a five-minute lab (examples/lab, documented on the "Try it in five minutes" page): three kubectl apply commands start a throwaway Postgres, a demo app and the radar in any Kubernetes cluster, ship a deploy whose migration drops an index, and show the radar detecting it, naming the deploy and reporting the Index Scan -> Seq Scan plan change. It needs no database, ArgoCD, Slack or Helm of your own. (#229)

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text:
• Fixed regressions being hidden by the cumulative average: the collector now measures each query from the change in calls and total time between scrapes, and recognises counter resets (including stats_since on PostgreSQL 17+) so they no longer look like latency changes. (#209)
  • Fixed the plan-diff summary on a detected regression, which with the default --min-samples almost never had a "before" plan and could read "root node type unchanged" after an index drop. The plan history now records one entry per distinct plan instead of one per scrape, so the plan from before the change is still there when detection fires. (#228)

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Added GET /api/v1/queries/{queryId}/samples for per-query sample history, enabled CORS on every dashboard API route, and changed queryId to a JSON string across the API so large pg_stat_statements ids no longer get silently rounded by JavaScript clients. (#162)
  • Added internal/telemetry/promsource, an opt-in correlation.SampleSource backed by PromQL queries against a Prometheus HTTP API, for fleets that already run an OpenTelemetry Collector and would rather not run a second pg_stat_statements scraper against the same database. Not yet wired into cmd/manager; that's a follow-up PR. (#163)
  • Wired internal/telemetry/promsource into the CRD-driven cmd/manager path: PostgresWatch.spec.sampleSource.type: prometheus now selects it as an opt-in alternative to internal/collector.Collector, skipping dsn/dsnSecretRef entirely and rejecting capturePlans: true (which needs a direct database connection this mode doesn't have) with a clear error instead of ignoring it. (#164)
  • Completed multi-cluster (fleet) support: a new reconciler proactively health-checks every registered cluster's kubeconfig, PostgresWatch.spec.cnpgClusterRef validates a remote CloudNativePG Cluster before a watch starts, and both are wired into the Helm chart and a new real two-kind-cluster end-to-end CI workflow. (#174)
  • Added a backport release-X.Y pull request label: a maintainer can say exactly which supported tool versions a merged fix should also reach, and the fix is automatically cherry-picked onto each release-X.Y maintenance branch (opening a draft pull request for manual resolution on a conflict). Every pull request's branch is also now deleted automatically once it closes. (#176)

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text:
• Fixed a self-feedback loop where the collector's own EXPLAIN plan-capture queries were recorded as new pg_stat_statements entries, which could grow into repeated capture failures or a false-positive regression of their own; these ghost entries are now excluded from both sampling and plan capture, with a new metric tracking how often it happens. (#161)
  • Fixed PostgreSQL collection for unprivileged roles by skipping statistics rows with hidden query IDs, allowing their own queries to be scraped in single-cluster and remote fleet deployments. (#175)

docs.title: Features
docs.text: • Added a read-only dashboard HTTP API (GET /api/v1/regressions, /deploys, /queries, /watches), enabled with the new --dashboard-addr flag on the operator and manager, so the observability dashboard can read regression, deploy, query-sample, and watch data without inventing any metric the correlation engine doesn't already compute. (#159)

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Alerting destinations can now be governed by a configurable destinationPolicy. Three modes are available:

  • permissive (default): unchanged behaviour — any URL that passes the built-in SSRF blocklist is accepted. Fully backward-compatible.

  • allowlist: the webhook URL's host must appear in --alerting-allowed-destinations. Reconciliation fails fast with a clear error when the host is outside the list. Intended for multi-tenant clusters where only a pre-approved set of receivers should be reachable.
  • relay-only: per-watch spec.alerting.url is ignored entirely; all alerts are forwarded to the fixed relay endpoint in --alerting-destination-policy-relay-url. The manager and operator both fail at startup if the relay URL is missing, surfacing misconfiguration before any watch is reconciled.

The policy is configured via two new flags shared by both the manager and the standalone operator:

--alerting-destination-policy=<permissive|allowlist|relay-only>
--alerting-destination-policy-relay-url=<url>          # required for relay-only

PostgresWatch.spec.alerting.destinationPolicy mirrors these values at the per-watch level and is honoured when no manager-level policy is set.

See Alerting: destination policies and Security model for configuration examples and deployment guidance.

(#136) - Introduces the PostgresRadarCluster CRD so administrators can pre-register remote clusters; PostgresWatch now references them by name via spec.remoteClusterRef, eliminating the confused-deputy risk of direct kubeconfig Secret access. (#138) - Operators can now cryptographically verify every released artifact. All five container images and the Helm OCI chart are signed with Cosign keyless signing; each image carries an attached SPDX SBOM attestation. A new docs/supply-chain.md page documents the trust model and step-by-step cosign verify commands. A companion scripts/verify-release.sh automates the checks. (#139) - Completed the final security-roadmap deployment gaps by adding Helm controls for alerting destination policies and ServiceAccount token automount, plus release provenance attestations for published images and the Helm OCI chart. (#141)

docs.title: Features
docs.text: • Added a sample Kyverno ClusterPolicy for restricting who can apply the pg-regression-radar.io/allow-postgreswatch-access consent label, and documented it as a recommended hardening control for multi-tenant clusters. (#122)

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text:
• Replaced bare http.ListenAndServe in the collector metrics server with a timeout-aware *http.Server (setting ReadHeaderTimeout, ReadTimeout, WriteTimeout, and IdleTimeout) and added graceful shutdown on context cancellation, resolving gosec G114 / CWE-676. Also added the same timeout fields to httpRunnable in the operator manager, resolving the companion G112 / CWE-400 finding. (#108)
  • CaptureGenericPlan and CapturePlan now accept a NormalizedQueryText value instead of a bare string, enforcing at compile time that only text originating from pg_stat_statements reaches the EXPLAIN statement. This closes the SQL-injection path (CWE-089 / CodeQL go/sql-injection alert #3) reported against internal/planner/genericplan.go. (#109)
  • The Helm chart Secret template now includes the pg-regression-radar.io/allow-postgreswatch-access: "true" consent label, fixing out-of-the-box breakage where the controller rejected the chart-created Secret on every reconciliation loop. (#110)
  • Added the pg-regression-radar.io/allow-postgreswatch-access: "true" consent label to the Helm chart's Secret template so a default mode: manager install works without manual post-install patching. (#115)
  • Added an opt-in alerting destination allowlist for operator and manager mode, and clarified that the built-in webhook URL validation is only a best-effort SSRF mitigation that should be paired with stricter network or admission controls in multi-tenant clusters. (#119)
  • BuildNotifier now treats an empty webhook URL as alerting disabled, returning a no-op notifier and rejecting empty URLs during direct webhook validation. (#125)

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text:
• PostgresWatch now requires Secrets referenced by dsnSecretRef or remoteClusterSecretRef to carry an explicit consent label before the manager will read them, closing a confused-deputy path. Remote kubeconfigs using exec-based or auth-provider credential plugins, or setting proxy-url, are now rejected outright instead of being trusted. (#94)
  • Alert webhook URLs are now validated against SSRF-prone destinations, deploy-event HTTP servers enforce request-size and timeout limits, the standalone ingester can gate /events behind the same webhook secret, the Helm chart runs pods with hardened non-root security defaults, and the Kubernetes-native watcher no longer drops events when multiple DeploySources target the same workload. (#96)

docs.title: Features
docs.text: • Added Prometheus counters for detected regressions and webhook notification successes or failures, so operators can alert on broken delivery paths and chart alerting reliability from /metrics. (#87)

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text:
• Webhook notifications now drain response bodies before closing them so Go can reuse keep-alive HTTP connections between alerts. (#89)
  • Malformed PostgreSQL DSNs that look like redacted or broken connection URIs are now rejected at operator startup with a clear parse error instead of silently falling back to localhost until scrape time. (#90)
  • Collector scrapes now cap pg_stat_statements query text at the configured --max-query-text-len budget instead of always asking PostgreSQL for up to 500 characters per row. (#91)
  • Manager startup failures that prevent controller informers from reaching the Kubernetes API now best-effort mark existing PostgresWatch and DeploySource resources with a non-empty degraded status instead of leaving them blank. (#92)
  • Periodic regressions now carry the configured namespace, so alerts, queries, and Kubernetes resources stay scoped to the same namespace as the PostgresWatch or operator configuration. (#93)

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Alerting now supports more than Slack: --alert-format/spec.alerting.format selects between slack (default, unchanged), teams (Microsoft Teams Incoming Webhook), pagerduty (Events API v2, opens/updates an incident), or custom (a user-supplied Go text/template, for any destination that isn't one of the built-in three). slackWebhookUrl/--slack-url keep working exactly as before. See Alerting for the full field/flag reference and the custom template's available fields. (#71)
  • Regression detection no longer requires a tracked deploy. --periodic-detection/spec.periodicDetection.enabled runs the same E-divisive/Welch's-t-test analysis on a rolling schedule, per query, independent of any DeployEvent — catching regressions with no deploy behind them (autovacuum lag, index bloat, stale planner stats, organic growth) that were previously invisible to this tool. A re-arm state machine suppresses repeat alerts for an ongoing episode until the query recovers. Deploy-triggered detection is unaffected either way; the two paths run side by side. See Periodic Detection for configuration and the false-positive caveat, and ADR-0001 for the design rationale. (#73)

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Make deploy-event retry analysis observable: the operator and manager now log when a deploy event is registered for retry and when its analysis window elapses, and expose a pg_regression_radar_pending_deploy_events gauge, so an operator can tell "still waiting for data" apart from a silent failure and confirm memory stays bounded over long uptimes. (#65)
  • Add a native Kubernetes watch deploy source: setting sourceType: kubernetes on a DeploySource CR watches a Deployment or StatefulSet directly and emits a deploy event once its rollout completes, so clusters with no ArgoCD, Argo Rollouts, or Flux installed can still be correlated against — no webhook required. (#66)
  • Add opt-in Argo Rollouts auto-abort: setting autoAbort.enabled on a PostgresWatch now aborts the Argo Rollouts canary behind a sufficiently confident detected regression automatically, instead of only alerting and waiting for a human to act, with its own confidence threshold and RBAC gate, and the outcome recorded on the resulting PerformanceRegression. (#67)

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text: • Fix regression detection silently missing real regressions: both operator and manager used to analyse a deploy event exactly once, immediately on arrival, well before enough post-deploy data could exist — now analysis retries every poll tick until the deploy's analysis window closes, deduplicating notifications so a detected regression is still only ever reported once. (#64)

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text: • Add a separate docker/login-action step to the release workflow's Helm chart job, so cosign can find registry credentials it needs to sign the chart — helm registry login alone writes to a config file cosign never reads, which made the chart-signing step fail with an authentication error on every release. (#60)

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Add spec.capturePlans to PostgresWatch, so the CRD-driven manager mode can attach a plan-diff summary to a detected PerformanceRegression's status.planDiffSummary, matching the standalone operator CLI's existing --capture-plans behavior. (#51)
  • Add spec.remoteNamespace to PostgresWatch, letting a fleet's remote-cluster DSN Secret live in a differently-named namespace than the hub-side PostgresWatch, instead of requiring matching namespace names on both sides. (#58)
  • Fleet mode now evicts a remote cluster's cached client immediately after it fails a real request, so a transient network blip or a genuinely rotated kubeconfig no longer keeps a broken connection in circulation until a future reconcile happens to notice. (#59)

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text: • Evict entries from the manager's remote-cluster client cache after an hour of disuse, so a rotated-away kubeconfig or a deleted fleet member's cached client no longer stays in memory for the life of the manager process. (#52)

docs.title: Detection & Correlation
docs.text:
• Deduplicate PerformanceRegression findings across a queryid rotation, which previously produced one duplicate finding per rotated queryid for what was really a single ongoing regression (fix(correlation), 4c62488).
  • Add EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON, GENERIC_PLAN)-based plan-diff correlation (PostgreSQL 16+): captures and diffs a query's execution plan around a detected regression, an estimate-based fallback source (feat, PR #31, 84dc8e8).
  • Add pg_store_plans as the preferred plan-diff capture source over the GENERIC_PLAN estimate above, when the extension is installed — it records the real, previously-executed plan with real parameter values instead of the planner's generic estimate (feat(planner), b611f50).
  • Backfill cmd/manager's in-memory Collector/Engine state from the Postgres persistence backend on restart, so a manager restart no longer silently resets detection state to empty — landed iteratively across two commits plus the merges that reconciled the feature branch with main mid-flight (feat(operator), 14c3574 and 5007b66; merge commits eaca170, a1b5340).

docs.title: Multi-cluster (Fleet)
docs.text: • Add spec.remoteClusterSecretRef support: PostgresWatchReconciler can now resolve a PostgresWatch's DSN Secret from a different Kubernetes cluster than the manager itself, via a kubeconfig Secret in the hub cluster — closing the gap where the only prior option was manually copying the Secret between clusters (feat(controller), bc0ab5f).

docs.title: Security
docs.text: • Add X-Webhook-Token bearer-token authentication to the ingester's webhook endpoint, closing the gap where any network path to the ingester could post a deploy-event webhook with no authentication at all (fix(ingester), faf94e4).

docs.title: Performance & Scalability
docs.text:
• Replace the O(n³) inner loops of the E-Divisive change-point algorithm with an O(n²) formulation (perf, 627d5cb).
  • Replace Store.All()-based O(N) poll loops with a cursor-based Store.Since() across the collector/ingester poll path (perf, PR #27, 9a80538).
  • Cursor-based poll draining and binary-search EventsInRange in the ingester, replacing a linear scan (perf, 6dd4659).
  • Replace an O(N×M) latestSampleTime computation with an O(1) Collector.LastScrapeTime() (perf, 0b27f86).
  • Halve Engine.Analyse's SamplesInRange lock acquisitions (fix(correlation), af9d21e).
  • Pre-allocate slices in ingester.Store and the in-memory stores to reduce GC pressure under load (perf, 0226995).

docs.title: CLI & Developer Experience
docs.text:
• Add a unified pg-regression-radar CLI so go install sets up all subcommands from a single binary instead of four separate go install targets (feat(cli), 6cac0e9).
  • Add --version and --dry-run flags to all four binaries (feat(cli), d973795).

docs.title: CI/CD & Quality
docs.text:
• Add a real kind + CloudNativePG cluster e2e validation for cmd/manager (.github/workflows/e2e-kind.yml): a real cluster, a real CloudNativePG operator and Cluster, the Helm chart, and a PostgresWatch reading its DSN from the CloudNativePG-generated Secret (ci(e2e), PR #37, 66261fb).
  • Document and enforce a PostgreSQL 16/17/18 + EDB Postgres Advanced/Extended Server support matrix in CI, including a matrixed integration-test job (docs(support-matrix), ae93e47).
  • Expand e2e coverage for recently-landed features against a real PostgreSQL instance — landed iteratively across two commits (test(e2e), 30b63fe and PR #42, 2e57051).
  • Use structurally distinct probe queries in e2e tests so pg_stat_statements can't merge them into one queryid (fix(e2e), PR #29, a6e82a4).
  • Resolve golangci-lint findings and pin a patched Go toolchain version in CI (fix(ci), PR #28, 2c50107).

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
• Add a structured docs/ site built with MkDocs Material, slim down README.md to a quick-start pointer at it (docs, 4a22bbc), and follow-on styling/nav fixes: true black/white palette with backdrop blur (c673b27), transparent tabs bar (fffe907), thinner active-tab underline (c02fffe), an Installation page plus active-tab contrast fix (068eff5), collapsing overflowing nav tabs into a real hover mega-menu across four follow-up fixes (a4f86d5, fd60fe9, a5f1d79, c9454b1).
  • Move .github/BRANCH_PROTECTION.md's content into the docs site and delete the standalone file (docs(ci), e474939; housekeeping merge/delete 6175a0f, 05d4f40).
  • Document least-privilege PostgreSQL role guidance for --dsn (docs, 2dbc330).
  • Document the PostgresWatch/DeploySource/PerformanceRegression v1alpha1 CRD compatibility policy (docs(api), 5a4a744; review-nit follow-up dccabcd).
  • Fix the Flux Provider authentication example in the webhooks doc to use the headers field, matching the new webhook-token auth above (docs(webhooks), 1196f20).
  • Fix a typo (fix(doc), b749609 — originally committed as fiz(doc), a typo in the commit type itself).

docs.title: Dependencies & Chores
docs.text:
• Weekly Dependabot bumps to five github-actions dependencies: actions/setup-python 5→7 (5304ae3), actions/upload-pages-artifact 3→5 (73c5383), actions/deploy-pages 4→5 (bf75348), actions/upload-artifact 4→7 (e52fab1), actions/download-artifact 4→8 (9ea1bab).
  • Fix dependabot.yml formatting (fix, edcb2eb; merged back in via c1e8543).

MVP: Collector + Ingester + Correlation Engine + Slack alerting + Helm chart, plus Argo Rollouts/Flux deploy-source support and the real PostgresWatch/DeploySource/PerformanceRegression CRD-driven controller-runtime mode — see docs/roadmap.md for what's shipped since. Predates this file; not reconstructed here since git-cliff's useful range starts at this tag.

docs.title: CI/CD
docs.text: Every GitHub Actions workflow in this repo, what it checks, and when it runs.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
pg-regression-radar runs fifteen workflows plus Dependabot. This page is a map of what each one does; see Testing for how to reproduce the test-related ones locally, Branch Protection for how (and whether) they're actually enforced as required checks on main, Backporting for the two workflows (backport.yml, release-branches.yml) and the release-prep.yml changes that exist specifically to support shipping a fix to an already-released tool version, and branch-cleanup.yml below for how this repo keeps disposable branches (including the ones those two workflows create) from piling up.

Security scanning, end to end: this repo uses only tools that are free for a public repository, spread across the layer each is actually good at — no single tool covers all of these:

Layer Tool Where Blocking? Go source (semantic SAST) CodeQL codeql.yml No — code scanning alerts, by design (see below) Go source (pattern-based security linter) gosec go-quality.yml Not yet — first run, no baseline (see below) Go dependencies (known, reachable CVEs) govulncheck go-quality.yml Not yet — first run, no baseline (see below) Go dependencies (version currency) Dependabot dependabot.yml N/A — opens update PRs, doesn't gate CI Container base images (version currency) Dependabot (docker ecosystem) dependabot.yml N/A — opens update PRs, doesn't gate CI Built container images (known CVEs in OS packages/libraries) Trivy release.yml Yes — CRITICAL-severity finding fails the images job, nothing is pushed

CodeQL findings are never blocking by design — github/codeql-action/analyze only fails the workflow on a tool/build error, never on an actual finding; results surface as Security tab alerts instead, the same UX as Dependabot alerts. gosec and govulncheck, by contrast, can fail their own step (continue-on-error: true is what's currently absorbing that) — both are first-time additions to this repo with no established clean baseline yet, so they start in report-only mode. Once a run of each comes back clean (or any real findings are triaged and fixed/suppressed), removing continue-on-error: true from that job is the one-line change that makes it a real gate. Trivy in release.yml predates this and already gates for real, because it was added with a known-clean baseline from the start.

docs.title: ci.yml — on every push/PR to main or a release-* branch
docs.text:
Also runs against release-* branches (not just main) so a backport pull request gets the exact same build/test gate before merging into a maintenance line — see Backporting for the full rationale and which checks are not extended this way.

Job What it proves Build & Test go build ./..., go vet ./..., go test -race ./... against fakes/mocks — no external services. Integration tests (real PostgreSQL) A postgres-version: [16, 17, 18] matrix — runs the integration-tagged tests in internal/storage/postgres, internal/collector, and internal/e2e against a real postgres:16/postgres:17/postgres:18 container (one job per version) with pg_stat_statements preloaded. See Support Matrix for why 16 is the floor. Integration tests (EDB Postgres) Same integration test suite, run against EDB Postgres Advanced Server and EDB Postgres Extended Server images — but only when the EDB_SUBSCRIPTION_TOKEN repository secret is configured (those images live behind a private, authenticated registry), and with continue-on-error: true so an absent secret or a real failure here can't break CI for anyone else. See Support Matrix for the full rationale. Integration tests (real pg_store_plans extension) Builds a real PostgreSQL 17 server with the real, upstream pg_store_plans extension compiled via PGXS (scripts/pg_store_plans), and runs internal/planner's pg_store_plans-specific integration test against it — proving CapturePlanFromStorePlans reads back a real plan for a real, actually-executed query, not just a fake *sql.DB. Unlike the EDB job above, everything this pulls from is public and unauthenticated, so it runs unconditionally, with no continue-on-error. See Testing and Roadmap. Controller tests (real kube-apiserver) Runs internal/controller's TestEnvtest_* suite against a real, locally-provisioned kube-apiserver + etcd via controller-runtime's envtest.

Every go test-based job above (every row except Helm render tests, which is shell, not Go) runs its tests through gotestsum instead of plain go test, producing a real JUnit XML report alongside the usual console output. Each job uploads its report as a build artifact (junit-unit, junit-integration-postgres-16/17/18, junit-integration-edb-epas/pge, junit-integration-pg-store-plans, junit-envtest) with if: always(), so a report exists whether the job passes or fails. test-report.yml below turns these into GitHub Check Runs.

docs.title: test-report.yml — on ci.yml's completion
docs.text:
A separate workflow_run-triggered workflow that downloads every junit-* artifact ci.yml uploaded and feeds each one to dorny/test-reporter, producing one GitHub Check Run per job — a pass/fail/skipped count, a per-test-case listing, and inline annotations pointing at the exact test (and, where the stack trace allows it, the exact source line) that failed. This replaces the single opaque pass/fail tick a plain go test step leaves behind with the kind of structured, drill-down test report CI for a project like this should have.

It's a separate workflow (triggered by workflow_run, not a job appended to ci.yml) specifically so it always runs with this repository's own read-write GITHUB_TOKEN, even when the triggering ci.yml run came from a pull request opened from a fork. GitHub Actions always gives a pull_request-triggered workflow a read-only token on fork PRs — which can never create a Check Run regardless of the permissions: block — but a workflow_run workflow always executes against this repo's default branch with its own normal permissions, no matter whose fork triggered the run it's reporting on. This is dorny/test-reporter's own documented pattern for public repositories (see its README's "Recommended setup for public repositories" section).

One consequence: a PR that only changes this file won't see it react to its own ci.yml run until after it's merged — workflow_run always resolves the workflow definition from the base branch, never the PR branch.

docs.title: go-quality.yml — on every push/PR to main or a release-* branch
docs.text:
Also extended to release-* branches for the same reason as ci.yml above — a backport PR's lint/vuln/security gate shouldn't be weaker than a normal PR's.

Job What it proves golangci-lint Static analysis beyond go vet (pinned version v2.12.2, no repo-specific config — runs with the tool's default linter set, which does not include a security-focused linter; that's what gosec below is for). gofmt Every tracked .go file is gofmt-clean. govulncheck Whether any dependency in go.sum has a known vulnerability that's actually reachable from this code's own call graph (not just present in the dependency tree) — see the Security scanning table above for why it's report-only for now. gosec Pattern-based security static analysis (hardcoded credentials, weak crypto, SQL string concatenation, etc.) — see the Security scanning table above for why it's report-only for now. Findings are uploaded as SARIF to Security -> Code scanning regardless of outcome.

docs.title: pr-title.yml — on PR open/edit/sync, targeting main
docs.text: Validates the PR title against Conventional Commits using the exact types/scopes documented in CONTRIBUTING.md — the title becomes the squash-merge commit message on main, so it's enforced the same way a commit message would be. Scoped to pull requests targeting main only: a backport pull request's title ([Backport release-X.Y] <original title>, generated by backport.yml) isn't itself Conventional-Commits-shaped, and doesn't need to be — see Backporting.

docs.title: changelog-fragment-check.yml — on PR open/edit/sync
docs.text:
Enforces the "changeset"/news-fragment convention described in CONTRIBUTING.md: any PR whose title's Conventional Commits type is feat, fix, or perf must add exactly one file to changelog.d/ named <PR-number>.<type>.md, and that file's content must pass seven format rules (single paragraph, capitalized, ends in ./!/?, no heading, no code block, doesn't repeat the type prefix, 20-400 characters). PRs of any other type (docs, test, refactor, chore, ci) are exempt — they don't describe anything an end user would see in release notes.

Step What it does Determine PR type Parses the PR title with the same type vocabulary pr-title.yml's types: list uses (kept manually in sync — see the comment in both files). Gate Only feat/fix/perf require a fragment; anything else short-circuits with a no-op pass. Find the fragment Diffs the PR against its base ref for added files under changelog.d/, and fails with a specific message if none, more than one, or a wrongly-named file was added. Validate content Runs scripts/check_changelog_fragment.py <file> — a small stdlib-only Python script (no towncrier dependency needed for this part) that checks each of the seven content rules independently and fails with the exact rule number and a human-readable reason (e.g. [3-ends-with-punctuation]), plus a link back to CONTRIBUTING.md.

This is a separate workflow from pr-title.yml (rather than a job appended to it) because pr-title.yml runs on pull_request_target (needed so it can comment on forked PRs without leaking secrets), while this check only ever needs to read the PR's own diff and is safer as plain pull_request.

docs.title: codeql.yml — on push/PR to main, plus a weekly schedule
docs.text:
Semantic SAST for Go via GitHub's own CodeQL engine — see the Security scanning table above for how this fits alongside gosec/govulncheck/Trivy. Runs the security-and-quality query suite (CodeQL's default, not the broader security-extended suite — same "keep signal-to-noise high, no repo-specific config" preference as golangci-lint's default linter set). The weekly schedule (Mondays) catches new findings against unchanged code when CodeQL's own query packs are updated upstream, the same rationale as running Dependabot/govulncheck on a cadence rather than push-only.

Findings appear under Security -> Code scanning alerts, never as a failed check — see the Security scanning table above for why that's true of code scanning generically, not a severity threshold that could be tuned.

One-time manual note

If this repo ever enables "Default setup" for code scanning in Settings -> Code security, GitHub manages its own CodeQL workflow and this file becomes redundant with it — the two should not both run. No such setup exists yet, so codeql.yml is the only CodeQL workflow.

docs.title: dco.yml — on every PR to main
docs.text: Verifies every commit in the PR carries a Signed-off-by: trailer (DCO), via a hand-rolled git/grep check rather than a third-party Action — DCO enforcement is simple enough that pulling in an external dependency for it isn't worth the supply-chain surface.

docs.title: release-prep.yml — on push to main or a release-* branch touching changelog.d/
docs.text:
Automates the one manual step the changelog.d/ fragment system was always meant to make possible to automate: building CHANGELOG.md. On every push to main or any release-X.Y maintenance branch that touches changelog.d/ (and via workflow_dispatch on demand), it checks whether any real fragment is pending (anything besides changelog.d/README.md), and if so:

Step What it does Compute next version Runs git describe --tags --abbrev=0 --match 'v*' — relative to the current ref, not a repo-wide tag search — to find the latest version reachable from here, then bumps it: any pending *.feat.md fragment means a minor bump (patch resets to 0); fix/perf-only fragments mean a patch bump. Same convention as semantic-release/Conventional Commits — the highest-impact pending fragment type decides the bump. There's no major-bump case, since this repo's fragment vocabulary (towncrier.toml) has no "breaking" type yet. On a release-X.Y branch, this always resolves to a patch bump regardless of fragment type (a maintenance line only ever ships patches), and the workflow fails loudly if that branch's own name ever disagrees with the major.minor of the latest tag it can actually reach — a mismatch there means the branch is misconfigured, not something to silently paper over. Build CHANGELOG.md towncrier build --version vX.Y.Z --yes — the exact command the repo owner used to run by hand. Pin the lab Where scripts/build_lab.sh exists, regenerates examples/lab/00-radar.yaml with the manager image pinned to the version being prepared (LAB_IMAGE_TAG=vX.Y.Z), so the commit that gets tagged carries a lab manifest matching its own release. The image appears only after release.yml finishes, so the lab on that branch cannot pull it for a few minutes after the PR merges. Skipped on maintenance branches that predate the lab. Open or update a PR peter-evans/create-pull-request pushes the result to a reused release-prep-${{ github.ref_name }} branch (based off whichever ref triggered the run) and opens (or updates, if one's already open) a PR titled ci: prepare release vX.Y.Z, signed off as github-actions[bot] so dco.yml passes it.

If another feat/fix/perf PR merges while the release-prep PR is still open, the next run recomputes the version and content from scratch and updates the same PR — there is never more than one open at a time per ref (concurrency: group: release-prep-${{ github.ref_name }} also prevents two runs against the same branch from racing to push it, while letting main and every release-X.Y line prepare their own release independently of each other).

This automates building the changelog, not deciding when to release: a person still reviews the compiled CHANGELOG.md diff like any other PR, merges it, and only then tags — see CONTRIBUTING.md. Full auto-tagging (building the changelog and creating/pushing the vX.Y.Z tag with no review step) was deliberately not chosen: it would need CI to either force-push a moved tag or bypass this repo's own branch protection to push straight to main/release-X.Y, both of which trade away the review step for not much real benefit — the changelog-building half was the actual repetitive manual work, and this workflow already removes exactly that.

One-time manual prerequisite

Same shape as release.yml's GHCR note: Settings → Actions → General → Workflow permissions must allow "Read and write permissions", and "Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests" must be checked — without the latter, create-pull-request fails to open the PR even though this workflow's own permissions: block is otherwise sufficient.

See Backporting for the full walkthrough of cutting a patch release from a release-X.Y branch once one or more backport PRs have merged into it.

docs.title: backport.yml — on a PR merging into main
docs.text:
Implements the backport release-X.Y label described in full on Backporting. Triggered by pull_request_target: types: [closed], scoped to PRs targeting main, and gated on github.event.pull_request.merged — closing a PR without merging it never does anything here.

Job What it does validate-targets Reads every backport <branch> label on the merged PR, parses it against ^backport (release-\d+\.\d+)$, de-duplicates, and confirms each named branch actually exists (GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/branches/{branch}) — a label naming a branch that was never created (typo, or a line nobody's maintaining) fails the job with a comment on the PR explaining exactly which label is wrong, rather than silently skipping it or letting the backport action fail deeper into its own run. Outputs the validated, space-delimited branch list. backport Only runs if validate-targets succeeds. Invokes korthout/backport-action@v4 with target_branches set to that validated list (its own independent label_pattern matching is disabled — validate-targets is the single source of truth for targets), cherry_picking: auto (picks the one squash-merge commit; see CONTRIBUTING.md: Squash merge only), and experimental.conflict_resolution: draft_commit_conflicts so a cherry-pick that doesn't apply cleanly becomes a draft PR with the conflict committed as-is, instead of a bare failed Actions run.

concurrency: group: backport-${{ github.event.pull_request.number }} ensures re-runs for the same PR (e.g. a label added after the fact) queue rather than race each other; it never cancels an in-flight backport (cancel-in-progress: false), since a half-applied cherry-pick is worse than a slightly delayed one.

docs.title: release-branches.yml — on pushing a v* tag
docs.text:
Keeps the set of valid backport release-X.Y targets up to date with zero manual branch-cutting. Triggered by the same push: tags: v* event release.yml reacts to, but is a fully independent workflow file with no shared jobs — see Backporting: the release job is unaffected for why this can't regress release.yml itself.

For a pushed tag vX.Y.Z: pre-release tags (containing -, e.g. v2.0.0-rc1) and patch releases (Z != 0) are skipped — only the first release of a minor/major line (vX.Y.0) does anything. For such a tag, it idempotently (checking first, so a re-run or a manually pre-created branch/label is a no-op, not an error):

  • creates branch release-X.Y pointed at that tag's commit, and
  • creates the matching backport release-X.Y label.

See Backporting: Maintenance branches for the full lifecycle this feeds into.

docs.title: branch-cleanup.yml — on a PR closing (merged or not)
docs.text:
Deletes a pull request's head branch the moment it closes, whether merged or closed without merging — feature branches, backport.yml's own per-target branches, and release-prep.yml's reused release-prep-${{ github.ref_name }} branch all get cleaned up this way instead of piling up indefinitely.

Deliberately a workflow rather than just the repository's native Settings → General → "Automatically delete head branches" toggle (which is not enabled on this repo): that setting only fires on merge, never on a PR closed without merging, and this repo wants both. Keeping it as one workflow, rather than a mix of that setting plus a workflow for the other case, avoids two independent mechanisms that could ever disagree.

Triggered by pull_request: types: [closed] with no branch filter, so it reacts to a PR closing against main, a release-X.Y branch, or anywhere else:

Safeguard Why Job gated on head.repo.full_name == github.repository A PR opened from a fork has its head branch in the fork, not this repo — never attempted, and couldn't succeed with this repo's own token anyway. main and any release-\d+\.\d+ branch name are never deleted These are long-lived branches this repo depends on, even in the unusual case one of them is ever a PR's head rather than its usual role as a base (e.g. a hypothetical "merge release-1.6 fixes forward into main" PR). Note this regex deliberately does not match release-prep-main/release-prep-release-1.6 — those are meant to be cleaned up. This name-based check is the only protection mechanism: it deliberately does not also query the real branch protection/ruleset API as a second check — that endpoint requires administration: read, a permission the default GITHUB_TOKEN can never be granted (confirmed in production: the very first run of this workflow 403'd attempting exactly that call, for every branch, not just a protected one — so the check was removed rather than left in place, always failing). Already-deleted branch (404/422 from the delete call) Treated as a no-op, not a failure — e.g. if someone already clicked GitHub's own "Delete branch" button.

docs.title: e2e-manual.yml — manual only (workflow_dispatch)
docs.text: The containerized, real-artifact end-to-end smoke test — see Testing for the full description. Deliberately not wired to push/PR: it spins up multiple long-lived containers and sleeps through real wall-clock windows, so it's opt-in rather than adding minutes to every PR.

docs.title: e2e-kind.yml — manual (workflow_dispatch) or opt-in via the run-e2e-kind PR label
docs.text:
The real-Kubernetes end-to-end test for the CRD-driven mode (cmd/manager) — see Testing for the full description. Creates a real kind cluster, installs the real CloudNativePG operator and a real Cluster, installs pg-regression-radar via the Helm chart, and asserts a real PerformanceRegression CR is created. Real ArgoCD and pg_store_plans are deliberately out of scope for this first pass — see Roadmap. Same opt-in reasoning as e2e-manual.yml: this is even heavier (a full cluster plus two operators), so it doesn't run on every push/PR by default.

It's opt-in on a per-PR basis, though: adding the run-e2e-kind label to a pull request runs this workflow against it, and every subsequent push to that PR re-runs it automatically for as long as the label stays attached (the job's if: checks the label on both the labeled and synchronize pull_request events — see the workflow's own header comment). Adding any other label never triggers it. Remove the label, or never add it, and this workflow costs nothing on that PR.

On every run (manual or label-triggered), a final Collect cluster diagnostics step writes everything useful the kind cluster still knows — the PostgresWatch/DeploySource/PerformanceRegression resources, the CloudNativePG Cluster's full YAML and describe output, cluster events, and the manager's and CloudNativePG controller's logs — to files, which an if: always() step then uploads as the e2e-kind-diagnostics-<run-id>-<attempt> build artifact. This matters specifically here because helm/kind-action tears the entire kind cluster down the instant the job ends (pass or fail): anything not captured to a file before that happens is gone for good, so this is the only way to debug a failure (or confirm a pass for the right reason) after the fact.

docs.title: lab-smoke.yml — lab manifests on every relevant PR, kind smoke test opt-in
docs.text:
Guards the lab under examples/lab. Two jobs:

  • manifests runs on every pull request that touches examples/lab/, the Helm chart or scripts/build_lab.sh. It re-renders examples/lab/00-radar.yaml from the chart with scripts/build_lab.sh --check (keeping whatever image tag the file already pins) and fails if the checked-in file is stale; run scripts/build_lab.sh and commit the result to fix it. (The Go test in examples/lab validates the hand-written manifests on every go test ./....)
  • smoke runs the lab on a real kind cluster exactly as the page describes (three kubectl applys, a three-minute wait, then the bad deploy) and asserts a Detected PerformanceRegression tied to the orders-api rollout, a plan diff showing Index Scan and Seq Scan, the alert in the sink, and that kubectl rollout undo brings the index back. It takes about ten minutes, so it is opt-in: run it manually, add the run-lab-smoke label to a PR, or rely on the weekly schedule, which runs it against the published image so a lab that breaks for users is noticed even when nobody touched it. Manual and labelled runs build the manager image from the commit under test.

docs.title: e2e-kind-multicluster.yml — manual (workflow_dispatch) or opt-in via the run-e2e-kind-multicluster PR label
docs.text:
The real-two-cluster end-to-end test for fleet mode — see Testing for the full description. Creates two real kind clusters (hub, spoke): the spoke runs the real CloudNativePG operator and a real Cluster; the hub runs this commit's manager (via the Helm chart) with a PostgresWatch that reaches across to the spoke using remoteClusterRef and the new cnpgClusterRef. Asserts both PostgresWatch.status.phase=Running and PostgresRadarCluster.status.ready=true, then rotates the registered kubeconfig to an invalid credential and back to prove the health-check reconciler both detects and recovers from a real credential rotation. Same opt-in reasoning as e2e-kind.yml, on its own label so either suite can be run independently: this one stands up two clusters instead of one, so it's heavier still.

It's opt-in on a per-PR basis: adding the run-e2e-kind-multicluster label to a pull request runs this workflow against it, and every subsequent push to that PR re-runs it automatically for as long as the label stays attached — identical labeled/synchronize gating to e2e-kind.yml, just on its own label. A final Collect cluster diagnostics step uploads the e2e-kind-multicluster-diagnostics-<run-id>-<attempt> build artifact before both kind clusters are torn down, for the same reason as e2e-kind.yml's equivalent step.

docs.title: release.yml — on pushing a v* tag
docs.text:
Publishes a release: builds, scans, signs, and pushes every artifact this repo ships, gated on pushing a tag matching v* (e.g. git tag vX.Y.Z && git push origin vX.Y.Z) — never on an ordinary merge to main, so there is no continuously-updated "edge" image, only real tagged releases. See Installation for the resulting pull/install commands.

Job What it does images (matrix: cli/operator/manager/collector/ingester × linux/amd64/linux/arm64) For each of the Dockerfile's five --target values, on each platform: builds the arch-specific image (loaded into the runner's local Docker daemon, not yet pushed — cross-compiled via the Dockerfile's --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM build stage + GOARCH=$TARGETARCH, not run under QEMU emulation, though docker/setup-qemu-action is still registered defensively), generates an SPDX SBOM with anchore/sbom-action (Syft under the hood — retried once automatically on failure, since this step's syft download from github.com's Releases CDN has hit a transient connection failure in a real release run before; a second consecutive failure still fails the job for real), scans it with aquasecurity/trivy-action and fails the job on any CRITICAL-severity finding (nothing is pushed if this fails), then — only once the scan passes — pushes it under an arch-specific tag, ghcr.io/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/<target>:<tag>-<arch> (never directly as :<tag>/:latest — see manifests below), signs that digest keylessly with cosign, attaches the SBOM as a signed in-toto attestation (cosign attest), and publishes build provenance attestations via actions/attest-build-provenance (SLSA format). manifests (needs images; matrix: cli/operator/manager/collector/ingester) Combines each target's two already-pushed, already-scanned arch-specific images into the single multi-arch :<tag> and :latest tags everything else in this repo actually references, via docker buildx imagetools create — a registry-side operation with no rebuilding, re-pulling, or re-scanning. Also cosign-signs the resulting manifest-list digest and publishes a provenance attestation for that digest, so both signature and SLSA provenance verification work directly against the plain :<tag>/:latest tag most people pull. helm-chart (needs manifests) Packages deploy/helm/deploylens with --version/--app-version derived from the pushed tag (chart version strips the tag's leading v for SemVer compliance; appVersion keeps it, matching the image tags), pushes it as an OCI artifact to oci://ghcr.io/joao00001/charts, parses the digest out of helm push's own Digest: sha256:... output line, signs that digest keylessly with cosign, and publishes a provenance attestation for that digest. Runs after manifests so a chart is never published pointing at images that failed to build/scan/publish/combine. release-notes (needs images, manifests, helm-chart) Extracts the section of CHANGELOG.md matching the pushed tag (from its ## vX.Y.Z - <date> heading up to, but not including, the next ## heading, via a small awk script) and publishes it as the body of a GitHub Release via softprops/action-gh-release. That section only exists because release-prep.yml (below) built it and it was merged to main before the tag was pushed — this job fails loudly (rather than publishing an empty release) if no matching section is found. Runs last, after every other artifact-publishing job, so a release is never announced before its images/manifests/chart actually exist.

Release notes are CHANGELOG.md-derived, not generated from commit history in this workflow. An earlier draft of this workflow considered generating release notes directly from commit messages via git-cliff (with a checked-in cliff.toml), but that never actually landed on main, and the changelog.d/ fragment system above supersedes it: fragments are written by a human in user-facing language and enforced per-PR in CI (changelog-fragment-check.yml), which a commit-message-driven changelog can't guarantee. There is no git-cliff usage or cliff.toml anywhere in this repo.

Supply chain and signing: every artifact published by this workflow is cryptographically signed with Cosign using keyless signing — the runner exchanges its own GitHub Actions OIDC token for a short-lived certificate from Sigstore Fulcio, and the signature is recorded in the public Rekor transparency log. No stored private key is needed or used. Signing covers: each per-arch image digest (in the images job), each multi-arch manifest-list digest (in the manifests job), and the Helm OCI artifact digest (in the helm-chart job). Each per-arch image also carries an SPDX-JSON SBOM attached as a signed in-toto attestation via cosign attest, and release artifacts now also receive build provenance attestations via actions/attest-build-provenance (SLSA format). The SBOM is generated by anchore/sbom-action (Syft) from the locally-built image before it is pushed; a persistent generation failure (after one automatic retry) fails the job and blocks the release. See Supply Chain Verification for the verification commands.

Permissions: packages: write (images, manifests, and helm-chart, to push to ghcr.io), id-token: write (images, manifests, and helm-chart, for cosign's OIDC-to-Fulcio exchange), and contents: write (release-notes only, for softprops/action-gh-release to create the Release). All three are satisfied entirely by the built-in GITHUB_TOKEN — no registry credential secret is configured or needed, since GHCR is free for public repositories and accepts GITHUB_TOKEN directly.

One-time manual prerequisite

GHCR pushes need Settings → Actions → General → Workflow permissions set to "Read and write permissions" on this repository — that setting can't be applied from workflow YAML, and without it every push in this workflow fails with 403 regardless of the permissions: block above. See the workflow's own top comment.

Chart versioning: deploy/helm/deploylens/Chart.yaml's checked-in version/appVersion are development-time placeholders only — helm package --version --app-version overrides both unconditionally from the pushed git tag at release time, so they never need editing in lockstep with a release. This is a deliberate design choice, not a gap.

Proven against real releases: this workflow has run for real against v1.0.0 and v1.0.1 — real pushes to ghcr.io, real keyless signing via GitHub's OIDC-to-Fulcio exchange, and a real Helm OCI chart push all succeeded, including the linux/arm64 cross-compilation. The one real failure found so far was in v1.0.0's helm-chart job: cosign sign failed with UNAUTHORIZED because helm registry login writes credentials to a different config file than cosign's default keychain reads. Fixed in v1.0.1 by adding a separate docker/login-action step before the cosign step. Not independently confirmed: an actual arm64 machine pulling and running the resulting multi-arch image, as opposed to the cross-platform build itself succeeding.

docs.title: docs.yml — check (every PR/push), deploy (release tags) and deploy-unversioned (home + roadmap)
docs.text:
Builds this documentation site with MkDocs Material and publishes a permanently versioned copy of it to GitHub Pages at https://joao00001.github.io/pg-regression-radar/ using mike — every tag gets its own browsable, never-overwritten copy of the site, a version selector renders in the header (Material's native mike integration, see mkdocs.yml's extra.version block), and a latest alias always points at the newest stable release.

This used to be one job that redeployed the live site on every push to main touching docs/**. That meant the public site could describe a feat that had merged but not shipped in any tagged image yet — nothing enforced "the docs you're reading match something you can actually install." It's now split into two jobs specifically to close that gap:

Job Trigger Publishes? check Push or PR to main (PRs path-filtered to docs/**/mkdocs.yml/hooks.py/requirements-docs.txt; plain pushes to main unconditionally, matching ci.yml's own pattern) No — mkdocs build --strict only, same broken-link/nav gate as before, just never publishes anything. deploy Push of a v* tag, or workflow_dispatch with an explicit tag input (for re-running a failed deploy — it checks out that exact tag, never whatever ref the workflow happens to run from) Yes — via mike deploy, straight to the gh-pages branch. deploy-unversioned Every push to main, and after every deploy (so after a tag push or manual run) Yes — the unversioned pages only, built from main; a no-op when nothing changed.

deploy runs unconditionally on every tag push, with no path filter (mirroring release.yml's own tag-triggered, always-runs behavior) — a release always gets a matching docs deploy, even when that specific tag's commit didn't touch anything under docs/.

Stable vs. pre-release tags: a tag containing a - (this repo's existing release-candidate convention, e.g. v1.0.0-rc1) is deployed as its own permanent, linkable version but never becomes the latest alias — only a tag with no - (a real vX.Y.Z release) moves latest, and with it, what a visitor sees at /latest/.

One-time manual prerequisite

Settings → Pages → Source must be "Deploy from a branch", branch gh-pages, folder / (root) — not "GitHub Actions". mike commits the built site directly to the gh-pages branch itself (see mike's own "How It Works"); there's no artifact-upload step here for the old "GitHub Actions" Pages source to serve.

docs.title: Unversioned pages (home, roadmap, playground, our math and contribute)
docs.text:
The home page (docs/index.md), the Roadmap (docs/roadmap.md) and the Playground (docs/playground.md) Our math (docs/our-math.md) and Contribute (docs/contribute.md) are not versioned. They describe the project, not a particular release — editing the roadmap has nothing to do with how a given version works — so they look the same whichever version a reader picks in the version selector, and a change to them is live as soon as it merges, without waiting for a release.

  • Layout on gh-pages: the unversioned pages are the site root (/, /roadmap/, /playground/, /our-math/ and /contribute/); mike's versions live in their own directories next to them (/latest/, /v1.5.0/, ...). Visiting /latest/ lands on the home page for versions cut before the split, and on that version's first docs page for newer ones, since their build has no home page of its own. mike set-default is deliberately not used — it would make the root a redirect to latest.
  • Two builds: mkdocs.yml builds the versioned docs and excludes those three pages (exclude_docs); mkdocs-unversioned.yml (which INHERITs mkdocs.yml) builds only them. Both run in check.
  • Links across the boundary are rewritten by hooks.py's on_page_markdown, so pages keep using ordinary relative links: a versioned page's [Roadmap](roadmap.md) becomes the root roadmap URL, and the unversioned pages' links to any other page point at the latest docs. The versioned nav's top level is the header's tab bar: "Home", "Playground" and "Roadmap" are absolute links to the root pages, and everything else sits under "Docs" (the left sidebar). The tab bar is Material's second header row (navigation.tabs.sticky), restyled in extra.css as a thin transparent strip with the header's backdrop blur. The three unversioned pages hide the left sidebar (hide: navigation), since it would only list themselves.
  • The playground's WebAssembly module: the Playground runs the real correlation engine in the browser. scripts/build_playground.sh compiles it (with the matching wasm_exec.js) into git-ignored files under docs/assets/playground/; check and deploy-unversioned both run it after setup-go and before building the unversioned site, so a change that breaks the js/wasm build fails the docs check. Because the page is unversioned it always runs the engine from main, which can be ahead of the latest release. To preview it locally, run the script and then mkdocs serve -f mkdocs-unversioned.yml.
  • Our math stays in step with the engine: the figures on Our math run docs/assets/math/math-core.js, a port of the change-point and t-test code in internal/correlation/engine.go. TestMathPageMatchesEngine (internal/correlation/mathpage_test.go) feeds series generated by that module (testdata/mathpage_fixtures.json) to the real engine and fails if the verdict, factor, change point or p-value differ. After changing either side on purpose, regenerate the fixtures with node internal/correlation/testdata/gen_mathpage_fixtures.js.
  • Publishing: scripts/publish_unversioned_docs.py replaces everything at the gh-pages root that isn't a mike version, alias or versions.json, so removed or renamed unversioned files don't linger. It also turns the roadmap/index.html of every already-published version that still contains its own copy (releases cut before this split) into a redirect to the root roadmap, so the roadmap changes retroactively too. It also points each version's own index.html (its bare root, which the version selector links to) at that version's installation/ page, so choosing a version lands in that version's docs, not on the home page. The menu's "Home" link goes straight to the site root, so no version root has to stand in for the home page. The "Docs" tab of the version-less pages (docs/javascripts/docs-version.js) returns to the version the reader last used, which version-flyout.js records in localStorage.

The docs-unversioned label: apply it to a pull request that only edits docs/index.md, docs/roadmap.md, docs/playground.md, docs/our-math.md and/or docs/contribute.md (and, with them, the files only the unversioned build uses: docs/stylesheets/roadmap.css, docs/javascripts/roadmap.js, docs/stylesheets/contribute.css, docs/javascripts/contribute.js, the playground's docs/assets/playground/ scripts and styles, the math page's docs/assets/math/ scripts, styles and font, and mkdocs-unversioned.yml), to flag that merging it changes those pages for every docs version at once. Everything else under docs/ is versioned and reaches the site only with a release, so such edits belong in a separate PR.

docs.title: docs-unversioned-guard.yml — on PR label changes
docs.text:
Runs on pull_request_target (so it can comment on fork PRs; nothing from the PR is ever checked out or executed — it only reads the PR's file list through the API) whenever a PR to main is opened, reopened, pushed to, labeled or unlabeled. If the PR carries the docs-unversioned label and changes any file other than docs/index.md, docs/roadmap.md, docs/playground.md, docs/our-math.md and the unversioned build's own assets (UNVERSIONED_ASSETS in the script; a renamed file's old path counts too), scripts/check_docs_unversioned.py posts a warning comment listing the offending files. The comment is kept up to date on every push and deleted once the PR only touches those files again or the label is removed. It never fails the check — it's an alert for the author and reviewers, who decide whether to split the PR or drop the label.

Changelog, on the site itself: docs/changelog.md isn't a real file in the repo — hooks.py's on_pre_build hook copies the root CHANGELOG.md into it at build time (rewriting the two relative links that would otherwise break a directory level deeper: CONTRIBUTING.md → an absolute GitHub blob URL, docs/roadmap.md → roadmap.md) and it's listed in mkdocs.yml's nav as a top-level "Changelog" page. Because it's built fresh per version, each mike-deployed version of the site shows CHANGELOG.md exactly as it existed at that tag — a real per-release changelog, not just a link out to GitHub.

Version indicator: the version a visitor is looking at is shown by Material's version selector (top of every page), sourced from mike's versions.json. The release-specific values inside the pages follow it: docs/installation.md and docs/supply-chain.md write image tags, chart versions and the go install pin as the release_tag placeholder (the tag, e.g. v1.8.0) and the release_version placeholder (the same without the leading v), both written in double curly braces, and hooks.py replaces them while building with the version being built: the PGRR_DOCS_VERSION environment variable (set by docs.yml's deploy job to the tag it deploys), else the tag that is checked out, else the most recent v* tag, else the literal vX.Y.Z. So /v1.6.0/installation/ shows v1.6.0, /latest/ shows the latest release, and a local mkdocs serve of unreleased work shows the most recent release. Write new release-specific commands with the placeholders, not with a hard-coded number.

Outdated-version warning banner: overrides/main.html (wired in via mkdocs.yml's theme.custom_dir: overrides) overrides Material's outdated block so a visitor browsing any version other than the one aliased latest sees a banner above the header linking back to the site root — see Material's version-warning docs. The banner's markup is baked into every version's build identically; Material's own client-side JS decides at page-load time (by comparing the current version against versions.json) whether to actually unhide it, so this needs no per-version build logic of its own.

docs.title: Dependabot (.github/dependabot.yml)
docs.text:
Weekly update checks for gomod, github-actions, and docker ecosystems, with chore(deps) / ci(deps) commit-message prefixes matching this project's Conventional Commits convention. The docker entry covers the base image(s) in the repo-root Dockerfile's FROM lines — the same five-target multi-stage build release.yml publishes from — so a base-image security patch shows up as an ordinary Dependabot PR, the same way a vulnerable Go dependency would.

This is version-currency only (opens a PR when a newer version exists); it's not what actually blocks a known-vulnerable dependency or image from shipping — see the Security scanning table above for govulncheck (Go deps) and Trivy (built images), which check for actual CVEs rather than just staleness.

docs.title: Branch protection
docs.text: None of the above has real effect unless main's (and, where applicable, each release-X.Y branch's) ruleset/branch protection actually requires each check by name — see Branch Protection for the exact check names and which settings are worth enabling alongside them.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
