docs.title: Collector Internals
docs.text: Row identity, retention behaviour, queryid instability, and PostgreSQL version handling — the details worth knowing when tuning --retention-minutes or debugging a "missing data" report.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The collector (internal/collector) keeps a bounded, in-memory time series of pg_stat_statements observations per queryid. Before combining rows into that series, it calculates intervals independently for each statistics entry. Retention is bounded, queryid is not stable across every deploy, and column availability varies by PostgreSQL major version.

docs.title: Row identity before aggregation
docs.text:
pg_stat_statements keeps separate cumulative counters for (dbid, userid, queryid, toplevel). Two roles running the same query can therefore return two rows with the same queryid. The collector subtracts each row's own previous counters first, then sums interval calls and execution time into one sample per queryid per scrape. Its interval mean is summed execution time divided by summed calls; it is not an unweighted average of the rows' means. A reset of one role does not restart another role's counters.

The first scrape, a changed set of rows, or an expired predecessor leaves that query's interval unknown. Such samples are excluded from interval analysis even when every interval in a window is unknown. Missing rows are forgotten after a successful scrape, so a returning row establishes a new baseline. A failed or incomplete scrape does not advance any row's predecessor.

The SQL still selects the 500 rows with the greatest cumulative execution time, not 500 distinct query IDs. Several roles can occupy slots for one query; aggregation can therefore yield fewer than 500 samples. Changes at that selection boundary can leave an interval unknown. The row-predecessor cache holds only the last successful scrape and is bounded by the same row limit.

docs.title: Retention, not an unbounded log
docs.text:
Every scrape, samples older than now - RetentionDuration are pruned (a single reslice per queryid, since samples are always appended in chronological order — no O(n²) scan), and any queryid left with zero samples (e.g. one that fell out of pg_stat_statements's top-500 ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC LIMIT 500) is removed from the map entirely, so both the data volume and the number of tracked keys stay bounded under long-running, continuous scraping.

The default of 180 minutes is 3x the full before+after span of the default 30-minute analysis window (2 x 30 = 60 min), giving headroom for delayed deploy-event ingestion/processing and for the queryid-fingerprint fallback below to have data on both sides of a rotation. If you run with a larger --window-minutes, size --retention-minutes to stay comfortably above 2 * window-minutes.

Two Prometheus gauges expose current state:

  • pg_regression_radar_collector_tracked_queries — distinct queryids retained.
  • pg_regression_radar_collector_retained_samples_total — total samples retained across all queryids.
  • pg_regression_radar_collector_explain_statements_skipped_total — pg_stat_statements rows skipped because their query text is itself an EXPLAIN statement, so it's never retained as a sample or handed to plan capture. See Detection Algorithm § Excluding capture's own footprint from tracking for why these rows exist at all and why they're excluded.

docs.title: queryid is not a stable identifier across a deploy
docs.text:
Per the PostgreSQL documentation, queryid "is not safe to assume... will be stable across major versions of PostgreSQL", and it also changes if a referenced object (e.g. a table touched by a migration) is dropped and recreated between executions — which can happen in the middle of the very deploy this tool is trying to analyze.

The collector guards against this by also computing a text-normalized FingerprintQuery hash (see internal/collector/fingerprint.go) for every sample. When SamplesInRange(queryID, from, to) finds few samples directly under queryID in range, it additionally merges in same-range samples recorded under any other queryid that currently shares that fingerprint, so a query whose queryid rotated mid-window doesn't look like it has "no data" on one side of the rotation. This is fully internal to the collector: the public SampleSource interface consumed by internal/correlation (SamplesInRange/AllQueryIDs) is unchanged.

Because the collector truncates QueryText to --max-query-text-len before fingerprinting, extremely small values for that flag increase the chance that distinct queries share the same truncated prefix and therefore the same fallback fingerprint. The default (200) leaves plenty of shape information intact; values below roughly 20 characters are where collision risk becomes materially easier to trigger in practice.

Deduplicated at the correlation-engine layer

AllQueryIDs() still lists the old and new queryids separately, so a rotated query is still analyzed once per queryid, each pulling in the same merged data — but internal/correlation.Engine.Analyse now recognizes this by fingerprint and reports it at most once, under whichever queryid most recently received a sample (the "live" identity). See Detection Algorithm for how.

docs.title: pg_stat_statements column names vary by PostgreSQL major version
docs.text:
PostgreSQL 13 split the old total_time/mean_time columns into total_plan_time/total_exec_time and mean_plan_time/mean_exec_time (compare the PG12 and PG13 column references).

CloudNativePG's currently supported releases only ship PostgreSQL 14+ (see Supported releases), and PostgreSQL 13 itself reached community end-of-life on 2025-11-13, so a query hard-coded to the modern column names is already safe for every CloudNativePG-managed cluster in support today. The collector nonetheless detects server_version_num once at startup and falls back to the legacy column names below PostgreSQL 13, so it also works against older or self-managed Postgres instances.

docs.title: Counters, resets and interval latency
docs.text:
Version detection enables toplevel on PostgreSQL 14+ and stats_since on PostgreSQL 17+. Before PostgreSQL 14, row identity uses the three available fields and a constant toplevel=true. If version lookup fails, the scrape fails and retries lookup on the next attempt rather than silently combining top-level and nested entries.

calls and total_exec_time accumulate until the entry is reset or evicted, so the collector stores each scrape's cumulative values and derives the latency of the calls made since the previous scrape. On PostgreSQL 17+ it also reads stats_since to recognise a reset that the counters alone would not reveal. See Detection Algorithm for the formula, the reset rules and their limits.

docs.title: Versioning & dry-run
docs.text:
All four binaries share two flags:

  • --version prints a one-line <binary> <version> (commit <sha>, built <date>) string and exits immediately, before any other flag is validated. A build made without the Dockerfile's --build-arg VERSION/COMMIT/DATE (e.g. a local go build) reports dev/none/unknown rather than a misleading guess.
  • --dry-run validates configuration and (where applicable) live connectivity — Postgres reachability and the pg_stat_statements extension for operator/collector, source-type/address validity for ingester, Kubernetes API config resolution for manager — then exits with status 0 on success or 1 (with a logged error) on failure, without starting any server. Useful in CI or an init container to fail fast on a bad DSN or typo'd --source-type before the real process starts.

docs.title: Tuning notes for less-frequently changed collector/operator flags
--max-query-text-len
docs.text:
• What it does: Caps the stored query text length per sample before the collector truncates it and computes the fallback fingerprint.
  • Default / valid values: 200; any positive integer number of characters.
  • When to change it: Raise it if your workload has long query texts where the distinguishing part often appears after the first 200 characters and you need better alert/debug context.
  • Caveats: Setting it very low reduces the amount of text available to the fingerprint fallback described in Collector Internals. Values below roughly 20 characters materially increase the chance that different queries collapse onto the same truncated prefix and get merged together incorrectly.

docs.title: --capture-plans
docs.text:
• What it does: Enables periodic plan capture so detected regressions can include a short plan-diff summary alongside the latency change.
  • Default / valid values: false; set to true to enable it.
  • When to change it: Turn it on when plan context will help an operator quickly tell whether a regression lines up with an index choice, join strategy, or other planner change.
  • Caveats: It is a no-op below PostgreSQL 16 (logged once at startup/scrape time) and it adds one extra planner invocation per tracked query per scrape cycle, so leave it off if you do not need the extra diagnostic signal.

docs.title: --changepoint-tolerance
docs.text:
• What it does: Limits how far the detected change point may land from a deploy timestamp and still be attributed to that deploy.
  • Default / valid values: 0 (auto), which resolves to 20% of --window-minutes with a minimum of 2 minutes; any non-negative Go duration string is accepted.
  • When to change it: Increase it for slow rolling deploys or event sources whose timestamps lag the actual traffic shift; decrease it when closely spaced deploys are being merged too aggressively.
  • Caveats: Larger tolerances make it easier to attribute a genuine regression to the wrong deploy when multiple changes happen near each other.

docs.title: --state-prune-interval
docs.text:
• What it does: Controls how often the postgres state backend sweeps old samples and deploy events past --state-retention.
  • Default / valid values: 15m; Go duration strings, with non-positive values falling back to the default 15-minute sweep interval in the prune loop.
  • When to change it: Shorten it if you need expired state cleared sooner to keep the backing tables smaller; lengthen it if you would rather do fewer background deletes and can tolerate stale rows lingering a little longer.
  • Caveats: More frequent pruning means more frequent DELETE ... WHERE recorded_at < now()-retention work against the state database; less frequent pruning leaves more expired rows behind between sweeps.

Never merged by the manager — see Attribution engine periodicDetection.enabled false Also run regression detection on a rolling schedule, independent of any tracked deploy — see Periodic Detection periodicDetection.windowMinutes 60 Split-window size for periodic detection; only meaningful alongside periodicDetection.enabled periodicDetection.intervalMinutes 15 How often a full periodic-detection pass runs; only meaningful alongside periodicDetection.enabled sampleSource.type "collector" Sample source backing the Correlation Engine: collector (default — internal/collector.Collector scrapes pg_stat_statements directly) or prometheus (internal/telemetry/promsource — see OpenTelemetry / Prometheus Sample Source). dsn/dsnSecretRef are not required when this is prometheus; capturePlans: true is rejected when combined with it sampleSource.prometheus.url (required with type: prometheus) Prometheus HTTP API base, e.g. http://prometheus:9090 sampleSource.prometheus.metricName (required with type: prometheus) Prometheus metric to read samples from — see OpenTelemetry / Prometheus Sample Source: The real gap for why there's no safe default sampleSource.prometheus.queryIDLabel "queryid" Label carrying the queryid sampleSource.prometheus.queryTextLabel "query" Label carrying the query text; set to "-" to disable sampleSource.prometheus.stepSeconds 15 query_range resolution sampleSource.prometheus.bearerTokenSecretRef (none) name/key of a Secret holding a bearer token for Prometheus. Needs the pg-regression-radar.io/allow-postgreswatch-access=true label otlpExport.endpoint (none — export disabled) OTLP/HTTP endpoint that receives one log record per detected regression (/v1/logs is appended); subject to the alert-destination SSRF checks and rejected under relay-only — see OTLP Regression Export otlpExport.encoding protobuf protobuf or json otlpExport.headersSecretRef (none) name/key of a Secret whose value is k=v,k2=v2 request headers (e.g. authorization=Bearer …). Needs the consent label otlpExport.gzip false Gzip-compress request bodies otlpExport.timeoutSeconds 10 Per-attempt timeout, 1–120

docs.title: DeploySource spec fields
docs.text: Field Default Description postgresWatchRef (required) Name of the PostgresWatch (same namespace) to correlate against sourceType generic argocd, argo-rollouts, flux, generic, kubernetes, otlp — see Deploy Sources & Webhooks: Native Kubernetes watch for kubernetes appName "" (all apps) Narrow correlation to a single application. When sourceType is kubernetes, this is the Deployment/StatefulSet's name and is required workloadKind "" Deployment or StatefulSet. Only meaningful (and required) when sourceType is kubernetes otlp (none) Required (with at least one of spanNames/matchAttributes) when sourceType: otlp; rejected otherwise. Fields: spanNames, matchAttributes, includeFailedSpans, timestamp, appAttribute, namespaceAttribute, clusterAttribute, revisionAttribute, imageTagAttribute — see OTLP Deploy Events webhookSecret "" Shared secret for this source's webhook, equivalent to --webhook-secret above. Not meaningful when sourceType is kubernetes (that mode has no webhook route to protect). Store the value in a Secret and reference it with valueFrom.secretKeyRef rather than inlining it — see Deploy Sources & Webhooks: Webhook authentication

docs.title: Source-type capabilities by mode
docs.text:
sourceType / --source-type means different things depending on which binary or field is reading it, and the two don't accept the same set of values:

Where it's set Accepted values Accepts kubernetes? operator --source-type / ingester --source-type (CLI flag, validated by --dry-run) argocd, argo-rollouts, flux, generic, otlp No — kubernetes isn't in ValidSourceTypes, so --dry-run rejects it outright, and without --dry-run it would silently fall through to generic-style webhook parsing instead of doing anything kubernetes-specific DeploySource.spec.sourceType (CRD field, manager mode only) argocd, argo-rollouts, flux, generic, kubernetes, otlp Yes — this is the only place kubernetes is meaningful. It skips webhook route registration entirely and instead watches the Deployment/StatefulSet named in appName directly — see Deploy Sources & Webhooks: Native Kubernetes watch

In short: if you're running the standalone operator/ingester binaries, kubernetes is not a valid --source-type no matter what — that capability only exists behind the manager/CRD path.

docs.text:
• Getting Started — these flags/fields used in full runnable commands.
  • Detection Algorithm — what --window-minutes, --min-samples, --min-executions, --latency-threshold, --changepoint-tolerance, --multiple-testing and --adjust-autocorrelation actually control.
  • Persistence — the --state-* flags in depth.
  • Deploy Sources & Webhooks — --source-type and sourceType per webhook source.
  • Auto-Abort (Argo Rollouts) — autoAbort.enabled/autoAbort.confidenceThreshold in depth, including the RBAC gate.
  • Attribution engine — attribution.enabled, attribution.mode, the verdict endpoint and the metric.
  • Periodic (Deploy-Independent) Detection — --periodic-detection/periodicDetection.* in depth, including the false-positive caveat and re-arm suppression model.
  • Multi-Cluster (Fleet) Mode — remoteClusterRef, cnpgClusterRef, and cluster health checks in depth, including the hub-spoke RBAC split.
  • API Versioning & Compatibility — what v1alpha1 guarantees (and doesn't) for the CRDs documented above.

docs.title: Dashboard
docs.text: A local web page, read-only toward your cluster, that shows what the radar saw, what it decided, why, and what it did. One command opens it.

docs.title: Try it without a cluster
docs.text:
pg-regression-radar dashboard --fixture internal/observe/testdata/recorded-sim.json --open

The page says Recorded sample, not a live cluster whenever it shows recorded data, so a sample is never mistaken for your system.

The recording is fixed: it answers with what was captured and nothing new arrives, so the page does not change by itself. The time range, the boards, the focus view with its settings and queries, and layout editing all work on it. Live updates and real history need a cluster (next section).

docs.title: Open it on your cluster
docs.text:
Before you start:

  • The manager is installed and running in the cluster (the chart's manager mode, cmd/manager). The dashboard does not install or start anything: it reads the manager's Observe API, which is on by default (--observe-addr, 127.0.0.1:8083; an empty value turns it off) and is served only by the manager's leader.
  • Your Kubernetes user has the permissions listed below, in the manager's namespace.
  • The radar has deploys to show. They come from the deploy sources you configured (see Deploy Sources & Webhooks), and the radar judges one about ten minutes after it is registered. Until then the panels say No deploys in this time range; widen the range or wait for the next deploy.
pg-regression-radar dashboard --namespace <manager-namespace> --open
# another cluster:
pg-regression-radar dashboard --context <kube-context> --namespace <manager-namespace> --open

What the command does:

  1. Reads the manager's leader-election Lease (pg-regression-radar-manager.radar.pgregressionradar.io) to find the leader pod, because only the leader runs the evaluators.
  2. Opens a port-forward to that pod with your own kubeconfig. The manager's Observe API listens on 127.0.0.1 inside the pod (--observe-addr, default 127.0.0.1:8083), so there is no Service, Ingress or token to leak.
  3. Serves the page on 127.0.0.1:8765 (--port).
  4. If the leader changes, it finds the new one and the page shows Reconnecting; if the manager's API version is not one the dashboard understands, it says Incompatible and names the versions it supports.

Your Kubernetes user needs: get on leases (coordination.k8s.io), get on pods, and create on pods/portforward. Without --namespace the command looks for the Lease in every namespace you may list.

Flag Meaning --namespace, --context, --kubeconfig, --lease-name Where the manager is and how to reach it --url http://host:port Skip the port-forward and read an Observe API you exposed yourself --port, --listen, --open Where the page is served; --listen must be a loopback address unless you add --insecure-listen --config FILE Boards and panels from a file (below) --data-dir DIR, --no-save Where your edits are kept between runs (default: pg-regression-radar/dashboard in your user configuration directory), or --no-save to keep them in the browser only. See Your edits are kept between runs --show-queries Show normalised SQL text. The manager must allow it too (--observe-allow-queries)

The page has no sign-in. Anyone who can reach it sees your deploys, which is why it refuses a non-loopback --listen unless you pass --insecure-listen, and why it rejects requests whose Host is not this machine (DNS rebinding).

docs.title: What the page shows
docs.text:
• Now: is the radar watching and fresh, which deploys it is judging, the picked deploy's grade, the canary-against-stable chart, why it decided that, the evidence per query, and what it did.
  • Case: the same evidence for one deploy, full width, with every evaluation, a ratio chart of all queries and the activity feed beside the deploy list. Open it from a deploy with Open as a case; the address (#/case/<id>) can be shared.
  • Source health: whether each source the radar reads is answering, what the radar may do (mode, actuation, breaker, namespaces) and the activity feed.

When a source is not healthy, or the radar may not act, the row says why in words and shows the reason code of the matching condition on the PostgresWatch (ScrapeStale, ArmsLogStale, ActuationNotAsked, BreakerOpen, and so on). The code links to its entry in Reason codes, which lists the causes, how to confirm each and the fix. The What the radar did panel shows the reason code of each action the same way, so a line in the manager log and a line on the dashboard can be matched by code. A manager older than 1.9.2 sends no codes; the dashboard then shows the same rows without them.

docs.title: Alerts
docs.text:
The few situations that need a person stay at the top right of every board, whichever board or time range is open, until they are dealt with. There is at most one alert per deploy, and its wording follows how far the radar got:

Alert Raised when Goes away when Regression detected the engine reads a deploy as regressed and has not acted the deploy is read as healthy again, or you dismiss it Regressed, rollout paused or aborted the radar paused or aborted the rollout and the deploy is still regressed the deploy is read as healthy again (the abort worked, or a later evaluation came back clean), or you dismiss it Still regressed after the abort the check after an abort found the regression still there the deploy is read as healthy again, or you dismiss it Could not pause or abort the rollout the call to the Rollout failed the deploy is read as healthy again, or you dismiss it The radar stopped acting by itself the circuit breaker of a watch is open the breaker is closed, or you dismiss it. The card carries the BreakerOpen code and the command that closes it

A few rules keep this quiet enough to trust:

  • It stays until it is over. An alert is not a toast that fades. It is removed on its own only when the engine reads the deploy as healthy; an inconclusive reading is not an all-clear, so the alert stays.
  • Dismissing is yours. The × removes one alert, Clear all removes those shown. By default a dismissed alert does not come back on the next refresh or after a reload (the browser remembers it for 30 days; Settings can make it come back on reload). It does come back if things get worse, for example Still regressed after the abort after you dismissed Regressed, rollout aborted, and if the same deploy regresses again after it had recovered.
  • Silence is not an all-clear. If the manager stops reporting a deploy (it restarted, and the history is kept in memory by default), its alert stays and says so, until you dismiss it.
  • A long list is folded. Three are shown on a wide screen by default (you can choose 1, 2, 3 or 5) and one on a phone, the worst first and then the newest; the rest is behind N more alerts.
  • Screen readers are told, politely, when an alert appears and when one is removed because the deploy recovered.

The page behind the alerts is blurred, more strongly towards the cards and fading to nothing at their edges, instead of the cards casting a shadow. With reduce transparency set in the system, or without support for backdrop blur in the browser, the page is not blurred and the cards get a plain shadow.

Each card names how bad it is (Alert or Critical) in the colour of its shape, then what happened, where, and what the radar did. When trouble clears by itself the card does not just vanish: its shape turns into a teal circle, the text changes to Healthy, and after a moment it slides away. Where the system asks for reduced motion the same happens without the movement.

Each alert links to the deploy's case and, when the radar acted, shows the reason code of the action. Alerts are read from the Observe API for the last 90 days, so they do not depend on the time range of the board.

Every panel has an info button at its top right. Hover it, or focus it with the keyboard, to read what the panel shows and how to read it; click to keep the text open (Escape or a click elsewhere closes it). A panel's own description in the file replaces the built-in text.

docs.title: Look at one panel
docs.text:
Click a panel (on its text or its chart, not on a button or list inside it), press V while the pointer is over it, or use the expand button that appears beside its info button. The panel opens alone, large, with its settings on the right. Esc, Back to the board or the browser's Back button return to the board. The address (#/now?view=canary) can be shared.

The settings pane is organised in groups you can fold, with a search box:

  • Visualization: how the panel is drawn. The deploy list is cards or a compact list; the canary chart is a line chart or a table; evidence is a table or a ratio chart; activity is a feed or a table.
  • Data: which rows (all, only problems, only flagged queries…), their order and how many.
  • Display: what the picture carries (the baseline, the sample bars, the axis from zero, the columns, the figures).
  • Panel: the panel's own title and description, which the info button shows.

A setting that does not apply to the chosen visualization is hidden. A changed setting is marked and has its own Reset. Changes apply at once and are saved like any other layout edit; Discard changes goes back to how the panel was when you opened it, Reset to defaults clears the panel's settings, and Copy as YAML gives the panel as the lines the dashboard file holds. A panel that shows one deploy has a deploy picker beside it, and choosing there chooses for the whole board.

docs.title: Change what a panel shows: the query
docs.text:
Under a panel in focus there is a Query field, as in Grafana's panel editor. It is not SQL: the dashboard only reads what the Observe API already serves, so the field takes a short filter language over that data. Click it and it lists the fields it understands; type app: and it lists the values that exist right now, with how many deploys or queries each matches, and it keeps up as the data changes. Under the field the panel says what it now shows ("Shows checkout · payments · 09:00, the newest deploy that matches"), or why the query cannot run (the column, what is wrong, what to write). A query that cannot run is never applied, so the panel keeps showing what it showed.

app:checkout                         # one application
app:checkout app:search              # same field twice: either one
app:checkout state:regressed         # different fields: both must hold
statement:UPDATE table:orders        # evidence for one kind of statement on one table
deploy:checkout-7f9c query:"SELECT*" # one deploy, queries whose name starts with SELECT
  • A term is field:value; a value with spaces is "quoted" (\" and \\ inside). At most 12 terms and 200 characters. Text is matched without regard to case; * matches any text in the free-text fields (app, namespace, query, statement, table, deploy).
  • Fields: app, namespace, state (regressed, acted, watching, healthy, inconclusive), grade (A to D), deploy (one deploy, by its id), query (a query by its name on the panel, its base name or the start of its fingerprint), statement (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) and table.
  • Each panel type takes the fields that make sense for it. List panels (deploys, activity, summary) are only filtered. Panels that show one deploy (deploy, canary, evidence, ratio chart, evaluations, figures, why, ledger) show the picked deploy of the board unless their query names one: deploy: chooses that deploy, and app:, namespace:, state: or grade: choose the newest deploy that matches. The deploy picker is disabled on such a panel, since its query decides. Panels that draw one query's measurements (canary, evidence, ratio chart, evaluations) also filter by query, statement and table. The radar state, safety and source health panels have nothing to filter and show no field. dashboard config dump --catalog prints the fields of each panel type.
  • A panel with a query says so in its info text, and the query is saved with the panel as query: in the layout file, so it is part of what Copy as YAML and Export give.
  • Because a query can name a deploy that is not on the board, such a panel fetches that deploy's own series. This only works for deploys the page already holds (the newest 30 in the time range and the picked one); outside those, the panel says the deploy is not in the range.

Queries are named by statement and table (SELECT on orders; two that would read the same are numbered), because the SQL text is hidden unless you ask for it.

docs.title: Your edits are kept between runs
docs.text:
Everything you change in the page (a panel's settings and visualization, its title and description, its query, positions and sizes, the time range of each board) is saved on its own, a moment after the change, in the dashboard's data directory. Close the dashboard, run the command again and the page opens as you left it, in any browser.

  • The directory is pg-regression-radar/dashboard inside your user configuration directory (~/.config on Linux, ~/Library/Application Support on macOS, %AppData% on Windows). Choose another with --data-dir DIR, which can be a mounted volume. The command prints the file it uses when it starts.
  • One file per dashboard: dashboard-default.json for the built-in boards, and dashboard-file-<id>.json for each --config file (the id comes from the file's path, so two files do not share edits). The directory is private to you (mode 0700, file 0600). The file is small JSON that the page reads and writes; to carry a dashboard to another machine or into version control, use Export and --config.
  • If the --config file changes after you made edits, your edits are dropped and the page says so: the file wins. Undo my edits removes them from disk too.
  • --no-save writes nothing to disk and keeps edits in the browser only (as earlier versions did). The same happens, with a message at start, if the directory cannot be written.
  • The dashboard is still read-only toward your cluster and the radar. The one thing it writes is this file, only from this page's own requests (the server refuses writes from any other site), only at this fixed path, at most 256 KiB, and only a layout that passes the same checks as a dashboard file.

What is in the file, and what to do about it. It holds your layout, each panel's settings, titles, descriptions and queries, and the time range of each board. Those are names you typed or picked, so they can name your applications, namespaces and tables: treat the file as you would your deploy list. It never holds credentials, kubeconfig data, DSNs, deploy or evaluation data, or SQL text, so it is safe to leave on your disk, but do not type secrets into a title or description, because they are stored in clear text.

  • The file is 0600 in a directory created 0700. A directory that already existed keeps its own permissions, so if you point --data-dir at a shared or synced folder, make sure that is what you want. Exclude it from file sync or backups, or use --no-save, if those names must not leave your machine.
  • With --insecure-listen the dashboard does not save: the page has no sign-in, so anyone who could reach it could overwrite your edits. The command says so, and edits stay in the browser.
  • A file that was edited by hand, or damaged, is checked like a dashboard file before the page uses it. If it cannot be used, the page says why and shows the standard layout; the file is left alone until your next change replaces it.
  • To forget everything: Undo my edits removes the layout from the file; deleting the file (or the data directory) removes it all. Nothing expires on its own.
  • The full threat table is in the security model.

Every board has a time range (15 minutes to 90 days, or an absolute range). It is remembered per board. If the manager keeps less history than the range, the page says so rather than showing a short list as complete.

docs.title: History
docs.text:
The manager keeps history behind --observe-history:

Setting Behaviour memory (default) A bounded ring (--observe-history-max-deploys, 500). Lost on restart; the dashboard says so. postgres Survives restarts. Needs --observe-history-dsn-file (a mounted Secret holding the DSN; a DSN on the command line would show in the pod spec).

--observe-history-retention (default 30 days) applies to both. Writing history never delays a decision: if the store is down the radar keeps acting and the dashboard says history is not being recorded. Only deploys in attribution.actuate.namespaces are served, on every endpoint including the event stream.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
The gear at the top right opens a page of settings, laid out like the other boards (it is not a tab: the tabs are the boards of the dashboard file). They belong to the person looking, not to the dashboard file, so they are kept in the browser's local storage only and are never sent anywhere. Each setting that is not at its default shows the accent bar and a Reset link, as the settings of a panel do.

Panel Setting Choices Appearance Theme System (the default), Light, Dark. This replaces the sun and moon button that used to sit in the header Time Time zone Browser time (the default, as before), UTC, or one of fourteen cities from Los Angeles to Auckland, each with its current offset Alerts When an alert clears by itself Say so, then remove it (default), Remove it quietly, or Keep it until I dismiss it, which turns the card to healthy and leaves it so you can see what cleared while you were away Alerts Alerts to show All (default), or Critical only Alerts Most at once 1, 2, 3 (default) or 5; a phone always shows one Alerts An alert you dismissed Stays hidden for 30 days (default), or Comes back on reload. An alert that gets worse is shown again either way Sound Play a sound with alerts Off by default. When on: a volume, and a switch and a Play button for each of three sounds: a new alert, a critical one (also when an alert gets worse), and an alert that is healthy again

The time zone applies to every clock time on the page: the cards, the charts and their tooltips, the alerts, the case view and the custom time range (what you type in it is read in that zone). Times such as 3m ago do not depend on it. The zone in use is written next to the Live indicator (for example UTC or UTC−03:00); click it to change it.

The sounds are generated in the browser, so there is nothing to download. They go with the card: the sound for a new alert plays as it appears, and the one for healthy plays as the card turns. When several happen at once only the most important is played. Browsers keep a page silent until you have clicked on it once, and the page says so when that is why nothing plays. Nothing is played when the page first loads, only for what changes while it is open.

Where they are kept: in the browser's local storage, under pgrr-dashboard-settings-v1 (everything but the theme), pgrr-theme (the theme, in its own key so it is applied before the page is first drawn) and pgrr-dashboard-dismissed-v1 (dismissed alerts, only while they are set to stay hidden). Local storage belongs to one browser and one address, port included, so another browser, another computer or a private window starts from the defaults, and clearing the site's data resets them. If the browser blocks storage the page works and simply forgets on reload. They are not part of the dashboard file and not saved by pgrr dashboard, so --no-save does not affect them.

docs.title: Make it yours
docs.text:
Boards are a grid of panels, 12 columns wide, rows 40 px high.

  • Edit layout (top right, wide screens): drag a panel by its bar, resize from the corner, move with the arrow keys (Shift+arrows to resize), hide with ×, add from the list. Undo my edits returns to the served layout. Edits are saved to your data directory (see Your edits are kept between runs).
  • Export YAML in edit mode writes the file below. It is byte-for-byte what config dump prints for the same layout.
  • Start from a file:
pg-regression-radar dashboard config dump > my-dashboard.yaml
pg-regression-radar dashboard config validate my-dashboard.yaml
pg-regression-radar dashboard --config my-dashboard.yaml

The file is read again on every page load, so editing it and reloading is enough. A file with problems is never half used: the page lists them, with line and column.

apiVersion: pgrr.io/v1
kind: Dashboard
boards:
  - id: now
    title: Now
    range: 6h              # 1m..90d, for example 15m, 6h, 7d
    panels:
      - id: summary
        type: summary
        at: [0, 0, 12, 4]  # x, y, width, height in cells
      - id: canary
        type: canary-chart
        at: [0, 4, 8, 10]
        description: "Canary against stable for the picked deploy."   # shown by the info button, 300 characters at most
        options: {viz: chart, unit: first, zero: false}
      - id: checkout-latency
        type: canary-chart
        at: [8, 4, 4, 10]
        title: "Checkout"
        query: "app:checkout namespace:payments"   # fields per panel type: dashboard config dump --catalog

Rules the validator enforces: at most 12 boards and 40 panels per board; unique ids; panels may not overlap or leave the 12 columns; each panel type has a minimum size; a panel's title is at most 80 characters and its description 300; unknown fields are reported with a suggestion (unnit → unit); a query must parse and use only fields its panel type takes (the error gives the column), an option's value must be one the panel type lists (dashboard config dump --catalog prints each option's label, group, values, default and, when it applies only to one visualization, when). dashboard config dump --catalog lists the panel types, their options and sizes. A file written for an older format is migrated; one written for a newer format is refused with the version it needs.

On narrow screens (under 900 px) panels stack in order and editing is hidden.

docs.title: Add a panel type
docs.text:
1. Go: add an entry to the catalog in internal/dashboard/layout/catalog.go: type name, title, default and minimum size, options (each with its kind and limits, a Label, a Group and a Doc sentence that the settings pane shows; viz is the choice of visualization, .when("viz=table") limits an option to one of them) and Help, the text its info button shows (a few sentences on what it shows and how to read it).
  2. UI: add internal/dashboard/ui/js/panels/<type>.js exporting build(type, host, ctx) that returns {render(view)}, and register it in panels/registry.js. A panel only reads the view it is given; it never fetches. Read its settings from ctx.options (defaults filled in) when it is built: a panel is built again whenever its title, description or settings change, so it never has to react to them. The settings pane needs no change.
  3. Add the panel to a preset in presets.go if it should ship by default, then regenerate the golden files:
go test ./internal/dashboard/layout -run Golden -update
  1. Add a case to internal/dashboard/uitest/panels-model.test.mjs for any logic, and check it by eye with the smoke test (DASHBOARD_URL=… SHOTS=dir node internal/dashboard/uitest/smoke.playwright.cjs).

An unknown type in a user's file is a validation error, not a crash; the UI shows a placeholder if the server and the page ever disagree.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Read-only toward the cluster: nothing in the page or the Observe API changes cluster state. The dashboard writes one thing, its own profile file in the data directory.
  • The real port-forward needs a real cluster; it is covered in tests by a fake API server, and by --url for everything else.
  • No user-written queries: panels read the datasets the Observe API serves.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• ADR-0002: A live dashboard — why it is local, read-only toward the cluster and opened with one command.
  • Security model — the dashboard's trust boundary, and how the file it saves is protected.
  • Persistence — the radar's optional Postgres state store, which is separate from the dashboard's own edits file.

docs.title: Deployment security hardening (Helm)
docs.text:
This guide covers optional Kubernetes hardening layers exposed by the Helm chart:

  • NetworkPolicy (default-deny + explicit allow rules)
  • ResourceQuota
  • LimitRange
  • Pod Security Standards (PSS) restricted

docs.title: NetworkPolicy
docs.text:
NetworkPolicy is disabled by default and can be enabled per release:

helm upgrade --install radar deploy/helm/deploylens \
  --set mode=manager \
  --set networkPolicy.enabled=true \
  --set networkPolicy.ingressCIDR=10.0.0.0/24 \
  --set networkPolicy.egress.postgresCIDRs[0]=10.10.0.0/16 \
  --set networkPolicy.egress.apiServerCIDRs[0]=10.20.0.0/16 \
  --set networkPolicy.egress.alertRelayCIDRs[0]=10.30.0.0/16

When enabled, the chart renders:

  • a mode-specific default-deny policy (Ingress + Egress)
  • a mode-specific allow policy with:
  • ingress for webhook and metrics ports
  • egress for PostgreSQL, API servers (manager mode), DNS, and alert relay CIDRs
flowchart LR
  IN["Webhook senders<br/>and Prometheus"]:::ext
  POD["radar pod<br/>default deny, plus allows"]:::radar
  PG[("PostgreSQL<br/>5432")]:::ext
  API["Kubernetes API server<br/>manager mode only"]:::ext
  DNS["Cluster DNS<br/>53 TCP and UDP"]:::ext
  AR["Alert relay<br/>and OTLP endpoint"]:::ext
  IN -->|"ingress: webhook and metrics ports"| POD
  POD -->|"egress"| PG
  POD -->|"egress"| API
  POD -->|"egress"| DNS
  POD -->|"egress"| AR

Everything not drawn is denied once the policy is enabled.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• networkPolicy.ingressCIDR is optional. If empty, ingress rules allow from any source.
  • DNS egress is enabled by default (kube-system namespace, port 53 TCP/UDP).
  • Keep CIDRs narrow and explicit for production.

docs.title: ResourceQuota and LimitRange
docs.text:
Enable namespace guardrails directly from chart values:

helm upgrade --install radar deploy/helm/deploylens \
  --set resourceQuota.enabled=true \
  --set limitRange.enabled=true

Defaults can be overridden in values:

  • resourceQuota.hard for aggregate namespace limits
  • limitRange.limits for per-container default requests/limits

See docs/examples/values-hardened.yaml for a complete example.

docs.title: Pod Security Standards (PSS) restricted
docs.text:
The chart defaults are compatible with PSS restricted expectations:

  • runAsNonRoot: true
  • runAsUser/runAsGroup: 65532
  • seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault
  • allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
  • capabilities.drop: [ALL]
  • readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
  • serviceAccount.automountServiceAccountToken: true (configurable)

Apply namespace Pod Security Admission labels as needed:

apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: pg-regression-radar
  labels:
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted

docs.title: ServiceAccount token automount
docs.text:
The chart now exposes serviceAccount.automountServiceAccountToken on both the ServiceAccount and Pod specs.

  • mode: manager: keep this true (required for in-cluster Kubernetes API access, reconciliation, and leader election).
  • mode: operator: can be set to false to reduce credential exposure when running without in-cluster API usage.

docs.title: Hardened values example
docs.text:
Use:

helm upgrade --install radar deploy/helm/deploylens \
  -f docs/examples/values-hardened.yaml

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
helm lint deploy/helm/deploylens
helm template radar deploy/helm/deploylens -f docs/examples/values-hardened.yaml >/dev/null

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• No NetworkPolicy created: verify networkPolicy.enabled=true.
  • Pods cannot reach PostgreSQL/API/relay: confirm destination CIDRs and ports in networkPolicy.egress.*.
  • DNS resolution failures: confirm cluster DNS runs in kube-system or adjust networkPolicy.egress.dns.namespace.
  • ResourceQuota/LimitRange missing: verify resourceQuota.enabled / limitRange.enabled.
  • PSS restricted rejection: check overridden security context values in custom values.yaml.

docs.title: Detection Algorithm
docs.text: The two-stage statistics behind every PerformanceRegression, why both stages have to agree, and how a regression gets a plan-diff attached.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Correlation Engine (internal/correlation) doesn't just compare a before/after mean — a naive comparison alone is prone to false positives whenever an unrelated latency shift happens to overlap the analysis window. This page explains the real two-stage pipeline it runs instead, inspired by Hunter — DataStax Labs and the accompanying ICPE'23 paper, "Hunter: Using Change Point Detection to Hunt for Performance Regressions".

flowchart TB
  A["Deploy event<br/>(or a periodic tick)"]:::radar
  B["Enough samples and<br/>executions in both windows?"]:::gate
  X["InsufficientData<br/>(retried until the window closes)"]:::gate
  C["Stage 0, pre-filter:<br/>mean changed by the threshold or more?"]:::gate
  D["Stage 1, E-divisive means:<br/>locate the change point"]:::radar
  E["Change point within the<br/>tolerance of the deploy?"]:::gate
  F["Stage 2, Welch t-test on the<br/>two real segments: significant?"]:::radar
  M["Multiple-testing control<br/>(opt-in): survives?"]:::gate
  Y["NoRegression"]:::gate
  G["Detected<br/>alert + PerformanceRegression"]:::out
  A --> B
  B -->|"no"| X
  B -->|"yes"| C
  C -->|"no"| Y
  C -->|"yes"| D
  D --> E
  E -->|"no"| Y
  E -->|"yes"| F
  F -->|"no"| Y
  F -->|"yes"| M
  M -->|"no"| Y
  M -->|"yes"| G

A query is reported only when every gate agrees: precision over recall.

docs.title: What a latency sample is
docs.text:
pg_stat_statements does not report the latency of the last scrape interval. calls and total_exec_time are counters that accumulate from the last reset, and mean_exec_time is their ratio, an average over the query's whole history. Feeding that value to a change-point test hides regressions: after a million calls at 10 ms, a query that becomes 5x slower for fifteen minutes moves the all-time mean from 10.0 ms to about 10.4 ms. A reset has the opposite effect and shows up as a step in the series that looks like a latency change.

The Collector therefore calculates the activity since the previous snapshot of each (dbid, userid, queryid, toplevel) row, then combines those intervals per queryid:

row interval calls = calls_now - calls_prev
row interval time  = total_exec_time_now - total_exec_time_prev
query interval mean = sum(row interval time) / sum(row interval calls)

The engine runs its statistics on this series:

  • Interval means are the series. Stage 1 and stage 2 read the per-interval mean. The reported MeanLatencyBefore/MeanLatencyAfter are total time over total calls in each window, so busy intervals weigh more than quiet ones.
  • Intervals with no calls are dropped. They carry no latency information. The first scrape of a queryid, a changed set of constituent rows, or an expired predecessor leaves an unknown interval, which is dropped too. Unknown collector intervals never fall back to cumulative-mean analysis. --min-samples and --min-executions are checked against what remains, see Minimum samples and minimum executions.
  • Resets are detected, not trusted. The counters are considered restarted when calls or total_exec_time decreases (pg_stat_statements_reset(), a crash, or eviction once pg_stat_statements.max is exceeded), or, on PostgreSQL 17+, when stats_since changes. The second signal also catches a reset whose counters have already climbed past their old values by the next scrape. After a reset the counters start from zero, so the new values are the activity since the reset and are used as that interval. Each detection increments pg_regression_radar_collector_stats_resets_detected_total.
  • History survives restarts. New persisted samples retain the calculated interval fields and their known/unknown state. Backfill preserves them instead of subtracting aggregate cumulative counters, which would mishandle independent row resets. Old cumulative-only records keep the legacy reconstruction behavior; missing row identities cannot be recovered retroactively. The first live scrape after restart establishes fresh row baselines.

Reset detection happens per row before aggregation. The aggregate marks a reset if any constituent row reset; its other rows still contribute only their own increments. See Collector Internals for the 500-row selection limit and row-membership changes.

The collector also exports the latest value as pg_regression_radar_query_interval_mean_exec_time_ms{queryid}.

Samples that carry no interval data (a source that only exposes a mean, such as the OTel/Prometheus source) are analysed on that value as before. For that source, the configured metric must already be a per-interval mean.

Limits: the series is made of interval means, so the t-test measures variation between scrape intervals, not between individual calls, and a long gap between scrapes yields one interval that spans the gap. Per-call variance (stddev_exec_time) is not used yet.

docs.title: Minimum samples and minimum executions
docs.text:
Two floors, applied to each of the pre- and post-deploy windows, decide whether a query has enough data for a verdict. A query that misses either one is reported as InsufficientData and, for deploy-triggered analysis, retried until the window closes.

Floor Flag Default Counts Samples --min-samples 10 Observations: scrape intervals in which the query ran at least once. Executions --min-executions 100 Calls to the query, summed over those observations.

They protect different things, which is why one number cannot do both jobs. Ten observations may be ten calls or ten million, and neither tells you how well the window's mean latency is known.

Samples protect the machinery. E-divisive means and Welch's t-test estimate a spread from the observations themselves, so they need enough points to do it. The R ecp package, the reference implementation of E-divisive means (Matteson and James, 2014), defaults to a minimum of 30 observations between change points; MongoDB's production deployment of the same method (Daly et al., ICPE 2020) lowered it to 3 in exchange for faster notification. The default of 10 sits between them and matches what --min-executions effectively enforced before the two were separated.

Executions protect the precision of the mean. The standard error of a mean of N calls is CV / sqrt(N), where CV is the coefficient of variation of per-call latency. To detect a relative change of delta with 5% significance and 80% power, each window needs roughly

N = 2 * (1.96 + 0.84)^2 * CV^2 / delta^2  ~=  15.7 * CV^2 / delta^2
Relative change to detect CV = 1 CV = 2 20% (the default --latency-threshold) ~390 ~1,570 30% ~175 ~700 50% ~63 ~250

Below that, the test is not wrong, it is underpowered: a "no regression" verdict would mean "could not tell". The default of 100 is a floor under which a verdict is not worth reporting, not a promise of 80% power. Raise it for queries with heavy-tailed latency or when you need to catch small changes; lower it for demos and tests.

What the floors do not do:

  • They do not control false positives. The p-value threshold does that. In simulations of per-call log-normal latency with Poisson traffic, Welch's t-test on per-interval means stayed close to its nominal 5% size even with one-call intervals, and a traffic step with no latency change stayed near 0% Detected through the full pipeline. Both results assume independent noise; with serially correlated noise the false-positive rate is higher (see what the p-value and the confidence score mean). The floors decide when to answer, not how often a wrong answer is raised.
  • They do not merge intervals. Merging consecutive intervals until each holds a minimum number of calls was tested and rejected: it left the test size unchanged, reduced the number of observations, cost power, and delayed detection (at 3 calls per interval, a +50% regression was found in 78% of trials unmerged and 0% when merged to 30 calls per observation, which left about a dozen observations per window).
  • They need call counts. Executions are known only for samples the Collector produced. A source that reports just a mean, such as the OTel/Prometheus source, is gated by --min-samples alone.

docs.title: Stage 0: cheap pre-filter
docs.text: The naive mean latency over the whole pre-deploy window is compared against the naive mean over the whole post-deploy window. If the relative change is below LatencyChangeThreshold (default 20%), the query is rejected immediately without running the more expensive stages below.

docs.title: Stage 1: E-divisive means (locate)
docs.text:
For queries that pass the pre-filter, the pre- and post-deploy samples are merged into a single chronologically-ordered series covering the whole analysis window, and the E-divisive means algorithm (energy-statistic based change-point detection; Matteson & James, 2014, JASA) locates the single most significant change point in that series.

Crucially, this does not assume the shift happens exactly at the deploy timestamp — rolling updates, connection draining, and collector scrape lag all delay the observable effect of a deploy by anywhere from seconds to a few minutes. The located change point must fall within ChangePointTolerance of the deploy timestamp (default: 20% of the analysis window, floored at 2 minutes) to be considered related to that deploy at all.

If E-divisive finds no change point, or the one it finds is too far from the deploy, the query is marked NoRegression — even if the naive pre/post means from stage 0 looked like a regression.

docs.title: Stage 2: Welch's t-test (confirm)
docs.text: The two segments actually defined by the change point E-divisive found (not the naive deploy-timestamp split) are compared with Welch's t-test to confirm the difference in means is statistically significant (configurable p-value threshold, default p < 0.05). The p-value is reported as pValue, and ConfidenceScore is derived from it as 1 - pValue; read What the p-value and the confidence score mean before relying on either.

docs.title: What the p-value and the confidence score mean
docs.text:
pValue is the probability of seeing a latency difference at least as large as the one observed between the two segments if the query's latency had not changed at all. confidenceScore is 1 - pValue, kept as a convenient number that grows with significance. It is not a probability, and it should not be read as one:

  • It is not the probability that the regression is real. A p-value conditions on "nothing changed"; the probability that something changed requires a prior, which the test does not have. The American Statistical Association's statement on p-values (Wasserstein and Lazar, 2016) names this misreading among its principles. The calibration of Sellke, Bayarri and Berger (2001) shows how far apart the two can be: for p below 1/e and a broad class of alternatives (symmetric and unimodal around "no change"), the evidence against "no change" is at most 1 / (-e * p * ln p), so with even odds of a change beforehand the probability that nothing changed is at least:
pValue confidenceScore Lowest possible probability that nothing changed 0.05 0.95 29% 0.02 0.98 18% 0.01 0.99 11% 0.001 0.999 1.8%

A confidenceScore of 0.98 therefore leaves at least a one-in-six chance that the shift is noise, under that prior, and usually more. - It is optimistic, because the split was chosen from the same data. Stage 1 picks the most extreme split and stage 2 tests it as if it had been fixed in advance. This is the known problem of maximally selected statistics, whose p-values need a correction that accounts for the search (Miller and Siegmund, 1982; Lausen and Schumacher, 1992; see the R maxstat package). E-divisive means itself judges significance with a permutation test over the whole search, not with a t-test at the chosen split. Measured with this project's own E-divisive and Welch code on series with no change at all (1,500 per row, 30 to 240 points): with independent noise, 35-39% had p < 0.05 and 11-17% had p < 0.01 at the split E-divisive chose; with first-order autocorrelation of 0.5 and 0.8, 60-90% and 85-99% had p < 0.05. Through the whole engine (120 samples per side, --latency-threshold 0.20, change-point tolerance, p threshold), the share of no-change analyses reported as Detected was 0-2% with independent noise but up to 8% with autocorrelated, heavy-tailed noise, and lowering the p threshold from 0.05 to 0.01 barely changed that (5.5-6%). Those false detections have tiny p-values, so they also clear autoAbort.confidenceThreshold. These are simulated series (AR(1) log-latency, 100 calls per interval), not production traces. See the Roadmap for the calibration work. - It says nothing about the cause. The deploy is blamed because the change point falls close to it in time. A confident shift near a deploy can still come from load, a plan flip or a neighbour. - It is per query. Across hundreds of queries and many deploys, some will clear any threshold by chance; the p-value does not account for that. Controlling false positives across many queries describes the opt-in correction.

In practice: treat pValue as the number to read, confidenceScore as a threshold knob (autoAbort.confidenceThreshold: "0.99" means pValue <= 0.01), and the change factor and detectedChangeAt as the evidence a person should look at. pValue is absent, not zero, when the test did not run, for example for an InsufficientData result.

docs.title: Controlling false positives across many queries
docs.text:
One pass judges every tracked query, up to the top 500 that pg_stat_statements keeps, and periodic detection repeats that on every tick. Each query is tested against pValueThreshold on its own, so the chance that some unchanged query is reported grows with the number of queries. Two opt-in settings address the two ways the per-query p-value goes wrong at that scale. Both are off by default, and with both off every p-value and verdict is exactly what it was before they existed.

Setting Flag / PostgresWatch field What it does Multiple-testing control --multiple-testing / multipleTesting: none (default), bh, by Applies the Benjamini-Hochberg (bh) or Benjamini-Yekutieli (by) step-up across the queries of one pass, at level pValueThreshold, and demotes the detections that do not survive to NoRegression. Autocorrelation adjustment --adjust-autocorrelation / adjustAutocorrelation Widens Welch's t-test for correlation between consecutive scrapes.

docs.title: Multiple-testing control
docs.text:
The step-up procedures bound the expected share of false detections among the queries a pass reports (the false-discovery rate), not the chance of any false detection, which is what a Bonferroni correction would bound and is far stricter. bh (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995) is valid when the p-values are independent or positively dependent, which is the usual situation for queries that share one server's load (Benjamini and Yekutieli, 2001). by divides the level by the harmonic sum 1 + 1/2 + ... + 1/m, which makes it valid under any dependence and costs a factor of about seven at 500 queries.

The family is every query the pass could judge, meaning every result that is not InsufficientData. A query that failed a gate (too small a change, no change point, a change point far from the deploy) counts toward m as a test that did not reject. Only queries already marked Detected can be rejected, so the correction can remove a detection but never add one. A demoted result keeps its raw pValue, so it can still be inspected, and loses its confidenceScore and detectedChangeAt.

Counting the unrejected queries is what makes the statement hold for the whole pass, and it is also what makes it strict: among 500 judged queries the smallest p-value must be below 0.05 / 500 = 0.0001 to survive. That is the intended trade, and it has a real cost in sensitivity for modest regressions in noisy queries (see the table below). It does not correct across passes: a deploy that is re-analysed as its post-deploy window fills, and each periodic tick, is a new pass.

docs.title: Autocorrelation adjustment
docs.text: Consecutive scrapes of one query are not independent, since a cache warming, a batch job or a noisy neighbour moves many scrapes the same way, and Welch's test treats each scrape as a new observation. With --adjust-autocorrelation each segment's n observations are replaced by an effective sample size n (1 - r) / (1 + r), where r is the lag-1 autocorrelation of the two segments pooled, each around its own mean (the AR(1) correction of Zwiers and von Storch, 1995). The effective size is held between 2 and n, and a negative r is not used to enlarge the sample, so the adjustment can only raise a p-value. On pairs of equal-mean AR(1) segments of 30 points with r = 0.7, plain Welch called 43% significant at 0.05 and the adjusted test 11% (4,000 pairs). The correction is approximate: with short segments r is estimated with a downward bias, so the test stays somewhat liberal, and it does nothing about the selection effect described under what the p-value means.

docs.title: What it buys and what it costs
docs.text:
The table runs this project's own engine on 500 simulated queries per pass with no change at all, plus five queries with a real +50% regression at the deploy, over 120 passes (deploy-triggered, 30-minute windows, one-minute scrapes, 200 calls per scrape). Each cell is false detections per pass / share of the five real regressions found. The noise is simulated (lognormal latency, AR(1) where stated), not production traces.

Noise in each query's latency none bh adjustment only bh + adjustment independent, CV 15% 0 / 100% 0 / 100% 0 / 100% 0 / 100% independent, CV 30% 2.9 / 95% 0.5 / 91% 2.9 / 95% 0.4 / 88% independent, CV 60% 15.4 / 57% 0.2 / 7% 14.0 / 56% 0.1 / 5% 5% of scrapes spike 4x, CV 15% 7.7 / 80% 0.0 / 15% 6.0 / 77% 0.0 / 14% autocorrelated, r = 0.7, CV 30% 32.6 / 64% 31.1 / 63% 21.5 / 55% 3.2 / 17%

Three things stand out. Quiet queries produce no false detections to begin with, because the latencyChangeThreshold gate removes them. For independent but noisy queries, bh removes nearly all the chance detections. For autocorrelated queries bh alone does almost nothing, because the p-values are already too small before it runs and a correction cannot repair them; it works only together with the adjustment. And in every noisy case the cost is sensitivity: a +50% regression in a query whose latency varies by 60% is not distinguishable from noise across 500 tests, and the table shows it. If that matters more than the false detections, leave the settings off and rank by the change factor instead.

The comparison is a design choice grounded in the literature on change-point detection for performance testing. MongoDB's deployment and DataStax's Hunter do not apply false-discovery-rate control; they filter on a minimum effect size, rank by magnitude and work on reducing noise, and both state that the method does not handle correlated noise. Online false-discovery-rate procedures such as ADDIS assume independent p-values, which overlapping analysis windows do not give, and exact post-selection p-values for change points (Jewell, Fearnhead and Witten) assume independent Gaussian noise with a known variance and cover other detection algorithms than E-divisive means.

docs.title: Both stages must agree
docs.text:
A PerformanceRegression is only marked Detected when the change point is found, lies near the deploy, and the t-test on the real segments is significant. This two-stage design prioritises precision over recall to avoid alert fatigue.

The change point's own timestamp is preserved on the result as DetectedChangeAt, so you can see exactly when the shift was located — which may differ slightly from the deploy event's timestamp, within the configured tolerance.

docs.title: Detection and attribution are different questions
docs.text: The two stages above answer did this query's latency change near this deploy? They cannot answer did the deploy cause it?: a statistics refresh, a load shock, a cold cache or a concurrent deploy produces the same step, and a query whose text changed has a new queryid and no history. The opt-in attribution engine asks the second question, by comparing each query with what a control built from untouched queries (or a canary arm) says it would have done without the deploy. It runs next to this detector: Detected and its alerts are unchanged, and the engine only ever acts through a verdict that a rollout controller chooses to read.

docs.title: Plan-diff correlation (optional)
docs.text: A PerformanceRegression says that a query got slower and roughly when, but not why on its own. Opt-in, default off, adds a short plan-diff hint by periodically capturing an execution plan for each tracked queryid and diffing the snapshot from just before the detected change point against the most recent one (internal/planner.Diff) — --capture-plans on the standalone operator CLI, or spec.capturePlans: true on a PostgresWatch in the CRD-driven (cmd/manager) mode. Both paths call the same internal/planner/Collector.PlansAround machinery and land the result in the same place: the standalone CLI's Slack notification gets a "Plan Diff" field, and a PostgresWatch's resulting PerformanceRegression custom resource gets status.planDiffSummary.

docs.title: Two sources, in order of preference
docs.text:
There are two ways to get that plan, and they are not equally trustworthy:

Source What it captures Reliability pg_store_plans (planner.CapturePlanFromStorePlans) The real plan PostgreSQL actually used for a past execution of that queryid, read from the pg_store_plans contrib-style extension's pg_store_plans view — the same idea as pg_stat_statements, but for plans. High — this is what really ran. EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON, GENERIC_PLAN) (planner.CaptureGenericPlan) An estimated plan the planner produces right now, without executing the query, for the normalized query text pg_stat_statements recorded. pg_stat_statements normalises query text, replacing every literal value with a $1/$2/... placeholder — a plain EXPLAIN cannot run against that text without real bound parameter values, so it fails with "there is no parameter $1". PostgreSQL 16 added GENERIC_PLAN specifically to solve this (see pganalyze's writeup and Cybertec's). Requires PostgreSQL 16+. Lower — table statistics, index availability, and even the query's own parameter values may have changed since the original slow execution, so the estimate is not guaranteed to match the plan that actually caused the regression.

internal/planner.CapturePlan(ctx, db, queryID, queryText) is the facade the collector calls: it tries pg_store_plans first and falls back to GENERIC_PLAN on any failure (extension missing, untrusted, no row yet, or an unexpected database error), returning an error only when neither source produces a plan — CloudNativePG supports PostgreSQL 14+, and below PG16 without a usable pg_store_plans install, that error is ErrUnsupportedVersion, logged once at Info level, and the collector otherwise runs exactly as before. Every PlanSnapshot carries a Source field ("pg_store_plans" or "generic_plan") precisely so a caller — or a Slack alert rendering Diff's output — can flag when a diff is being shown on an estimate rather than a real execution; Diff itself appends a caution line whenever either side of the comparison is "generic_plan".

docs.title: Why pg_store_plans isn't always trusted just because it's installed
docs.text:
pg_store_plans's queryid column is, in current releases, the same core-generated query identifier pg_stat_statements uses — the upstream docs state this plainly and even show JOIN pg_store_plans USING (queryid) against pg_stat_statements as the intended usage. That compatibility is not unconditional, though, so internal/planner (detectStorePlans in storeplans.go) checks three things before trusting a pg_store_plans queryid enough to correlate it with a pg_stat_statements queryid from the collector:

  1. Extension version >= 1.6. Per the pg_store_plans 1.6 release notes, that release "removed the column queryid_stat_statements and now the column queryid shows the core generated query id." Before 1.6, pg_store_plans computed its own queryid with its own algorithm and needed the separate queryid_stat_statements column specifically to cross-reference pg_stat_statements — meaning a pre-1.6 queryid is not safe to join directly. (The upstream HTML docs still contain a sentence claiming queryid "is calculated ... in a different algorithm" than pg_stat_statements, which reads as leftover pre-1.6 prose that contradicts the same page's own column reference table; we treat the release notes and column table as authoritative and the stray sentence as a documentation bug, but fail closed on old versions regardless.)
  2. Server is PostgreSQL 14+. Upstream's docs explicitly scope the queryid-join guarantee to "PostgreSQL 14 or later" — consistent with 14 being the first version with the core compute_query_id GUC that pg_store_plans >= 1.6 relies on.
  3. compute_query_id is not off. Upstream: "pg_store_plans requires the GUC variable compute_query_id to be 'on' or 'auto'. If it is set to [off], pg_store_plans is silently disabled." A disabled extension can still be present in pg_extension and even still hold stale rows, so this is checked explicitly rather than inferred from installation alone.

If any of these don't hold, CapturePlanFromStorePlans returns ErrQueryIDUnreliable (with a specific reason) instead of a snapshot, and CapturePlan falls back to GENERIC_PLAN. This version/GUC gating is validated against a real pg_store_plans install, not just a fake *sql.DB — see Testing → Real pg_store_plans extension for the real, PGXS-compiled server internal/planner/storeplans_integration_test.go runs against in CI, which executes a real parameterized query and asserts CapturePlanFromStorePlans reads back the exact real plan pg_store_plans recorded for it.

docs.title: What it captures, and how much
docs.text:
Once per scrape cycle (not once per query — this stays bounded), the collector runs CapturePlan for every query already in that cycle's pg_stat_statements read (the same top-500 set the scrape itself uses, no separate query universe) and retains the last 5 plan snapshots per queryid in a small in-memory ring — plans change far less often than latency samples, so this doesn't need --retention-minutes' time-based mechanism.

When a regression is Detected, the operator's poll loop compares the plan the query had before its most recent plan change with the current plan, provided that change was first seen within the analysis window before the change point or the deploy (otherwise the plan is stable and the diff reads "unchanged"). The plan history is change-based, one entry per distinct plan stamped with when it first appeared, so a deploy that flips a plan is not lost by the time --min-samples post-deploy scrapes have accumulated. The diff covers: whether the root plan node changed, whether the estimated cost moved meaningfully, and — per the caution line above — whether either side is only an estimate. The result is attached to the PerformanceRegression as PlanDiffSummary and included in the Slack message when non-empty.

docs.title: Excluding capture's own footprint from tracking
docs.text:
When CapturePlans is enabled, the collector's GENERIC_PLAN capture literally runs EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON, GENERIC_PLAN) <query text> against the target database. If pg_stat_statements.track is set to all (rather than the default top) — or anything else that tracks utility statements — that EXPLAIN call gets recorded by pg_stat_statements as a brand-new query in its own right, distinct from the query it was EXPLAINing. Left alone, this causes two problems on the next scrape cycle:

  • Plan capture would try to EXPLAIN that ghost entry too, producing EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON, GENERIC_PLAN) EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON, GENERIC_PLAN) <original query>, which PostgreSQL correctly rejects with a syntax error. Harmless by itself, but it grows without bound every cycle capture runs, and it's noise that obscures whether capture is actually working for real queries.
  • The correlation engine would keep accumulating that ghost entry's own latency samples, which could in principle trip stage 0/1/2 above and produce a PerformanceRegression for a query that was never really run by the application — a false positive with no real query behind it.

internal/collector.isExplainStatement guards against both: any pg_stat_statements row whose (trimmed, case-insensitive) query text starts with EXPLAIN is skipped entirely during scrape — excluded from both ingestSample (so it can never feed the correlation engine) and the tracked-query list capturePlans consumes (so it's never re-EXPLAIN'd). Skipped rows increment the pg_regression_radar_collector_explain_statements_skipped_total counter metric; a sustained non-zero rate is expected whenever CapturePlans is on under track=all, and would only be worth investigating if it appears with CapturePlans off (which would mean something other than this collector is issuing raw EXPLAINs against the tracked database).

docs.title: Honest limitations
docs.text:
• GENERIC_PLAN, when that's the source actually used, is an estimate, not a real one. It reflects the planner's default, parameter-independent cost estimate — it can differ from the plan Postgres would actually choose for a real, skewed parameter value (e.g. a highly selective vs. a common value for the same column). Treat a "generic_plan"-sourced diff as a hint pointing you toward EXPLAIN ANALYZE-ing the real query yourself, not a substitute for it. This caveat does not apply when Source is "pg_store_plans", since that plan is what actually ran.
  • No real auto_explain integration. This deliberately does not ingest real auto_explain log output, which would give a third, independent way to recover a real per-parameter plan. That remains a heavier lift (a log-shipping pipeline) left as a documented follow-up — see Roadmap.

docs.title: Deduplicating a queryid rotation
docs.text:
pg_stat_statements' queryid is not guaranteed stable across a deploy (see Collector Internals), so AllQueryIDs() can enumerate both the pre-rotation and post-rotation queryid for what is really a single query. Once the collector's fingerprint-merge fallback has kicked in for either side, SamplesInRange for both queryids returns the identical merged sample set — so evaluating both, unguarded, would run the two-stage pipeline above twice on the same data and emit two PerformanceRegressions for one real regression.

Engine.Analyse prevents this: before evaluating a queryid, it looks at the Fingerprint of the most recently recorded sample in its (possibly merged) sample set. The first queryid — in sorted, deterministic order — to surface a given fingerprint is evaluated; every later queryid sharing that fingerprint is skipped, since it would only re-evaluate the same merged data. The one PerformanceRegression that is produced is reported under whichever queryid most recently received a sample (not necessarily the queryid that happened to win the dedup check), so it points at the "live" identity still receiving traffic in pg_stat_statements rather than one that may have already aged out.

This guarantees at most one PerformanceRegression per distinct query per Analyse call, regardless of how many queryids pg_stat_statements currently associates with it.
