docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: Prerequisites and the fastest path to a running pg-regression-radar, in any of its three supported forms.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
pg-regression-radar ships two runnable entrypoints (operator and manager) plus a Helm chart that wraps both. This page assumes you already have the binaries, the container image, or a clone of the repo — see Installation if you don't yet. It covers the minimal command to get each form running; see Architecture Overview for which one to pick, and Configuration Reference for every flag and CRD field used below.

The commands below use go run ./cmd/operator/go run ./cmd/manager, which assume a clone of the repo. If you installed the unified CLI instead (see Installation, option 1), replace go run ./cmd/operator with pg-regression-radar operator and go run ./cmd/manager with pg-regression-radar manager — every flag below is identical either way.

If your goal is to prove end-to-end behavior (regression detection + deployment attribution) instead of only bringing services up, follow Quickstart Validation and Example regression scenario after startup.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Go 1.22+ (only needed to build from source; the Dockerfile needs no local Go install)
  • A Postgres cluster with pg_stat_statements enabled — see Support Matrix for officially supported versions/distributions
  • A least-privilege Postgres role for --dsn — see the Creating a least-privilege Postgres role section in the Installation guide. Never use a superuser or application-owner DSN.
  • (Optional) ArgoCD, Argo Rollouts, or Flux for real deploy-event webhooks — see Deploy Sources & Webhooks

docs.title: Run the all-in-one operator
docs.text:
go run ./cmd/operator \
  --dsn "postgres://user:password@localhost:5432/mydb?sslmode=disable" \
  --cluster-name my-cluster \
  --namespace production \
  --webhook-listen :8080 \
  --metrics-listen :9090 \
  --slack-url https://hooks.slack.com/services/XXX/YYY/ZZZ \
  --source-type argocd \
  --window-minutes 30 \
  --min-samples 10 \
  --min-executions 100 \
  --latency-threshold 0.20

docs.title: Run the manager (CRD-driven, HA)
docs.text:
# 1. Install the CRDs (also done automatically by the Helm chart below).
kubectl apply -f config/crd/bases/

# 2. Create a Secret holding the DSN, a PostgresWatch, and a DeploySource.
kubectl create secret generic my-cluster-dsn \
  --from-literal=dsn="postgres://user:password@cnpg-cluster-rw.production:5432/mydb?sslmode=require"

cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: radar.pgregressionradar.io/v1alpha1
kind: PostgresWatch
metadata:
  name: my-cluster
  namespace: production
spec:
  clusterName: cnpg-cluster
  dsnSecretRef:
    name: my-cluster-dsn
    key: dsn
  windowMinutes: 30
  minSamples: 10
  minExecutions: 100
  latencyChangeThreshold: "0.20"
  slackWebhookUrl: "https://hooks.slack.com/services/XXX/YYY/ZZZ"
---
apiVersion: radar.pgregressionradar.io/v1alpha1
kind: DeploySource
metadata:
  name: my-cluster-argocd
  namespace: production
spec:
  postgresWatchRef: my-cluster
  sourceType: argocd
EOF

# 3. Run the manager (in-cluster it reads a ServiceAccount token
#    automatically; --kubeconfig is only for out-of-cluster/local runs).
go run ./cmd/manager \
  --leader-elect=true \
  --leader-election-namespace=production \
  --webhook-bind-address=:8080 \
  --pg-metrics-bind-address=:9090

# 4. Watch it come up and, later, watch regressions land as CRs.
kubectl get postgreswatch,deploysource -n production
kubectl get performanceregressions -A

docs.title: Deploy on Kubernetes via Helm
docs.text:
helm install pg-regression-radar ./deploy/helm/deploylens \
  --set postgres.dsn="postgres://user:password@cnpg-cluster-rw.production:5432/mydb?sslmode=require" \
  --set postgres.clusterName=cnpg-cluster \
  --set postgres.namespace=production \
  --set alerting.slackWebhookUrl=https://hooks.slack.com/services/XXX/YYY/ZZZ

The chart's mode value picks the entrypoint (operator, the default above, or manager). In manager mode it also installs the CRDs (deploy/helm/deploylens/crds/), the RBAC the manager needs, and — unless manager.createDefaultWatch=false — a PostgresWatch + DeploySource pair from the same postgres.*/analysis.*/alerting.* values:

helm install pg-regression-radar ./deploy/helm/deploylens \
  --set mode=manager \
  --set manager.replicaCount=2 \
  --set postgres.dsn="postgres://user:password@cnpg-cluster-rw.production:5432/mydb?sslmode=require" \
  --set postgres.clusterName=cnpg-cluster \
  --set alerting.slackWebhookUrl=https://hooks.slack.com/services/XXX/YYY/ZZZ

For hardened alert egress in Helm, set alerting.destinationPolicy (allowlist or relay-only) and the matching companion values (alerting.allowedDestinations and/or alerting.destinationPolicyRelayUrl) — see Alerting: destination policies.

Note

Helm only installs a chart's crds/ directory on helm install, never on helm upgrade — this is a deliberate Helm safety behaviour, not a bug in this chart (see the Helm docs on CRDs). To pick up CRD schema changes after upgrading the chart, apply deploy/helm/deploylens/crds/*.yaml (or config/crd/bases/*.yaml, the same files) with kubectl apply -f directly.

docs.title: Simulate a deploy event (for testing)
docs.text:
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/webhook \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "app": "my-app",
    "namespace": "production",
    "revision": "abc123def456",
    "imageTag": "my-app:v42",
    "timestamp": "2026-08-11T12:00:00Z"
  }'

That payload matches the generic source type (the default), which accepts a DeployEvent shape directly — see API Reference.

docs.title: What "detecting a regression" looks like
docs.text:
In practice, successful detection means more than "the process stayed running." You should eventually observe:

  • a specific query identified as regressed,
  • measurable before/after latency change,
  • deploy metadata (app/namespace/revision/image) attached to the same finding.

Depending on mode and configuration, this appears in logs, in PerformanceRegression resources (manager mode), and/or in alert destinations (for example Slack). For a reproducible validation flow with expected outcomes, follow Quickstart Validation.

docs.title: Troubleshooting common setup issues
docs.text:
A short list of first-run symptoms. For the full guide, see Troubleshooting.

  • No deploy events are being ingested: verify your webhook URL/path (/webhook), source type, and authentication header if --webhook-secret is enabled.
  • No regression detected yet: increase traffic volume for the target query, verify pg_stat_statements is enabled, and check detection thresholds (windowMinutes, minSamples, minExecutions, latency threshold).
  • Manager exits with address already in use on startup: the health probe endpoint listens on :8081 by default (--health-probe-bind-address). If that port is already taken (for example by another manager instance), set a free port, for example --health-probe-bind-address=:18081.
  • Manager mode does not produce resources: confirm CRDs are installed and check namespace-scoped PostgresWatch/DeploySource reconciliation status.
  • Helm manager mode seems missing CRDs on upgrade: Helm installs crds/ only on initial install; apply updated CRDs manually as noted above.
  • Alerts not delivered: validate webhook destination config and any egress/destination policy restrictions.

docs.title: Index 1
docs.text:
PostgreSQL on Kubernetes # pg-regression-radar

Detects PostgreSQL query performance regressions and pinpoints which Kubernetes deployment caused them.

[Get started](installation.md){ .md-button .md-button--primary } [How it works](#how-it-works){ .md-button } Example alertRegression QuerySELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = $1 Latency4.1 ms → 38.6 ms×9.4 Deploycheckout-api · revision=v2 Confidence0.97

Illustrative values.

## The problem Teams running Postgres on Kubernetes (CloudNativePG, Zalando, Crunchy, Percona...) deploy applications many times a day via GitOps (ArgoCD, Flux, Argo Rollouts). When query latency spikes, the first question in every post-mortem is:

Which deploy caused this?

Today that question is answered manually: open Grafana, look at `pg_stat_statements`, try to recall when the last deploy happened, cross-reference timestamps by eye. No open-source tool closes that loop automatically. **pg-regression-radar does.** ## Regression capture Watching 4 queries Inject deploy

Simulated data. Hover the chart to pause and inspect it, pick a query, then inject a deploy.

## How it works pg-regression-radar architecture Postgres and deploy sources feed the Collector and the Deploy Event Ingester, which write into an in-memory time-series store read by the Correlation Engine, which fires Alerting and, in manager mode, a PerformanceRegression status. A rolling schedule can also trigger the Correlation Engine directly, independent of any deploy. scrape webhook / watch samples deploy events on a schedule alert manager mode Postgres pg_stat_statements Deploy sources ArgoCD, Rollouts, Flux, K8s Collector bounded in-memory series Deploy event ingester normalised DeployEvent records Rolling schedule periodic, no deploy needed Correlation engine E-divisive change point + Welch's t-test Alerting Slack, Teams, PagerDuty, custom Regression status PerformanceRegression CRD 1 Collector

Scrapes `pg_stat_statements` on an interval and keeps a bounded in-memory time series per `queryid`.

[Architecture Overview](architecture.md) [Collector Internals](collector-internals.md)

2 Deploy Event Ingester

Receives webhooks from ArgoCD, Argo Rollouts, and Flux and stores normalised `DeployEvent` records.

[Deploy Sources & Webhooks](webhooks.md)

3 Correlation Engine

Runs a real two-stage detection for every deploy event: E-divisive change-point location, then Welch's t-test confirmation.

[Detection Algorithm](detection-algorithm.md)

4 Alerting

Fires a Slack-compatible webhook with the query text, latency before/after, change factor, and confidence score.

[Alerting](alerting.md)

## Where to go next - New to the project? Start with [Installation](installation.md), then [Getting Started](getting-started.md). - Deciding between the two ways to run it? See [Architecture Overview](architecture.md). - Looking for a specific flag or CRD field? See [Configuration Reference](configuration.md). - Want to contribute? See [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) in the repo root.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: How to obtain the binaries, the container image, or the Helm chart.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Every tagged release (git tag vX.Y.Z, matching CI/CD's release.yml workflow) publishes five container images and one Helm chart to ghcr.io/joao00001 — see Option 3 and Option 4 below. Building from source (cloning the repo, or go install directly from the module proxy) still works exactly as before and is the only option for anything unreleased. This page covers obtaining pg-regression-radar; see Getting Started for actually running it once installed.

flowchart TB
  Q1["Running in Kubernetes?"]:::gate
  Q2["Need a container image?"]:::gate
  Q3["Need unreleased code?"]:::gate
  H["Option 4: Helm chart"]:::out
  I["Option 3: container image"]:::out
  S["Option 2: build from source"]:::out
  G["Option 1: go install"]:::out
  Q1 -->|"yes"| H
  Q1 -->|"no"| Q2
  Q2 -->|"yes"| I
  Q2 -->|"no"| Q3
  Q3 -->|"yes"| S
  Q3 -->|"no"| G

Pick the first option that fits; go install is the simplest when none of the others applies.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Go 1.22+ (to build from source)
  • Docker (to build the container image)
  • A Postgres cluster with pg_stat_statements enabled — see Support Matrix for officially supported PostgreSQL versions (16, 17, 18) and distributions (community, CloudNativePG, EDB Postgres Advanced/Extended Server)
  • kubectl and/or helm (only for the Kubernetes-deployed paths)

docs.title: Creating a least-privilege Postgres role
docs.text:
pg-regression-radar only needs to read pg_stat_statements and a handful of catalog views — it never writes to user data. Do not use a superuser or a role with broad privileges for --dsn. If the connection string is ever leaked (e.g. via a misrouted Secret), the blast radius should be limited to read-only statistics access.

Create a dedicated role before installing pg-regression-radar:

-- Create the role with login but no superuser privileges.
CREATE ROLE pgrr_monitor WITH LOGIN PASSWORD 'change-me';

-- Built-in role that grants read access to pg_stat_statements, pg_stat_*
-- views, and other monitoring functions — exactly what pg-regression-radar needs.
GRANT pg_monitor TO pgrr_monitor;

-- If pg_stat_statements is installed in a non-public schema, also grant USAGE.
-- GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA extensions TO pgrr_monitor;

Using spec.capturePlans / --capture-plans? pg_monitor alone is not enough

pg_monitor grants read access to catalog/statistics views, but not SELECT on ordinary user tables. Plan-diff capture runs EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON, GENERIC_PLAN) <query> against every tracked query, and PostgreSQL checks table-level SELECT privilege for every table an EXPLAIN'd statement references — even though EXPLAIN never executes the statement. Without it, capture fails per-query with pq: permission denied for table ... (42501), logged at DEBUG (so it's easy to miss), and planDiffSummary is left permanently at "no plan captured on either side of the regression" for any query touching a real table. (Queries with no table reference, like SELECT pg_sleep($1), are unaffected — this is why capture can appear to "work" in a quick smoke test and then silently fail on real workload queries.)

If you enable plan-diff capture, also grant read access to the tables you want plan diffs for:

-- Existing tables in the schema:
GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public TO pgrr_monitor;

-- So newly created tables get it automatically too (adjust FOR ROLE to
-- whatever role actually creates your application's tables):
ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE app_owner IN SCHEMA public
  GRANT SELECT ON TABLES TO pgrr_monitor;

Then use that role in your DSN:

postgres://pgrr_reader:password@host:5432/mydb?sslmode=require

Warning

Never pass a superuser or application-owner connection string. A leaked DSN with superuser access gives an attacker full control of the database; a pg_monitor DSN limits exposure to read-only statistics.

docs.title: Option 1: Go install — one command, one binary (recommended)
docs.text:
The simplest way to get pg-regression-radar: a single unified CLI, pg-regression-radar, with each run mode as a subcommand. No clone needed — go install resolves the tagged release directly from the repository's tags via the Go module proxy:

go install github.com/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/cmd/pg-regression-radar@latest
# or pin the release these docs describe: @v1.9.2

This places a single pg-regression-radar binary in $(go env GOPATH)/bin. From there:

command not found?

go install puts the binary in $(go env GOPATH)/bin (or in $GOBIN, if you set it), and a fresh Go install doesn't have that directory on your PATH. Add it, for example export PATH="$PATH:$(go env GOPATH)/bin" in ~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc, and open a new terminal.

pg-regression-radar operator --dsn "postgres://user:password@host:5432/dbname?sslmode=disable"
pg-regression-radar manager --leader-elect=true
pg-regression-radar collector --dsn "..."
pg-regression-radar ingester --source-type argocd
pg-regression-radar version
pg-regression-radar help

version says dev: that is expected

A binary installed with go install prints pg-regression-radar dev (commit none, built unknown), whichever release you installed. The version, commit and build date are stamped in at build time with -ldflags, which go install doesn't pass; the published container images (Option 3) are built with them. To check which release a go install binary came from, run go version -m $(go env GOPATH)/bin/pg-regression-radar and read its mod line.

Every subcommand accepts its own --help, --version, and (except manager) --dry-run — see Configuration Reference.

If you'd rather have four separate binaries (e.g. to match the container images described in Option 3), the same code is also available as four standalone commands:

go install github.com/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/cmd/operator@latest
go install github.com/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/cmd/manager@latest
go install github.com/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/cmd/collector@latest
go install github.com/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/cmd/ingester@latest

Both forms run identical code (internal/cli) — pg-regression-radar operator ... and the standalone operator ... behave the same way.

docs.title: Option 2: Build from source
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/joao00001/pg-regression-radar.git
cd pg-regression-radar
go build -o bin/pg-regression-radar ./cmd/pg-regression-radar
# or the four standalone binaries individually:
go build -o bin/operator  ./cmd/operator
go build -o bin/manager   ./cmd/manager
go build -o bin/collector ./cmd/collector
go build -o bin/ingester  ./cmd/ingester

Useful if you want to build against an unreleased commit, or need the CRD manifests and Helm chart alongside the binaries (both live in the same clone — see options 3 and 4).

docs.title: Option 3: Pull or build the container image
docs.text:
Pull a published release (every vX.Y.Z tag publishes all five images — see CI/CD):

docker pull ghcr.io/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/operator:v1.9.2
docker pull ghcr.io/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/manager:v1.9.2
docker pull ghcr.io/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/collector:v1.9.2
docker pull ghcr.io/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/ingester:v1.9.2
docker pull ghcr.io/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/cli:v1.9.2

These commands use the release this documentation describes (v1.9.2); use :latest for the most recent release instead (there is no rolling/"edge" image — every published tag corresponds to a real vX.Y.Z release). docker run ghcr.io/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/cli:v1.9.2 operator --dsn ... runs the unified CLI image; the other four are single-mode images matching the Dockerfile's other --target values.

Verify the signature and SBOM before trusting a pulled image. Every published image is keyless-signed with cosign using the publishing GitHub Actions run's own OIDC identity (no shared private key to leak or rotate), and carries an attached SBOM attestation:

# Verify the image was signed by this repo's release.yml workflow, specifically
# (not just "signed by someone with a GitHub account").
cosign verify ghcr.io/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/operator:v1.9.2 \
  --certificate-identity-regexp "^https://github.com/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/.github/workflows/release.yml@.*" \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com

# Fetch and inspect the attached SPDX SBOM attestation.
cosign verify-attestation ghcr.io/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/operator:v1.9.2 \
  --type spdxjson \
  --certificate-identity-regexp "^https://github.com/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/.github/workflows/release.yml@.*" \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com \
  | jq -r '.payload | @base64d | fromjson | .predicate'

Every image is also scanned with Trivy at release time and the release job fails outright on any CRITICAL-severity finding (see CI/CD) — a published image never carries a known CRITICAL CVE as of its release date, though new CVEs can of course be disclosed later against the same fixed image bytes.

Build locally, e.g. to test an unreleased commit:

git clone https://github.com/joao00001/pg-regression-radar.git
cd pg-regression-radar
docker build --target operator -t pg-regression-radar/operator .
docker build --target manager  -t pg-regression-radar/manager  .

See the Dockerfile for the other --target values (collector, ingester, and cli for an image running the unified pg-regression-radar binary).

docs.title: Option 4: Install the Helm chart
docs.text:
From the published OCI chart (published alongside the images by every release — see CI/CD):

helm install pg-regression-radar oci://ghcr.io/joao00001/charts/pg-regression-radar \
  --version 1.9.2 \
  --set postgres.dsn="postgres://user:password@cnpg-cluster-rw.production:5432/mydb?sslmode=require" \
  --set postgres.clusterName=cnpg-cluster \
  --set alerting.slackWebhookUrl=https://hooks.slack.com/services/XXX/YYY/ZZZ

--version here is the chart's SemVer version (the release tag without its leading v — release v1.9.2 publishes chart version 1.9.2; see CI/CD for why the two differ by that one character). No helm repo add is needed for an OCI registry — helm install/helm pull reference oci:// URLs directly. The chart's image.tag values default to the chart's own appVersion (the release tag with the v, e.g. v1.9.2), which already matches the images published in the same release, so you don't need to set image.tag/manager.image.tag explicitly unless you want to run a different image tag than the chart's own release.

The chart also exposes alert destination-policy controls used by both entrypoints:

  • alerting.destinationPolicy: "" (default permissive), allowlist, or relay-only
  • alerting.allowedDestinations: manager/operator allowlist used by allowlist policy
  • alerting.destinationPolicyRelayUrl: required when policy is relay-only

Example (mode=manager, force all alerts through a relay):

helm upgrade --install pg-regression-radar oci://ghcr.io/joao00001/charts/pg-regression-radar \
  --version 1.9.2 \
  --set mode=manager \
  --set alerting.destinationPolicy=relay-only \
  --set alerting.destinationPolicyRelayUrl=https://relay.example.com/webhook

Verify the chart's signature before trusting it, the same way as the container images above — the published Helm OCI artifact is keyless-signed with cosign too, using the chart's SemVer version as the tag (same one --version above installs):

cosign verify ghcr.io/joao00001/charts/pg-regression-radar:1.9.2 \
  --certificate-identity-regexp "^https://github.com/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/.github/workflows/release.yml@.*" \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com

From a local clone, e.g. to test unreleased chart changes:

git clone https://github.com/joao00001/pg-regression-radar.git
helm install pg-regression-radar ./pg-regression-radar/deploy/helm/deploylens \
  --set postgres.dsn="postgres://user:password@cnpg-cluster-rw.production:5432/mydb?sslmode=require" \
  --set postgres.clusterName=cnpg-cluster \
  --set alerting.slackWebhookUrl=https://hooks.slack.com/services/XXX/YYY/ZZZ

See Getting Started for the full set of values, including switching to manager mode.

docs.title: Pod/container security defaults
docs.text:
podSecurityContext/securityContext default to runAsNonRoot: true (UID/GID 65532), allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, readOnlyRootFilesystem: true, capabilities.drop: [ALL], and seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault — matching how every image this chart deploys already runs regardless (all five binaries build on gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot, which sets USER nonroot:nonroot and has no writable-filesystem tooling to begin with), just enforced by Kubernetes instead of merely true by accident. None of the binaries write to the local filesystem, so readOnlyRootFilesystem costs nothing. Override either value back to {} only if your environment's own admission policy conflicts with these fields.

serviceAccount.automountServiceAccountToken defaults to true for backward compatibility. Keep it true in mode: manager (the manager talks to the Kubernetes API for leader election and reconciliation). In mode: operator, you can safely set it to false when you do not need in-cluster API access.

If ingester.webhookSecret is left empty, helm install/helm upgrade prints a warning that the deploy-event webhook (and, in mode: operator, GET /events) are unauthenticated — see Deploy Sources & Webhooks: Webhook authentication. That's expected and fine as long as the Service stays cluster-internal (the default service.type is ClusterIP); set the secret before exposing it further.

docs.title: Try it in five minutes (lab)
docs.text:
The fastest way to see pg-regression-radar do its job: a throwaway lab that runs in any Kubernetes cluster (kind, minikube, k3d, Docker Desktop) and needs nothing but kubectl. No Postgres of your own, no ArgoCD, no Slack, no credentials, no helm.

The story it plays out:

  1. A small app, orders-api, runs the same lookup query against a Postgres database about ten times a second. The radar learns what "normal" looks like.
  2. You ship version 2 of orders-api. Its database migration drops an index. The code and the queries are unchanged, but every lookup now scans the whole table.
  3. The radar notices the slowdown, ties it to that rollout, and tells you what changed in the query plan: Index Scan -> Seq Scan.

Everything lives in the pgrr-lab namespace and is deleted with it. The manifests are in examples/lab.

sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  participant You
  participant K as Kubernetes
  participant R as Radar
  participant P as Postgres
  participant S as alert-sink
  loop every 5 s, about 3 minutes
    R->>P: scrape pg_stat_statements
  end
  Note over R: baseline learned
  You->>K: apply 20-bad-deploy.yaml
  K-->>R: rollout finished on a new revision
  R->>P: keep scraping
  R->>R: compare latency before and after
  R->>K: create PerformanceRegression
  R->>S: alert with the plan diff

The lab in time order: learn a baseline, ship the bad deploy, and the radar ties the slowdown to that rollout.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
You need a cluster you can throw things at and kubectl pointed at it. If you have none, kind is the quickest:

kind create cluster --name pgrr-lab

The lab pulls postgres:16, python:3.12-alpine and the radar's manager image from ghcr.io, so the cluster needs internet access. About 1 CPU and 1.5 GiB of memory are enough.

docs.title: Step 1: install the radar
docs.text:
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/main/examples/lab/00-radar.yaml

kubectl wait --for=condition=Established --timeout=60s \
  crd/postgreswatches.radar.pgregressionradar.io \
  crd/deploysources.radar.pgregressionradar.io \
  crd/performanceregressions.radar.pgregressionradar.io

kubectl -n pgrr-lab rollout status deployment/pgrr-manager

This creates the namespace, the radar's custom resources (CRDs), its permissions and the radar itself, running in manager mode. The kubectl wait matters: the next step creates objects of the new types, which only works once the CRDs are registered.

docs.title: Step 2: start the lab
docs.text:
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/main/examples/lab/10-lab.yaml

kubectl -n pgrr-lab wait --for=condition=Available deployment --all --timeout=300s
kubectl -n pgrr-lab get postgreswatch,deploysource

This starts Postgres (seeded with 400,000 orders and an index on orders.order_ref), the orders-api workload, and alert-sink, a small receiver that prints the alerts the radar sends, in place of Slack. It also tells the radar what to watch: a PostgresWatch that scrapes the database every 5 seconds, and a DeploySource that treats every rollout of the orders-api Deployment as a deploy.

Wait about three minutes now. The radar has to see the query running normally before a change means anything. (It also records the first rollout of orders-api as a deploy; waiting lets that one expire so it cannot be mistaken for the bad deploy below.)

In a second terminal, follow the alerts:

kubectl -n pgrr-lab logs -f deployment/alert-sink

docs.title: Step 3: ship the bad deploy
docs.text:
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/main/examples/lab/20-bad-deploy.yaml

kubectl -n pgrr-lab get performanceregressions -w

Version 2 rolls out, its migration drops the index, and within about a minute a PerformanceRegression appears with status Detected. Look at it:

kubectl -n pgrr-lab describe performanceregressions

The fields to look at in Status: Latency Change Factor (how many times slower), Confidence Score, P Value, and Plan Diff Summary, which names the plan change. In the other terminal, the alert arrives, in the same shape it would have in Slack:

================================================================
:rotating_light: *pg-regression-radar* — performance regression detected on cluster *orders*
  Deploy Event     k8s-Deployment-pgrr-lab-orders-api-orders-api-2
  Query (excerpt)  SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE order_ref = $1
  Latency Before   0.05 ms
  Latency After    18.00 ms
  Change Factor    360.00x
  Plan Diff        plan diff for queryid ...:
      root node type changed: "Index Scan" -> "Seq Scan"

(The numbers depend on your machine; the shape does not.)

docs.title: Undo and run it again
docs.text:
kubectl -n pgrr-lab rollout undo deployment/orders-api

Version 1's migration recreates the index and the query is fast again. To repeat the demo, wait three minutes so the radar sees the healthy baseline again, then re-apply step 3.

docs.title: Clean up
docs.text:
kind delete cluster --name pgrr-lab      # if you used kind
# otherwise:
kubectl delete -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/main/examples/lab/00-radar.yaml

docs.title: If something looks wrong
docs.text: Symptom Check A pod stays Pending or ImagePullBackOff kubectl -n pgrr-lab describe pod <name>: the cluster needs to reach ghcr.io and Docker Hub. postgreswatch never reaches Running kubectl -n pgrr-lab describe postgreswatch orders and kubectl -n pgrr-lab logs deployment/pgrr-manager. Step 2 fails with "no matches for kind PostgresWatch" Step 1's kubectl wait did not finish; re-run step 2. No regression after five minutes You applied step 3 before the baseline was learned, or Postgres was not ready. Check kubectl -n pgrr-lab get pods, undo, wait three minutes and repeat. The plan diff says Gather instead of Seq Scan Only if you changed the Postgres settings: the lab turns parallel query off so the plan stays readable.

docs.title: What is in the manifests
docs.text:
File What it is 00-radar.yaml Namespace, CRDs, permissions and the manager. Generated from the Helm chart by scripts/build_lab.sh; do not edit by hand. 10-lab.yaml Postgres, orders-api v1, alert-sink, the PostgresWatch and the DeploySource. 20-bad-deploy.yaml orders-api v2: identical to v1 except that its migration drops the index.

The deploy is detected with sourceType: kubernetes (see Webhooks): the radar watches the Deployment itself, so the lab needs no webhook sender. The settings in the PostgresWatch (5 second scrapes, three samples) are sized for a demo; the defaults are meant for production traffic.

When you are ready for your own database, continue with Installation and Getting Started.

docs.title: Multi-Cluster (Fleet) Mode
docs.text: How one cmd/manager in a hub cluster watches Postgres/CloudNativePG clusters living in other ("spoke") Kubernetes clusters.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
cmd/manager can reconcile any number of PostgresWatch CRs at once, each with its own Collector/Engine/Notifier/ingester.Store (see Architecture Overview and internal/controller/registry.go). When a Postgres cluster's DSN Secret lives in a different Kubernetes cluster than the manager, the fleet mode described on this page applies.

Two approaches are supported:

Approach Field When to use Cluster registry (recommended) spec.remoteClusterRef An administrator pre-registers the cluster; watch creators pick from the approved list. Direct Secret reference (deprecated) spec.remoteClusterSecretRef Backward compatibility — still works in controlled security-profile mode, rejected in hardened mode.

On top of resolving a DSN across clusters, fleet mode also covers two related concerns, each with its own section below: validating that a referenced CloudNativePG Cluster actually exists and is healthy (spec.cnpgClusterRef), and continuously verifying that a registered cluster's kubeconfig is still good (cluster health checks) — independent of whether any PostgresWatch currently references that cluster.

flowchart LR
  subgraph HUB["Hub cluster"]
    PW["PostgresWatch<br/>remoteClusterRef"]:::k8s
    MGR["manager"]:::radar
    PRC["PostgresRadarCluster<br/>(cluster-scoped)"]:::k8s
    KS["kubeconfig Secret<br/>needs the consent label"]:::k8s
  end
  subgraph SPOKE["Spoke cluster"]
    DS["DSN Secret<br/>read through the kubeconfig"]:::ext
    PG[("PostgreSQL")]:::ext
  end
  PW -->|"1 reconcile"| MGR
  MGR -->|"2 look up"| PRC
  PRC -->|"3 kubeconfigSecretRef"| KS
  MGR -->|"4 read the DSN"| DS
  MGR -->|"5 scrape with the DSN"| PG

The manager only ever reads one Secret from a spoke cluster; the connection to Postgres itself is a separate network path that you provide.

docs.title: Registering a cluster
docs.text:
An administrator creates a PostgresRadarCluster resource (cluster-scoped) for each remote cluster. Only users with create/update/delete access to PostgresRadarCluster can add or change cluster registrations — watch creators have no say in which clusters are reachable.

apiVersion: radar.pgregressionradar.io/v1alpha1
kind: PostgresRadarCluster
metadata:
  name: prod-eu-west
spec:
  kubeconfigSecretRef:
    namespace: pg-radar-system   # namespace of the kubeconfig Secret in the HUB cluster
    name: prod-eu-west-kubeconfig
    key: kubeconfig
  namespace: postgres            # optional: default namespace on the remote cluster for DSN Secrets

The kubeconfig Secret must carry the consent label and must contain only static credentials (bearer token or client certificate). See Kubeconfig restrictions for what is rejected and why.

kubectl create secret generic prod-eu-west-kubeconfig \
  --from-file=kubeconfig=./spoke-scoped.kubeconfig \
  -n pg-radar-system

kubectl label secret prod-eu-west-kubeconfig \
  pg-regression-radar.io/allow-postgreswatch-access=true \
  -n pg-radar-system

docs.title: Referencing a registered cluster
docs.text:
A PostgresWatch references a registered cluster by name via spec.remoteClusterRef:

apiVersion: radar.pgregressionradar.io/v1alpha1
kind: PostgresWatch
metadata:
  name: prod-eu-west
  namespace: default
spec:
  clusterName: prod-eu-west
  remoteClusterRef: prod-eu-west     # must match a PostgresRadarCluster name
  dsnSecretRef:
    name: prod-eu-west-app-superuser # Secret name on the SPOKE cluster
    key: uri

If the named PostgresRadarCluster does not exist, reconciliation fails with status.phase: Failed and a clear error message, exactly like any other DSN resolution failure.

docs.title: Security profiles
docs.text:
The manager and operator support a --security-profile flag that controls whether the deprecated remoteClusterSecretRef path is still accepted:

  • controlled (default): both remoteClusterRef and remoteClusterSecretRef work. A deprecation warning is logged whenever the old field is used. This is the backward-compatible default for existing installations.
  • hardened: remoteClusterSecretRef is rejected outright with a clear error. Only the cluster registry path (remoteClusterRef) is allowed.

Use hardened in new installations and in clusters where you want to enforce that only pre-registered clusters are reachable.

docs.title: RBAC for cluster administrators
docs.text:
Only bind create/update/delete on postgresradarclusters to administrators — watch creators need no write access to this resource. The Helm chart creates a ClusterRole for this purpose:

kubectl create clusterrolebinding pg-radar-cluster-admins \
  --clusterrole=<release>-cluster-registry-admin \
  --group=cluster-admins

The manager's own ServiceAccount only needs get;list;watch on postgresradarclusters (already included in the generated ClusterRole).

docs.title: The hub-spoke model
docs.text:
• Hub cluster: where cmd/manager (the Deployment, its ServiceAccount, and its RBAC) actually runs. This is the only cluster the manager's own Kubernetes client (r.Client in internal/controller/postgreswatch_controller.go) can talk to.
  • Spoke cluster(s): any number of other Kubernetes clusters, each typically running its own CloudNativePG installation and Postgres cluster(s). The manager never runs anything in a spoke cluster; it only reads one Secret from it.

docs.title: What actually happens on reconcile
docs.text:
PostgresWatchReconciler.resolveDSN → dsnSecretClient (internal/controller/postgreswatch_controller.go) decide, on every reconcile, which Kubernetes API server to read spec.dsnSecretRef from:

  1. remoteClusterRef set (recommended): look up the named PostgresRadarCluster, read its kubeconfig Secret (from the hub cluster, in whatever namespace the PostgresRadarCluster.spec.kubeconfigSecretRef.namespace specifies), build (or reuse a cached) client.Client, and read spec.dsnSecretRef through that remote client. The PostgresRadarCluster must exist; if it doesn't, Reconcile marks the watch Failed immediately.
  2. remoteClusterSecretRef set (deprecated): read the kubeconfig Secret it names — in the hub cluster, in the PostgresWatch's own namespace — then follow the same build/cache/read path as above. Accepted in controlled profile (default), rejected in hardened profile.
  3. Neither set (default): read the DSN Secret with the manager's own (hub) client, exactly as before fleet mode existed. Zero behavior change, zero new RBAC needed.

In all cases, spec.remoteNamespace (if set alongside a remote cluster path) overrides which namespace on the remote cluster is used to look up the DSN Secret — see the remoteNamespace field in the Configuration Reference.

Any failure in that chain — the PostgresRadarCluster doesn't exist, its kubeconfig Secret is missing, the kubeconfig is malformed, or the remote API server is unreachable — is treated exactly like any other DSN resolution failure: Reconcile calls markFailed, setting status.phase: Failed, status.message to the error, and returning it so controller-runtime's rate limiter retries with backoff.

docs.title: Generating and storing the kubeconfig Secret
docs.text:
The kubeconfig you put in the Secret should be scoped down to the bare minimum on the spoke side — least privilege lives entirely in the kubeconfig's own embedded credentials/RBAC, not in anything the hub cluster enforces (the hub cluster has no way to know or limit what a kubeconfig can do once it's handed to a remote API server). A reasonable way to build one:

# On/against the SPOKE cluster:
kubectl create serviceaccount pg-regression-radar-reader -n <spoke-namespace>

kubectl create role pg-regression-radar-dsn-reader \
  --verb=get --resource=secrets \
  --resource-name=<dsn-secret-name> \
  -n <spoke-namespace>

kubectl create rolebinding pg-regression-radar-dsn-reader \
  --role=pg-regression-radar-dsn-reader \
  --serviceaccount=<spoke-namespace>:pg-regression-radar-reader \
  -n <spoke-namespace>

# Only needed when the PostgresWatch also sets spec.cnpgClusterRef — see
# "Remote CloudNativePG Cluster validation" below. Grants get on exactly
# one named Cluster object, nothing else (no access to the Cluster's own
# spec beyond what `get` on this one object implies, and no access to any
# other CloudNativePG resource type).
kubectl create role pg-regression-radar-cluster-reader \
  --verb=get --resource=clusters.postgresql.cnpg.io \
  --resource-name=<cnpg-cluster-name> \
  -n <spoke-namespace>

kubectl create rolebinding pg-regression-radar-cluster-reader \
  --role=pg-regression-radar-cluster-reader \
  --serviceaccount=<spoke-namespace>:pg-regression-radar-reader \
  -n <spoke-namespace>

# Mint a kubeconfig for that ServiceAccount only (exact steps depend on your
# cluster's token/cert issuance setup — a short-lived ServiceAccount token
# via `kubectl create token`, or a long-lived one via a Secret of type
# kubernetes.io/service-account-token, both work as the "users.user.token"
# field of a kubeconfig).

# On the HUB cluster:
kubectl create secret generic prod-eu-west-kubeconfig \
  --from-file=kubeconfig=./spoke-scoped.kubeconfig \
  -n default

# Required — see "Secret consent label" below: without this label the
# manager refuses to read this Secret at all, regardless of RBAC.
kubectl label secret prod-eu-west-kubeconfig \
  pg-regression-radar.io/allow-postgreswatch-access=true \
  -n default

The Roles above each grant get on exactly one named object — the DSN Secret, and (only if cnpgClusterRef is set) the CloudNativePG Cluster — nothing else. Neither should grant list/watch on all objects of that type, access to any other resource type, or any verb beyond what's needed to read those two specific objects. This is an operational responsibility of whoever creates the kubeconfig Secret, not something cmd/manager or its own RBAC can enforce from the hub side.

docs.title: RBAC: two separate concerns
docs.text:
It's easy to conflate "the manager's own RBAC" with "what the manager can reach in a spoke cluster" — they are unrelated:

Grants Enforced by Hub ServiceAccount RBAC (config/rbac/role.yaml, +kubebuilder:rbac marker above PostgresWatchReconciler.Reconcile) Read access to Secrets in the hub cluster — this already covered dsnSecretRef before this feature, and now also covers reading the remoteClusterSecretRef kubeconfig Secret. Nothing about this RBAC changes what can be reached in a spoke cluster. The hub cluster's API server The kubeconfig's own embedded credentials Whatever the spoke cluster's API server decides that identity can do — should be scoped to get on exactly the one Secret dsnSecretRef names, per the previous section. The spoke cluster's API server

config/rbac/role.yaml's existing secrets: get;list;watch ClusterRole rule is unchanged by this feature — it was already necessary and sufficient for dsnSecretRef, and the exact same rule is what makes remoteClusterSecretRef kubeconfig Secrets readable too, since both live in the hub cluster. If you're running a hardened setup that narrows that ClusterRole to specific Secret names (e.g. via resourceNames), remember to include your kubeconfig Secrets in that list alongside your DSN Secrets.

docs.title: Secret consent label
docs.text:
That cluster-wide secrets: get;list;watch grant means anyone who can create or edit a PostgresWatch in a namespace — a much weaker permission than being able to read Secrets in that namespace directly — could otherwise name any Secret there in dsnSecretRef or remoteClusterSecretRef and have the manager read it on their behalf: a classic confused-deputy path, since it's the manager's own broader Secret-read privilege being exercised at the referencer's request, not the Secret owner's.

internal/controller/secret_consent.go closes this: before either Secret's contents are used, the manager checks it carries the label

pg-regression-radar.io/allow-postgreswatch-access: "true"

If the label is missing, resolveDSN/dsnSecretClient return an error (surfaced the same way any other DSN resolution failure is — status.phase: Failed, status.message set) instead of using the Secret's contents. This applies to both dsnSecretRef (the DSN Secret itself) and remoteClusterSecretRef (the kubeconfig Secret) — whoever owns a Secret must explicitly opt it in before any PostgresWatch can reference it, in the hub cluster or, via a remote kubeconfig, in a spoke cluster's own Secrets:

kubectl label secret prod-eu-west-app-superuser \
  pg-regression-radar.io/allow-postgreswatch-access=true \
  -n <namespace>

This is a namespace-local decision the Secret's own owner makes (labeling a Secret requires the same patch/update permission on that Secret that creating it did), independent of whatever RBAC governs who can create PostgresWatch CRs — it doesn't replace narrowing that RBAC or the ClusterRole above where you can, it closes the gap for installations where you can't (or haven't yet).

For multi-tenant clusters, treat that label as a privileged capability: add an admission policy so only approved identities can set it. A ready-to-adapt Kyverno example (edit its allowed-identity list for your environment) lives at docs/policies/kyverno-consent-label-policy.yaml.

docs.title: Kubeconfig restrictions
docs.text:
Because a remoteClusterSecretRef kubeconfig comes from a Secret a PostgresWatch's owner controls — untrusted input from the manager's perspective, even after the consent label above — buildRemoteClient (internal/controller/remote_client.go) rejects any kubeconfig that would hand the manager process more capability than "talk to a remote API server with a static credential":

Rejected Why users[].exec (exec-based credential plugins) client-go would execute it as a local process inside the manager's own pod every time the resulting client authenticates — a kubeconfig-controlled arbitrary command, not just a credential. users[].auth-provider (deprecated auth-provider plugins) Same "plugin decides how to authenticate" shape as exec; some implementations shell out too. clusters[].proxy-url Would route the manager's API traffic for that cluster through a proxy endpoint the kubeconfig's author chooses, not the cluster operator — a network egress redirection risk.

Static-credential kubeconfigs — bearer token, client-certificate, or username/password users[] entries, with no proxy-url — are unaffected; those are exactly the shapes the previous section's kubectl create token-based example produces. A rejected kubeconfig surfaces the same way any other DSN resolution failure does (status.phase: Failed), with an error naming the specific user/cluster entry and restriction that was violated.

docs.title: Remote CloudNativePG Cluster validation
docs.text:
PostgresWatch.spec.cnpgClusterRef names a real CloudNativePG Cluster object (postgresql.cnpg.io/v1) that must exist and be healthy before the watch is allowed to start — a cross-cluster complement to dsnSecretRef, since clusterName by itself is only ever a free-text label on metrics/PerformanceRegression CRs, not a live reference to anything.

apiVersion: radar.pgregressionradar.io/v1alpha1
kind: PostgresWatch
metadata:
  name: prod-eu-west
  namespace: default
spec:
  clusterName: prod-eu-west
  remoteClusterRef: prod-eu-west
  cnpgClusterRef: prod-eu-west-pg    # the CloudNativePG Cluster's own name
  dsnSecretRef:
    name: prod-eu-west-app-superuser
    key: uri

validateCNPGCluster (internal/controller/cnpg_cluster.go) reads the named Cluster through the exact same client dsnSecretRef was just resolved through — the hub's own client when remoteClusterRef/remoteClusterSecretRef are unset, or the cached remote client for the spoke cluster otherwise — and in the exact same namespace dsnSecretRef was read from (spec.remoteNamespace, or the watch's own namespace by default). Nothing here reads the Cluster from a different cluster or namespace than the DSN itself came from.

"Healthy" is decided in two steps, matching how kubectl get cluster itself reports status:

  1. If status.conditions contains a condition with type: Ready, its status is authoritative: True means healthy, anything else means not — the error message includes that condition's reason/message verbatim, so it reads the same as kubectl describe cluster would show.
  2. Otherwise (an older CloudNativePG release that predates the Ready condition, or a cluster that hasn't reported status yet at all), fall back to status.phase: empty means not yet reconciled far enough to report anything (treated as unhealthy — the cluster "may still be initialising"), a phase containing "fail" (case-insensitive — CloudNativePG's own failed-state phase string is "Cluster in failed state") is unhealthy, and any other non-empty phase (including CloudNativePG's several transient "setting up.../switching.../waiting for..." phases) is treated as healthy. This fallback is deliberately permissive: the point is catching a genuinely broken or missing target, not gating on every transient reconciliation phase of a cluster that's simply still starting up.

cnpgClusterRef requires no additional hub-side RBAC: PostgresWatchReconciler reads Cluster objects through whichever client it already built to resolve dsnSecretRef, the same way it reads Secrets. What it does require, when used alongside remoteClusterRef/remoteClusterSecretRef, is an additional grant in the kubeconfig's own embedded RBAC — get on the one named Cluster object, in addition to get on the DSN Secret — see Remote cluster RBAC above for the exact recipe. No consent label is required for the Cluster object itself (unlike dsnSecretRef/kubeconfig Secrets): it carries no credentials, and the confused-deputy concern the consent label exists for doesn't apply to a read-only health check of an object the kubeconfig's own RBAC already had to explicitly grant access to.

A missing Cluster, one without CloudNativePG CRDs installed at all, or one reporting unhealthy, all surface exactly like any other DSN resolution failure: status.phase: Failed with status.message naming the Cluster, its namespace, and precisely what was wrong.

docs.title: Cluster health checks
docs.text:
Before PostgresRadarClusterReconciler existed, a registered cluster's kubeconfig going bad — rotated away from, revoked, or simply pointed at an address that stopped answering — was only ever discovered reactively, the next time some PostgresWatch's resolveDSN happened to need that cluster, and never surfaced anywhere an administrator watching PostgresRadarCluster.status directly would see it independent of any particular watch.

PostgresRadarClusterReconciler (internal/controller/postgresradarcluster_controller.go) closes that gap by periodically re-probing every registered PostgresRadarCluster on its own schedule, regardless of whether any PostgresWatch currently references it:

  • The probe itself is a single discovery.ServerVersion() call — deliberately the least-privileged check possible, since every Kubernetes cluster's default RBAC bindings expose the version/discovery endpoints to any authenticated identity (system:discovery bound to system:authenticated). A least-privilege kubeconfig built strictly per Remote cluster RBAC above (whose only grants are get on one Secret and, optionally, one Cluster) still satisfies this check — the health check never requires broader RBAC than the workload itself already needs.
  • It runs on --cluster-health-check-interval (default 5m — see Configuration Reference), both for the very first probe after a PostgresRadarCluster is created and for every subsequent re-probe of an already-healthy cluster. An unhealthy result is re-probed on the same steady interval rather than any tighter backoff: the failure mode being watched for (an expired or rotated credential) doesn't resolve itself by retrying sooner.
  • It builds its own fresh client per probe rather than reusing PostgresWatchReconciler's remoteClientCache — that cache is sized and keyed around many reconciles sharing one hot client on a sub-minute cadence, whereas this reconciler runs per cluster on a multi-minute interval, so the cache's actual value proposition (TTL'd reuse) barely applies here.

The result is written to PostgresRadarCluster.status:

status:
  ready: true
  lastProbeTime: "2026-01-15T10:32:07Z"
  conditions:
  - type: Ready
    status: "True"
    reason: HealthCheckSucceeded
    lastTransitionTime: "2026-01-15T10:32:07Z"
    message: "cluster responded to a discovery.ServerVersion() probe"

status.ready and status.conditions are kept in sync (status: "True" on the Ready condition implies ready: true) purely so anything that already reads the plain boolean doesn't need to walk conditions — kubectl get postgresradarcluster prints status.ready as its Ready column for exactly this reason. status.lastProbeTime is set on every probe regardless of outcome, so a PostgresRadarCluster that has simply never been reconciled yet (lastProbeTime absent) stays distinguishable from one that was just probed and found unhealthy (lastProbeTime recent, ready: false).

A failing probe does not itself evict anything from remoteClientCache or otherwise affect any in-flight PostgresWatch reconcile — it is a read-only, side-effect-free signal for observability and alerting (e.g. kubectl get postgresradarcluster -o jsonpath='{.items[?(@.status.ready==false)].metadata.name}' in a cron-based check, or a Prometheus alert over kube_customresource_* metrics if you export controller-runtime's own metrics alongside this project's), independent of and complementary to the evict-on-failure behavior described below, which remains the mechanism that actually protects a live PostgresWatch reconcile from reusing a known-broken client.

docs.title: Operational considerations
docs.text:
These are permanent, by-design characteristics of this feature, not open work tracked on the Roadmap — understanding them matters for running fleet mode safely in production:

  • Kubeconfig rotation/expiration is detected, not auto-refreshed. Cluster health checks above proactively surface a rotated, revoked, or expired kubeconfig on PostgresRadarCluster.status on a steady interval, independent of whether any PostgresWatch happens to be using it — but no code running in the hub cluster has the authority to mint a fresh credential for a spoke cluster it doesn't control, so actually refreshing the kubeconfig Secret's content remains an operational responsibility, same as rotating dsnSecretRef itself. The request-path behavior this used to be the only word on is still true and still matters alongside the health check: the moment a cached remote client fails a real request (resolveDSN), its entry is evicted from remoteClientCache immediately (remoteClientCache.evict, internal/controller/remote_client.go), rather than waiting for a future reconcile to keep reusing a client already known to be broken — so (a) a transient failure gets a genuinely fresh connection/transport on the very next attempt instead of reusing one that just failed, and (b) once an external rotator does rewrite the kubeconfig Secret with fresh credentials, the next reconcile picks that new content up immediately with no orphaned old entry left sitting in the cache. Exec-based kubeconfig auth plugins, which would otherwise get transparent, automatic refresh from client-go itself with no evict/re-fetch cycle needed at all, remain rejected outright, precisely because that same "runs a local process to get fresh credentials" mechanism is what makes them unsafe to accept from a tenant-controlled Secret.
  • The remote client cache's time-based eviction is independent of the health check. Entries unused for over an hour are swept out (internal/controller/remote_client.go's Start, registered as a manager-owned background task in SetupWithManager, running every 10 minutes) — a kubeconfig still referenced by a live PostgresWatch gets its cache entry refreshed at least every 30 seconds (the reconciler's status-refresh cadence), so this only ever reclaims clients for kubeconfigs that were rotated away from or whose PostgresWatch/Secret was deleted, never one still genuinely in use. By design, eviction isn't triggered directly by a Secret's deletion (it just stops being asked for and ages out on the next sweep), and cluster health checks above — a proactive, read-only reachability signal on PostgresRadarCluster.status — don't feed back into evicting or refreshing this cache; the two mechanisms serve different purposes (observability vs. request-path correctness) and are intentionally kept decoupled.
  • DSN-to-Postgres network reachability is always the operator's responsibility. remoteClusterRef/cnpgClusterRef only ever grant the hub cluster Kubernetes API access to the spoke (an authenticated HTTPS call to read a Secret or a Cluster's status) — they say nothing about, and cannot provide, network routability for the actual Postgres wire-protocol TCP connection the Collector makes once resolveDSN hands it a connection string. A DSN naming CloudNativePG's default in-cluster Service DNS host (<cluster>-rw.<namespace>.svc) is only resolvable and routable inside the spoke cluster itself; reaching it from the hub requires some real cross-cluster network path already in place (a shared VPC, a service-mesh multi-cluster mesh, Submariner, a VPN, or a CloudNativePG Service of type LoadBalancer/ExternalName with a genuinely routable address) — see Real two-cluster end-to-end test for exactly this constraint surfacing (and a CI-only workaround) in a kind-based test rig specifically. This is an inherent property of running two separate Kubernetes clusters, not something a future version of this feature could remove.

docs.title: Migration from remoteClusterSecretRef to remoteClusterRef
docs.text:
The remoteClusterSecretRef field on PostgresWatch is deprecated. It continues to work in controlled security-profile mode (the default), but will be rejected in hardened mode. Migrating is a two-step process:

Step 1 — Register the cluster as a PostgresRadarCluster.

Move the kubeconfig Secret to the administrator-managed namespace (e.g. pg-radar-system) if it isn't there already, and create the PostgresRadarCluster:

# Move the kubeconfig Secret if needed (or create a new one in the admin namespace)
kubectl create secret generic prod-eu-west-kubeconfig \
  --from-file=kubeconfig=./spoke-scoped.kubeconfig \
  -n pg-radar-system

kubectl label secret prod-eu-west-kubeconfig \
  pg-regression-radar.io/allow-postgreswatch-access=true \
  -n pg-radar-system

# Create the PostgresRadarCluster
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: radar.pgregressionradar.io/v1alpha1
kind: PostgresRadarCluster
metadata:
  name: prod-eu-west
spec:
  kubeconfigSecretRef:
    namespace: pg-radar-system
    name: prod-eu-west-kubeconfig
    key: kubeconfig
EOF

Step 2 — Update each PostgresWatch to use remoteClusterRef.

kubectl patch postgreswatch prod-eu-west \
  --type=merge \
  -p '{"spec":{"remoteClusterRef":"prod-eu-west","remoteClusterSecretRef":null}}'

Or apply a new manifest replacing remoteClusterSecretRef with remoteClusterRef:

spec:
  remoteClusterRef: prod-eu-west    # replaces remoteClusterSecretRef
  dsnSecretRef:
    name: prod-eu-west-app-superuser
    key: uri

After migration, the old kubeconfig Secret in the watch's namespace can be removed (once no other watch references it).
