docs.title: OpenTelemetry / Prometheus Sample Source
docs.text: internal/telemetry/promsource — an opt-in SampleSource that reads query samples from Prometheus instead of scraping pg_stat_statements directly; for fleets that already run an OpenTelemetry Collector.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
internal/correlation.Engine depends only on a two-method SampleSource interface (SamplesInRange, AllQueryIDs — internal/correlation/engine.go), not concretely on internal/collector.Collector. internal/telemetry/promsource.Source is a second implementation of that same interface, backed by PromQL queries against a Prometheus HTTP API instead of a direct database connection. This page covers what it does and, more importantly, what it currently cannot do without extra setup — that second part matters more here than for most pages.

flowchart LR
  PG[("PostgreSQL<br/>pg_stat_statements")]:::ext
  subgraph OTEL["OpenTelemetry Collector"]
    RC["postgresqlreceiver<br/>top_query log records"]:::ext
    TR["transform and<br/>signal_to_metrics"]:::ext
    EX["prometheusexporter"]:::ext
  end
  PR["Prometheus<br/>recording rule"]:::ext
  subgraph RADAR["pg-regression-radar"]
    SRC["promsource.Source"]:::radar
    ENG["Correlation Engine"]:::radar
  end
  PG --> RC
  RC --> TR
  TR -->|"calls and exec time per queryid"| EX
  EX -->|"scraped"| PR
  PR -->|"PromQL"| SRC
  SRC -->|"samples"| ENG

The radar reads latency from Prometheus instead of connecting to Postgres; the Collector pipeline has to produce a per-query metric first.

docs.title: The real gap: per-query attribution isn't there yet, out of the box
docs.text:
opentelemetry-collector-contrib's postgresqlreceiver scrapes pg_stat_statements and exposes postgresql.query.execution.time — but as of this writing that metric is a cumulative Sum scoped to db.namespace (the database) only. It carries no queryid and no query text. Per-query detail (queryid, calls, exec time, query text) exists only on the receiver's db.server.top_query log record, and a metrics-only Prometheus exporter never sees log records.

Concretely: pointing promsource.Config.MetricName at postgresql_query_execution_time_seconds_total (the Prometheus-exported name of that metric, per the OTel-to-Prometheus translation rules) will not work — there is no queryid label on it to select by, so SamplesInRange would only ever see one series per database, never per query.

promsource.Source does not hardcode that broken assumption. Config.MetricName and Config.QueryIDLabel are both required configuration, not defaults pointing at the receiver's stock metric — see the package doc comment on internal/telemetry/promsource/promsource.go for the full reasoning. To actually get a usable feed, an operator needs one of:

  • A custom OTel Collector pipeline that promotes db.server.top_query's postgresql.queryid (and, ideally, db.query.text) attributes onto a metric with per-query cardinality — for example a transform processor turning that log record into a metric point, exported by prometheusexporter as usual.
  • A Prometheus recording rule computed over whatever that custom pipeline exposes, producing the mean-execution-time-in-milliseconds shape promsource.Source expects (see below) — keeping the PromQL complexity in Prometheus config rather than in this project's Go code.
  • A future postgresqlreceiver release that adds per-query attribution to the metric itself, at which point Config.MetricName/Config.QueryIDLabel point at it directly with no code change here.

This is deliberately staying "bring your own per-query metric" rather than "here's a broken one-liner that looks like it works." The seam is real, and the moment any of the three options above exists in a given fleet, this package is what plugs it in — no changes to internal/correlation or to this package itself.

docs.title: Worked example: PostgreSQL → OTel Collector → Prometheus
docs.text:
docs/examples/otel/ ships a complete, validated pipeline that produces exactly the metric this source reads:

File Role otel-collector.yaml postgresqlreceiver (with db.server.top_query enabled) → transform (promotes postgresql.queryid/db.query.text to queryid/query) → signal_to_metrics connector (calls and exec-time counters per queryid) → delta_to_cumulative → prometheusexporter. prometheus.yml Scrapes the Collector's exporter. prometheus-rules.yaml Recording rule pg_regression_radar_query_mean_exec_time_ms{queryid,query}.

Things the example gets right that are easy to miss:

  • The per-query signal is a log record, so the Collector needs the signal_to_metrics connector to turn it into metrics; prometheusexporter alone never sees it.
  • postgresql.total_exec_time is in seconds, so the recording rule multiplies by 1000 to produce the milliseconds this source expects.
  • prometheusexporter only exposes cumulative counters, hence delta_to_cumulative.
  • The monitoring role needs pg_monitor; without it other roles' statements show up as <insufficient privilege> and are dropped.

scripts/validate-otel-example.sh runs the whole stack in Docker (PostgreSQL, Collector contrib, Prometheus), slows a probe query from ~10 ms to ~60 ms mid-run, and asserts through the Prometheus API that the recording rule carries numeric queryid labels, query text and values that track the slowdown. Point metricName at pg_regression_radar_query_mean_exec_time_ms to consume it.

docs.title: Value semantics: mean exec time in milliseconds, per point
docs.text:
Whatever metric is configured must report a per-scrape, per-queryid mean execution time in milliseconds — the same shape as pg_stat_statements.mean_exec_time, which is the only field internal/correlation.Engine's detection math actually reads (extractLatencies in internal/correlation/engine.go). A raw cumulative counter is the wrong shape and must be turned into a mean before Prometheus scrapes it — for example, at the recording-rule layer:

avg by (queryid) (
  rate(some_per_query_exec_time_seconds_total[5m])
  /
  rate(some_per_query_calls_total[5m])
) * 1000

promsource.Source.SamplesInRange then reads that recording rule's raw values back with a query_range request and maps each returned point to one collector.QuerySample directly — it does not itself rate() or average anything, exactly mirroring how one collector.Collector.Scrape() call stores one raw observation per queryid.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: Field Default Notes BaseURL (required) Prometheus HTTP API base, e.g. http://prometheus:9090. Must be http(s) and must not embed credentials; a trailing slash is trimmed. MetricName (required) See above — no default is safe to assume. QueryIDLabel queryid Label carrying the queryid as a base-10 integer string. Always parsed with strconv.ParseInt, never through a JSON-number/float path, so values past 2^53 (routine for pg_stat_statements queryids, which are int64) don't silently lose precision. QueryTextLabel query Optional; set to - to disable. Populates QuerySample.QueryText/Fingerprint for display and for the queryid-rotation fallback described in Collector Internals — a queryid-only feed still satisfies SampleSource without it. Step 15s query_range resolution; should match or exceed the underlying scrape interval. BearerToken (none) Sent as Authorization: Bearer … for Prometheus endpoints behind an authenticating proxy. From a PostgresWatch, set spec.sampleSource.prometheus.bearerTokenSecretRef (see below). HTTPClient / Timeout 10s timeout HTTPClient set explicitly takes precedence; set its own Timeout in that case.

docs.title: Using it from a PostgresWatch CRD (cmd/manager)
docs.text:
The CRD-driven cmd/manager path (PostgresWatch) selects this source declaratively via spec.sampleSource, instead of any Go code:

apiVersion: radar.pgregressionradar.io/v1alpha1
kind: PostgresWatch
metadata:
  name: widgets-prod
spec:
  clusterName: widgets-prod
  sampleSource:
    type: prometheus
    prometheus:
      url: http://prometheus.monitoring.svc:9090
      # A custom recording rule's output, not the stock
      # postgresql_query_execution_time_seconds_total metric — see
      # "The real gap" above for why.
      metricName: pg_regression_radar_query_mean_exec_time_ms
      queryIDLabel: queryid
      queryTextLabel: query
      stepSeconds: 15
  windowMinutes: 30
  minSamples: 10

dsn/dsnSecretRef are not required, and not read, when sampleSource.type is prometheus — internal/controller.PostgresWatchReconciler skips DSN resolution entirely in that mode (see usesPrometheusSampleSource in internal/controller/postgreswatch_controller.go). capturePlans: true combined with sampleSource.type: prometheus is rejected at reconcile time with a clear error, rather than silently ignored: EXPLAIN-based plan-diff capture needs the direct database connection this mode deliberately doesn't have. Every other field (windowMinutes, minSamples, alerting, autoAbort, periodicDetection, …) works exactly the same regardless of which sampleSource is active — the only things this field changes are which correlation.SampleSource implementation internal/correlation.Engine runs against and whether a direct database connection exists at all.

bearerTokenSecretRef (name + key) reads a bearer token from a Secret in the watch's namespace. Like dsnSecretRef, the Secret must carry the label pg-regression-radar.io/allow-postgreswatch-access=true, otherwise the watch fails with a consent error; the token's value is part of the spec hash, so rotating it restarts the watch's workers.

See SampleSourceConfig in api/v1alpha1/postgreswatch_types.go for the full field reference (type, and prometheus.{url,metricName,queryIDLabel,queryTextLabel,stepSeconds,bearerTokenSecretRef}), each mirroring promsource.Config one-to-one.

docs.title: Usage example (direct Go construction)
docs.text:
Outside the CRD path — the standalone operator CLI, a custom binary, or a smoke test against a real Prometheus — internal/telemetry/promsource is used the same way any other correlation.SampleSource implementation is: constructed directly and passed to correlation.New, in place of an *internal/collector.Collector.

package main

import (
    "log/slog"
    "os"
    "time"

    "github.com/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/internal/correlation"
    "github.com/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/internal/telemetry/promsource"
)

func main() {
    logger := slog.New(slog.NewTextHandler(os.Stdout, nil))

    src, err := promsource.New(promsource.Config{
        BaseURL: "http://prometheus.monitoring.svc:9090",
        // A custom recording rule's output, not the stock
        // postgresql_query_execution_time_seconds_total metric — see
        // "The real gap" above for why.
        MetricName:     "pg_regression_radar_query_mean_exec_time_ms",
        QueryIDLabel:   "queryid",
        QueryTextLabel: "query",
        Step:           15 * time.Second,
    })
    if err != nil {
        logger.Error("configuring promsource", "error", err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }

    engine := correlation.New(correlation.Config{
        WindowMinutes: 30,
    }, src, logger)

    // engine.Analyse(...) / engine.AnalysePeriodic(...) from here on,
    // exactly as with the default internal/collector.Collector-backed
    // SampleSource — see Detection Algorithm.
    _ = engine
}

Calling SamplesInRange/AllQueryIDs directly (e.g. for a smoke test against a real Prometheus) looks like:

now := time.Now()
ids := src.AllQueryIDs()
for _, qid := range ids {
    samples := src.SamplesInRange(qid, now.Add(-30*time.Minute), now)
    logger.Info("samples in range", "queryid", qid, "count", len(samples))
}

docs.title: Failure behavior
docs.text:
SamplesInRange and AllQueryIDs still return nil on any error — unreachable Prometheus, a non-success API response, a malformed body, or the wrong resultType — to match correlation.SampleSource's signature and the "unknown queryid returns nothing" contract of internal/collector.Collector. Failures are no longer silent, though:

  • Counter pg_regression_radar_promsource_query_errors_total{operation} (samples_in_range or all_query_ids) increments on every failed query, so "no data in range" can be told apart from "Prometheus is unreachable".
  • A warning is logged at most once per minute per operation. A 401/403 adds a hint to check the bearer token.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• OTLP Deploy Events and OTLP Regression Export — the other two OpenTelemetry integration points.
  • Collector Internals — the existing, default SampleSource implementation this package is an alternative to, including the queryid-fingerprint fallback this package's QueryTextLabel also participates in.
  • Detection Algorithm — how SamplesInRange's output is actually consumed.

docs.title: OpenTelemetry Deploy Events (OTLP)
docs.text: sourceType: otlp — turn the OpenTelemetry spans your pipeline already emits for a deploy into DeployEvents, with no per-tool webhook template.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Every other DeploySource type parses one tool's webhook payload (ArgoCD, Flux, Argo Rollouts, or a generic JSON body). sourceType: otlp instead makes the DeploySource route an OTLP/HTTP traces receiver. Anything that can export OpenTelemetry traces — an OpenTelemetry Collector's otlphttp exporter, a CI/CD pipeline instrumented with an OTel SDK, a release script — can point at it, and the spans you select become v1alpha1.DeployEvents through exactly the same ingester.Store.Add path as every other source. Detection is unchanged: the Correlation Engine only ever sees a DeployEvent.

Only the OTLP/HTTP trace encodings are implemented, at the wire level (no gRPC, no OpenTelemetry SDK dependency):

Request Supported Content-Type application/x-protobuf, application/json (anything else → 415) Content-Encoding none, identity, gzip (anything else → 415) Size limit 8 MiB on the wire and after decompression (413 otherwise), so a gzip bomb is rejected Success response 200 with an empty ExportTraceServiceResponse; spans that matched the mapping but are unusable are reported via OTLP partial_success (rejected_spans), so the sender logs it instead of retrying forever Malformed body 400 (never retried by compliant exporters)

The X-Webhook-Token shared secret applies exactly as for the other source types.

flowchart LR
  CI["CI/CD pipeline or<br/>release script (OTel SDK)"]:::ext
  subgraph OC["OpenTelemetry Collector"]
    F["filter: keep spans<br/>named deploy"]:::ext
    X["otlphttp exporter"]:::ext
  end
  subgraph RADAR["pg-regression-radar"]
    R["DeploySource route<br/>sourceType: otlp"]:::radar
    M["match spanNames or<br/>matchAttributes"]:::radar
    E["DeployEvent"]:::out
  end
  CI -->|"OTLP traces"| F
  F --> X
  X -->|"POST /webhook, OTLP/HTTP"| R
  CI -.->|"or straight to the radar"| R
  R --> M
  M -->|"one event per matching span"| E

Only spans selected by spanNames or matchAttributes become deploys, so a full trace stream does not turn every span into one.

docs.title: Selecting which spans are deploys
docs.text:
An OTLP endpoint usually receives a whole trace stream, so the mapping must be explicit. A mapping with neither spanNames nor matchAttributes is rejected at configuration time (a CRD reports phase Failed, reason InvalidSpec; the CLI exits non-zero) — it would otherwise turn every span into a deploy.

Field Meaning spanNames Span names (exact match) that represent a deploy. Any one matching is enough. matchAttributes key: value pairs that must all match. Looked up on the span first, then on its resource. includeFailedSpans Also accept spans with status ERROR. Off by default — a failed deploy did not change what the database runs.

When both are set, a span must satisfy both (name in spanNames and every matchAttributes pair).

docs.title: Field mapping
docs.text:
DeployEvent field Source (span attribute, then resource attribute) Override app (required) service.name appAttribute namespace k8s.namespace.name namespaceAttribute cluster k8s.cluster.name, falling back to the handler's cluster name (--cluster-name / the DeploySource's watch) clusterAttribute revision vcs.ref.head.revision, then service.version revisionAttribute imageTag container.image.tags (first element), then container.image.tag imageTagAttribute timestamp span end time (the moment the deploy finished) timestamp: start id otlp-<traceId>-<spanId> —

Details worth knowing:

  • Retries are idempotent. The event ID is derived from the span's trace/span IDs, so an exporter that retries a batch overwrites the same event instead of creating duplicates. A span with no IDs gets a stable hash of its name, app, namespace, revision and time.
  • Timestamps are clamped to "now" so a sender with a skewed clock cannot create a deploy in the future.
  • A matched span without the app attribute is rejected (counted in partial_success), not silently stored under an empty application name.
  • The appName filter of the DeploySource (--app-name on the CLI) still applies after mapping.
  • Attribute values are matched as strings; integer, double and bool attribute values are compared by their canonical string form.

docs.title: Linking a regression back to the deploy trace
docs.text: Because the event ID embeds the span's trace and span IDs, a PerformanceRegression caused by an OTLP-sourced deploy can be exported (see OpenTelemetry Regression Export) as a log record carrying that same trace_id/span_id. A backend such as Grafana, Tempo or Datadog can therefore jump from the deploy trace to the regression it caused.

docs.title: Using it from a DeploySource CRD
docs.text:
apiVersion: radar.pgregressionradar.io/v1alpha1
kind: DeploySource
metadata:
  name: checkout-deploys
spec:
  postgresWatchRef: checkout-prod
  sourceType: otlp
  otlp:
    spanNames: ["deploy"]
    matchAttributes:
      cicd.pipeline.name: release
    timestamp: end          # or "start"

The manager registers two routes for the DeploySource, because the OpenTelemetry otlphttp exporter appends /v1/traces to whatever endpoint it is given:

  • /webhook/<namespace>/<name>
  • /webhook/<namespace>/<name>/v1/traces

so the exporter's endpoint is simply http://<manager>:8080/webhook/<namespace>/<name>.

docs.title: Using it from the standalone binaries
docs.text:
operator --dsn "$POSTGRES_DSN" --source-type otlp \
  --otlp-span-name deploy \
  --otlp-match-attribute cicd.pipeline.name=release
# ingester accepts the same flags

The receiver is served on /webhook and /webhook/v1/traces of --webhook-listen. Further flags: --otlp-include-failed, --otlp-timestamp, and --otlp-{app,namespace,cluster,revision,image-tag}-attribute. --dry-run validates the mapping.

With the Helm chart, set ingester.sourceType: otlp and ingester.otlp.* (see values.yaml).

docs.title: OpenTelemetry Collector example
docs.text:
A Collector that receives spans from your CI/CD tooling, keeps only the deploy spans, and forwards them:

receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      http:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4318

processors:
  filter/deploys:
    error_mode: ignore
    traces:
      span:
        - 'name != "deploy"'
  batch: {}

exporters:
  otlphttp/radar:
    endpoint: http://pg-regression-radar.monitoring.svc:8080/webhook
    compression: gzip            # also accepted: none
    encoding: proto              # or json
    headers:
      X-Webhook-Token: ${env:RADAR_WEBHOOK_TOKEN}

service:
  pipelines:
    traces/deploys:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [filter/deploys, batch]
      exporters: [otlphttp/radar]

Filtering in the Collector is optional: the DeploySource's spanNames/matchAttributes already ignore non-deploy spans. It just avoids shipping the rest of the trace stream.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Nothing shows up in /events / no regressions. Send one request by hand and read the response. A body {} with HTTP 200 and no event means no span matched — check spanNames against the exact span name and matchAttributes against span and resource attributes.
  • partialSuccess.rejectedSpans in the response: spans matched but lack the application attribute. Set appAttribute or add service.name to the resource.
  • 415 — the sender is using gRPC or an unsupported Content-Type. Use the otlphttp exporter, not otlp (gRPC).
  • 401 — missing/incorrect X-Webhook-Token.
  • 404 on /v1/traces — the DeploySource is not sourceType: otlp, or (CRD mode) its PostgresWatch is not yet Running.

docs.title: OpenTelemetry Regression Export (OTLP)
docs.text: Emit every detected PerformanceRegression as an OTLP log record, so any OpenTelemetry-native backend can consume it without this project's own dashboard API.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
When a regression is detected — from either the deploy-triggered or the periodic path, regardless of which SampleSource fed it — it is sent to the existing alert notifier and, when configured, also exported as one OTLP/HTTP log record. This is complementary to Slack/Teams/PagerDuty alerting, not a replacement; the two are independent, so a failing OTLP endpoint never delays or suppresses an alert (and vice versa).

Only OTLP/HTTP is implemented (binary protobuf or JSON, optional gzip), at the wire level — no gRPC and no OpenTelemetry SDK dependency. The export goes to the standard POST <endpoint>/v1/logs of any OpenTelemetry Collector or OTLP-capable backend.

flowchart LR
  ENG["Correlation Engine<br/>regression detected"]:::radar
  AL["Alert notifier"]:::radar
  EXP["OTLP exporter"]:::radar
  CH["Slack, Teams,<br/>PagerDuty, webhook"]:::out
  OC["OpenTelemetry Collector<br/>or OTLP backend"]:::ext
  ENG --> AL
  ENG -.->|"when configured"| EXP
  AL --> CH
  EXP -->|"one log record, POST /v1/logs"| OC

OTLP export is in addition to the alert, never instead of it.

docs.title: PostgresWatch (cmd/manager)
docs.text:
apiVersion: radar.pgregressionradar.io/v1alpha1
kind: PostgresWatch
metadata:
  name: checkout-prod
spec:
  # ...
  otlpExport:
    endpoint: https://otel-collector.observability.svc:4318
    encoding: protobuf        # or json (default: protobuf)
    gzip: true
    timeoutSeconds: 10        # per attempt, 1-120
    headersSecretRef:         # optional; OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS format
      name: otlp-headers
      key: headers

headersSecretRef points to a Secret in the PostgresWatch's namespace whose value is k=v,k2=v2 (for example authorization=Bearer abc). Like every Secret a PostgresWatch references, it must carry the consent label pg-regression-radar.io/allow-postgreswatch-access: "true". Rotating the Secret restarts the watch's worker on the next reconcile.

The endpoint is chosen by whoever can create a PostgresWatch but requested by the manager, so it is held to the same manager-wide outbound policy as alert destinations:

  • http/https only, no embedded credentials (use headers);
  • loopback, link-local (including the 169.254.169.254 cloud metadata address) and metadata hostnames are refused;
  • when --alerting-allowed-destinations is set, the host must be on that allowlist;
  • under --alerting-destination-policy=relay-only, spec.otlpExport is rejected outright.

A violation puts the PostgresWatch in phase Failed with the reason in status.message; nothing is started.

docs.title: Standalone operator
docs.text:
operator --dsn "$POSTGRES_DSN" \
  --otlp-endpoint http://localhost:4318 \
  --otlp-encoding protobuf --otlp-gzip --otlp-timeout 10s

Headers come from --otlp-headers, or — preferably, to keep credentials out of the process list — the standard OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_LOGS_HEADERS / OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS environment variables. Export is only enabled by --otlp-endpoint; ambient OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT variables (usually set for a pod's own tracing) are deliberately not honoured. The destination rules above apply to the extent the standalone binary has the corresponding flags; a localhost collector sidecar is accepted when no allowlist is set.

docs.title: Helm
docs.text: otlpExport.* in values.yaml. otlpExport.headers is stored in the chart Secret (never rendered into arguments or the CR), and networkPolicy.egress.otlpCIDRs/otlpPorts opens the matching egress rule.

docs.title: What is exported
docs.text:
One log record per regression, in a Resource identifying this project (service.name=pg-regression-radar, service.version, plus k8s.namespace.name, k8s.cluster.name and pg_regression_radar.watch.name when known) and scope github.com/joao00001/pg-regression-radar.

Log record field Value event_name pg_regression_radar.performance_regression severity_number / severity_text 13 / WARN time_unix_nano when the change point was detected (falling back to creation time) observed_time_unix_nano export time body human-readable summary, e.g. Query 123 latency regressed 3.00x (mean 10.00 ms -> 30.00 ms) after deploy otlp-…, confidence 0.97, p-value 0.03 trace_id / span_id present when the triggering deploy came from an OTLP span; links the regression to the deploy trace Attribute Type Notes db.system.name string always postgresql db.query.text string truncated query text, when known pg_regression_radar.regression.name / .status / .trigger_type string trigger_type is deploy or periodic pg_regression_radar.query_id int pg_stat_statements queryid pg_regression_radar.confidence double 1 - p_value; a significance score, not a probability pg_regression_radar.p_value double Welch's t-test p-value; omitted when the test did not run pg_regression_radar.latency.before_ms / .after_ms / .change_factor double pg_regression_radar.deploy_event_id string when deploy-triggered pg_regression_radar.detected_change_at string RFC 3339 pg_regression_radar.external_cause_suspected bool pg_regression_radar.auto_abort.triggered / .error bool / string .error only when set pg_regression_radar.plan_diff_summary string only when plan capture produced one

Query text is already truncated by the collector before it reaches any notifier; the same value is exported. Do not enable the export towards a destination you would not also trust with the Slack alert.

docs.title: Delivery guarantees
docs.text:
Export is asynchronous and bounded; it never blocks detection.

  • A bounded in-memory queue (256 regressions) feeds one worker. When it is full the regression is dropped and counted, rather than growing memory or stalling the poll loop.
  • Network errors and 429/502/503/504 responses are retried with exponential backoff (4 attempts in total, first retry after 500 ms), honouring Retry-After. Any other non-2xx status — including 400, 401, 403, 404 — is permanent and not retried.
  • Redirects are never followed, so a collector cannot bounce the request (and its auth headers) to another host.
  • On shutdown or when a watch is stopped or reconfigured, queued records are flushed for up to 5 seconds; retries are aborted at that deadline.
  • Delivery is at-least-once per detection but not durable: records queued when the process is killed, or still failing after the retries, are lost. The alert notifier and the PerformanceRegression resource remain the durable record.

Metric pg_regression_radar_otlp_export_total{result="success|failed|dropped"} counts outcomes per exporter; alert on a growing failed or dropped rate. Each retry is logged at WARN, a record abandoned after the last attempt at ERROR (both with the endpoint and the cause), and a full queue at WARN.

docs.title: OpenTelemetry Collector example
docs.text:
A Collector receiving the log records and forwarding them to a logging backend:

receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      http:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4318

processors:
  batch: {}

exporters:
  debug:
    verbosity: detailed
  # otlphttp/loki, datadog, ... — any logs exporter

service:
  pipelines:
    logs/regressions:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [batch]
      exporters: [debug]

Filter on event_name == "pg_regression_radar.performance_regression" (or attributes["db.system.name"] == "postgresql") to route regressions separately from other log traffic.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• pg_regression_radar_otlp_export_total{result="failed"} grows. Check the operator/manager log for the status code: 401/403 → headers; 404 → the endpoint must be an OTLP/HTTP receiver (port 4318, not the gRPC port 4317); 415 → try encoding: json or protobuf to match what the backend accepts.
  • PostgresWatch is Failed with spec.otlpExport.endpoint rejected. The endpoint is loopback/metadata or not on the allowlist; use an in-cluster Service DNS name or IP.
  • ... has no key / consent-label error. The headers Secret needs the key named in headersSecretRef.key and the consent label.
  • dropped is non-zero. The collector is slower than detection for a sustained period; investigate the collector, or lower detection volume.

docs.title: Periodic (Deploy-Independent) Detection
docs.text: Regression detection that doesn't need a deploy at all.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
By default, this project only ever analyses a query around a tracked DeployEvent: Engine.Analyse builds a window around the deploy's timestamp and only confirms a regression whose change point falls close enough to it. That means a real, significant latency regression with no deploy behind it — autovacuum falling behind, index/table bloat, stale planner statistics, organic data growth, a connection-pool or traffic-pattern change — goes completely undetected, and using this feature at all requires wiring up a DeploySource, even for clusters that don't want deploy correlation specifically.

Periodic detection is a second, independent trigger path: Engine.AnalysePeriodic runs the same E-divisive-change-point-plus-Welch's-t-test machinery on a rolling schedule, per tracked query, with no DeployEvent involved at all. It is additive, not a replacement — deploy-triggered detection keeps working exactly as before, unaffected by whether periodic detection is enabled. A PostgresWatch (or the CLI) can have either, both, or neither active. See ADR-0001 for the full design rationale.

This is opt-in, on purpose:

  • Disabled by default, both on the CLI (--periodic-detection) and the CRD (spec.periodicDetection.enabled).
  • Per-watch/per-process. Enabling it for one PostgresWatch, or one cmd/operator process, doesn't affect any other.
  • Available in both run modes at once (see Architecture Overview) — this was a deliberate scope decision (see ADR-0001), not staged.
flowchart LR
  T["Every tick"]:::radar
  W["Window of 2 x windowMinutes<br/>ending now"]:::gate
  O["Older half<br/>baseline"]:::gate
  N["Newer half<br/>compared with it"]:::gate
  S["Same statistics<br/>as deploy-triggered"]:::radar
  R["Detected,<br/>if not already flagged"]:::out
  T --> W
  W --> O
  W --> N
  O --> S
  N --> S
  S --> R

With no deploy to anchor on, the engine splits a window in half and compares the two halves.

docs.title: How the window works
docs.text:
Each tick, the engine looks at a window of 2 * windowMinutes ending now, and splits it in half: the older half is the baseline, the newer half is what gets compared against it. There is no deploy timestamp to anchor the split on, so windowMinutes defaults to 60 — double the deploy-triggered default of 30 — since a shorter window would be noisier with nothing narrowing down where to look.

This is a genuinely simpler baseline than deploy-triggered detection's: it's vulnerable to ordinary daily/weekly traffic-pattern shifts producing a "detected" result with nothing actually wrong (a start-of-business-hours load ramp is the obvious failure case). It is mitigated, not eliminated, by a longer default window and by the existing latencyChangeThreshold/pValueThreshold significance bar — the same statistical test deploy-triggered detection uses, just without a deploy to check the change point against. Treat the defaults as a starting point to tune against your own traffic, not a validated answer, especially in the first few weeks of using this. Every tick judges every tracked query, so if the noise is a problem, see Controlling false positives across many queries.

docs.title: Suppression: re-arm, not cooldown
docs.text:
A query that trips periodic detection stays flagged internally until it recovers — it will not re-fire on every subsequent tick just because the same underlying condition is still present. Once a tick shows the query's latency has come back down within latencyChangeThreshold of a fresh baseline, it re-arms, so a later, genuinely new episode of regression fires again. This was a deliberate choice over a fixed time-based cooldown, which either re-alerts on a schedule with nothing new to say, or goes silent well past the point someone fixed and then re-broke the same thing.

This suppression state is in-memory, matching the rest of this project's default runtime state (the Collector's samples, PendingSet's dedup) — it resets on restart. A regression already in progress at restart time will fire one more alert rather than staying silently suppressed forever.

docs.title: cmd/operator (CLI mode)
docs.text:
--periodic-detection
--periodic-window-minutes=60
--periodic-interval-minutes=15
Flag Default Description --periodic-detection false Turns on periodic detection for this process. --periodic-window-minutes 60 Split-window size; the engine compares the most recent half of 2 * this value minutes against the older half. --periodic-interval-minutes 15 How often a full pass over every tracked query runs.

docs.title: PostgresWatch (manager/CRD mode)
docs.text:
apiVersion: radar.pgregressionradar.io/v1alpha1
kind: PostgresWatch
metadata:
  name: prod-db
spec:
  clusterName: prod
  dsnSecretRef: {name: prod-db-dsn, key: dsn}
  periodicDetection:
    enabled: true
    windowMinutes: 60      # optional; this is the default
    intervalMinutes: 15    # optional; this is the default
Field Default Description enabled false Turns on periodic detection for this watch. windowMinutes 60 Same meaning as --periodic-window-minutes. intervalMinutes 15 Same meaning as --periodic-interval-minutes.

docs.title: Telling periodic and deploy-triggered regressions apart
docs.text:
Every PerformanceRegression now carries triggerType: deploy (the default, matching every regression created before this field existed) or periodic. A periodic regression's deployEventId is always empty — there is no deploy event to reference. Alerts (Slack/Teams/PagerDuty/custom) and kubectl get performanceregressions both surface triggerType, so it's always clear which path fired.

Unlike deploy-triggered regressions, which are named after the triggering deploy event so each deploy is its own record, a periodic regression uses one stable name per query (periodic-q<queryID>). Repeated episodes for the same query update that same object rather than accumulating a new PerformanceRegression on every tick — periodic detection has no natural "this episode is over" boundary the way a deploy's fixed analysis window does.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• ADR-0001: Deploy-independent regression detection — the design decisions and trade-offs behind this feature.
  • Detection Algorithm — the E-divisive/Welch's-t-test core both trigger paths share.
  • Configuration Reference — the full flag/field reference across every binary and CRD.
  • Auto-Abort (Argo Rollouts) — auto-abort only ever acts on deploy-triggered regressions; a periodic-triggered regression is never auto-aborted, since there is no deploy to abort.

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text: The optional Postgres-backed state store: what it persists, its schema, retention, and current trade-offs.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
By default (--state-backend=memory) all state lives only in process memory: the Collector keeps its per-queryid samples in an in-memory map, and the Ingester keeps deploy events in an in-memory slice. That means a pod restart loses all history, and running multiple replicas gives each one an inconsistent, independent view of the world. Setting --state-backend=postgres additionally persists both to Postgres, so history survives restarts and can be inspected/shared across replicas.

flowchart LR
  subgraph PROC["operator process"]
    COL["Collector<br/>samples per queryid"]:::radar
    ING["Ingester<br/>deploy events"]:::radar
  end
  ST[("Postgres schema<br/>regression_radar")]:::ext
  COL -.->|"writes, with --state-backend=postgres"| ST
  ING -.->|"writes"| ST
  ST -.->|"Backfill on startup"| COL
  ST -.->|"Backfill on startup"| ING

With the default memory backend nothing is persisted and a restart starts cold; with the Postgres backend history survives restarts.

docs.title: Configuring it
docs.text:
operator --dsn "postgres://user:password@host:5432/monitored_db?sslmode=disable" --state-backend postgres
# --state-dsn defaults to --dsn above: state lives in the SAME Postgres
# cluster being monitored. To isolate it, point at a separate instance:
# --state-dsn "postgres://user:password@host:5432/pgrr_state?sslmode=disable"
  • Same Postgres as the monitored cluster (default, --state-dsn empty): simplest to operate — one connection string, one cluster. Trade-off: the tool's own write traffic shows up in the very pg_stat_statements it watches, and an outage of the monitored cluster also takes down the history.
  • Separate Postgres instance (--state-dsn set): isolates storage load and availability from the cluster under observation, at the cost of running a second Postgres.

docs.title: Schema
docs.text:
Everything lives in its own schema so it never collides with application tables and can be dropped cleanly:

CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS regression_radar;

CREATE TABLE regression_radar.query_samples (
    id                  BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    query_id            BIGINT NOT NULL,
    query_text          TEXT NOT NULL,
    calls               BIGINT NOT NULL,
    total_exec_time_ms  DOUBLE PRECISION NOT NULL,
    mean_exec_time_ms   DOUBLE PRECISION NOT NULL,
    recorded_at         TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    interval_computed   BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE,
    interval_known      BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE,
    interval_calls      BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    interval_total_ms   DOUBLE PRECISION NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    interval_mean_ms    DOUBLE PRECISION NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    reset_detected      BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE
);
CREATE INDEX idx_query_samples_queryid_recorded_at ON regression_radar.query_samples (query_id, recorded_at);
CREATE INDEX idx_query_samples_recorded_at         ON regression_radar.query_samples (recorded_at);

CREATE TABLE regression_radar.deploy_events (
    id               TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    source           TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
    app              TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
    cluster          TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
    namespace        TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
    revision         TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
    image_tag        TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
    event_timestamp  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX idx_deploy_events_event_timestamp ON regression_radar.deploy_events (event_timestamp);

Why not pg_regression_radar?

PostgreSQL reserves the literal pg_ prefix for its own system schemas — CREATE SCHEMA pg_regression_radar is rejected outright with "unacceptable schema name". The schema is named regression_radar for exactly this reason.

The schema is applied automatically on startup (internal/storage/postgres) using hand-rolled, idempotent DDL (CREATE ... IF NOT EXISTS) rather than a migration framework like golang-migrate/goose — both tables are append-mostly, derived/observational data that evolves purely additively, so the extra machinery of a versioned migration runner isn't earning its keep yet. If the schema ever needs a genuinely breaking change (rename, backfill, tightened constraint), that's the point to introduce one.

docs.title: Retention
docs.text: Old rows are pruned periodically (--state-prune-interval, default 15 min) using a DELETE ... WHERE recorded_at < now() - retention sweep, where retention defaults to 7 days (--state-retention).

docs.title: Trade-offs and limitations
docs.text:
• Not a replacement for leader election. Pointing multiple operator replicas at the same state backend makes the data consistent and durable, but each replica still independently scrapes pg_stat_statements and runs the correlation engine — so you'd get duplicate scrapes and duplicate alerts. Preventing that requires only one replica being active at a time (leader election), which cmd/manager provides via controller-runtime's built-in leader election, not this package. Don't run N unattended cmd/operator replicas against a shared backend.
  • Extra write load. Every scrape/webhook now also does a write to Postgres. The connection pool used for this is intentionally small (see internal/storage/postgres.Open) to keep the footprint low, especially when reusing the monitored cluster's own Postgres.

docs.title: Backfill on startup
docs.text:
When --state-backend=postgres, RunOperator loads recent history from the store and seeds the live in-memory Collector/Ingester with it before the webhook/metrics servers or the deploy-event poll loop start:

  • collector.Collector.Backfill seeds the per-queryid sample history (covering the last --retention-minutes), so the correlation engine's view isn't empty for the first --window-minutes after a restart. It does not touch the live Prometheus gauges (pg_regression_radar_query_mean_exec_time_ms/..._calls_total) — those reflect the most recent live scrape, and overwriting them with historical values would misrepresent current server state to anything scraping /metrics before the first real scrape completes.
  • ingester.Store.Backfill seeds deploy-event history the same way, and returns the resulting event count, which becomes the poll loop's initial DrainSince cursor. This matters for correctness, not just completeness: DrainSince treats anything past its cursor as newly-arrived work to analyse and potentially alert on. Backfilling events without also advancing the cursor past them would make every historical deploy event look brand new on restart, re-running correlation and potentially re-sending duplicate Slack alerts for regressions already reported in a previous process lifetime.

Both backfills are best-effort: a failure to load either kind of history is logged at Warn and the process starts with a cold in-memory view for that piece, exactly like before this existed, rather than failing startup outright.

New sample records preserve the per-row-derived interval after aggregation, including unknown intervals and reset detection. interval_computed distinguishes an intentionally unknown interval from a legacy record that never stored interval fields. Existing tables receive these columns additively; old rows and writes from older binaries retain the false/zero defaults. Legacy cumulative-only rows still use the old backfill reconstruction, but it cannot repair previously mixed row counters. Recorded intervals are never re-derived from aggregate totals. Row predecessor state is not persisted, so the first live scrape after restart establishes a new baseline before subsequent intervals can be calculated.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Configuration Reference — the full --state-* flag list.
  • Collector Internals — the in-memory samples this store durably copies.
  • Roadmap — other known gaps.

docs.title: Quickstart Validation
docs.text: Step-by-step validation flow for external users to confirm that pg-regression-radar detects a regression and links it to a deployment event.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This guide is a practical checklist for validating the product's core capability in a local or test environment: detect a query-latency regression and identify the deployment that introduced it. It is written for users who only have public repo/docs access and does not require internal setup knowledge.

Use this page together with the full walkthrough in Example regression scenario. The steps below show how to run that same validation flow in all three supported run modes: operator, manager, and Helm.

docs.title: 1) Prepare a test PostgreSQL and baseline workload
docs.text:
Follow Example regression scenario to:

  1. Start PostgreSQL with pg_stat_statements enabled.
  2. Create test data and an indexed query path.
  3. Run a short baseline workload (fast query execution).

Use placeholder credentials in docs/examples only, for example:

postgres://user:pass@localhost:5432/mydb?sslmode=disable

docs.title: Option A: operator mode
docs.text:
go run ./cmd/operator \
  --dsn "postgres://user:password@localhost:5432/mydb?sslmode=disable" \
  --cluster-name demo-cluster \
  --namespace demo \
  --webhook-listen :8080 \
  --metrics-listen :9090 \
  --source-type generic \
  --window-minutes 15 \
  --min-samples 5 \
  --min-executions 5 \
  --latency-threshold 0.20

docs.title: Option B: manager mode (CRD-driven)
docs.text:
kubectl apply -f config/crd/bases/

kubectl create namespace demo
kubectl create secret generic demo-db-dsn -n demo \
  --from-literal=dsn="postgres://user:password@localhost:5432/mydb?sslmode=disable"

cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: radar.pgregressionradar.io/v1alpha1
kind: PostgresWatch
metadata:
  name: demo-db
  namespace: demo
spec:
  clusterName: demo-cluster
  dsnSecretRef:
    name: demo-db-dsn
    key: dsn
  windowMinutes: 15
  minSamples: 5
  minExecutions: 5
  latencyChangeThreshold: "0.20"
---
apiVersion: radar.pgregressionradar.io/v1alpha1
kind: DeploySource
metadata:
  name: demo-generic
  namespace: demo
spec:
  postgresWatchRef: demo-db
  sourceType: generic
EOF

go run ./cmd/manager \
  --webhook-bind-address=:8080 \
  --pg-metrics-bind-address=:9090

docs.title: Option C: Helm
docs.text:
helm install pg-regression-radar ./deploy/helm/deploylens \
  --set mode=operator \
  --set postgres.dsn="postgres://user:password@localhost:5432/mydb?sslmode=disable" \
  --set postgres.clusterName=demo-cluster \
  --set ingester.sourceType=generic

docs.title: 3) Reproduce a deployment-associated regression
docs.text:
Execute the full scenario from Example regression scenario:

  1. Emit a baseline deploy event (revision=v1).
  2. Intentionally slow the query path.
  3. Emit a second deploy event (revision=v2).
  4. Continue query traffic until analysis runs.

Tip

For fast local demos, run with --scrape-interval 1s and keep each baseline/regression traffic phase long enough to cover at least 3–4 scrape windows; short single-burst traffic usually does not produce enough time-series shape for E-divisive detection.

docs.title: 4) Validate that detection worked
docs.text:
Use mode-appropriate checks:

  • operator: check process logs and alert outputs.
  • manager: check logs and created PerformanceRegression resources: 
    kubectl get performanceregressions -A
  • Helm: use the same checks as whichever chart mode you selected (operator or manager).

Expected outcome in all modes:

  • At least one regression is reported for the slowed query.
  • The reported deploy metadata points to the simulated deployment event (for example revision=v2).

docs.title: 5) What "successful detection" looks like in practice
docs.text:
A successful validation is not only "an alert fired." You should also see:

  • Query identity (query text and/or query ID).
  • Measured latency change (before vs after, with change factor/percent).
  • Deployment identity (app/namespace/revision/image tag or equivalent fields from the deploy event).
  • Timestamp/correlation context showing the regression tied to the specific deployment window.

docs.title: Security and production-use context
docs.text:
The commands on this page are intentionally minimal for testing and validation. Do not treat these defaults as production-ready.

For production use, at minimum:

  • Protect webhook ingest with a shared secret (--webhook-secret or spec.webhookSecret) and only trusted senders.
  • Use least-privilege RBAC and explicit Secret-access consent controls where applicable.
  • Apply Kubernetes hardening controls (Pod Security, NetworkPolicy, resource boundaries, and egress controls).
  • Restrict alert destinations and review outbound webhook policy.

For hardened production configuration, see:

  • Deployment security hardening (Helm)
  • Security Model & Threat Model

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Getting Started — run commands for each supported mode.
  • Example regression scenario — reproducible end-to-end validation workflow.
  • Alerting example — concrete alert delivery and interpretation walkthrough.
  • Deploy Sources & Webhooks — webhook source wiring and authentication.

docs.title: Security Model & Threat Model
docs.text: Formal threat model and security contract for who may configure pg-regression-radar, which Secrets it may read, and where it may connect in each supported security profile.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This page defines the security contract for cmd/manager mode: trust assumptions, protected assets, authorization boundaries, and profile-specific operational rules. It is intentionally concrete: an administrator should be able to answer (a) who can create each CRD, (b) which Secrets may be read, (c) where the manager may connect, and (d) what changes between controlled, hardened, and relay-only.

The model applies to the Kubernetes/CRD deployment path (PostgresWatch + DeploySource), including fleet mode via spec.remoteClusterRef (and deprecated spec.remoteClusterSecretRef for backward compatibility) plus the optional spec.cnpgClusterRef remote CloudNativePG Cluster health check, which reuses the same kubeconfig and trust boundary. It does not cover host/OS hardening, cloud IAM design outside Kubernetes, or arbitrary third-party webhook endpoints beyond the controls listed here.

flowchart LR
  T["Tenant<br/>creates a PostgresWatch"]:::ext
  M["manager<br/>broad Secret read"]:::radar
  SP["Spoke cluster<br/>Kubernetes API"]:::ext
  AE["Alert endpoint"]:::ext
  T -->|"consent label required on the Secret"| M
  M -->|"kubeconfig auth restrictions"| SP
  M -->|"URL validation and optional allowlist"| AE

Each arrow is a trust boundary and is labelled with the control that guards it.

docs.title: Security profiles
docs.text: Profile Intended environment Trust assumption Tenancy model Default recommendation controlled Single-tenant cluster or one trusted platform team People with namespace write access are trusted operators Single team or tightly coordinated teams Good baseline when operational simplicity matters most hardened Shared cluster with multiple teams and sensitive production workloads CRD authors are not automatically trusted to select any Secret/destination Multi-team, namespace-isolated Recommended for most production shared clusters relay-only Highly restricted environments (regulated or strict network controls) Manager should not be used as a direct cross-cluster credential broker Multi-team with central integration point Use when direct DB Secret access by manager is not acceptable

docs.title: controlled profile (single-tenant, trusted teams)
docs.text:
Supported:

  • PostgresWatch and DeploySource can be created by trusted team operators in their namespace.
  • spec.remoteClusterRef is preferred; deprecated spec.remoteClusterSecretRef is allowed only when the same trusted team also owns the remote-cluster kubeconfig lifecycle.
  • Alert destinations may be team-defined, still subject to built-in URL checks.

Practical example:

  • A single platform team runs one cluster, owns all namespaces, and uses one manager instance to watch multiple Postgres clusters (including one remote spoke) using team-managed kubeconfig Secrets.

docs.title: hardened profile (multi-team, sensitive production)
docs.text:
Supported:

  • Teams may create PostgresWatch/DeploySource only in their own namespace.
  • Only approved identities may apply the Secret consent label (pg-regression-radar.io/allow-postgreswatch-access=true).
  • Remote-cluster references are allowed only for platform-approved kubeconfig Secrets.
  • Alert destinations are restricted with --alerting-allowed-destinations and the allowlist destination policy. Set --alerting-destination-policy=allowlist alongside a non-empty --alerting-allowed-destinations so every reconciled watch fails fast if its URL is not pre-approved — see Alerting: destination policies.

Practical example:

  • Team A can create a PostgresWatch, but cannot force the manager to read Team B's Secret because unlabeled Secrets are rejected and consent labeling is centrally restricted by admission policy.

docs.title: relay-only profile (highly restricted)
docs.text:
Supported:

  • Teams may define correlation intent (PostgresWatch + DeploySource) through platform-approved templates/policies, but should not manage remote-cluster references directly.
  • Tenant-managed remote-cluster references (spec.remoteClusterRef/deprecated spec.remoteClusterSecretRef) are disallowed by policy (admission/RBAC convention) unless approved as break-glass by platform admins.
  • Manager network egress is restricted to approved alert relays and required in-cluster APIs.

Not supported (by contract):

  • Tenant-managed direct remote-cluster kubeconfig usage.
  • Arbitrary tenant-defined external alert endpoints.

Practical example:

  • A regulated environment routes all alerts through an internal relay service; teams cannot point alerting.url to internet endpoints and cannot attach remote kubeconfigs to watches.
  • Configure the manager with --alerting-destination-policy=relay-only --alerting-destination-policy-relay-url=https://relay.example.com/webhook. Any destinationPolicy or url set in a PostgresWatch spec is ignored; all alert traffic flows through the single relay. The manager fails at startup if the relay URL is empty, catching misconfigurations before any watches are reconciled — see Alerting: destination policies.

docs.title: Actors
docs.text: Actor Typical identity Trusted for Not trusted for (without extra controls) Cluster administrator Cluster-admin / platform SRE Cluster-wide RBAC, admission policy, namespace boundaries Day-to-day app release intent in every team Team lead Namespace admin role Creating team-scoped watches/sources, selecting approved Secrets Global Secret brokering across namespaces/teams Application developer CI/CD or developer role with limited namespace write Proposing DeploySource changes for owned app Choosing privileged Secrets or remote kubeconfigs Operator (manager ServiceAccount) manager-role ClusterRole binding Reading referenced Secrets and reconciling CRDs within granted RBAC Making trust decisions beyond configured labels/RBAC/policies

docs.title: Protected assets
docs.text: Asset Why sensitive PostgreSQL DSN credentials (dsnSecretRef) Direct database access; may include high-privilege roles Remote-cluster kubeconfig Secrets (remoteClusterRef registry entry or deprecated remoteClusterSecretRef) Delegates Kubernetes API access to spoke clusters Alert destination configuration (alerting.url, webhook targets) Potential data exfiltration/SSRF route Deployment metadata (DeployEvent, app/revision/cluster mapping) Operational intelligence about release cadence and topology The dashboard's saved profile (layout edits, panel queries, time ranges) Holds no credentials, but its panel titles, descriptions and queries name applications, namespaces and tables, so it is topology metadata of the same kind as deploy metadata, on the user's disk. See What the dashboard saves

docs.title: Trust boundaries
docs.text: Boundary Crossing event Main risk Mitigation Tenant authoring CRDs -> manager reading Secrets A PostgresWatch references dsnSecretRef plus remoteClusterRef/deprecated remoteClusterSecretRef Confused deputy (manager reads Secrets broader than author's own rights) Secret consent label check before use (Multi-Cluster: Secret consent label) Hub cluster -> spoke cluster Kubernetes API Kubeconfig from remoteClusterRef registry (or deprecated remoteClusterSecretRef) is used to build remote client, to read dsnSecretRef and, when cnpgClusterRef is set, a CloudNativePG Cluster's status Credential/plugin abuse, proxy-based traffic redirection Kubeconfig auth restrictions (exec, auth-provider, proxy-url rejected) (Multi-Cluster: Kubeconfig restrictions) Dashboard page -> dashboard server (the one write) The page saves the user's edits with PUT/DELETE /dashboard/profile; a page on another site, or another process, tries the same Overwriting or reading someone's profile; writing outside the data directory; using a forged request from a browser tab Fixed path, marker header that forces a CORS preflight the server never answers, same-origin Origin/Sec-Fetch-Site, Host check, size limit, validation before write; saving off under --insecure-listen (below) Manager -> external alert endpoint Notifier sends payloads to configured destination SSRF/data exfiltration to unsafe endpoints URL validation + optional strict allowlist (Alerting: Destination validation)

docs.title: Operator responsibilities vs Kubernetes responsibilities
docs.text: Concern Kubernetes platform is responsible for pg-regression-radar operator is responsible for Who can create/modify CRDs RBAC/admission for PostgresWatch and DeploySource Respecting CRD intent, not bypassing API authorization Secret ownership and eligibility Secret creation rights, namespace isolation, consent-label policy Refusing unlabeled Secrets before reading contents Remote cluster access scope Issuing least-privilege kubeconfigs in spoke clusters Rejecting unsafe kubeconfig auth/proxy mechanisms Network destination control NetworkPolicy, egress firewall, DNS policy Rejecting obviously unsafe alert destinations; honoring allowlist config

docs.title: Permission matrix (security contract)
docs.text: Capability controlled hardened relay-only Create PostgresWatch resource ✓ Cluster admin, Team lead ✓ Team lead in own namespace; Cluster admin ✓ Team lead in own namespace; Cluster admin Create/modify DeploySource resource ✓ Cluster admin, Team lead, App developer (team policy) ⚠ Team lead/App developer in own namespace only, with stricter admission ⚠ Team lead/App developer in own namespace only, often templated via platform workflow Manager reads DSN Secret (spec.dsnSecretRef) ✓ If Secret is consent-labeled ✓ If Secret is consent-labeled and label assignment is restricted ⚠ Prefer platform-managed relay/credentials; direct reads only for explicitly approved Secrets Configure remote cluster reference (spec.remoteClusterRef or deprecated spec.remoteClusterSecretRef) ✓ Trusted team operators or Cluster admin ⚠ Platform-approved identities only; tenant use gated by policy ✗ Tenant-managed remote references; break-glass platform admin only

docs.title: Which Secrets may be read
docs.text:
The manager may read only Secrets that satisfy all of the following:

  1. Are reachable through manager RBAC in the hub cluster (config/rbac/role.yaml for hub reads).
  2. Are explicitly consent-labeled: pg-regression-radar.io/allow-postgreswatch-access=true.
  3. When remote-cluster mode is used, are reachable by the kubeconfig identity in the spoke cluster.

In short: label consent is required, RBAC scope still applies, and remote access is additionally constrained by spoke-side RBAC.

docs.title: Where the manager may connect
docs.text: Connection target controlled hardened relay-only Hub Kubernetes API Required Required Required Spoke Kubernetes API via remoteClusterRef (or deprecated remoteClusterSecretRef) Allowed Allowed only for platform-approved references Disallowed by default PostgreSQL endpoint from DSN Allowed per referenced Secret Allowed per approved Secret + tighter namespace policy Usually via approved internal path only Alert endpoints (alerting.url) Team-defined with built-in validation Restricted allowlist + network egress controls Internal relay destinations only

docs.title: Reading the Postgres log (optional, off by default)
docs.text: attribution.arms reads the database's JSON log, either through the Kubernetes pods/log subresource or from a file. A Postgres log can hold anything the server logs, so the access is broad, and the chart grants it only with manager.arms.rbacEnabled: true (cluster-wide get/list on pods and get on pods/log; narrow it to a Role in the database's namespace if you can). What the manager keeps from it: when a statement ran, its application_name, its query_id and its duration. It does not keep the statement text or the bind parameters, a line over 1 MiB is skipped, and the number of distinct application_name/query_id pairs is bounded so a client cannot grow the manager's memory by putting a request id in its application_name. The file path comes from the PostgresWatch, so whoever may create one chooses a file the manager reads: it must be an absolute, clean path to a regular file, and what is read from it is only parsed as log lines, but treat the right to create a PostgresWatch with arms.file as the right to point the manager at any file it can open, or use podLogs. It writes nothing to the database or the cluster.

docs.title: The Observe API and the dashboard (read-only)
docs.text:
The manager serves a read-only Observe API (/observe/v1) on --observe-addr, 127.0.0.1:8083 by default, so it is reachable only from inside the pod. There is no Service or Ingress for it and the chart adds none. The dashboard reaches it through a Kubernetes port-forward with the user's own kubeconfig, which needs get on leases, get on pods and create on pods/portforward in the manager's namespace; whoever lacks that permission cannot see it.

  • Nothing in the API changes cluster state. It serves only deploys in attribution.actuate.namespaces when that list is set, on every endpoint including the event stream.
  • Normalised SQL text is off unless both the manager (--observe-allow-queries) and the dashboard (--show-queries) ask for it.
  • History in Postgres (--observe-history=postgres) reads its DSN from a file (--observe-history-dsn-file, for example a mounted Secret), never from a flag.
  • The dashboard binds to loopback, checks the Host header, accepts only GET and HEAD (and the one save request described next), and sets a strict Content-Security-Policy. It has no sign-in, so --insecure-listen exposes it to anyone who can reach the address; for that reason it also turns saving off.
  • It is read-only toward the cluster and the radar. The only thing it writes is the user's own profile file, in its data directory, described in the next section.

docs.title: What the dashboard saves, and how it is protected
docs.text:
The dashboard keeps the user's edits between runs in one small JSON file per dashboard source, dashboard-default.json or dashboard-file-<id>.json, in --data-dir (default pg-regression-radar/dashboard under the user's configuration directory). See Dashboard: your edits are kept between runs for how a user works with it.

What the file holds: the layout (board and panel ids, types, positions and sizes), each panel's settings, its title, description and query text, the time range of each board, and a fingerprint of the layout it was edited on. Titles, descriptions and queries are text the user typed, so they can name applications, namespaces and tables.

What it never holds: credentials of any kind (the kubeconfig, DSNs, tokens, the history DSN), Observe API data (deploys, evaluations, series, decisions), normalised SQL text, or anything the manager serves. The page does not put such data in the profile and the server accepts only the fields listed above. Do not type secrets into a title or description: they are stored in clear text and shown on the page.

Threat How it is handled Residual risk A web page on another site makes the user's browser write or read the profile A write needs the X-Requested-By: pgrr-dashboard header, which a browser sends cross-site only after a preflight the server never answers; Origin and Sec-Fetch-Site, when present, must be this page's own; the Host check refuses DNS-rebound names for reads and writes; no CORS headers are sent Browsers and extensions that do not enforce CORS are outside this model Another local user reads the file Directory created 0700 and file 0600; the file holds no credentials An existing directory keeps its own permissions (a shared or world-readable --data-dir exposes the file's contents, not secrets); keep the directory private Another local user replaces or tampers with the file Everything read from the file is re-validated: known fields only, a layout that passes the dashboard-file validator, plain ranges, at most 256 KiB; the page sanitises it again and draws all text as text (no HTML), under a strict Content-Security-Policy; an unusable file is reported and left alone until the next save Someone who can write the user's configuration directory can change what the user's own dashboard shows (hide a panel, change a title or query); they can also edit the user's other files Remote users on an exposed dashboard overwrite the profile --insecure-listen turns saving off (the page then keeps edits in the browser) and the command says so None for the file; the page itself is still readable by anyone who can reach it A request names a file to write, or escapes the directory The path is fixed (dashboard-<key>.json in the data directory; the key is default or a digest of the --config path); no request carries a path; writes go to a temporary file in the same directory and are renamed over it A data directory that is itself a symlink or a mount points where the user pointed it A large or malformed body fills the disk or crashes the server At most 256 KiB, a single JSON object, validated before anything is written, one file per source The user can still fill their own disk by other means The file is copied by backup or file-sync software Nothing in it is a credential It is copied like any other file in the configuration directory; point --data-dir somewhere excluded, or use --no-save, where topology names must not leave the machine

Retention and deletion. The file lives until it is removed; there is no expiry and no history. Undo my edits drops the layout from it, and deleting the file (or the data directory) resets everything. --no-save writes nothing to disk and keeps edits in the browser only. In a container or on a read-only file system, an unwritable directory is reported at start and the dashboard falls back to the browser; mount a volume and pass --data-dir to keep edits.

docs.title: Actions on the outside world (optional, off by default)
docs.text:
Two optional features of the attribution engine can change things outside the manager. Both need attribution.mode: enforce on the watch, so a default install does neither.

Capability What it can do What it cannot do Stop it attribution.actuate Set spec.paused or status.abort on an Argo Rollouts rollout reported by an argo-rollouts DeploySource, once per deploy Create, delete, scale, resume or roll back a Rollout; touch any other kind Set actuate.enabled: false, or annotate the PostgresWatch with pg-regression-radar.io/actuation-paused="true" (no restart). Without manager.autoAbort.rbacEnabled the RBAC is not even granted attribution.revert Open a draft pull request that reverts the commit behind a convicted deploy, at most maxPerDay per day, using the token in tokenSecretRef Merge or approve it. It creates a revert branch and a draft pull request (GitHub's revertPullRequest), and only for the merge commit of a merged pull request Remove revert, or revoke the token. Give the token only the access to open pull requests on that one repository

Every pause and abort is recorded in the action ledger (GET /api/v1/attribution/actions) and in pg_regression_radar_attribution_actions_total, and an abort that did not help counts toward a circuit breaker that stops further action. The endpoints that serve the verdict and the ledger are read-only and unauthenticated: expose them only inside the cluster (a ClusterIP Service) and restrict them with a NetworkPolicy.

docs.title: Namespace isolation assumptions
docs.text:
• PostgresWatch and DeploySource are namespace-scoped resources; this model assumes teams do not get arbitrary write across other teams' namespaces.
  • In fleet mode, default remote Secret lookup uses the same namespace name as the watch unless remoteNamespace is explicitly set (Multi-Cluster: What actually happens on reconcile).

docs.title: Multi-tenancy restrictions by profile
docs.text:
• controlled: relies mostly on trust and process; technical controls are still present but may be less restrictive operationally.
  • hardened: requires admission/RBAC reinforcement around consent label use and remote reference ownership.
  • relay-only: intentionally removes tenant-controlled remote references and external destination freedom.

docs.title: Scope limits of this model
docs.text:
This document defines the contract for CRD-driven access mediation and manager connection surfaces. It does not guarantee:

  • host-level compromise resistance,
  • protection from all DNS rebinding variants,
  • automatic remote kubeconfig credential rotation,
  • full policy examples for every admission controller product.

docs.title: Existing security controls and where they live
docs.text: Control Purpose Documented in Implemented in Secret consent label (pg-regression-radar.io/allow-postgreswatch-access=true) Prevent confused-deputy Secret reads from arbitrary references Multi-Cluster: Secret consent label, Configuration Reference internal/controller/secret_consent.go, enforced in internal/controller/postgreswatch_controller.go Optional admission policy restricting consent label setters Ensure only approved identities can opt Secrets in docs/policies/kyverno-consent-label-policy.yaml Cluster admission engine (example policy file in repo) Kubeconfig restrictions for remote cluster refs Block exec plugins, auth-provider, and proxy-url in tenant-supplied kubeconfigs Multi-Cluster: Kubeconfig restrictions internal/controller/remote_client.go (validateKubeconfigAuth) Alert destination validation and allowlist support Reduce SSRF/exfiltration risk for alerting destinations Alerting: Destination validation internal/alerting notifier construction and destination validation path Webhook shared-secret authentication Prevent unauthenticated deploy-event injection Deploy Sources & Webhooks: Webhook authentication internal/cli/ingester.go (X-Webhook-Token constant-time check) Dashboard profile write protection (marker header, same-origin check, fixed path, validation, 0600 file, saving off under --insecure-listen) Keep the dashboard's one write from being forged, redirected or abused Security model: What the dashboard saves, Dashboard internal/dashboard/profile.go, internal/dashboard/server.go, internal/cli/dashboard.go Manager RBAC split (hub Secrets vs spoke kubeconfig rights) Clarify and constrain what manager SA can do in hub cluster Multi-Cluster: RBAC config/rbac/role.yaml + spoke-cluster RBAC provided by kubeconfig owner

docs.title: Hardened-mode deployment: admission + RBAC for consent labeling
docs.text: Use these policy examples to ensure tenants cannot self-approve Secret access by setting pg-regression-radar.io/allow-postgreswatch-access=true themselves.

docs.title: Option A: Kyverno policy
docs.text:
1. Apply RBAC example identities: 
    kubectl apply -f docs/policies/rbac-consent-labeler-example.yaml
  2. Apply Kyverno policy: 
    kubectl apply -f docs/policies/kyverno-consent-label-policy.yaml
  3. Verify enforcement: 
    kubectl get cpol restrict-postgreswatch-consent-label
kubectl describe cpol restrict-postgreswatch-consent-label

docs.title: Option B: Kubernetes ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (CEL)
docs.text:
1. Ensure your cluster supports ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (Kubernetes 1.26+ with feature enabled).
  2. Apply RBAC example identities: 
    kubectl apply -f docs/policies/rbac-consent-labeler-example.yaml
  3. Apply CEL policy + binding: 
    kubectl apply -f docs/policies/validating-admission-policy-consent-label.yaml
  4. Verify enforcement: 
    kubectl get validatingadmissionpolicy restrict-postgreswatch-consent-label
kubectl get validatingadmissionpolicybinding restrict-postgreswatch-consent-label

docs.title: RBAC strategy (least privilege)
docs.text:
• Use a dedicated identity for labeling (docs/policies/rbac-consent-labeler-example.yaml).
  • Keep tenant PostgresWatch authors in roles that exclude Secret mutation (create, update, patch, delete on Secrets).
  • Treat break-glass labeler identities as audited, short-lived operational paths.
  • Policy allowlists in examples match exact Kubernetes usernames (system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<name>); adapt to group-based checks if your platform standard prefers groups.

docs.title: Validate policy behavior with kubectl --dry-run=server
docs.text:
Note

Replace <ns> with a namespace where your policy applies.

Attempt without consent label (should be admitted; controller will still refuse to use it):

cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -n <ns> --dry-run=server -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: dry-run-without-consent
type: Opaque
stringData:
  dsn: postgres://example
EOF

Attempt with consent label as unauthorized identity (should be denied):

cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -n <ns> --as=system:serviceaccount:team-a:app-operator --dry-run=server -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: dry-run-unauthorized-labeler
  labels:
    pg-regression-radar.io/allow-postgreswatch-access: "true"
type: Opaque
stringData:
  dsn: postgres://example
EOF

Attempt with consent label as approved labeler identity (should succeed):

cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -n <ns> --as=system:serviceaccount:platform-security:secret-consent-labeler --dry-run=server -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: dry-run-authorized-labeler
  labels:
    pg-regression-radar.io/allow-postgreswatch-access: "true"
type: Opaque
stringData:
  dsn: postgres://example
EOF

docs.title: Troubleshooting common misconfigurations
docs.text:
• Policy appears inactive: ensure Kyverno is healthy (kubectl -n kyverno get pods) or that ValidatingAdmissionPolicy feature is enabled on API server.
  • Unexpected deny: confirm caller identity (kubectl auth whoami) and compare to the allowlist in the policy file.
  • Unauthorized users can still label: verify their RBAC grants do not include Secret mutation verbs.
  • Manager still rejects a Secret: confirm exact label key/value is present: pg-regression-radar.io/allow-postgreswatch-access=true.
