docs.title: Supply Chain Verification
docs.text:
How to confirm that a pg-regression-radar artifact you downloaded matches what was built from the source commit you expect.

Every artifact published by a release — container images, Helm chart, and attached SBOM/provenance attestations — is cryptographically signed and traceable back to the exact source commit and GitHub Actions run that produced it. This page explains the trust model and gives the exact commands to verify each artifact type.

flowchart LR
  TAG["Git tag vX.Y.Z"]:::ext
  subgraph REL["release.yml, GitHub Actions"]
    B["Build images<br/>and chart"]:::radar
    S["Trivy scan:<br/>fail on CRITICAL"]:::radar
    SG["Sign keyless (Fulcio),<br/>SBOM and SLSA provenance"]:::radar
  end
  REG["ghcr.io<br/>image, chart, signatures"]:::out
  LOG["Rekor<br/>transparency log"]:::ext
  YOU["You: cosign verify<br/>against release.yml"]:::gate
  TAG --> B
  B --> S
  S --> SG
  SG --> REG
  SG --> LOG
  REG --> YOU
  LOG --> YOU

Verification checks that the artifact was signed by this repository's release workflow and that the signature is in the public log.

docs.title: Trust model
docs.text:
Signing uses Cosign in keyless mode: instead of a stored private key (which can be stolen, rotated, or mis-scoped), the GitHub Actions runner exchanges its own OIDC token for a short-lived signing certificate from Sigstore's public Fulcio CA. The certificate's Subject Alternative Name encodes the exact workflow URL and Git ref at build time. Every signature is recorded in Rekor, Sigstore's public, append-only transparency log, so it can be audited independently.

What this guarantees when you run cosign verify:

  • The artifact was signed during a run of .github/workflows/release.yml in this repository (not just "any GitHub Actions workflow, anywhere").
  • The signing certificate was issued for the exact ref and SHA you expect (visible in the verified output).
  • The signature is present in the public Rekor log — it cannot be back-dated or silently removed.

What this does not guarantee:

  • That the tag commit itself is correct — verify the Git tag signature with git tag -v <tag> if your threat model includes a compromised GitHub account pushing a bad tag.
  • That new CVEs have not been disclosed against the published image bytes after release date — scan locally with Trivy if you need a current view.

docs.title: Artifact inventory
docs.text:
Artifact Registry path Signed? SBOM? Provenance? cli image (amd64 + arm64) ghcr.io/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/cli:<tag> ✓ keyless ✓ SPDX attached ✓ SLSA attestation operator image (amd64 + arm64) ghcr.io/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/operator:<tag> ✓ keyless ✓ SPDX attached ✓ SLSA attestation manager image (amd64 + arm64) ghcr.io/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/manager:<tag> ✓ keyless ✓ SPDX attached ✓ SLSA attestation collector image (amd64 + arm64) ghcr.io/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/collector:<tag> ✓ keyless ✓ SPDX attached ✓ SLSA attestation ingester image (amd64 + arm64) ghcr.io/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/ingester:<tag> ✓ keyless ✓ SPDX attached ✓ SLSA attestation Helm chart (OCI) ghcr.io/joao00001/charts/pg-regression-radar:<chart-version> ✓ keyless — ✓ SLSA attestation

Per-architecture images (:v1.9.2-amd64, :v1.9.2-arm64) are signed individually during the build job. The multi-arch manifest lists (:v1.9.2, :latest) are additionally signed after assembly — so cosign verify works whether you pin the multi-arch tag or a specific arch digest.

Chart versions use SemVer without a leading v (e.g. 1.9.2), matching what helm install --version accepts. The image tag (:v1.9.2) and chart version (1.9.2) are always derived from the same Git tag.

docs.title: Finding the digest
docs.text:
Every GitHub Release page lists the pushed tag name and links to the Actions run. To resolve the exact digest of any image:

# Print the digest for the multi-arch manifest list
docker buildx imagetools inspect \
  ghcr.io/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/operator:v1.9.2 \
  --format '{{json .Manifest}}' | jq -r '.digest'

# Or with crane (faster, no daemon needed)
crane digest ghcr.io/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/operator:v1.9.2

For the Helm chart:

helm show chart oci://ghcr.io/joao00001/charts/pg-regression-radar --version 1.9.2 \
  | grep -E '^(version|appVersion):'

docs.title: Verifying image signatures
docs.text:
These examples use v1.9.2, the release this documentation describes; replace it with the release tag you are verifying. The --certificate-identity-regexp must match the release workflow path exactly; the --certificate-oidc-issuer must be GitHub's Actions token endpoint.

IMAGE=ghcr.io/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/operator:v1.9.2

cosign verify "$IMAGE" \
  --certificate-identity-regexp \
    "^https://github.com/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/tags/v" \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com

A successful verification prints the JSON payload of each matching signature, which includes the workflow ref, run URL, and SHA. A failure (wrong issuer, wrong identity, or no recorded signature) exits non-zero and prints an error — there is no silent pass on mismatch.

Verify a per-arch image by digest instead of tag:

DIGEST=$(docker buildx imagetools inspect \
  ghcr.io/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/operator:v1.9.2-amd64 \
  --format '{{json .Manifest}}' | jq -r '.digest')

cosign verify "ghcr.io/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/operator@${DIGEST}" \
  --certificate-identity-regexp \
    "^https://github.com/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/tags/v" \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com

docs.title: Verifying the Helm chart signature
docs.text:
The Helm chart is published as an OCI artifact to ghcr.io/joao00001/charts/pg-regression-radar. Cosign signs any OCI artifact by digest, so cosign verify works identically to images:

cosign verify ghcr.io/joao00001/charts/pg-regression-radar:1.9.2 \
  --certificate-identity-regexp \
    "^https://github.com/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/tags/v" \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com

docs.title: Inspecting the SBOM
docs.text:
Each image digest has an SPDX-JSON SBOM attached as a signed in-toto attestation. Fetch and inspect it:

IMAGE=ghcr.io/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/operator:v1.9.2

cosign verify-attestation "$IMAGE" \
  --type spdxjson \
  --certificate-identity-regexp \
    "^https://github.com/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/tags/v" \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com \
  | jq -r '.payload | @base64d | fromjson | .predicate'

The predicate output is an SPDX document listing every OS package and Go module baked into the image at build time. To extract just the package list:

cosign verify-attestation "$IMAGE" \
  --type spdxjson \
  --certificate-identity-regexp \
    "^https://github.com/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/tags/v" \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com \
  | jq -r '.payload | @base64d | fromjson | .predicate.packages[].name'

SBOM files are also uploaded as GitHub Actions artifacts during the release run and attached to the GitHub Release for offline inspection (named sbom-<target>-<arch>-<version>.spdx.json).

docs.title: Verifying provenance attestations (SLSA)
docs.text:
Releases also publish provenance attestations via actions/attest-build-provenance. Verify them with:

IMAGE=ghcr.io/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/operator:v1.9.2

gh attestation verify "$IMAGE" \
  --owner joao00001

For the Helm chart OCI artifact:

CHART=ghcr.io/joao00001/charts/pg-regression-radar:1.9.2

gh attestation verify "$CHART" \
  --owner joao00001

docs.title: Scanning locally for vulnerabilities
docs.text:
To check a released image for CVEs beyond those known at release date:

trivy image ghcr.io/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/operator:v1.9.2

The release pipeline already scans every image at build time and fails on any CRITICAL-severity finding, so the image was clean at release date. trivy image here gives you a current view (new CVE disclosures may have occurred since).

docs.title: Provenance: connecting source commit to built artifact
docs.text:
Build arguments VERSION, COMMIT, and DATE are injected at build time (see the Build step in .github/workflows/release.yml):

  • VERSION — the pushed Git tag (e.g. v1.9.2)
  • COMMIT — the full Git SHA of the tagged commit (github.sha)
  • DATE — RFC 3339 UTC timestamp of the build start

These values are baked into each binary's --version output via internal/buildinfo. To confirm the binary in a pulled image was built from the commit you expect:

docker run --rm ghcr.io/joao00001/pg-regression-radar/cli:v1.9.2 pg-regression-radar version
# Expected output includes: version=v1.9.2  commit=<sha>  date=<timestamp>

Cross-reference commit with the GitHub Release's linked tag commit SHA to confirm they match.

docs.title: Automated verification script
docs.text:
scripts/verify-release.sh automates the checks above. It requires cosign and jq to be installed:

./scripts/verify-release.sh v1.9.2

The script verifies signatures for all five images (multi-arch manifest lists) and the Helm chart, then prints a summary. Pass --help for usage.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
cosign verify exits with "no matching signatures"

The image was either not pushed by release.yml (e.g. a local build), or the --certificate-identity-regexp does not match. Verify you are using the exact URL pattern shown above, including the trailing /refs/tags/v anchor. Signatures are not stored in the image itself — they live in the registry's referrers API and in the public Rekor log. If the image was re-tagged or mirrored to a different registry, signatures do not follow.

cosign verify-attestation exits with "no matching attestations"

The SBOM attestation is attached to the per-arch digest, not the manifest-list tag. If you are verifying a manifest-list reference (:v1.9.2) and your registry/cosign version does not traverse the index, pin to a per-arch digest instead (:v1.9.2-amd64 or :v1.9.2-arm64).

helm push digest not parseable (historic release gap)

Before v1.0.1, the Helm chart signing step was missing a separate Docker registry login for cosign, causing the sign step to fail with UNAUTHORIZED. The chart was pushed but unsigned. Starting with v1.0.1, cosign verify against the chart passes. Images were signed from the first release.

docs.title: Support Matrix
docs.text: Officially supported PostgreSQL versions and distributions, what "supported" means for each, and which project features require which minimum version or extension.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This page is the single source of truth for "will pg-regression-radar work against my Postgres, and how thoroughly is that combination actually tested." It covers two independent axes — PostgreSQL major version and distribution (community/vanilla, CloudNativePG, EDB Postgres Advanced Server, EDB Postgres Extended Server) — plus a feature-by-feature breakdown of minimum version/extension requirements, since "supported" doesn't mean every feature is available on every combination.

docs.title: Officially supported PostgreSQL versions
docs.text:
Version Status Verified in CI 16 Officially supported Yes — every PR (integration-postgres matrix, .github/workflows/ci.yml) 17 Officially supported Yes — every PR (integration-postgres matrix, .github/workflows/ci.yml) 18 Officially supported Yes — every PR (integration-postgres matrix, .github/workflows/ci.yml)

16 is the floor of the officially tested matrix, not an arbitrary cutoff: it's the minimum version required by this project's newest feature, EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON, GENERIC_PLAN)-based plan-diff capture (see Feature requirements by version below). Rather than support a matrix where some officially-listed versions can't run every feature, the floor was raised to match the newest requirement already in the codebase.

PostgreSQL versions below 16 — degraded mode, not refused

pg-regression-radar does not refuse to connect to, or artificially block, a PostgreSQL server older than 16. internal/collector detects server_version_num at startup and already falls back to the pre-13 total_time/mean_time pg_stat_statements column names when needed (see Collector Internals), and internal/planner.CapturePlan returns planner.ErrUnsupportedVersion (logged once at Info, not fatal) rather than failing the scrape when the server is older than 16 (see Detection Algorithm).

In practice, a server on PostgreSQL 14 or 15 gets full regression detection (collector, correlation engine, alerting) exactly as documented, minus:

  • The optional --capture-plans plan-diff hint (EXPLAIN GENERIC_PLAN, PostgreSQL 16+ only).
  • Any assumption this matrix's CI coverage says about that specific version — a pre-16 server has never been exercised by integration-postgres, only by ad hoc local testing, if at all.

Versions below 14 are untested and unsupported in any sense — CloudNativePG's own currently-supported releases only ship PostgreSQL 14+ (see Collector Internals), so there is no realistic deployment target below that line anyway.

docs.title: CloudNativePG: deployment target and validation coverage
docs.text: pg-regression-radar's Helm chart, CRDs, and docs consistently treat CloudNativePG as the reference way to run Postgres on Kubernetes, and nothing in the codebase is CloudNativePG-specific in a way that would make it not work (it talks to Postgres over a normal DSN, exactly the same as any other Postgres). This is backed by a real, automated proof, not just that reasoning: e2e-kind.yml creates a real kind cluster, installs the real CloudNativePG operator and a real Cluster, installs pg-regression-radar via the Helm chart in mode=manager, and asserts a real PerformanceRegression CR is produced from real traffic — and e2e-kind-multicluster.yml extends that same proof across two real clusters (fleet mode's hub/spoke split). Both are label-gated/manual rather than running on every PR (real kind clusters are comparatively heavy for a per-push check) — see Roadmap → Known robustness gaps for exactly what each workflow does and does not cover (real ArgoCD, pg_store_plans on the CloudNativePG operand image, and each workflow's own "not yet proven green on a real runner" status are the remaining honest gaps).

docs.title: CI coverage for EDB distributions
docs.text:
EDB Postgres Advanced Server and EDB Postgres Extended Server images are not publicly pullable: they live behind docker.enterprisedb.com, which requires an authenticated EDB subscription (docker login -u k8s -p <token>) to pull at all — see EDB's private registry docs. GitHub Actions never exposes repository secrets to pull_request runs triggered from a fork, so essentially every external contributor's PR runs with no way to authenticate to that registry.

To keep the matrix honest without breaking CI for the common case (no EDB subscription configured), .github/workflows/ci.yml has a separate integration-edb-postgres job that:

  1. Only runs if the EDB_SUBSCRIPTION_TOKEN repository secret is non-empty — otherwise the job is skipped entirely (shows as skipped in the Actions UI, not failed, and doesn't block merging).
  2. Runs with continue-on-error: true even when it does run, so a mismatch between this workflow's docker run invocation and the real EDB image's entrypoint conventions (which this environment could not verify against the real, credential-gated image) can't turn an otherwise-green PR red.

Maintainers with an EDB subscription: configure the EDB_SUBSCRIPTION_TOKEN secret under the repository's Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions to enable this job's coverage. Until that's done, EPAS and PGE remain documented as officially supported distributions, but are not verified automatically on every PR — only community postgres:16/17/18 get that automatic, unconditional coverage. This mirrors the same "opt-in when it needs resources not every environment has" pattern e2e-manual.yml already uses for its own credential/resource-heavy checks (see CI/CD).

docs.title: Feature requirements by version or extension
docs.text: Feature Minimum requirement Notes pg_stat_statements Required, all supported versions The core data source for every sample the Collector reads; there is no code path that runs without it. Must be loaded via shared_preload_libraries (a server restart, not just ALTER SYSTEM + reload — see the comment in .github/workflows/ci.yml's integration-postgres job). Attribution engine (attribution.enabled) The watch's own collector (not a Prometheus sample source); about 45 minutes of history before hold and pause are possible Opt-in. Validated against PostgreSQL 16 under synthetic load; see the roadmap Rollout actuation (attribution.actuate) Argo Rollouts Rollout objects with spec.paused and status.abort, and manager.autoAbort.rbacEnabled Opt-in, enforce mode only. The pause and abort calls were checked against the Argo Rollouts CRD on a real API server Arm-labelled evidence (attribution.arms) PostgreSQL 15 or newer with compute_query_id = on and a jsonlog destination; the log read from a file or, in Kubernetes, from the pods' pods/log. Argo Rollouts pods whose application_name begins with the pod name. CloudNativePG's wrapped JSON log is unwrapped but not yet verified against a live cluster pg_stat_statements column names PostgreSQL 13+ uses total_exec_time/mean_exec_time; below that, total_time/mean_time Handled automatically — the collector detects server_version_num once at startup and picks the right column names (see Collector Internals). Every version in the officially supported matrix (16-18) uses the modern names; this only matters for the degraded-mode case below 16. EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON, GENERIC_PLAN) PostgreSQL 16+ The plan-diff capture source behind the optional --capture-plans flag (internal/planner.CapturePlan) — see Detection Algorithm. Returns planner.ErrUnsupportedVersion below PostgreSQL 16; this is exactly why the matrix floor above is 16. pg_store_plans extension (optional) pg_store_plans >= 1.6 on PostgreSQL 14+ before its queryid is trusted as joinable against pg_stat_statements; older versions/servers fall back to GENERIC_PLAN automatically Implemented and verified against a real, PGXS-compiled install (internal/planner.CapturePlanFromStorePlans, preferred over GENERIC_PLAN-based plan-diff whenever installed and trusted — see Detection Algorithm): scripts/pg_store_plans builds a real PostgreSQL 17 with the real upstream extension, and the integration-pg-store-plans CI job runs internal/planner's integration test against it on every PR — not just a fake *sql.DB. See Testing for how to run it locally. --state-backend=postgres (optional durable state) No extra version requirement beyond the base matrix above Plain DDL/DML against a regression_radar schema — see Persistence. Works identically across 16/17/18 and, in degraded mode, below 16 too.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: Every layer of test coverage this project runs, from plain go test to a real containerized end-to-end run and a real Kubernetes cluster, and how to reproduce each one locally.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: pg-regression-radar has five distinct layers of testing, each catching a different class of bug. This page lists all five and how to run each locally; see CI/CD for which of them run automatically and when.

docs.title: Unit tests (fakes/mocks, no external services)
docs.text:
go test ./...       # run all tests
go vet ./...        # static analysis
go build ./...      # build all binaries

These cover collector, correlation, ingester, alerting, storage, controller, and CLI-flag/--dry-run logic against synthetic data and fakes — fast (the whole suite runs in well under a second), and safe to run with no external services. .github/workflows/ci.yml's build-and-test job runs this exact command on every push/PR and posts a per-package coverage breakdown to the job's summary (go tool cover -func, plus the raw profile as a downloadable artifact) — visibility, not a hard-blocking threshold.

docs.title: Coverage philosophy
docs.text:
There is no single repo-wide coverage percentage this project targets, deliberately: unit coverage means genuinely different things depending on what a package actually does, and a blanket target (99%, say) would either be impossible for some packages or actively counterproductive for others.

  • Pure logic — internal/correlation's statistics (E-divisive, Welch's t-test, its p-value machinery), internal/collector's query fingerprinting, internal/alerting's formatters, internal/ingester's payload parsing, internal/cli's flag validation and --dry-run checks — has no real dependency (no network, no database, no Kubernetes API) standing between it and a fast, deterministic unit test. This is where high unit coverage (90-100%) is both achievable and worth pursuing, and where a coverage number going down on a PR diff is a meaningful signal worth looking at.
  • Real-infrastructure-dependent code — internal/collector's actual pg_stat_statements scrape, internal/storage/postgres's SQL, internal/controller's envtest-based reconciliation — correctly shows up as low/zero in the unit-only coverage number above, because faking away a real Postgres/Kubernetes API to chase that number would mean testing the fake, not the code. This is covered instead, deliberately, by the real-infrastructure integration tests, the envtest suite, and the two full end-to-end workflows below — see CI/CD for which of those actually run automatically.
  • Wiring/glue code — cmd/*/main.go's few-line wrappers, generated code (zz_generated.deepcopy.go), SetupWithManager calls — isn't meaningfully unit-testable at all (there's no logic to assert on beyond "does it call the thing it's supposed to call"), and its correctness is instead proven by the fact the real binary starts up and reconciles for real in the real-cluster end-to-end test below. No coverage target applies here, and none should.

docs.title: Real-infrastructure integration tests
docs.text:
Gated behind the integration build tag so go test ./... stays safe with no database or Kubernetes API available:

# Real PostgreSQL (internal/storage/postgres, internal/collector, and
# internal/e2e — the last one runs the full Collector -> correlation.Engine
# -> alerting pipeline against real pg_stat_statements data, the closest
# thing to a proof that regressions are actually detected end to end).
# CI runs this same command against postgres:16, postgres:17, and
# postgres:18 (see the integration-postgres matrix in ci.yml) — pick
# whichever tag locally, they're all officially supported; see the
# support matrix doc for the full version/distribution matrix, including
# the separate, secret-gated job that also runs this suite against EDB
# Postgres Advanced Server and EDB Postgres Extended Server.
docker run -d --name pgrr-test -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=test -p 5432:5432 \
  postgres:16 postgres -c shared_preload_libraries=pg_stat_statements
export PGRR_TEST_DSN="postgres://postgres:test@localhost:5432/postgres?sslmode=disable"
go test -tags=integration ./internal/storage/... ./internal/collector/... ./internal/e2e/... ./internal/cli/...

docs.title: Real pg_store_plans extension
docs.text:
internal/planner.CapturePlanFromStorePlans (see Detection Algorithm) prefers the real, previously-executed plan pg_store_plans records over an EXPLAIN (GENERIC_PLAN) estimate — but none of the plain postgres:16/17/18 images the integration tests above run against ship that third-party C extension at all. scripts/pg_store_plans builds a server that does, compiling the real upstream source via PGXS:

docker build -t pgrr-pg-store-plans scripts/pg_store_plans
docker run -d --name pgrr-test-storeplans -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=test -p 5432:5432 \
  pgrr-pg-store-plans
export PGRR_STOREPLANS_TEST_DSN="postgres://user:password@localhost:5432/postgres?sslmode=disable"
go test -tags=integration -run StorePlans -v ./internal/planner/...

internal/planner/storeplans_integration_test.go skips automatically if PGRR_STOREPLANS_TEST_DSN is unset (a plain go test ./... or the integration-postgres run above never needs it), but fails loudly — rather than silently falling back to GENERIC_PLAN — if it's set and pointed at a server that doesn't actually have a reliable pg_store_plans installed. .github/workflows/ci.yml's integration-pg-store-plans job runs this exact sequence on every push/PR, unconditionally: everything it pulls from (Debian's own deb.debian.org archives and the public pg_store_plans GitHub repo) is public and unauthenticated, unlike the secret-gated EDB job below, so there's no reason to gate it behind a repository secret or continue-on-error.

scripts/pg_store_plans/Dockerfile deliberately isn't FROM postgres:17: that image's apt source (apt.postgresql.org/PGDG) ships pre-built server binaries only, with no postgresql-server-dev-17 headers to compile a PGXS extension against, and depending on network/DNS configuration that registry isn't always reachable at all. Debian trixie's own archives ship postgresql-17 and postgresql-server-dev-17 built from the exact same source at the exact same version, which is what makes the PGXS build reliably load into that same server — see the Dockerfile's own comments for the full rationale.

# Real kube-apiserver + etcd (internal/controller):
go install sigs.k8s.io/controller-runtime/tools/setup-envtest@latest
export KUBEBUILDER_ASSETS="$(setup-envtest use 1.31.0 -p path)"
go test ./internal/controller/... -run TestEnvtest -v

docs.title: Diagnosing a failure: internal/testlogger
docs.text:
Every test in this section (plus the envtest suite and the rest of internal/controller's reconciler-backed tests) builds its *slog.Logger via testlogger.New(t) instead of constructing one directly. It behaves exactly like a discarded logger while a test passes — nothing extra printed, no change to the fast path — but if the test fails, t.Cleanup dumps everything the code under test logged during that test through t.Log, right next to the failing assertion:

--- FAIL: TestEnvtest_PostgresWatch_RemoteClusterSecretRef_FetchesDSNFromRemoteAPIServer (4.07s)
    remote_cluster_envtest_test.go:142: reconcile: dsn secret default/remote-dsn is missing the required consent label ...
    testlogger.go:78: --- captured application logs (only shown because this test failed) ---
    testlogger.go:79: time=... level=INFO msg="resolving dsn secret" secret=default/remote-dsn
                      time=... level=ERROR msg="secret consent check failed" secret=default/remote-dsn

Before this, a failing integration/envtest test's only diagnostic output was whatever single line its own t.Fatalf/t.Errorf happened to include — the reconciler's, collector's, or ingester's own logging was silently thrown away unconditionally, on both success and failure. If you're writing a new integration or internal/controller test, use testlogger.New(t) rather than reaching for slog.New(slog.NewTextHandler(io.Discard, nil)) directly.

docs.title: Why internal/e2e exists
docs.text:
Every other test in this project stops short of proving the full detection pipeline works:

  • internal/correlation's tests feed the engine hand-built QuerySample slices, so they validate the statistics but never touch a real Collector or a real Postgres.
  • internal/collector's integration test proves scrape() reads pg_stat_statements correctly, but stops there — it never feeds those samples into correlation.Engine.
  • internal/controller's tests (fake client and envtest) deliberately use an unreachable DSN so no scrape ever fires; they prove the Kubernetes reconciliation state machine, not detection.

internal/e2e/pipeline_integration_test.go closes that gap: it drives a real Collector against a real Postgres, feeds the real samples into a real correlation.Engine, and asserts a real HTTP POST fires from alerting.WebhookNotifier — with a control query that must not be flagged, so the test can't pass just by flagging everything indiscriminately after any deploy.

docs.title: OpenTelemetry pipeline validation
docs.text:
The OTLP pieces are unit-tested with httptest servers and a test-only protobuf reader (internal/telemetry/otlpdeploy, internal/telemetry/otlpexport, internal/ingester/otlp_test.go, internal/controller/otlp_export_test.go). Beyond that, scripts/validate-otel-example.sh runs the worked example from OpenTelemetry / Prometheus Sample Source against real containers (PostgreSQL, OpenTelemetry Collector contrib, Prometheus) and needs only Docker, curl and python3:

bash scripts/validate-otel-example.sh

The OTLP deploy and export paths were also checked by hand against a real Collector (otlphttp exporter → ingester with --source-type otlp; the controller's exporter → a Collector with the debug exporter), in both protobuf+gzip and JSON encodings. deploy/helm/deploylens/tests/otlp.sh renders the chart's OTLP values (needs helm).

docs.title: Manual end-to-end smoke test (real container)
docs.text:
None of the tests above build the Docker image or run it as a container — they exercise Go source directly. The "Manual E2E (real container)" workflow (.github/workflows/e2e-manual.yml) does: it builds the operator image from the Dockerfile, runs it as a real container against a real PostgreSQL container (pg_stat_statements preloaded), generates real before/after query traffic, POSTs a real deploy webhook to the running container's /webhook endpoint, and asserts a real alert HTTP request lands on a mock receiver — the operator treated as an opaque black box, the same way it runs in Kubernetes.

It runs as two jobs (build-image, then e2e) so a failure to build the image and a failure to detect the regression show up as two distinct, independently-inspectable results in the Actions UI, with the image crossing the job boundary via docker save/upload-artifact and download-artifact/docker load.

It's workflow_dispatch-only (not on every push/PR, since it spins up several containers and sleeps through real wall-clock windows): trigger it from the Actions tab -> "Manual E2E (real container)" -> Run workflow.

To build the image locally:

docker build --target operator -t pg-regression-radar/operator .
docker build --target manager  -t pg-regression-radar/manager  .

It deliberately uses --source-type=generic with an explicit, already-elapsed deploy timestamp rather than --source-type=argocd: cmd/operator's ingester-poll loop analyses a deploy event exactly once, on the first 5s poll tick that observes it, with no retry. An argocd-shaped webhook always stamps the deploy timestamp at receipt time, which would race that fixed poll interval against however much "after" traffic had been generated so far. Recording the timestamp after both traffic phases have already happened removes that race entirely.

docs.title: Real-cluster end-to-end test (kind + CloudNativePG)
docs.text:
Everything above proves either the Go source directly (go test) or the built container image against plain Docker (the manual e2e above) — neither ever touches a real Kubernetes API server, a real CRD, or a real CloudNativePG installation, so neither can catch a bug specific to cmd/manager/PostgresWatchReconciler's Kubernetes integration (RBAC, CRD schema, Secret lookups against a real operator-managed Secret, the webhook route a DeploySource registers, and so on). The "E2E (kind + CloudNativePG)" workflow (.github/workflows/e2e-kind.yml) closes that gap:

  1. Creates a real kind (Kubernetes-in-Docker) cluster.
  2. Installs the real CloudNativePG operator from its official upstream manifest and applies a real Cluster CR — a real PostgreSQL instance, managed by a real operator, with pg_stat_statements enabled via CloudNativePG's own managed-extension mechanism.
  3. Builds this commit's manager image from the Dockerfile and loads it into the kind cluster with kind load docker-image — no registry involved.
  4. Installs pg-regression-radar the same way Installation and Getting Started document: the Helm chart in deploy/helm/deploylens, mode=manager, which installs the CRDs, the manager's RBAC, and the manager Deployment/Service.
  5. Applies a PostgresWatch CR whose dsnSecretRef points directly at the Secret CloudNativePG itself generated for the Cluster (<cluster-name>-app, key uri) — proving the DSN-from-a-real-operator-managed-Secret integration path, not a hand-written one.
  6. Generates real "before"/"after" query traffic against the real Postgres from a throwaway client Pod, sends a real HTTP webhook to the manager's real /webhook/<namespace>/<name> route via kubectl port-forward, and asserts a real PerformanceRegression CR lands with status.status: Detected.

Deliberately out of scope for this first pass — see Roadmap for both tracked as explicit follow-ups:

  • No real ArgoCD. Standing up ArgoCD's Application controller and its Notifications engine (the part that actually emits an on-sync-succeeded webhook — see Deploy Sources & Webhooks) is a second, mostly-orthogonal integration surface. This workflow posts a sourceType: generic payload directly to the DeploySource webhook route instead — the same deliberate choice the manual e2e workflow above documents for the same reason (a generic payload carries an explicit, already-elapsed timestamp, avoiding a race against the reconciler's fixed 5s poll interval that an argocd-shaped payload would reintroduce).
  • No pg_store_plans on the CloudNativePG instance specifically. It's a C extension not compiled into CloudNativePG's default operand images; building and maintaining a custom CloudNativePG operand image just for this smoke test wasn't judged worth it yet. This is narrower than "is pg_store_plans validated against a real server at all" — see Real pg_store_plans extension above, which validates the real extension outside of CloudNativePG specifically, and Roadmap for the full history.

It's workflow_dispatch-only by default, for the same reason as the manual e2e above: creating a Kubernetes cluster, installing two operators, and sleeping through real traffic-generation windows takes several minutes. It's also opt-in on a per-PR basis, though — adding the run-e2e-kind label to a pull request runs it against that PR, and re-runs it on every subsequent push for as long as the label stays attached. See CI/CD for the exact trigger conditions, and that same section for what the Collect cluster diagnostics/Upload cluster diagnostics steps persist as a build artifact before the kind cluster is torn down.

docs.title: Running it locally
docs.text:
You need kind, kubectl, helm, and docker installed. This mirrors the CI workflow's steps exactly:

# 1. Build the manager image and create a kind cluster.
docker build --target manager -t pg-regression-radar/manager:e2e-kind .
kind create cluster --name pgrr-e2e --wait 90s
kind load docker-image pg-regression-radar/manager:e2e-kind --name pgrr-e2e

# 2. Install CloudNativePG (check https://cloudnative-pg.io/documentation/current/installation_upgrade/
#    for the current release tag if this one has since been superseded).
kubectl apply --server-side -f \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cloudnative-pg/cloudnative-pg/release-1.30/releases/cnpg-1.30.0.yaml
kubectl rollout status deployment -n cnpg-system cnpg-controller-manager --timeout=180s

# 3. Create the namespace and a real Postgres Cluster with pg_stat_statements enabled.
kubectl create namespace pgrr-e2e
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: postgresql.cnpg.io/v1
kind: Cluster
metadata:
  name: pgrr-e2e-pg
  namespace: pgrr-e2e
spec:
  instances: 1
  storage:
    size: 1Gi
  postgresql:
    parameters:
      pg_stat_statements.max: "10000"
      pg_stat_statements.track: "all"
EOF
kubectl -n pgrr-e2e wait --for=condition=Ready cluster/pgrr-e2e-pg --timeout=300s

# 4. Install pg-regression-radar in manager mode, pointing at the local image.
helm install pgrr-e2e-mgr deploy/helm/deploylens \
  --namespace pgrr-e2e \
  --set mode=manager \
  --set fullnameOverride=pgrr-e2e-mgr \
  --set manager.image.repository=pg-regression-radar/manager \
  --set manager.image.tag=e2e-kind \
  --set manager.image.pullPolicy=Never \
  --set manager.replicaCount=1 \
  --set manager.leaderElection.enabled=false \
  --set manager.createDefaultWatch=false \
  --wait --timeout=180s

# 5. Point a PostgresWatch at the CloudNativePG-generated Secret directly.
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: radar.pgregressionradar.io/v1alpha1
kind: PostgresWatch
metadata:
  name: pgrr-e2e-watch
  namespace: pgrr-e2e
spec:
  clusterName: pgrr-e2e-pg
  dsnSecretRef:
    name: pgrr-e2e-pg-app
    key: uri
  scrapeIntervalSeconds: 5
  windowMinutes: 5
  minSamples: 5
  minExecutions: 1
---
apiVersion: radar.pgregressionradar.io/v1alpha1
kind: DeploySource
metadata:
  name: pgrr-e2e-deploysource
  namespace: pgrr-e2e
spec:
  postgresWatchRef: pgrr-e2e-watch
  sourceType: generic
EOF

# 6. From here, generate before/after traffic against the app Secret's DSN
#    and POST a deploy event to the webhook route — see
#    .github/workflows/e2e-kind.yml's "Generate ... traffic" and "Send the
#    deploy webhook" steps for the exact commands, then:
kubectl -n pgrr-e2e get performanceregressions

# 7. Tear down.
kind delete cluster --name pgrr-e2e

docs.title: Real two-cluster end-to-end test (fleet mode)
docs.text:
Everything above — including the real-cluster test directly above this section — runs the manager and the Postgres it watches in the same kind cluster. None of it can catch a bug specific to fleet mode (see Multi-Cluster (Fleet) Mode): resolving a DSN through a registered PostgresRadarCluster's kubeconfig, validating a cnpgClusterRef against a real CloudNativePG Cluster object reached over that same remote connection, or the health-check reconciler actually detecting a kubeconfig that stops authenticating. The "E2E (kind, multi-cluster fleet mode)" workflow (.github/workflows/e2e-kind-multicluster.yml) closes that gap:

  1. Creates two real kind clusters on one runner: hub (runs this commit's manager, via the Helm chart, as a real in-cluster Deployment) and spoke (runs the real CloudNativePG operator and a real Cluster).
  2. Builds a least-privilege kubeconfig scoped to exactly the one DSN Secret and the one Cluster object this run needs — the same recipe Multi-Cluster: Remote cluster RBAC documents — and registers it as a PostgresRadarCluster on the hub.
  3. Applies a PostgresWatch using both spec.remoteClusterRef and spec.cnpgClusterRef, and asserts it reaches status.phase: Running and that the PostgresRadarCluster reaches status.ready: true with a populated status.conditions/status.lastProbeTime — both resolved and validated entirely over the network against the spoke's real API server.
  4. Confirms status.trackedQueryIds rises above zero, proving the Collector is genuinely scraping the remote (spoke) Postgres through the cross-cluster DSN path, not a cached or stale value.
  5. Rotates the registered kubeconfig Secret to a deliberately invalid token and asserts PostgresRadarCluster.status.ready flips to false (and PostgresWatch.status.phase to Failed) within one health-check interval, then restores the original kubeconfig and asserts both recover — proving the health-check reconciler's detection and the existing evict-on-failure cache behavior against a real, live credential rotation, not a syntactically-valid-but-unreachable address.

Deliberately out of scope — see the workflow's own header comment for the full reasoning: a full traffic-generation/webhook/PerformanceRegression-detection pass (already proven by e2e-kind.yml above; re-proving it here would mostly duplicate that workflow, since nothing about regression detection changes based on which cluster the DSN came from) and spec.remoteClusterSecretRef (the deprecated path, already covered by internal/controller's own unit tests without needing a second real cluster).

Because both kind clusters in this test run on the same Docker network, but a real hub and spoke in production normally don't share one, the workflow also has to bridge the Postgres data-plane connection — CloudNativePG's own generated DSN Secret names an in-cluster Service DNS host, which only resolves inside the spoke cluster itself. The workflow exposes the Postgres primary via a fixed NodePort and publishes a second Secret with that externally-reachable address for dsnSecretRef to point at instead. This NodePort bridge is a CI-only stand-in for whatever real cross-cluster network path (shared VPC, service mesh, VPN, or a CloudNativePG Service of type LoadBalancer) a production hub/spoke deployment is expected to already have — not a deployment pattern to copy. See Multi-Cluster: The hub-spoke model for why: remoteClusterRef/cnpgClusterRef only ever grant the hub Kubernetes API access to the spoke (an authenticated HTTPS call to read a Secret or a CRD's status) — they say nothing about, and cannot provide, network routability for the plain Postgres TCP connection the Collector makes once it has the DSN in hand.

It's workflow_dispatch-only by default, opt-in via the run-e2e-kind-multicluster PR label — see CI/CD for the exact trigger conditions.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text: How to move a Helm install to a newer release safely: CRDs first, then the chart, with a way back.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Upgrading the radar is helm upgrade, with one extra step Helm does not do for you: updating the CRDs. Helm applies a chart's crds/ directory only on the first install, so a newer chart can arrive in a cluster that still has the old definitions. This page gives the order to follow and what to check before moving between releases. It applies to manager mode; in operator mode no CRDs are used and only the chart (or image) changes.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
The CRDs are v1alpha1, which means a schema can change in any release, including a patch, and there is no conversion webhook. Read the Changelog for every release between yours and the target, and look for a Breaking changes heading. See API versioning for what is and is not guaranteed.

helm list -n <ns>                                  # the chart version you run now
kubectl get postgreswatch,deploysource -A -o yaml > backup.yaml

The backup is your way back if a field was renamed or removed. With state.backend: postgres the sample history survives restarts; with the default memory backend a restart starts cold (Persistence).

docs.title: Upgrade steps
docs.text:
1. Get the new CRDs. They ship with the chart. Pull them from the matching tag or from the chart itself:

    helm pull oci://ghcr.io/joao00001/charts/pg-regression-radar --version <new-version> --untar
kubectl apply -f pg-regression-radar/crds/

    In a clone, the same files are in deploy/helm/deploylens/crds/. Use kubectl apply (or --server-side if you hit annotation size limits), never delete and recreate: deleting a CRD deletes every object of that kind.

  2. Wait until they are accepted:

    kubectl wait --for=condition=Established \
  crd/postgreswatches.radar.pgregressionradar.io \
  crd/deploysources.radar.pgregressionradar.io \
  crd/performanceregressions.radar.pgregressionradar.io \
  crd/postgresradarclusters.radar.pgregressionradar.io

  3. Compare your values with the new defaults:

    helm show values oci://ghcr.io/joao00001/charts/pg-regression-radar --version <new-version> > new-values.yaml
helm get values <release> -n <ns> > current-values.yaml
diff current-values.yaml new-values.yaml

  4. Upgrade the chart. Pass your values file each time; it is more predictable than --reuse-values, which ignores new chart defaults:

    helm upgrade <release> oci://ghcr.io/joao00001/charts/pg-regression-radar \
  --version <new-version> -n <ns> -f my-values.yaml

    The chart version is the release tag without the leading v. image.tag defaults to the chart's appVersion, so the image moves with it unless you pinned a tag.

  5. Check it came up:

    kubectl rollout status deployment -n <ns>
kubectl get pgw,pgds -n <ns>

    Every PostgresWatch should reach Running and every DeploySource Ready. If one is Failed, status.message says why.

docs.title: Minor and patch releases
docs.text: Patch releases usually change only the image. Minor releases can add fields or change defaults. Always run steps 1 and 2 anyway: applying an unchanged CRD is harmless, and skipping it is the common cause of "unknown field" errors after an upgrade.

docs.title: Major releases and v1alpha1 changes
docs.text:
A major release, or any release whose notes list a breaking change, can rename or remove fields. Before upgrading:

  • Edit your manifests (and GitOps repo) to the new schema.
  • If objects stored in the cluster no longer validate, update or re-create them from your backup after the CRDs are applied.
  • Upgrade in a non-production cluster first.

docs.title: Rolling back
docs.text:
helm history <release> -n <ns>
helm rollback <release> <revision> -n <ns>

Rollback restores the release's objects, not the CRDs. If the new CRDs changed the schema, re-apply the CRDs from the older version too, then restore backup.yaml if needed.
