docs.title: Deploy Sources & Webhooks
docs.text: How to wire ArgoCD, Argo Rollouts, Flux, or a custom system into the Deploy Event Ingester, including cluster attribution per source.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Ingester (internal/ingester) normalises webhook payloads (or OTLP trace spans) from five source types into a single DeployEvent — see API Reference for that shape. Every DeployEvent carries a cluster field so multi-cluster setups can tell deploys apart; this page covers how each source populates it.

A fifth source, OpenTelemetry spans, reuses the same /webhook route to accept OTLP/HTTP traces instead of a tool-specific payload (see OTLP Deploy Events). A sixth, Kubernetes-native watch, doesn't send a webhook at all — see below — and is only available in manager mode (CRD-driven), not via the standalone operator/ingester binaries' --source-type flag. See Configuration Reference: Source-type capabilities by mode for the full accepted-values comparison.

flowchart LR
  subgraph PUSH["Pushed to the radar"]
    A1["ArgoCD<br/>on-sync-succeeded"]:::ext
    A2["Argo Rollouts<br/>promotion"]:::ext
    A3["Flux<br/>notification"]:::ext
    A4["Custom CI<br/>generic JSON"]:::ext
    A5["OpenTelemetry<br/>deploy span"]:::ext
  end
  R["Ingester route<br/>POST /webhook"]:::radar
  subgraph PULL["Watched by the radar (manager mode)"]
    K["Deployment or StatefulSet<br/>finishes a rollout"]:::k8s
  end
  W["Workload watch<br/>sourceType: kubernetes"]:::radar
  E["DeployEvent<br/>app, revision, cluster"]:::out
  ENG["Correlation Engine"]:::radar
  A1 --> R
  A2 --> R
  A3 --> R
  A4 --> R
  A5 --> R
  K --> W
  R -->|"normalise"| E
  W -->|"synthesise"| E
  E --> ENG

Five sources push a payload that the Ingester normalises; the Kubernetes-native source needs no sender, because the radar watches the workload itself.

docs.title: Supported sources
docs.text: Source Trigger Notes ArgoCD on-sync-succeeded notification Configure in ArgoCD Notifications Argo Rollouts Rollout promotion webhook Set --source-type argo-rollouts Flux Notification Controller event Set --source-type flux Generic Any JSON matching DeployEvent schema Useful for custom CI systems OpenTelemetry (OTLP) A trace span (e.g. deploy) arriving over OTLP/HTTP Set --source-type otlp / sourceType: otlp; point an OTel Collector otlphttp exporter at /webhook — see OTLP Deploy Events Kubernetes-native Deployment/StatefulSet rollout completes manager mode only; sourceType: kubernetes on a DeploySource CR — no webhook, no GitOps tool required

docs.title: Cluster attribution
docs.text: Always run each ingester (or the operator binary) with --cluster-name <name> set to the identity of the Kubernetes cluster it's watching — this is the fallback used whenever the source payload itself doesn't carry destination-cluster identity. Where the source tool can report the target cluster in its webhook payload, the ingester prefers that value over the flag.

docs.title: ArgoCD
docs.text:
The notification template is a Go template you control (see Notifications templates), and every template has access to the full Application object as .app, including .app.spec.destination.name / .app.spec.destination.server — the actual target cluster of the sync. Configure your argocd-notifications-cm webhook template to include it:

apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: argocd-notifications-cm
data:
  template.on-sync-succeeded-webhook: |
    webhook:
      pg-regression-radar:
        method: POST
        body: |
          {
            "app": {
              "metadata": {
                "name": "{{.app.metadata.name}}",
                "namespace": "{{.app.metadata.namespace}}"
              },
              "spec": {
                "destination": {
                  "name": "{{.app.spec.destination.name}}",
                  "server": "{{.app.spec.destination.server}}"
                }
              },
              "status": {
                "sync": {"revision": "{{.app.status.sync.revision}}"},
                "summary": {"images": {{toJson .app.status.summary.images}}}
              }
            }
          }
  trigger.on-sync-succeeded: |
    - when: app.status.operationState.phase in ['Succeeded']
      send: [on-sync-succeeded-webhook]

The ingester reads app.spec.destination.name first and falls back to app.spec.destination.server (the API server URL) if the destination is addressed by server instead of by registered cluster name. If your ConfigMap doesn't populate spec.destination at all, the --cluster-name fallback is used instead.

docs.title: Argo Rollouts
docs.text:
A Rollout is not a cross-cluster deploy pointer the way an ArgoCD Application is: the controller and the Rollout it manages always live in the same cluster, so there is no destination/cluster field on the object to read (notification templates only expose .rollout and .recipient; see Argo Rollouts notifications).

If a single ingester fronts Rollouts from more than one cluster and you need to disambiguate per event rather than per ingester instance, add a top-level "cluster" field to your argo-rollouts-notification-configmap webhook body template (the same way this project already asks you to add imageTag, which also isn't a stock Rollout field):

apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: argo-rollouts-notification-configmap
data:
  template.pg-regression-radar-webhook: |
    webhook:
      pg-regression-radar:
        method: POST
        body: |
          {
            "rollout": {
              "metadata": {
                "name": "{{.rollout.metadata.name}}",
                "namespace": "{{.rollout.metadata.namespace}}"
              },
              "status": {"currentPodHash": "{{.rollout.status.currentPodHash}}"}
            },
            "cluster": "{{index .rollout.metadata.labels "cluster"}}"
          }

Otherwise, just rely on --cluster-name.

docs.title: Flux
docs.text:
The notification-controller's Event payload (API reference) is a fixed Go struct, not a customizable template, and has no cluster/destination field either — Flux is installed per-cluster with no built-in notion of a remote target. However, the Alert resource lets you merge static key/value pairs into every event it forwards via spec.eventMetadata (docs). Set a cluster key there and the ingester will pick it up automatically:

apiVersion: notification.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1beta3
kind: Alert
metadata:
  name: pg-regression-radar
  namespace: flux-system
spec:
  providerRef:
    name: pg-regression-radar-webhook
  eventMetadata:
    cluster: prod-cluster-1
  eventSources:
    - kind: Kustomization
      name: '*'
    - kind: HelmRelease
      name: '*'

Without eventMetadata.cluster, the --cluster-name fallback is used.

docs.title: Generic
docs.text: Set cluster directly in the JSON body; it is taken as-is and never overwritten by the fallback. This is also the source type used by the manual e2e workflow precisely because it accepts an explicit timestamp field, avoiding a race against the ingester's poll loop.

docs.title: Native Kubernetes watch (no webhook)
docs.text:
Every other source in this table exists to receive a webhook from something that already knows a deploy happened. If nothing in your cluster sends that webhook — no ArgoCD, no Argo Rollouts, no Flux, just plain kubectl apply or a CI pipeline rolling a Deployment/StatefulSet forward directly — there was previously no way to feed this project anything at all.

sourceType: kubernetes closes that gap by watching the workload itself instead of waiting for a notification about it. Set it on a DeploySource CR (manager mode only):

apiVersion: radar.pgregressionradar.io/v1alpha1
kind: DeploySource
metadata:
  name: checkout-native
  namespace: default
spec:
  postgresWatchRef: prod-db
  sourceType: kubernetes
  workloadKind: Deployment   # or StatefulSet
  appName: checkout          # the Deployment/StatefulSet's own name

WorkloadWatchReconciler watches apps/v1 Deployment and StatefulSet objects cluster-wide and, whenever the one named appName (in the same namespace as this DeploySource) finishes rolling out to a new revision, synthesises a DeployEvent exactly as if a webhook had arrived — revision is the Deployment's deployment.kubernetes.io/revision annotation, or the StatefulSet's status.updateRevision. "Finishes rolling out" means the full kubectl rollout status completion signal, not just "the spec changed" — a half-finished rollout never gets reported, since that would mix two revisions' data in the correlation engine's before/after windows.

Because there's no webhook payload to read a cluster field from, the event's cluster always comes from the owning PostgresWatch's spec.clusterName.

This mode needs read-only RBAC on apps/v1 deployments/statefulsets, already included in the manager's default ClusterRole (see Configuration Reference).

Two different DeploySources (each with its own postgresWatchRef) can watch the exact same Deployment/StatefulSet — e.g. two teams independently tracking the same shared workload against two different PostgresWatches. WorkloadWatchReconciler reports the rollout to every matching DeploySource on the same pass, each getting its own DeployEvent with a distinct id and source; a PostgresWatch that isn't registered yet on one of them doesn't block delivery to the others, though the reconcile does retry until every match has been delivered.

docs.title: When the watch behind a source is not running
docs.text: In manager mode, a DeploySource route hands each event to the event store of the PostgresWatch it references, looked up again on every request. While that watch is stopped (it is being deleted, or it is restarting because its spec changed), the route answers 503 Service Unavailable with Retry-After: 10 and logs ingester: deploy event not stored, instead of accepting an event that nothing would read. Senders that retry, such as Argo Rollouts notifications and OTLP exporters, deliver the event once the watch is back. In v1.9.0 and earlier, an event sent after a PostgresWatch spec change was accepted and never judged.

docs.title: Webhook authentication
docs.text: By default the /webhook endpoint accepts any POST request that reaches port 8080, which means any process that can route to that port can inject deploy events. To prevent event spoofing — spam alerts, or masking a real regression under noise — configure a shared secret.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Set the --webhook-secret flag (operator/ingester binary) or spec.webhookSecret (DeploySource CRD). The ingester then requires every POST to /webhook to include the secret verbatim in the X-Webhook-Token header. Requests without the header, or with a wrong value, are rejected with 401 Unauthorized. The comparison is constant-time to prevent timing-based secret inference.

The standalone ingester binary's GET /events route (lists the full deploy-event history — see Configuration Reference) is gated behind this same secret and header once --webhook-secret is set; it has no authentication of its own otherwise. /events doesn't exist in operator/manager mode, so this only applies to the standalone ingester binary.

docs.title: Operator / standalone ingester
docs.text:
Pass the secret via an environment variable to avoid exposure in process listings:

export WEBHOOK_SECRET="$(openssl rand -hex 32)"
operator --dsn=... --webhook-secret="$WEBHOOK_SECRET"

Or with the standalone ingester binary:

ingester --source-type=argocd --webhook-secret="$WEBHOOK_SECRET"

docs.title: Helm chart (mode: operator)
docs.text:
Set ingester.webhookSecret in your values.yaml override (or via --set). The chart stores the value in the existing <release>-secret Kubernetes Secret and injects it into the pod as the WEBHOOK_SECRET environment variable:

ingester:
  sourceType: argocd
  webhookSecret: "your-secret-here"   # generate with: openssl rand -hex 32

In production, avoid committing the secret to version control. Instead, pre-create the Kubernetes Secret and reference it directly, or use an external secrets operator to sync it.

docs.title: Configuring ArgoCD / Argo Rollouts / Flux to send the header
docs.text:
Each GitOps tool lets you add custom HTTP headers to its webhook notifications:

ArgoCD (argocd-notifications-cm):

service.webhook.pg-regression-radar: |
  url: http://pg-regression-radar:8080/webhook
  headers:
    - name: X-Webhook-Token
      value: $webhook-secret   # reference a secret key

Argo Rollouts (argo-rollouts-notification-configmap):

service.webhook.pg-regression-radar: |
  url: http://pg-regression-radar:8080/webhook
  headers:
    - name: X-Webhook-Token
      value: $webhook-secret

Flux (Provider resource):

apiVersion: notification.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1beta3
kind: Provider
metadata:
  name: pg-regression-radar-webhook
  namespace: flux-system
spec:
  type: generic
  address: http://pg-regression-radar:8080/webhook
  headers:
    - name: X-Webhook-Token
      value: your-secret-here   # replace with your actual secret

Flux ≥ 2.4 supports the headers field on the generic Provider, which lets you send a custom header verbatim. For earlier versions that only support secretRef (which sends Authorization: token <value> instead), use the generic-hmac provider type or upgrade Flux.

docs.title: Verifying the token with curl
docs.text:
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/webhook \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "X-Webhook-Token: your-secret-here" \
  -d '{"app":"my-app","revision":"abc123","timestamp":"2024-01-15T10:00:00Z"}'

A request without the header returns 401 Unauthorized; with the correct token it returns 204 No Content.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• API Reference — the DeployEvent JSON shape every source normalises into.
  • Configuration Reference — --source-type / sourceType.
  • Getting Started — simulating a deploy event with curl against the generic source.

docs.title: ADR-0001: Deploy-independent regression detection
docs.text: Status: Accepted Date: 2026-08-13 Deciders: Joao

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
pg-regression-radar's Correlation Engine (internal/correlation) only ever runs in response to a DeployEvent: Engine.Analyse(ev) builds a window symmetric around ev.Timestamp, and a detected regression is only confirmed when the E-divisive change point it finds lies within ChangePointTolerance of that timestamp. PendingSet exists purely to retry Analyse against the same event until its post-deploy window closes.

This hard-couples the tool's actual value (statistically confirming a real, significant latency shift) to one specific cause (a tracked Kubernetes deploy). Most real-world Postgres regressions have no deploy behind them at all — autovacuum falling behind, index/table bloat, stale planner statistics, organic data growth, a connection-pool/traffic-pattern change. None of those are detectable today, and the requirement to wire up a DeploySource (ArgoCD/Flux/Rollouts/native-K8s/generic webhook) is also the main reason the tool reads as Kubernetes-specific and narrow, even though the standalone operator/collector CLI binaries already work against any reachable Postgres DSN, no Kubernetes required.

This ADR is the first of three follow-ups from a broader "how do we make this tool matter to more people" discussion (see conversation history); the other two (a friction-free non-Kubernetes onboarding path, and prescriptive causes alongside detection) are out of scope here and will get their own ADRs.

Decisions on the three open questions below were made via direct discussion before writing this ADR (not re-litigated here, just recorded):

  • Baseline strategy: split-window (recent half vs. previous half of a single rolling window), not a longer trailing baseline or a time-of-day/day-of-week model.
  • Alert suppression: a re-arm state machine per query (alert once, stay "in regression" until latency recovers below threshold, then re-arm), not a fixed cooldown.
  • Scope: both the CLI (cmd/operator) and the CRD (cmd/manager, PostgresWatch) get this in the same effort, not staged.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Add a second, independent trigger path — periodic detection — that runs the existing E-divisive + Welch's t-test machinery on a rolling schedule, per tracked query, with no DeployEvent involved. It is additive, not a replacement: deploy-correlated detection (Analyse/PendingSet) keeps working exactly as today, unaffected by whether periodic detection is enabled. A PostgresWatch (or the CLI) can have either, both, or neither active.

Concretely:

  1. Engine refactor. Extract the part of evaluateQuery that is genuinely deploy-agnostic (stage-0 mean pre-filter, stage-1 E-divisive, stage-2 Welch's t-test) from the part that is not (the ChangePointTolerance-to-ev.Timestamp check, and populating DeployEventID/Namespace from ev). Deploy-triggered Analyse keeps the tolerance check; a new AnalysePeriodic skips it entirely — for a self-contained window with no external anchor, the change point is the finding, wherever it falls.
// engine.go — shape, not final code
func (e *Engine) Analyse(ev v1alpha1.DeployEvent) []v1alpha1.PerformanceRegression {
    // ... unchanged: builds window around ev.Timestamp, calls evaluateSeries,
    // then rejects if the change point isn't within ChangePointTolerance of ev.Timestamp.
}

func (e *Engine) AnalysePeriodic(now time.Time) []v1alpha1.PerformanceRegression {
    // window = [now - 2*PeriodicWindowMinutes, now], split at the midpoint
    // into "before"/"after" halves; same evaluateSeries core; no
    // deploy-timestamp proximity check at all.
}

  1. New config knob: PeriodicWindowMinutes (default 60 — deliberately double the deploy-mode default of 30, since there is no deploy prior narrowing where to look, so a shorter window would be noisier). Independent from WindowMinutes so tuning one never silently affects the other.

  2. Re-arm state machine. Deploy-correlated detection's dedup (PendingSet.notified map[int64]struct{}) is scoped to one deploy event's lifetime — it doesn't need to survive across events. Periodic detection has no such natural boundary, so it needs its own per-query state, kept for the life of the watch:

// correlation package — shape, not final code
type periodicState struct {
    inRegression map[int64]bool // queryID -> currently alerting (won't re-fire until recovered)
}

A query transitions false -> true (fires once) when AnalysePeriodic reports Detected; it stays true (suppressed) on every subsequent tick where the recent half is still significantly worse than a fresh baseline; it transitions back to false once a tick shows recent-half latency has recovered to within LatencyChangeThreshold of baseline, so a future regression can fire again. This needs a lightweight recovery check on every tick regardless of whether a new regression fires — effectively "is the query still bad" as well as "did it just become bad."

  1. CRD additions (PostgresWatchSpec):
periodicDetection:
  enabled: false          # default off; opt-in per watch, mirrors autoAbort's own opt-in pattern
  windowMinutes: 60        # optional; falls back to a 60m default
  intervalMinutes: 15      # how often a full pass over tracked queries runs

  1. CLI additions (cmd/operator): --periodic-detection (bool), --periodic-window-minutes, --periodic-interval-minutes — same shape as the existing --window-minutes/--min-executions flags.

  2. New poll path, separate from the existing deploy-triggered one in both internal/cli/operator.go and internal/controller/postgreswatch_controller.go: a ticker firing every intervalMinutes, calling AnalysePeriodic(time.Now()), running results through the re-arm state machine, then through the same alerting.Notifier/recordRegression paths already in place — no changes needed to alerting or to PerformanceRegression persistence beyond one new field (see below).

  3. PerformanceRegression gets one new field: TriggerType ("deploy" | "periodic"), so alerts/CRs make it obvious which detection path fired, and DeployEventID is simply empty for a periodic-triggered regression (it's already an optional-shaped string field, not a required one — no schema break).

docs.title: Option A: Split-window (chosen)
docs.text:
Dimension Assessment Complexity Low — reuses evaluateQuery's existing core almost unchanged False-positive risk Real, but bounded by using a longer default window (60m) than deploy mode and a conservative LatencyChangeThreshold/PValueThreshold to start Data/retention cost None beyond what deploy-mode already needs Time to ship Fastest of the three

Pros: minimal new code, no new retention requirements, directly reuses the statistically-validated E-divisive/Welch's-t-test core as-is. Cons: genuinely vulnerable to ordinary daily/weekly traffic-pattern shifts producing a "detected" result with nothing wrong — start-of-business-hours load ramps are the obvious failure case. Mitigated only by tuning (window size, thresholds), not eliminated.

docs.title: Option B: Recent vs. longer trailing baseline
docs.text:
Dimension Assessment Complexity Medium — needs a second, longer-lived sample store (hours, not the ~180m default retention) False-positive risk Lower — a real trailing average/stddev absorbs some daily variation Data/retention cost Meaningful — likely forces the postgres state backend rather than memory-only for anyone using this Time to ship Slower

Pros: meaningfully more robust to daily variation than Option A without the full complexity of Option C. Cons: retention-cost implications ripple into internal/storage, --retention-minutes defaults, and the memory-vs-postgres backend story — a bigger blast radius than this ADR's scope.

docs.title: Option C: Time-of-day/day-of-week baseline
docs.text:
Dimension Assessment Complexity High — needs weeks of retained history and a seasonality model False-positive risk Lowest of the three, by design Data/retention cost Highest — weeks of samples, not hours Time to ship Slowest — realistically its own multi-ADR effort

Pros: the only option that actually solves seasonality rather than working around it. Cons: scope of a standalone project, not a follow-up ADR item.

docs.title: Option A: Fixed cooldown
docs.text: Pros: trivial to implement and reason about (a timestamp + duration check). Cons: semantically wrong for a persisting condition — either re-alerts on a schedule while nothing changed (noisy), or, if the cooldown is long, stays silent well past the point a human already fixed and then broke it again.

docs.title: Option B: Re-arm state machine (chosen)
docs.text: Pros: matches what an operator actually wants — one alert per distinct episode of regression, re-firing only for a genuinely new episode, not a timer. Cons: needs an explicit recovery check every tick (not just a "did it get worse" check), and per-query state that must survive restarts as gracefully as the rest of this project's in-memory-by-default state does (i.e., accepted to reset on restart, matching PendingSet's and the Collector's own existing behavior, unless the postgres state backend is in use).

docs.title: Option A: CLI first, CRD later
docs.text: Pros: smaller first PR, faster feedback loop, matches the "low-friction non-K8s onboarding" thread from the same discussion. Cons: temporary feature gap between the two run modes.

docs.title: Option B: CLI + CRD together (chosen)
docs.text: Pros: no temporary gap; the re-arm state machine and engine refactor are shared code regardless, so the CRD wiring on top is comparatively small once the CLI side works. Cons: larger single PR/review; PostgresWatchSpec schema, deepcopy, Helm chart, and RBAC (none needed here, unlike auto-abort — periodic detection touches nothing outside Postgres/CRD-status) all need updating in the same pass.

docs.title: Trade-off Analysis
docs.text: The central trade-off is Option A vs. B/C on baseline strategy: A ships fastest and reuses the most existing, already-trusted code, but is the most exposed to false positives from ordinary traffic variation — exactly the failure mode that would erode trust in the tool fastest if it fires on "the store opened for the day" instead of "someone shipped a bad plan." B and C reduce that risk but pull in retention/storage changes this ADR deliberately keeps out of scope. Given this is genuinely new, unvalidated territory (unlike the alerting/actuation work, there's no existing production usage pattern to lean on yet), shipping A first — with conservative defaults and this ADR's own re-arm suppression softening the blast radius of a false positive to "one alert, then silence until it actually changes again" — is the right sequencing: validate the core mechanic against real traffic before paying for B/C's added retention cost.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Detecting a regression no longer requires wiring up a DeploySource at all — the tool's addressable use case grows from "Postgres + Kubernetes + a tracked deploy tool" to "any Postgres with pg_stat_statements."
  • PerformanceRegression.TriggerType becomes a new, permanent field every consumer (Slack/Teams/PagerDuty/custom formatters, kubectl get performanceregression -o yaml, the docs) needs to account for, even though none of the alerting work needs to change to support it (it's just one more piece of context in the same payload).
  • Periodic detection's false-positive risk is real and will need real tuning against real traffic once this ships — the initial defaults (60m window, existing LatencyChangeThreshold/PValueThreshold) are a starting point, not a validated answer, and should be called out as such in the docs.
  • A future ADR (Option B or C above) becomes the natural place to revisit baseline strategy if false positives prove to be a real adoption blocker — this ADR does not close that door, it deliberately defers it.
  • The re-arm state (periodicState) is in-memory by default, same as the rest of this project's runtime state (Collector, PendingSet) — it resets on restart, which means a regression already "in progress" at restart time will re-fire once rather than staying silently suppressed. This matches the project's existing "memory is the default, postgres backend is opt-in for durability" pattern (internal/storage) rather than introducing a new one.

docs.title: Action Items
docs.text:
1. [ ] internal/correlation/engine.go: extract the deploy-agnostic core of evaluateQuery into a shared helper; add AnalysePeriodic(now time.Time) and PeriodicWindowMinutes to Config.
  2. [ ] internal/correlation: new re-arm state type (periodicState or similar) with a recovery check, unit-tested for both the "fire once" and "recover, then re-fire" transitions.
  3. [ ] pkg/apis/v1alpha1 + api/v1alpha1: add PerformanceRegression.TriggerType; add PostgresWatchSpec.PeriodicDetection (Enabled, WindowMinutes, IntervalMinutes) with hand-edited deepcopy, mirrored CRD YAML (config/crd/bases + Helm copy).
  4. [ ] internal/cli/operator.go: --periodic-detection/--periodic-window-minutes/--periodic-interval-minutes flags, a new ticker-driven poll loop parallel to the existing deploy-triggered one, --dry-run validation.
  5. [ ] internal/controller/postgreswatch_controller.go: mirror the same poll loop into WatchRuntime/pollLoop, gated on spec.periodicDetection.enabled.
  6. [ ] Helm chart: analysis.periodicDetection.* values wired into both operator and manager mode, matching the autoAbort/alerting precedent.
  7. [ ] Docs: new docs/periodic-detection.md (mirroring docs/auto-abort.md's structure) explicitly documenting the false-positive caveat from Consequences above; docs/configuration.md field/flag tables; mkdocs.yml nav entry.
  8. [ ] Tests: engine-level (split-window detection, no-tolerance-check behavior), re-arm state machine (fire/suppress/recover/re-fire), CLI dry-run validation, controller reconcile wiring — following this session's existing pattern of fake-client/httptest-based unit tests plus real-Postgres integration coverage where the existing internal/e2e suite already does so for deploy-triggered detection.
  9. [ ] changelog.d/<PR>.feat.md fragment once a PR number is known.

docs.title: ADR-0002: A live dashboard, opened with one command
docs.text: Status: Accepted (implemented; amended 2026-11-26, see "Amendments") Date: 2026-11-26 Deciders: Joao

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The radar now decides and acts on its own: it assesses a deploy, grades the evidence (A to D), pauses or aborts a Rollout, verifies the abort and trips a circuit breaker. All of that is visible only in manager logs, a verdict endpoint and a ledger endpoint. A person watching a rollout, or arriving after one, cannot see what the radar saw, what it concluded, why, and what it did. The project says in its README that it "does not ship a dashboard"; that is now the biggest gap between what the engine does and what a user can trust.

What the repo already has and this builds on:

Reusable Where Used for Per-deploy assessments, decisions, action ledger, breaker state internal/attribution/shadow (Records, Actions, BreakerOpen), verdictapi the "what was decided and done" half Per-query samples and deploy events over HTTP internal/dashboardapi history and charts Log-arm source (canary vs stable) internal/pglog, attribution.arms the canary/stable chart and source health Chart code, design tokens, copy for the engine's concepts docs/assets/playground/* visual language; the playground already explains the engine in a browser A CLI entry point with subcommands cmd/pg-regression-radar, internal/cli the one command

Decisions made with the owner before this ADR (recorded, not re-litigated):

  • Data origin in v1: the real cluster. Demo and direct-Postgres origins come later through the same interface.
  • First screen: "what is happening now" (live), not post-mortem or long-term trend.
  • Flexibility: editable panels, saved and loaded as a declarative file. Not a user-written query language in v1.
  • Query text: hidden by default (--show-queries to reveal), as proposed.
  • History: kept the way Grafana does, read here as: retention is a configurable property of the data layer, the data lives outside the UI and the process, and every board has a time-range picker (last 15 minutes to 7 days, or an absolute range). See "History" below.
  • Scope: the Observe API respects the namespace allowlist (attribution.actuate.namespaces). See "Scope" below.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Ship a read-only, local web dashboard as pg-regression-radar dashboard, in three layers that can each be tested alone.

 browser (vanilla ES modules, SVG)       your laptop                      cluster
┌───────────────────────────────┐   ┌──────────────────────┐   SPDY    ┌────────────────────────┐
│ board = layout (grid) of      │   │ pg-regression-radar  │ port-fwd  │ manager (leader pod)   │
│ panels; panels read named     │◀─▶│ dashboard            │──────────▶│ observe API, bound to  │
│ datasets from the Observe API │   │  - embedded UI       │ (kube RBAC│ 127.0.0.1 in the pod   │
│ and live events (SSE)         │   │  - port-forward      │  pods/    │  - snapshot + SSE      │
│ layout saved in a data dir    │   │  - /api proxy        │  portfwd) │  - read-only           │
└───────────────────────────────┘   └──────────────────────┘           └────────────────────────┘

docs.title: 1. The Observe API (in the manager)
docs.text:
One versioned, read-only contract, /observe/v1, which the UI and any other client consume. Nothing in it can change cluster state.

Endpoint Returns GET /observe/v1/overview per watch: mode (shadow/enforce), actuation on/off, breaker state, kill-switch annotation state, allowlist; collector health (last scrape age, pg_stat_statements reachable, reset detected); arms health (log flowing, sample rate, settings issues) GET /observe/v1/deploys deploys the radar tracks, newest first: workload, revision, time, phase (observing, decided, acted, verified), next evaluation time, latest verdict, grade, impact, attribution, action wanted/taken GET /observe/v1/deploys/{id} the whole case: every evaluation in order, each with its decision and reasons, per-query verdicts (grade, ratio, interval, flags, cap reasons), actions and verification GET /observe/v1/deploys/{id}/series?unit=… the chart data for one query: treatment and control (canary/stable) series, the pre-deploy baseline and the engine's placebo band, the deploy marker GET /observe/v1/actions the ledger GET /observe/v1/events Server-Sent Events: deploy.registered, evaluation, decision, action, verification, health — what the live view subscribes to, so nothing polls

Every list endpoint takes from and to (RFC 3339 or a relative now-6h), which is what the time-range picker sends; the case, series and ledger endpoints are addressed by id and also honour them for what they return.

Rules for the contract:

  • Same data the engine used. A chart is drawn from the series the engine assessed, not recomputed by the UI, so the picture cannot disagree with the verdict. Each series carries its own sample counts so the UI can show how thin the evidence was.
  • Explanations are data, not UI copy. Decisions already carry Reasons; flags and cap reasons gain stable machine codes plus a short plain-language text, so a panel can say "capped at grade C: too few donors (7 queries)" and a user can search the docs for the code.
  • No query parameters, no SQL text by default. Queries are shown by fingerprint and table; the normalized text appears only when the dashboard is started with --show-queries.
  • Additive and versioned. /observe/v1 never removes a field; the dashboard refuses to talk to a manager whose GET /observe/version it does not understand and says which versions it supports.
  • Bounded memory. The in-process view is bounded (the evaluator's record list, today unbounded, gets a cap) and the live series are the ones the collector window and the log store already hold.

docs.title: History
docs.text:
The Observe API reads history through one seam, HistoryStore, with a retention that is a setting and not a constant:

  • Memory (default). A bounded ring of deploys, evaluations, actions and verifications. It is lost on restart, and the dashboard says so in the status strip ("history since 02:14, in memory") instead of showing a short list as if it were complete.
  • Postgres (opt-in). The same optional state backend the operator already has (--state-backend=postgres, the regression_radar schema, the existing prune loop and --state-retention), extended with attribution_deploys, attribution_evaluations (the assessment as JSONB, versioned), attribution_actions and a compact attribution_series written at each evaluation (the points the engine used, downsampled, so a chart of a past deploy needs neither the collector window nor the log store). Retention defaults to 30 days. Writing history is best effort and never blocks or delays a decision: if the store is down the radar keeps acting and the dashboard shows "history not recorded since …".

The time-range picker therefore means the same thing in both modes: it asks the store for a range, and the API answers with what exists, saying what is missing at either end.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: The Observe API serves only deploys in the namespaces of attribution.actuate.namespaces when that list is set (empty means every namespace the deploy sources report, as it does for actuation). The filter is applied inside the API, on every endpoint including the event stream and the history, not in the UI, so a client cannot ask around it. The status strip names the scope ("scoped to: checkout, payments") so a missing deploy is explained rather than mysterious. The cost is deliberate: a deploy outside the allowlist is still judged and logged by the manager but invisible here; a separate visibility list would be a different decision.

docs.title: 2. Reaching it: one command, no new exposure
docs.text:
pg-regression-radar dashboard [--context CTX] [--namespace NS] [--port 8765] [--open] [--config FILE] [--show-queries]

  • It finds the leader manager pod (the Lease holder, since only the leader runs the evaluators), opens a port-forward to it with the user's own kubeconfig, serves the UI on 127.0.0.1, and proxies /api to the forward.
  • The observe listener in the manager is bound to 127.0.0.1 inside the pod. No Service, no Ingress, no token to mint or leak: the only way in is the Kubernetes pods/portforward permission the user already has or does not have. This is also why the chart needs no new Service.
  • --url http://host:port skips the port-forward, for tests and for a user who exposed the API some other way.
  • If the leader changes mid-session the command re-resolves it and the UI shows a reconnecting state rather than stale data without saying so.
  • The dashboard binds to loopback only and refuses a non-loopback --listen unless --insecure-listen is passed, because the page shows an operator's view of production.

docs.title: 3. The UI: boards, panels, datasets
docs.text:
Plain ES modules and hand-written SVG, embedded in the binary with go:embed. No Node, no bundler, no runtime dependency, nothing downloaded at run time: the same constraint the docs playground already lives under, and the right one for a tool that runs next to production.

Three concepts, kept apart so each can be changed without touching the others:

  • Dataset: a named, typed slice of the Observe API (deploys, decisions, actions, source-health, unit-series, …). Datasets are the only thing panels read; they hide transport (snapshot then SSE patches).
  • Panel: a component with a type, a small schema of options and a dataset it binds to. Types for v1: deploy-cards, decision-feed, evidence-table, canary-chart, ratio-chart, safety, source-health, kpi.
  • Board: a grid of panels. Presets ship in the binary; a board is just data.
apiVersion: pgrr.io/v1
kind: Dashboard
boards:
  - id: now
    title: Now
    refresh: live
    panels:
      - {id: active,   type: deploy-cards,  at: [0, 0, 8, 4], options: {states: [observing, decided, acted]}}
      - {id: safety,   type: safety,        at: [8, 0, 4, 4]}
      - {id: feed,     type: decision-feed, at: [0, 4, 5, 6], options: {limit: 50}}
      - {id: evidence, type: evidence-table, at: [5, 4, 7, 6], options: {follow: active}}
      - {id: health,   type: source-health, at: [0, 10, 12, 2]}

Flexibility, in the order a user meets it: drag, resize, hide and re-add panels in the browser (saved in the command's data directory; see the amendment Saved edits); Export writes the YAML above; --config loads a file; pg-regression-radar dashboard config validate FILE checks it against the schema with line-numbered errors; … config dump prints the presets as files to start from. A panel's options are validated against its schema, an unknown panel type renders a clear placeholder instead of breaking the board, and a layout from an older version is migrated or reported, never silently dropped.

docs.title: 4. What the first board ("Now") shows, and why
docs.text:
A person watching a rollout asks four questions in order, so the board is laid out in that order:

  1. Is the radar alive and trustworthy right now? A top strip: data freshness, mode, actuation on/off, breaker, kill switch, log-arm health. If the data is stale or the arms are unusable, say so first, because everything below depends on it.
  2. What deploys is it watching, and where is each? One card per active deploy: workload and revision, phase and "next evaluation in 3m", verdict, grade as a badge, impact, attribution, and the action wanted vs taken. A card is not a number: it ends with one plain sentence ("Grade A: the canary is 2.3x slower than the stable pods on 3 queries; aborted at 02:19").
  3. Why? Selecting a card shows the evidence: the per-query table (grade, ratio, interval, flags) and the canary vs stable chart with the deploy marker and the pre-deploy placebo band. The grade is explained where it appears (what A/B/C/D mean here, and what caps this one).
  4. What did it do, and was it right? A live feed of evaluations and actions, and the verification result of each abort ("regression persisted after abort"), because trust in an agent that acts comes from seeing its mistakes as plainly as its saves.

Colour carries one meaning only (state: ok, watching, regressed, acted), never decoration; every colour has a text or shape twin so the board reads without colour; light and dark follow the system; the board is usable at laptop width without scrolling sideways.

A second preset, Case, is the same evidence full-screen for one deploy (the investigation view), and a third, Source health, is for debugging the radar itself.

docs.title: 5. How it is tested
docs.text:
• Contract: Go tests for each endpoint with golden JSON, a test that every field the UI reads exists in the golden, and an SSE test (ordering, resume after reconnect, slow-consumer drop).
  • Spec: table tests for schema validation and migration of config files, including bad files.
  • UI logic: the dataset layer and the layout engine run in Node without a DOM (the pattern playground-core.js already uses).
  • Visual: Playwright against a fixture source that replays recorded observe responses (from the real e2e runs in this repo, so the fixtures are real shapes, not invented ones). Screenshots at three widths in light and dark are reviewed by a person, together, before each milestone is called done.
  • End to end: the real-cluster harness already used for the arms test (real Postgres, API server, Rollout CRD, manager) with a canary regression, an A/A and an abort, checking that the dashboard shows the same verdict the ledger recorded. The port-forward itself cannot run in that harness (no kubelet), so it is tested against a recorded SPDY exchange and --url covers the rest; a real cluster run is a manual checklist item.

docs.title: 6. Milestones
docs.text:
Each ends with something that runs, is tested and is looked at before the next starts.

  1. Observe API + fixture source: contract, golden files, SSE, --url mode. No UI yet; curl shows the case.
  2. Shell and "Now" board, read-only: embedded UI, datasets, deploy-cards, decision-feed, safety, source-health.
  3. Evidence: evidence-table, canary-chart, ratio-chart, grade/flag explanations, the Case board.
  4. History store: the HistoryStore seam, the memory ring and the Postgres backend with retention, in step with the API.
  5. The command: leader discovery, port-forward, reconnect, version handshake, --open.
  6. Flexibility: edit/drag/resize/hide, export, --config, config validate|dump, migration.
  7. Hardening and docs: accessibility and width checks, loopback guard, docs page and screenshots, an "add a panel type" guide.

docs.title: Amendments (as built)
docs.text:
• Grid model. Boards are a fixed-row-height grid, as Grafana's: at: [x, y, w, h] in cells, 12 columns, rows 40 px, panels compacted upward. The earlier sketch (refresh: live, follow: options) is dropped: every board is live through the event stream, and panels follow the picked deploy.
  • Layout bundle. GET /dashboard/layout serves {layout, source, catalog, grid}: the layout (default preset or the --config file, re-read per request, 422 with line-numbered problems when invalid), the panel catalog and the grid constants, so the page and the validator cannot disagree. The UI's Export produces the same YAML as dashboard config dump; golden files pin it.
  • Preset boards are Now, Case and Source health. Panel types differ from the first list: summary, radar-state, deploy-cards, deploy-head, canary-chart, figures, why, evidence-table, ratio-chart, evaluations, ledger, decision-feed, safety, source-health.
  • History DSN. Resolves the first open question: the manager reads the Postgres DSN from a file (--observe-history-dsn-file), never from a flag, so it does not show in the pod spec. History is its own store (--observe-history=memory|postgres), independent of --state-backend.
  • Series. Series are recorded per evaluation for the units the engine keeps, downsampled; other units answer 404 and the UI says no series was recorded. Resolves the second open question as "only the units the engine keeps".
  • Info button. Each panel carries an info button (hover or focus shows, click pins) with a few sentences from the catalog (help), or the panel's own description from the file. It is how a board stays readable after someone else rearranged it.
  • Focus view. Clicking a panel anywhere that is not a button, a list, a link or the info button, pressing V over it, or its expand button opens it alone, large, with a settings pane on the right, as Grafana's view panel does. The address becomes #/<board>?view=<panel> (so it can be shared, and Back closes it); Escape and Back to the board leave. What we took from Grafana: the pane is organised in collapsible groups with a search box; the visualization is chosen first; each setting has a help sentence and a way back to its default; a changed setting is marked. What we did differently: a change applies at once and is kept like any other layout edit (it is the same localStorage entry, exported as the same YAML), with Discard changes back to how the panel was when the view opened, rather than Grafana's Save/Discard pair, because nothing here is saved on a server.
  • Settings are catalog data. Each option in the catalog carries label, group, doc, optional labels for enum values and an optional when: "viz=table" that hides it while another option has a different value. The pane is drawn from the catalog the server sends, so a new option on the Go side needs no change in the pane, only in the panel that reads it. The option named viz is the type's choice of visualization (deploy list as cards or compact list, canary as chart or table, evidence as table or ratio chart, activity as feed or table) and is drawn as a picker. Types that read one deploy carry followsDeploy, and the view then offers a deploy picker beside the panel. A panel is rebuilt when its title, description or settings change, so a panel never has to apply a change in place.
  • Panel queries. A panel in focus has a Query field under it (Grafana's place for it) holding a filter language, saved as query: in the layout. It is not SQL and cannot become it: the dashboard stays read-only over what the Observe API serves, which is what keeps GET-only, the allowlist and the hidden query text intact. Grammar: field:value terms, bare or quoted values, same field OR, different fields AND, * in free-text fields, at most 12 terms and 200 characters; fields app, namespace, state, grade, deploy, query, statement, table. The catalog lists which fields each panel type takes (query on the type, queryFields on the bundle carries each field's help and closed values), so the field's suggestions are drawn from the catalog and from the live view (values with counts, refreshed on every event). Go validates a layout's queries (ParseQuery, ValidateQuery, errors that name the column) and the page evaluates them; testdata/query-cases.json is a hand-written contract both sides run, so they cannot drift. Panels that show one deploy resolve it from the query (deploy: names one; other deploy fields pick the newest match) and otherwise from the board's pick; a pinned deploy fetches its own series through a small per-session cache. We chose a constrained language over free-form expressions because a card's data is already shaped by the API and the cards would otherwise each need their own interpreter; the cost is that a query cannot reach data the API does not serve, which is the intent. Radar state, safety and source health take no query because they have nothing to select.
  • Saved edits. Edits (layout, panel settings, queries, board ranges) are kept between runs in the command's own data directory, as one small JSON profile per dashboard source: dashboard-default.json, or dashboard-file-<digest of the --config path>.json. The directory is --data-dir, defaulting to pg-regression-radar/dashboard under the user's configuration directory (a mounted volume works), mode 0700, files 0600, written atomically. This replaces localStorage as the home of the profile; the browser's storage is now only the fallback (--no-save, or a directory that cannot be written, reported at start), and an earlier browser-only profile moves to disk once. The page reads GET /dashboard/profile at start and writes through PUT/DELETE about 350 ms after a change (and when the page is hidden). This is the dashboard's first write. "Read-only" now means toward the cluster and the radar; what makes the one write safe: the path is fixed and no request names a file; the Host check of the read paths applies; a write must carry X-Requested-By: pgrr-dashboard (a non-simple header, so a browser asks first and the server never answers the CORS question), a same-origin Origin and Sec-Fetch-Site when sent, and application/json; the body is at most 256 KiB and is validated as a profile (known fields, version, a layout that passes the dashboard-file validator, plain ranges) before anything is written; every other path stays GET/HEAD only. We did not write back into the --config file: that file is the person's, possibly in version control, and a page rewriting it would be surprising; Export remains the way to turn a profile into a file. A --config file that changed since the edits were made wins, as before (the profile stores the fingerprint of what it was edited on). With --insecure-listen saving is off, because with no sign-in anyone who can reach the page could rewrite the file; the page falls back to the browser. The profile holds no credentials and no Observe data, only names the user typed or picked (so topology metadata), and the file is 0600 in a 0700 directory; the threat table lives in docs/security-model.md (What the dashboard saves). Residual risks accepted: an existing directory keeps its own permissions, and anyone who can write the user's configuration directory can change what their dashboard shows.
  • Ranges. The range picker accepts 1 minute to 90 days; the page reports when history is shorter than the range.
  • Permissions of the command. get leases, get pods, create pods/portforward. The port-forward uses a WebSocket tunnel and falls back to SPDY.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A real trust surface for an agent that acts. The decision, its evidence and its consequence are one click apart, which is what makes enforce mode adoptable.
  • The manager grows a second HTTP surface, on loopback only. It is read-only and carries no query text by default, but it is new API to keep stable: hence the versioned contract and goldens.
  • Only the leader can answer, so the command depends on Lease inspection and a re-resolve on failover. A lost leader shows as "reconnecting", not as an empty board.
  • History is as long as the chosen store. In memory, a restart empties the case list and the dashboard says so; with the Postgres backend it survives restarts for the retention period, at the cost of a small write per evaluation and a schema to migrate. The manager does not yet have a state backend, so this adds its configuration.
  • Allowlist as visibility keeps the dashboard's reach equal to the radar's authority, at the price of hiding judged-but-out-of-scope deploys.
  • No JavaScript toolchain: smaller attack surface and an easy audit, at the price of writing the grid, the charts and the form controls ourselves and testing them well. The panel registry keeps that cost in one place.
  • Customisation is bounded on purpose. Users can rearrange, hide and configure panels and share the file; they cannot define new queries over the data in v1. The schema leaves room for it (a dataset can gain parameters) without breaking files written today.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• Grafana dashboards over Prometheus metrics. Familiar and cheap, but the interesting objects (a deploy's case, per-query evidence, canary vs stable series, an action and its verification) are not metrics, and "one command, no infrastructure" is lost. Metrics remain useful and remain exported; they are the wrong primary surface.
  • A React/Vite single-page app. Faster to a rich UI, but it brings a build toolchain, a large dependency tree and a bundle to audit into a security-sensitive operator tool, and breaks the "embed and ship one binary" simplicity. Revisit only if the panel registry becomes the bottleneck.
  • An in-cluster dashboard behind a Service/Ingress. Convenient for teams, but it needs authentication and authorisation the project does not have, and widens the exposure of an operator's view of production. A loopback port-forward reuses Kubernetes' own authentication; a shared deployment can be a later, explicitly secured option.
  • A user-written query language for panels now. Maximum flexibility, but a large surface to design, secure and test before the built-in panels have proven what users actually need. Deferred, with the dataset parameter as the extension point.
  • Direct Postgres or a demo world as the first origin. Both are cheap to add behind the same dataset interface and are worth having (onboarding, docs); they do not show the thing this ADR exists for, the radar's own decisions, so they follow the cluster origin.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• A shared, authenticated dashboard (in-cluster) remains a later, explicitly secured option.
  • User-defined datasets: the dataset parameter is the extension point; nothing is designed yet.

docs.title: Alerting example
docs.text: Concrete webhook alerting example that shows how to configure delivery, receive a regression alert, and identify the deployment that caused it.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This page demonstrates a practical alerting setup for regression notifications using a Slack incoming webhook. The same pattern works with other webhook-compatible destinations: configure alerting in your run mode, trigger a known regression scenario, and verify that the delivered alert includes enough deploy metadata to identify the faulty release.

Use this together with Example regression scenario so your alert test is repeatable.

docs.title: 1) Configure alert destination
docs.text:
Use a redacted placeholder webhook URL in docs/scripts:

https://hooks.slack.com/services/XXX/YYY/ZZZ

docs.title: operator
docs.text:
go run ./cmd/operator \
  --dsn "postgres://user:password@localhost:5432/mydb?sslmode=disable" \
  --cluster-name demo-cluster \
  --source-type generic \
  --alert-format slack \
  --alert-url https://hooks.slack.com/services/XXX/YYY/ZZZ

docs.title: manager (PostgresWatch.spec.alerting)
docs.text:
apiVersion: radar.pgregressionradar.io/v1alpha1
kind: PostgresWatch
metadata:
  name: demo-db
  namespace: demo
spec:
  clusterName: demo-cluster
  dsnSecretRef:
    name: demo-db-dsn
    key: dsn
  alerting:
    format: slack
    url: https://hooks.slack.com/services/XXX/YYY/ZZZ

docs.title: Helm
docs.text:
helm upgrade --install pg-regression-radar ./deploy/helm/deploylens \
  --set postgres.dsn="postgres://user:password@localhost:5432/mydb?sslmode=disable" \
  --set alerting.format=slack \
  --set alerting.url=https://hooks.slack.com/services/XXX/YYY/ZZZ

docs.title: 2) Trigger a known regression
docs.text:
Run the reproducible flow in Example regression scenario, including:

  1. baseline deploy event (revision=v1),
  2. query slowdown,
  3. second deploy event (revision=v2),
  4. continued query executions.

docs.title: 3) Confirm alert delivery
docs.text:
When the regression is detected, Slack receives a message similar to:

🚨 PostgreSQL Regression Detected
Cluster: demo-cluster
App: checkout-api
Namespace: demo
Revision: v2
Query ID: 123456
Latency: 3.1ms -> 48.7ms (15.7x)
Confidence: 98% (1 − p)
p-value: 0.02

If you are testing without a real Slack workspace, use a temporary webhook sink (for example, an internal relay or test endpoint) and confirm the same fields appear in the payload body.

docs.title: 4) Interpret which deployment is at fault
docs.text:
The key correlation fields are:

  • App + namespace: workload identity.
  • Revision / image tag: specific deployment candidate.
  • Regression timing + before/after latency: evidence that degradation aligns with that deployment window.

In this example, revision=v2 is the deployment to investigate/rollback first.

docs.title: 5) Common alerting validation issues
docs.text:
• No alert arrives: verify webhook URL, egress/network policy, and destination allowlist settings.
  • Detection happened but no destination accepted: check --alert-format/spec.alerting.format matches destination type.
  • Payload missing deployment info: confirm deploy events include app/namespace/revision fields.

docs.title: Example: let the radar pause a bad rollout
docs.text: A copy-and-adapt setup for the attribution engine in enforce mode: the radar watches your database, judges each deploy of an Argo Rollouts app, and pauses the rollout when a deploy slows queries down. Read the Attribution engine first for what the grades mean.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Postgres with pg_stat_statements, scraped by the watch's own collector (a Prometheus sample source is not enough for this engine).
  • A DeploySource of type argo-rollouts that reports your Rollout's deploys (Deploy Sources & Webhooks).
  • Updated CRDs (Upgrading, step 1).
  • Time: the engine needs about 45 minutes of history after the manager starts before it can pause, and about 15 minutes after a deploy to convict it.

docs.title: 1. Start in shadow mode
docs.text:
Shadow mode records what the engine would do and never acts. Run it for a while and compare its decisions with what actually happened.

apiVersion: radar.pgregressionradar.io/v1alpha1
kind: PostgresWatch
metadata:
  name: shop-db
  namespace: shop
spec:
  clusterName: shop-db
  dsnSecretRef:        # adapt to your Secret
    name: shop-db-dsn
    key: dsn
  attribution:
    enabled: true
    mode: shadow

Look for attribution (shadow): decision, not executed in the manager log, with wanted: hold on the deploys you consider bad.

docs.title: 2. Let the manager pause
docs.text:
Grant the Rollout RBAC in the chart, then switch the watch to enforce and turn actuation on, limited to the namespaces you choose:

# Helm values
manager:
  autoAbort:
    rbacEnabled: true   # grants get and patch on rollouts and rollouts/status

spec:
  attribution:
    enabled: true
    mode: enforce
    actuate:
      enabled: true
      namespaces: [shop]

docs.title: 3. Give the Rollout time to be judged
docs.text:
The engine cannot convict before about 15 minutes after a deploy, so the canary must not be promoted before that:

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata:
  name: checkout
  namespace: shop
spec:
  strategy:
    canary:
      steps:
        - setWeight: 20
        - pause: {duration: 25m}   # long enough for the engine to judge
        - setWeight: 50
        - pause: {duration: 10m}

docs.title: 4. See what it did
docs.text:
# Every pause or abort, newest first (port-forward the verdict port first)
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8082/api/v1/attribution/actions | jq .

# The Rollout it paused
kubectl -n shop get rollout checkout -o jsonpath='{.spec.paused}'

A person decides what happens next: kubectl argo rollouts promote checkout to continue, or kubectl argo rollouts abort checkout to stop it.

docs.title: Stopping it
docs.text:
kubectl -n shop annotate postgreswatch shop-db pg-regression-radar.io/actuation-paused=true

Remove the annotation (...actuation-paused-) to resume. No restart is needed.

docs.title: If it does not act
docs.text: See The engine only alerts and does not act.

docs.title: Example regression scenario
docs.text: Reproducible walkthrough that simulates a slower query after deployment and verifies that pg-regression-radar links the regression to that deployment event.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This scenario gives external users a deterministic way to validate end-to-end behavior in local/test environments. You will generate fast baseline query samples, emit a deploy event, intentionally slow the same query path, emit another deploy event, and then verify that pg-regression-radar attributes the regression to the second deployment.

The workflow is run-mode agnostic: operator, manager, and Helm all use the same database workload and webhook payloads. Only where you read results differs by mode.

Timing (E-divisive requirement)

Detection needs a time series that spans multiple scrape windows, not a single burst of queries in one scrape cycle. Keep each traffic phase running for at least 3–4 scrape intervals. For quick demos, start pg-regression-radar with --scrape-interval 1s and keep each phase running for ~20–30 seconds total.

sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  participant You
  participant P as Postgres
  participant R as Radar
  You->>P: 1 create test data and fast baseline traffic
  P-->>R: scrapes show normal latency
  You->>R: 2 deploy event v1 (baseline)
  You->>P: 3 slow the same query
  P-->>R: scrapes show higher latency
  You->>R: 4 deploy event v2
  R->>R: compare the windows around v2
  R-->>You: 5 PerformanceRegression attributed to v2

Each numbered step below matches a step in this sequence; the radar keeps scraping the whole time.

docs.title: 1) Set up PostgreSQL and test data
docs.text:
Start a local PostgreSQL for testing:

docker run --name radar-pg -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=pass -e POSTGRES_DB=mydb \
  -p 5432:5432 -d postgres:16 \
  -c shared_preload_libraries=pg_stat_statements \
  -c pg_stat_statements.track=all

Create schema, data, and an indexed query:

psql "postgres://user:password@localhost:5432/mydb?sslmode=disable" <<'SQL'
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_stat_statements;
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS orders (
  id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  amount_cents BIGINT NOT NULL
);
TRUNCATE orders;
INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, amount_cents)
SELECT (random() * 10000)::bigint, (random() * 100000)::bigint
FROM generate_series(1, 200000);
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_orders_customer_id ON orders(customer_id);
ANALYZE orders;
SQL

Generate baseline (fast) query executions:

for i in $(seq 1 600); do
  psql "postgres://user:password@localhost:5432/mydb?sslmode=disable" \
    -c "SELECT pg_sleep(0.04); SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42;" >/dev/null
done

docs.title: 2) Emit baseline deploy event (v1)
docs.text:
curl -sS -X POST http://localhost:8080/webhook \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "app": "checkout-api",
    "namespace": "demo",
    "revision": "v1",
    "imageTag": "checkout-api:v1",
    "timestamp": "2026-08-16T12:00:00Z"
  }'

docs.title: 3) Trigger a simulated regression
docs.text:
Remove the index so the same query becomes much slower:

psql "postgres://user:password@localhost:5432/mydb?sslmode=disable" \
  -c "DROP INDEX IF EXISTS idx_orders_customer_id;"

Drive post-change workload with the same query:

for i in $(seq 1 600); do
  psql "postgres://user:password@localhost:5432/mydb?sslmode=disable" \
    -c "SELECT pg_sleep(0.04); SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42;" >/dev/null
done

docs.title: 4) Emit deploy event for the regression window (v2)
docs.text:
curl -sS -X POST http://localhost:8080/webhook \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "app": "checkout-api",
    "namespace": "demo",
    "revision": "v2",
    "imageTag": "checkout-api:v2",
    "timestamp": "2026-08-16T12:10:00Z"
  }'

docs.title: Where to verify by run mode
docs.text:
Mode Where to look operator Process logs and configured alert destination output manager Controller logs plus PerformanceRegression CRs Helm (mode=operator) Same as operator Helm (mode=manager) Same as manager

Manager CR check:

kubectl get performanceregressions -A

A successful result should include:

  • the slowed query (query text and/or query ID),
  • before/after latency evidence,
  • deployment metadata matching checkout-api revision v2.

Example (illustrative only):

regression detected: app=checkout-api namespace=demo revision=v2 query_id=123456
latency_before_ms=3.1 latency_after_ms=48.7 change=15.7x confidence=0.98

docs.title: 6) Optional cleanup
docs.text: docker rm -f radar-pg

docs.text:

  • Getting Started — startup commands for operator, manager, and Helm.
  • Alerting example — concrete webhook/Slack alert configuration and interpretation.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Find what the radar is doing, why it is not doing what you expect, and what to change.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The radar reports on itself in several places, each suited to a different question. This section is organised the way you meet a problem: first where to look, then the symptom, then the catalogs that name every log line, reason and metric.

Before anything else, read the conditions of the watch. They answer the three questions most problems come down to, in one command:

kubectl get pgw <name> -n <ns> -o json \
  | jq '.status.conditions[] | {type, status, reason, message}'
Condition Question it answers Collecting Is the radar reading my database? ArmsLog Can it tell a canary from the stable pods? Actuating May it pause or abort a Rollout right now, and if not, why?

A condition that is not healthy has a reason and a message that ends with the link to its entry in Reason codes.

New in 1.9.2

Conditions, reason codes, one log format on every command, --log-level and --log-format, and the reset-breaker annotation. They change no CRD schema and no default.

docs.title: Start with a symptom
docs.text: Symptom Page I need to know where a given kind of information lives Where to look The radar will not start, cannot reach the database, or pg_stat_statements is not available Setup and the database It runs, and never reports a regression Nothing is detected A deploy happened and the radar did not judge it Deploy sources It judged a deploy and did not pause or abort it, or I want to turn enforce on Enforce mode A regression was found and no alert arrived, or the dashboard shows nothing Alerts and the dashboard I want to read the log, or ask for more detail Logs I want to ask for help Collect a report A short question FAQ

docs.title: Catalogs
docs.text:
These pages list everything, and a test keeps them equal to the code on every build.

Catalog What it lists Use it to Reason codes the stable name of each decision or fault, with its causes, how to confirm each, and the fix go from a reason in a log or a condition to what to do Log catalog every log message, its level, its fields and what it means find what a line you saw means Metrics every Prometheus metric, its type and labels choose what to graph and alert on

docs.title: Alerts and the dashboard
docs.text: A regression was found and nobody was told, or the dashboard does not show what you expect.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Alerts leave the radar for a destination you configured; the dashboard reads the manager. Both are ways to see what the radar found, and each has a few failure modes of its own. A detected regression is always written first as a PerformanceRegression, so if that object exists the detection worked and the problem is delivery.

kubectl get pgreg -n <ns>

docs.title: An alert did not arrive
docs.text:
Find out which of three things happened: it was never sent, it was sent and failed, or it was delivered and you did not see it.

kubectl logs -n <ns> -l app.kubernetes.io/component=manager --since=2h \
  | jq -c 'select(.msg | test("alert|notification|notify"))'
You see It means Fix nothing, and pgreg is empty nothing was detected Nothing is detected alerting: notification skipped; webhook url is not configured the watch has no alert URL set spec.alerting.url (or the legacy spec.slackWebhookUrl) postgreswatch: alert notify failed delivery failed AlertNotifyFailed: err has the status or the network error postgreswatch: failed to persist PerformanceRegression CR the alert went out and the object could not be saved RegressionPersistFailed alerting: notification sent with a status_code the destination accepted it look in the destination: the right channel, a filter, a rate limit the watch is Failed with build alert notifier the alert URL or policy is rejected when the watch starts WorkerStartFailed

A rejected URL is refused before any request is made: a scheme other than http or https, a literal loopback or link-local address, and the cloud metadata hostnames. A 3xx from the destination counts as a failure, because the radar never follows redirects. See Destination validation and Destination policies.

Counts over time:

  • pg_regression_radar_regressions_detected_total rises when a regression is found.
  • pg_regression_radar_notifications_total{status="success"} and {status="error"} count delivery attempts by outcome. Detections that rise with no success mean alerts are being lost.

For regressions exported as OTLP logs, pg_regression_radar_otlp_export_total{result} and the lines otlpexport: queue full, otlpexport: delivery failed, will retry and otlpexport: giving up on regression say what happened; see OTLP export.

docs.title: The dashboard
docs.text:
pg-regression-radar dashboard --namespace <manager-namespace> --open
The page says Cause Fix Reconnecting the leader changed, or the port-forward dropped wait; the command finds the new leader. The terminal logs dashboard: cannot reach the manager, then dashboard: connected to the manager Incompatible the manager speaks an Observe API version this dashboard does not upgrade the CLI to the manager's release; the page names the versions it supports No deploys in this time range no deploy has been registered, or it is not 10 minutes old yet widen the range; check A deploy never shows up history is not being recorded the history store is down HistoryNotRecording. Decisions are unaffected history is lost after a restart --observe-history=memory, the default set it to postgres the command cannot find the manager your user cannot read the Lease or port-forward needs get on leases and pods, create on pods/portforward query text is missing by design --show-queries on the dashboard and --observe-allow-queries on the manager

A regression, an abort that did not help, a failed pause or abort and an open breaker also appear as alerts at the top right of the dashboard, and stay until you dismiss them or the deploy is healthy again. See Alerts. If an alert you expected is not there, check that you did not dismiss it (the browser remembers dismissals), and that the deploy is read as regressed: Regressed in the deploy list.

When the dashboard shows a source as not healthy, or says the radar may not act, the row carries a reason code (ScrapeStale, ArmsLogStale, BreakerOpen and so on) that links to Reason codes. It is the same code as the reason of the matching condition in kubectl describe postgreswatch and of the log line, so you can look for it in either place. A manager older than 1.9.2 sends no codes.

The dashboard reads the leader only. If the manager has more than one pod, a port-forward to a standby shows nothing, which is why the command resolves the leader from the Lease itself. See Dashboard.
